en: The Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Volume One.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
The Supreme Worldly Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) are seven; the two Summits (mūrdhan) and the Heat (uṣmagata) [are as previously described].
The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), consisting of eleven types of views, is to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-prahātavya). It is requested that this chapter explain these in full:
what are the Supreme Worldly Dharmas?
Answer:

If the mind and mental factors—acting as the equal-and-immediate condition for entering into the state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma)—are called the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma). Some say this:

If the five faculties—acting as the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for entering into the state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*)—are called the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*). Within this context:

if the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*)—acting as the immediate antecedent condition for entering into the state of correctness and departure from birth—are called the Supreme Mundane Dharmas.
Why is it called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)? Answer:

Because these mental states and mental factors are the most excellent, the most superior, the longest-lasting, the most venerable, the highest, and the most sublime among all other mundane dharmas; therefore, they are called the Supreme Mundane Dharma.

Furthermore, these mental states and their concomitants act as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*): they abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and attain the nature of a noble one (*āryatva*);
they abandon the state of error (*mithyātva*) and attain the state of correctness (*samyaktva*), thereby being able to enter the state of certainty regarding the right nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Therefore, it is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Should the Supreme Mundane Dharma be said to belong to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Is it bound to the formless realm?
Answer: It should be said that it is bound to the form realm.
Why should this dharma not be said to be bound to the desire realm? Answer:

It is not by means of the path of the desire realm that one can sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and restrain the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), so as to prevent the envelopments of the desire realm from arising again.

Thus, by means of the path of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one is able to sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and restrain the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), causing the fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) not to arise again.
If, by means of the path of the desire realm, one is able to sever the hindrances and restrain the fetters, this likewise causes the fetters of the desire realm not to arise again.
Thus, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) should be said to be bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

However, it is not by means of a path belonging to the desire realm that one severs the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and restrains the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), thereby preventing the envelopments of the desire realm from arising again;

rather, it is by means of a path belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-mārga*) that one severs the hindrances and restrains the envelopments, thereby preventing the envelopments of the desire realm from arising again.
Therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) should not be said to be bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Why should this dharma also not be said to be bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)? Answer:

Entering into the state of right determination and departure from birth—first realizing the suffering of the desire realm as suffering, and subsequently realizing the suffering of the form and formless realms in combination—the Noble Path arises.
First, the matters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are analyzed; subsequently, the matters of the form (*rūpadhātu*) and formless (*ārūpyadhātu*) realms are analyzed together.

If one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)—first directly realizing (*abhisamaya*) the suffering of the formless realm as suffering, and subsequently realizing the suffering of the desire and form realms as suffering—the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) arises.

Having first analyzed the matters pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one subsequently analyzes the matters pertaining to the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*) together.
In this way, the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) should be said to belong to the formless realm.

However, upon entering the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma)—first directly realizing the suffering of the desire realm as suffering, and subsequently realizing the suffering of the form and formless realms in combination—the Noble Path arises.
Having first analyzed the matters of the desire realm, one subsequently analyzes the matters of the form and formless realms together.
Therefore, the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) should not be said to be bound to the formless realm.

Furthermore! Upon entering the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one eliminates the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*); yet, it is not by eliminating the perception of form that one can know the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If, taking this dharma as an object, one gives rise to the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), then, taking that same dharma as an object, one gives rise to the supreme mundane dharma (*laukika-agra-dharma*).
Should it be said that the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma) are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and with vicāra only,
or without both vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: One should say that it may be with vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is meant by "with vitarka and vicāra"?
Answer:

If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on a samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, that is the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukika-agra-dharma) attained therein.
What is "without vitarka and with only vicāra"?
Answer:

If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on a samādhi that is without vitarka and with only vicāra, that is the "worldly supreme dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma) obtained therein.
What, then, is [the samādhi] without vitarka and without vicāra?
Answer:

If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*),
is the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) attained therein to be said as being associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?
Is it associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)? Or is it associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)? Answer:

One should say that it is either associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), or associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
How is it associated with the faculty of pleasure? Answer:

If one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the third dhyāna, what is the relationship between the resulting "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)? Answer:

If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the first or second dhyāna, how is the worldly supreme dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) attained therein associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya)?
Answer:
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on either the *anāgamya* stage or the fourth dhyāna,
is the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) attained therein to be described as being of a single moment of mind?
"Are there many minds?
Answer: "One should say there is one mind."
Why is this dharma not characterized by multiple minds? Answer:
From this mind and its mental factors, no other mundane mind arises in immediate succession; only supramundane mind arises.
If one were to give rise to other mundane states of mind, they would be either inferior, equal, or superior.
If they were inferior, one would be unable to enter the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Why is this? It is because one cannot enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of regressing from the Path.
If it were otherwise, those who have attained equanimity would likewise be unable to enter the state of right determination.
Why is this? Because, by means of such paths previously [practiced], one cannot enter the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).

If they were indeed superior, then what was previously [regarded as] the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma) would not have been so, and only subsequently would it become the Supreme Mundane Dharmas.
Should it be said that the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) are subject to regression, or are they not? Answer:
One should say that it is non-retrogressive.
Why is this dharma fixed as non-retrogressive? Answer:
The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) accord with the Truths, tend toward the Truths, and are on the verge of entering the Truths.
Between these and those [Truths], there is no room for the arising of a dissimilar mind that would prevent one from entering the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths.
It is, for example, like a strong man crossing a river, a valley, a mountain, or a precipice; once he has crossed, nothing can turn him back midway.
His body returns to its original place, or he proceeds to another location.
The previously initiated superior bodily actions do not cease until they have reached their destination;
the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are likewise.
They accord with the truths, tend toward the truths, and are on the verge of entering the truths.
In the interval between this and that, there is no room for the arising of a dissimilar state of mind that would prevent one from entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths.
It is like the five great rivers of Jambudvīpa:
First is named Gaṅgā;
second is named Yamunā;
third is named Sarayū.
The fourth is named Aciravatī;
the fifth is named Mahī.

These five rivers—flowing toward the great ocean, heading toward the great ocean, and entering the great ocean—cannot be turned back midway. Their currents do not return to their original source, nor do they flow elsewhere; they are certain to flow into the great ocean.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is likewise.

It conforms to the Truths, tends toward the Truths, and is on the verge of entering the Truths; in the interval between these states, there is no room for an incongruous mind to arise that would prevent one from entering the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths.

Furthermore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) acts as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the Patience regarding the Knowledge of the Dharma concerning Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*). Since there is no phenomenon more swift in its revolution than the mind, nothing could possibly act as an obstacle at that moment to prevent one from entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths.
Therefore, this dharma is certain not to regress.
What is the "summit" (mūrdhan)? Answer:
One gives rise to a small measure of faith toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
As the Blessed One said to the young brahmin Bhāradvāja:
"If one gives rise to even a slight faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha..."
"Mañjuśrī, you should know that he has already attained the stage of the 'Summit' (mūrdhan).
What is meant by 'falling from the summit'? Answer:
For example, there is a certain class of persons who associate with virtuous friends, hear the true Dharma, and attend to it with correct mental attention;
they have faith in the Buddha’s enlightenment, that the Dharma is well-expounded, and that the Saṅgha practices the sublime way.
Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Thus is the truth of suffering well-established, and the truths of origin, cessation, and the path are well-established.
At another time, he does not associate with virtuous persons, does not hear the true Dharma, and does not attend to it correctly; consequently,
the mundane faith he had previously attained declines, is destroyed, shifts, and is lost.
Therefore, it is called "falling from the summit.
As the Buddha said to the young brahmin Bhāradvāja:
"If a person falls away from these three dharmas..."
"I say that those of such a kind should be known as 'fallen from the summit' (mūrdha-pratyāpanna).
What is 'Heat' (uṣmagata)? Answer:
If there is even a slight degree of faith and acceptance within the True Dharma and the Vinaya—
as the Blessed One said to the two bhikṣus Aśvajit and Puṣya:
"These two fools are as far from my True Dharma and Vinaya as the great earth is from space."
"These two fools possess not even a fraction of 'heat' within my True Dharma and Vinaya.
Of these twenty phrases of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), how many are views of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*)?
How many views of "mine" (mamakāra-dṛṣṭi) are there? Answer:
Five views of "self" (ātma-dṛṣṭi).
That is to say:
one regards form as self, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as self.
These are the fifteen views of "mine."
That is to say:

one contemplates thus—“I have form; form is mine; I am in form”—and likewise, “I have feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are mine; I am in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.”
If one views what is impermanent as permanent,
among the five views, by which view is it subsumed,
and by which view is it abandoned?

Answer: It is subsumed under the view of extremes and the view of eternalism, and is abandoned through the vision of suffering. This applies whether one holds the view that things are eternal or that they are non-eternal.
Regarding the five views—by which view are they subsumed?
By which view are they abandoned? Answer:
It is subsumed under wrong view and is abandoned through the vision of cessation;
it is the view that [there is] suffering or pleasure.
Regarding the five views—by which view are they subsumed?
By which view are they abandoned? Answer:
To grasp inferior phenomena as superior is subsumed under the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
It is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*). If one views suffering as pleasure;
Regarding the five views—by which view are they subsumed?
By which view are they abandoned? Answer:
It is subsumed under wrong view and is abandoned through the vision of cessation;
it is the view that what is impure is pure.
Regarding the five views—by which view are they subsumed?
By which view are they abandoned? Answer:
To grasp inferior phenomena as superior is subsumed under the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
It is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*). This includes views regarding what is pure or impure.
Regarding the five views—by which view are they subsumed?
By which view are they abandoned? Answer:
It is subsumed under wrong view.
This is of two kinds: if one says:
If one views cessation as impure, it is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).
If one claims that the path is impure, it is abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*).
If it is not the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*),
among the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭayaḥ*), under which view is it subsumed, and by the abandonment of which [of the four noble truths] is it eliminated?
Answer: It is comprised within the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha).
If it is not the view of causality regarding causes;
among the five views, by which view is it subsumed,
and by which view is it abandoned?
Answer: To regard what is not a cause as a cause is subsumed under the clinging to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa) and is abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
If one views what is not a cause as a cause,
among the five views, by which view is it subsumed, and by the abandonment of which view is it eliminated?
Answer: It is subsumed under wrong view and is abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
If there is the view of non-existence (*asaddṛṣṭi*);
among the five views, by which view is it subsumed,
and by which view is it abandoned?
Answer: It is subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This consists of four types:
If one says:
"There is no suffering"—this is abandoned by the vision of suffering.
If one says:
There is no origination—this is abandoned by the vision of origination.
If one says:
there is no cessation—this is abandoned by the vision of cessation.
If it is claimed that there is no Path— that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the Path—
then there would be no vision at all.
Regarding the five views—by which view are they subsumed?
By which view are they abandoned? Answer:
This is not vision; it is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
First, the causal conditions for the cognition of knowledge; second, the mental recollection of sacrifice;
third, the application of the three faculties (*indriya*) in the past; and doubt regarding the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).

The Buddha’s Reprimand of the Six Causes; the Latent Dispositions (*anuśaya*), the Mind, the Causes of Abandonment, the Objects of Abandonment, and the Meaning of Cognition—this chapter shall explain these fully.
Is there any single cognition that knows all phenomena?
Answer: No.
If this wisdom arises [realizing] that "all phenomena are not-self," what is there that this wisdom does not know?
Answer: It does not know its own nature, nor the various phenomena associated with and co-arising alongside it.
Is there perhaps a single consciousness that comprehends all phenomena?
Answer: There is none.
If this consciousness gives rise to the realization that "all phenomena are non-self," what is there that this consciousness does not understand?
Answer: It does not comprehend its own intrinsic nature, nor the various phenomena associated with and coexistent with it.
Is it possible for two minds to serve as causes for one another in a reciprocal manner?
Answer: No. Why is this so?
There is not a single person for whom two minds arise simultaneously, neither before nor after;
furthermore,
a subsequent mind does not serve as the cause for a preceding mind.
Is it possible for two minds to serve as mutual objects of cognition for one another? Answer: Yes.
For example:
when one gives rise to the thought "there is no future," one contemplates this and gives rise to a second thought.
For example:
When there is a mind that gives rise to the thought "there is a future," one contemplates this and gives rise to a second mind.
For example:
when there is a mind that gives rise to the thought "there is no future path," one contemplates this and gives rise to a second mind.
For example:
when a mind arises that thinks, "There is a future path," one contemplates this and gives rise to a second mind.
For instance:
There are two types of those who know the minds of others, and these two minds take each other as their objects.
Why is it that no single *pudgala* has two minds arising simultaneously—neither before nor after?
Answer: Because there is no second immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and because the mental continuum of sentient beings proceeds one moment after another;
since a person (*pudgala*) cannot be found, and furthermore, there is no prior mind that transmigrates to a subsequent mind, by what principle could one remember a deed performed in the past?
Answer:

Sentient beings, through the power of habitual practice regarding phenomena, attain such a cognition of commonality (*sabhāgatā-jñāna*) that they are able to know things accordingly as they encounter them.
For example:
There are two makers of seals who are able to understand the seal-syllables created by themselves and others; although those two persons do not go to meet one another, [they know each other's work].
Question:
How is it that you create these syllables, and yet they do not meet?
Answer: "I have thus fashioned these characters.
Then, by the power of habitual practice, those two persons attain a corresponding cognition (*sabhāga-jñāna*) that enables them to discern the stamped characters fashioned by themselves and others.
Sentient beings are likewise!
By the power of habitual practice, they attain such knowledge of commonality (*sabhāgatā*), whereby they are able to know things in accordance with their past experiences.
It is also like this:
There are two who possess the knowledge of others' minds and mutually know each other's thoughts; yet, although those two do not go to meet one another, [the question arises]:
"How do you know my mind, and why do we not meet?"
Answer: I know your mind in this way.
However, those two individuals, through the power of habitual practice, have attained such a shared cognition that they know each other's minds.
Sentient beings are likewise!
By the power of habitual practice, they attain such knowledge of a commonality (sabhāgatā), whereby they are able to know things according to their respective experiences.
Furthermore:
All mental states and their concomitants are fixed upon their objects and remain established therein.
Furthermore, by the causal power of the faculty of feeling and volition, mindfulness becomes strong and thus one does not forget.
For what reason do sentient beings forget and then remember again? Answer:
When the continuity of a sentient being’s homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) proceeds, they are able to give rise to a cognition and vision that establishes a connection with phenomena.
Furthermore, by taking the power of the intention to receive [the teaching] as the causal force, one remembers strongly and does not forget.
For what reason do sentient beings remember and yet again forget? Answer:
When the continuity of sentient beings undergoes transformation through different states, they do not give rise to a cognition or vision of connection regarding phenomena.
Furthermore, due to the causal power of the mind that experiences [them], inferior mindfulness is lost.
For what reason does an offering made to a hungry ghost reach it,
whereas it does not reach those in other realms? Answer:
It is the natural law of those destinies that they obtain such a place, object, birth, and personal identity; therefore, the sacrificial offering reaches them and no others.
For example, although swans, geese, peacocks, parrots, śāris, and jīvañjīvakas may fly freely through the sky at will, their supernatural power and majesty are not greater than those of humans.
However, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of that realm that one obtains such a location, object, birth, and personal identity, enabling one to fly through the air.
It is the same for the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*):
by the power of natural law, they arrive at the place of sacrifice.
Other realms of existence are not like this!
Furthermore,
there are certain types of hell-beings who are able to recollect their past lives and also know the minds of others.

Certain classes of animals and certain classes of hungry ghosts (preta) are able to recollect their past lives, know the minds of others, and produce smoke and flames, raise clouds and bring forth rain, and create cold and heat.
Although they are able to perform such deeds, their supernormal power and majesty are no greater than those of humans.
Nevertheless, it is the very nature of that realm (*gati*) that, having obtained such a station, object, birth, and personal identity (*ātmabhāva*), they are able to perform these deeds.
It is the same for the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati)!
By the power of the nature of things (dharmatā), they arrive when there is a sacrifice;
it is not so for the other realms!
Furthermore, there are those who for a long night have given rise to such desires and such inclinations:
"I shall take a wife; I shall take a wife for my son; I shall take a wife for my grandson, so that sons and grandsons may be born, ensuring that our lineage continues without interruption."
"After my life has ended, if I am reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, they will offer sacrifices to me because they remember me.
Because he has long harbored this desire and pleasure, the sacrifice reaches him; it does not reach anyone else!
Should it be said that one sees forms with one eye,
or that one sees forms with both eyes? Answer:
One should say that "the two eyes see forms.
Why is this? Because if one closes one eye and impure consciousness arises, when both eyes are opened, pure consciousness arises.
If such a consciousness arises when one eye is closed, and this same consciousness also arises when both eyes are open, then one should not say that "the two eyes see forms.
However, since an impure consciousness arises when one eye is closed, whereas a pure consciousness arises when both eyes are open, one should therefore say that "the two eyes see forms."
As with joining;
so too with covering, damaging, breaking, and destroying!
As when the eye sees forms;
The same applies to hearing sounds with the ear and smelling odors with the nose!
Are all those things of the past not manifest? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions:
there is that which is past, yet not non-manifest.
That is to say:
As the Venerable Udāyin said:
"All fetters have passed away; From the forest he has come out of the forest.
Delighting in renunciation, he has emerged from all desires, Like gold extracted from the mountain peak."
There is that which is not manifest, yet is not past.
That is to say:

there may be someone who, by means of supernormal powers, incantations, medicinal herbs, or knowledge acquired through such a place of birth, causes something to be concealed so that it does not appear.
There is that which is past and no longer manifest;

namely, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)— those already arisen and arising, already produced and being produced, already transformed and currently transforming, already accumulated and manifested, already passed away, already ceased and extinguished, and already undergone change.
This is—subsumed under the past, the past portion, and the past time.
There is that which is not past, yet is also not non-manifest.
That is to say:
Excluding the aforementioned cases:
Is everything that is past entirely exhausted? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions:
there is that which is past, yet not exhausted.
That is to say:
As the Venerable Udāyin said:
"All fetters have passed away...
and so forth, as explained at length.
There is exhaustion that is not of the past.
That is to say,
as the Buddha said:
"This noble disciple has exhausted hell, has exhausted the animal realm, has exhausted the realm of hungry ghosts, and has exhausted all the treacherous pits of the miserable destinies.
This [state] exists in the past and is also exhausted.
That is to say:
all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)—those already arisen and those currently arising...
[and so on, as extensively explained].
There is that which is neither past nor exhausted;
namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Furthermore, if one speaks in terms of the abandonment of fetters (*saṃyojana*):
there are fetters that are past, yet not exhausted.
That is to say:
there are fetters of the past that have not been abandoned, not fully understood, not extinguished, and not vomited out;
yet there is the exhaustion of fetters that is not of the past.
That is to say:
the fetters of the future have been abandoned, fully understood, extinguished, and vomited out.
The fetters of the past have also been exhausted.
That is to say:
those fetters of the past that have already been abandoned, already fully understood, already ceased, and already vomited out;
as well as those fetters that are not of the past and are not yet exhausted.
That is to say:
regarding future fetters—those not yet abandoned, not yet fully understood, not yet extinguished, and not yet vomited out—as well as present fetters;
are all those past [fetters] necessarily extinguished?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is that which is past, yet not ceased.
That is to say, as the Venerable Udāyin said:
"All fetters have passed away."
……and so on, as explained at length.
There is cessation that is not of the past.
That is to say:

Based on worldly convention, one speaks of "the destruction of the street," and so forth up to "the destruction of the eye," with respect to small streets, small houses, small vessels, and small eyes.
That which has passed away is likewise destroyed.
That is to say:
all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)—those already arisen and those currently arising...
[and so on, as extensively explained].
There are things that are neither past nor ceased;
namely, those cases other than the aforementioned characteristics.
Furthermore, if one speaks in terms of the abandonment of fetters (*saṃyojana*):
there are fetters that are past, yet not extinguished.
That is to say:
there are fetters of the past that have not been abandoned, not fully understood, not extinguished, and not vomited out;
there are also fetters that have been extinguished, but are not of the past.
That is to say:
the fetters of the future have been abandoned, fully understood, extinguished, and vomited out.
As for the fetters of the past, they too have been extinguished.
That is to say:
the fetters of the past have already been severed, already fully understood, already ceased, and already vomited out.
There are fetters that are neither of the past nor have they ceased.
That is to say:
the fetters of the future— which have not been abandoned, not fully understood, not extinguished, and not vomited out—
as well as the fetters of the present.
If one gives rise to doubt regarding suffering— thinking, "Is this suffering?
Or is this not suffering?"—
should it be said that this is a single mind?
"Are there many minds?
Answer: One should say:
He had many thoughts, namely: "Is this suffering?"
"This is one mind; 'Is this not suffering? is the second mind."
The same applies to the arising of doubt regarding the origin, cessation, and the path!
Is there any single moment of mind that both possesses doubt and is free from doubt? Answer:
There is none. Why is this?
It is because:
Regarding the Truth of Suffering— if one asks, "Is this suffering?"—
this mind harbors doubt.
If one says, "This is suffering," this mind is free from doubt.
If one says:
"Is this not suffering?"—
this mind harbors doubt;
if one says:
"This is not suffering"—this mind has no doubt.
One should know that it is likewise regarding the origin, cessation, and path.
What is meant by "a plurality of name-bodies"?
Answer: It refers to "multiple names and designations.
Synonyms, appellations, perceptions, conceptualizations, and conventional designations—these are called multiple name-bodies (*nāmakāya*).
What is a "group of many phrases" (*padakāya*)? Answer:
It refers to various phrases that fulfill meanings not yet fully realized; their concatenation therein is called a group of many phrases.
As the Blessed One said:
"Commit no evil; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
These four lines are each complete in themselves, yet they possess an unfulfilled meaning when combined within this context; this is called a *padakāya* (a group of multiple phrases).
What is the "multitude of phonemes" (vyañjana-kāya)? Answer:
The collection of all syllables is called the multitude of phonemes.
As the Blessed One said:
"The desire [to compose] is the basis of the verse; the phrasing is the syllables; the verse depends upon the names and the composer.
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, rebuked his disciples by calling them "fools," what is the meaning of this?
Answer: This is a term of reproach.
That is to say:

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, rebuked his disciples, calling them "fools," just as a preceptor or a teacher would today—should a disciple who dwells nearby or relies upon him commit various transgressions, he would rebuke him, saying:
"You are deluded; you lack clarity and virtue."
“The World-Honored One is likewise!
He rebukes his disciples, calling them ‘fools.
For what reason does the World-Honored One rebuke his disciples, calling them ‘fools’?”
Answer: Regarding the World-Honored One’s instructions and exhortations, they do not act in accordance with their meaning, do not comply with them, and do not maintain continuity with them.
Furthermore:
Regarding the holy teaching, he acts with folly; it is empty and without fruit, lacking emergence or flavor, and devoid of any benefit.
Having transgressed the Buddha’s instruction, he is unable to receive or train in the various precepts.
Therefore, the Buddha rebuked him, calling him a "foolish person.
There are six reasons for this, namely:
The associated cause... up to the enabling cause.
What is the associated cause? Answer:

Feeling is the associated cause for those phenomena associated with feeling, and those phenomena associated with feeling are the associated cause for feeling... [likewise for] perception, volition, contact, attention, desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration... and wisdom is the associated cause for those phenomena associated with wisdom, and those phenomena associated with wisdom are the associated cause for wisdom.
This is called the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
What is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)? Answer:
The mind is the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) of the mental factors (caitta-dharma), and the mental factors are the co-existent cause of the mind.
The mind is the co-existent cause of the bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind.

The mind is the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) for the non-associated formations that arise in accordance with it, and those non-associated formations that arise in accordance with the mind are the co-existent cause for the mind.
Furthermore:
The co-nascent four great elements are mutually simultaneous causes;
this is called the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
What is the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
Answer:
Formerly produced wholesome roots are the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for subsequently produced wholesome roots of their own realm, as well as their associated factors.
Past wholesome roots are the homogeneous cause for future and present wholesome roots of their own realm, as well as their associated factors.
Present wholesome roots and future wholesome roots of their own realm, along with their associated factors, serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As it is with wholesome roots,
so it is with unwholesome and neutral roots.
As for the distinction:
among the unwholesome [dharmas], excluding those of their own realm—
these are called similar-cause factors (sabhāga-hetu).
What is the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)? Answer:

The previously arisen universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) serve as the universal cause for the subsequently arisen proclivities and their associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) within one's own realm that are abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*), as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the past serve as the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) for the future and present latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and their associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) within one's own realm.

Present universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) serve as universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) for future latent dispositions and their associated factors within their own realm that are abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*), as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Just as it is for those abandoned through the vision of suffering,
so it is for those abandoned through the vision of origin;
this is called the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
What is the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*)? Answer:

It consists of all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), as well as the resultant matter (*vipāka-rūpa*), mental states and mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
These mental states and mental factors serve as the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) for that ripening result.

Furthermore, all bodily and vocal actions, as well as the material form that undergoes ripening, the mental states and mental factors, and the formations dissociated from mind [serve as ripening causes].
These bodily and vocal karmas serve as the ripening cause for that ripening result.
Furthermore,
all formations dissociated from mind experience the ripening of matter, mental states and their concomitants, and formations dissociated from mind.
These formations dissociated from mind act as the ripening cause for that ripening result;
this is called the ripening cause.
What is the efficient cause?
Answer: With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises.

This visual consciousness takes that eye and those visible forms, those associated mental factors, those coexistent factors, as well as the ear, sounds, and auditory consciousness [as its conditions].
The nose and odors, nose-consciousness;
the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness;
the body and tangibles, body-consciousness;
Mental phenomena (dharma) and mental consciousness;

material and immaterial phenomena; visible and invisible phenomena; resistant and non-resistant phenomena; outflowing and non-outflowing phenomena; conditioned and unconditioned phenomena—all such phenomena serve as the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu), with the exception of their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
As it is with visual consciousness,
so it is with auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness;
this is called the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
When various minds are called "minds with latent dispositions" (anuśaya) because they possess latent dispositions, do those latent dispositions increase (anuśerate) within these minds?
Answer: They either increase or do not increase.
How do they increase?
It means that those latent dispositions (anuśaya) are associated with this mind and have not yet been abandoned, and they take this mind as their object.
What is meant by "not increasing through association"?
It refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) which, having been associated with this mind, have already been abandoned.
If latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with a mind, is that mind called "a mind with latent dispositions" solely because of those [specific] latent dispositions?
Answer: It is either because of those and not others, or because of both those and others.
Why is it by that [mind] alone and not by any other?
It is because this mind has not yet been severed.
What is meant by "by that and others"?
It refers to the case where the knowledge of suffering has already arisen, but the knowledge of the origin [of suffering] has not yet arisen.

If a mind is an object of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
such that it is called a "mind with latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya-citta*) because of those latent dispositions,
will those latent dispositions be abandoned in relation to this mind?
Answer: Some are to be abandoned, while others are not to be abandoned.
What is to be abandoned?
That is to say:
those latent tendencies take this mind as their object.
How could they not be abandoned?
That is to say:
those latent dispositions (anuśaya) are associated with this mind.
By what means, then, should these latent dispositions be abandoned?
Answer: Due to the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Do you say that "the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) should be abandoned by means of their object-conditions"?
Answer: It is so. If that is the case!

Regarding those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) or the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) and which take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-ālambana*) as their object: by what cause should those latent dispositions be abandoned?
If one says that this [object] is abandoned and thereby that [disposition] is abandoned, neither case is logical.
Answer: The untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) proclivities abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path are abandoned by means of their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Because these are abandoned, those [proclivities] are also abandoned.
If a latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is to be abandoned in a mind, is that mind called "a mind with latent dispositions" solely because of that specific latent disposition?
Answer: It may be so because of that [specific one] and not others, or it may be so because of both that and others.
Why is it by that [path] alone and not by others?
It is because the mind is undefiled and is to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
What is meant by "by that and others"?
It refers to the defilement of the mind.
How is consciousness abandoned by means of its object? Answer:

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, if the mind has as its object that which is to be abandoned through the vision of origin or that which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering—this is called the abandonment of consciousness by means of its object.
Regarding this consciousness, how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase? Answer: Nineteen.
Is it with a single mind? Answer: No.
That is to say:
one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire;
for whom the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) has already arisen, but the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen.

If the mind is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
then regarding this consciousness abandoned through the vision of the origin, seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase.
One who is already free from the defilements of the desire realm but not yet free from the defilements of the form realm;
for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.

If the mind takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) or that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) within the form realm.

This refers to the consciousness that is abandoned by means of the object—namely, the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to the [defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

One has already become free from the defilement of the form realm; the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.

If the mind is [a consciousness] abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-heya) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), taking as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-heya)—
this consciousness, abandoned through the vision of origin in the formless realm, has six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that increase in accordance with it.
Dependent origination and its cessation are based on the mind;
when the mind is free from craving, one is liberated by depending on the perception of the elements.
In this chapter, it is intended to explain in full how a single person possesses the twelve links of dependent origination in this life—how many belong to the past?
How many are future?
How many are present? Answer:
Two belong to the past,
namely: ignorance and volitional formations.
The two future [links] are:
birth and old age and death.
Eight are present;
namely: consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and existence.
As the Blessed One said:
"Ignorance conditions volitional formations; grasping conditions existence.
In what way does ignorance condition volitional formations?
What is existence conditioned by clinging? Answer:
Ignorance conditions volitional formations:
This demonstrates karma—performed and accumulated in previous lives—which results in the maturation of the present existence and has already undergone that maturation.
Regarding "appropriation conditions becoming":
this demonstrates karma—performed and accumulated in the present life—which will result in the maturation of future existence.
What is the difference between "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) and "grasping conditions existence" (*upādāna-pratyayo bhavaḥ*)?
Answer: Regarding "ignorance conditions volitional formations":
The detailed explanation is as before.
Regarding this causal condition of karma, the Blessed One said:
"There is one affliction, namely, ignorance."
Regarding "existence conditioned by grasping":
it is explained at length as before.
As for this condition of karma, the Blessed One said:
"All afflictions refer to the various types of grasping"— this is the distinction.
Is there, however:
Is it that formations have ignorance as their condition, but do not have clarity as their condition? Answer: No.
Is there any case where volitional formations (saṃskāra) have clarity (vidyā) as their condition, but do not have ignorance (avidyā) as their condition? Answer:
No. Is it possible that conditioned by volitional formations there is ignorance, yet it is also conditioned by clarity?
Answer: There is. Is there such a case?
Do the formations not have ignorance as their object, nor do they have clarity as their object? Answer: No.

Why is this? Because there has not been a single sentient being since time immemorial who, having slandered the Noble Path by calling it no path, did not subsequently create and accumulate karma that brings about rebirth in the great hells.
Having first slandered the Path, they later performed and increased such actions.
At a later time, one may perform and increase karma that leads to rebirth as a minor king;
or at a later time, one may perform and increase karma that leads to rebirth as a great king;
or at a later time, one may perform and increase karma that leads to rebirth as a wheel-turning monarch.

By this cause, by this condition, and through that noble path, all things belonging to the great earth—cities, villages, humans, non-humans, livestock, grain crops, medicinal herbs, trees, and forests—are successively brought forth, increasing and flourishing.
Thus, the four conditions of the preceding mind serve as only a single dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) for the subsequent mind.
Furthermore, if one speaks in terms of causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya), is there any case where:
Is it the case that volitional formations have ignorance as their condition, but do not have clarity as their condition? Answer: Yes.
That is to say:
the maturation of ignorance and defiled formations.
Is there perhaps:
Is it that formations have clarity as their condition, rather than ignorance?
Answer: There is.
That is to say:
with the exception of the first illumination,
all other untainted (anāsrava) formations.
Is there any instance where volitional formations have ignorance as their condition and also have clarity as their condition? Answer:
No. Is there perhaps a case where formations do not have ignorance as their object, nor do they have clarity as their object?
Answer: There is. Namely:
Excluding the maturation of ignorance,
all other non-obscured neutral formations (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-saṃskāra*), as well as the initial light (*āloka*) and wholesome contaminated formations (*sāsrava-kuśala-saṃskāra*).
Should it be said that inhalation and exhalation proceed in dependence upon the body?
Does it revolve in dependence upon the mind?
Answer: It should be said:
It functions in dependence on both the body and the mind, as appropriate.
If inhalation and exhalation functioned only in dependence on the body and not in dependence on the mind,
then inhalation and exhalation would also have to function in those who are in the meditative attainments of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
If inhalation and exhalation were to proceed solely in dependence upon the mind and not in dependence upon the body,
then the inhalation and exhalation of sentient beings in the formless realm would also have to proceed.
If inhalation and exhalation were to proceed solely in dependence upon both the body and the mind, it would not be as it ought to be.

Furthermore, [the vital wind] should also circulate within the eggshell and the mother’s womb during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana, when the sense faculties are not yet complete or matured; it should likewise circulate during the inhalation and exhalation in the fourth dhyāna.
Because inhalation and exhalation—relying both upon the body and upon the mind, as well as according to what is appropriate—occur in this way;

therefore, from the Avīci Hell below up to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven above, for all sentient beings therein whose faculties are complete and matured, inhalation and exhalation proceed in reliance upon the body and the mind.
Just as for sentient beings with form, the continuity of the mind proceeds in dependence upon the body;
for sentient beings without form, in dependence upon what does the continuity of the mind proceed?
Answer: Based on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), and other such formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*),
when there is "craving for existence" (*bhavarāga*), should it be said that this is abandoned by insight (*darśanaprahātavya*)?
Is it abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: It should be said:
It is abandoned by cultivation.
Some say that craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) is either abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned by seeing?
It refers to craving for that which does not exist regarding phenomena abandoned by seeing.
What is that which is to be abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to craving for that which does not exist regarding phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation.
In this context, there is no "craving for existence" (*bhavarāga*); rather, it should simply be said to be "abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*).
You have stated:
"There is no craving for existence; it is abandoned solely by cultivation."
"Do those who have attained the stream-entry (srotāpanna) not yet abandon this craving? Answer: "It is so."
What is your position?
Do those who have attained the stream-entry ever give rise to such a thought as this:
"If, after my death, I am annihilated and cease to exist, would that not be peace and bliss?"
Answer: It is not so. Listen to what I say:
If it were the case that "non-existence— craving for existence— is abandoned solely through cultivation, and stream-enterers have not yet abandoned this craving," then one should say:
a stream-enterer would give rise to such a thought as, "If, after my death, I were to cease, perish, and no longer exist, would that not be peace and happiness?"
If a stream-enterer does not give rise to such a thought as, "If,
after my death, I am annihilated and cease to exist, would that not be peace and happiness?
then one should not say:
To say, "There is no craving for existence (*bhavarāga*);
it is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); and stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) have not yet abandoned this craving"—such statements are both unreasonable.
Do you also maintain that "the craving for the maturation of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts is abandoned only through cultivation,
and that stream-enterers have not yet abandoned this craving"?
Answer: It is so. What do you maintain?
Do those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry give rise to such thoughts as:
"I shall become the Naga King Elāpattra, the Naga King Supratiṣṭhita... or the Yama King of the Pretas, presiding over all sentient beings in the realm of ghosts"?
Answer: It is not so. Listen to what I say:
If the craving for the maturation of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts were to be abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
then it would follow that all stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) have not yet abandoned this craving;
thus, one should say:
A stream-enterer gives rise to such a thought: "I shall become the Naga King Elāpattra...
[and so on, as extensively explained].
If a stream-enterer does not give rise to such a thought: "I shall become the Naga King Elāpattra... [and so on].
...and so on, as explained at length.
Then one should not say:
"The craving for the maturation of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts is abandoned only by cultivation."
To say that "all stream-enterers have not yet abandoned this craving" is likewise unreasonable.
You yourselves also say:
"Is it because they are bound by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) that they take the lives of their parents, and are these fetters abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
such that even those who have attained the stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) have not yet abandoned them?"
Answer: It is so. What do you maintain?
Do those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) kill their parents because they give rise to such obsessions (paryavasthāna)? Answer: No.
Listen to what I say:
if one kills the lives of one's father or mother because of being "bound by the fetters" (*paryavasthāna*), these fetters are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
yet, those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) have not yet abandoned these fetters.
One should then say:
"It is because a stream-enterer gives rise to such fetters that they take the lives of their parents;
it is not because a stream-enterer fails to give rise to such fetters that they take the lives of their parents."
Then one should not say:
"Because they are bound by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), they take the lives of their parents; these fetters are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
and stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) have not yet abandoned these fetters."
To speak in such a manner is, in both cases, unreasonable.
You yourselves also state:
"Regarding phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation, there is craving for what does not exist; this craving is abandoned solely through cultivation."
"Is it not the case that all stream-enterers have not yet abandoned this greed? Answer: "It is so."
What is your position?
Do those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry give rise to craving conditioned by this? Answer:
Not so. Listen to what I say:
if there is craving for dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation that do not exist, this craving is abandoned solely by cultivation.
"If those who have attained the stream-entry (srotāpanna) have not yet abandoned this craving," then one should say:
"The stream-enterer gives rise to affection based on this."
If a stream-enterer does not give rise to craving with respect to this [object], then one should not say:
"Regarding phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation, there is greed for what does not exist; this greed is abandoned only by cultivation."
To say that "all stream-enterers have not yet abandoned this craving" is likewise unreasonable.
Since that [previous statement] is reasonable, this must also be so.
What dharma is called "non-existence"?
Answer: The impermanence of the three realms.
As the Blessed One said:
"The mind is liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion.
From what is the mind liberated?
Is there a mind possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion?
Or is it a mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion? Answer:
One attains liberation through a mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Some, however, maintain that liberation is attained by a mind associated with greed, hatred, and delusion.
One should not speak in that way.

Why is this? It is not the case that "because this mind is conjoined with, associated with, and mixed with greed, hatred, and delusion, and because greed, hatred, and delusion have not been abandoned, the mind is not liberated."
"When greed, hatred, and delusion are abandoned, the mind is liberated.
The Blessed One also said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
This disk of the sun and moon, when obscured by five veils, is neither bright nor illuminating, neither expansive nor pure. What are these five?
First, clouds.
Second, smoke;
third, dust;
fourth, mist.
"O Pañcahiraḥ Asura, it is as when the orbs of the sun and moon are not conjoined with, associated with, or mixed with the five obscurations.
As long as those obscurations have not been removed, these orbs of the sun and moon are not bright, do not shine, are not expansive, and are not pure."
"When that cataract is removed, this disk of the sun or moon shines with vast and pure brilliance.

In the same way, it is not the case that "this mind is conjoined with, associated with, and mixed with greed, hatred, and delusion, yet greed, hatred, and delusion have not been abandoned, and the mind is not liberated."
"When greed, hatred, and delusion are abandoned,
the mind is liberated. Is this mental liberation past,
or is it future?
Is it present? Answer:
At the time when a future mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) arises.
How is it that all obstacles are liberated? Answer:

It is like when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is about to cease, and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is about to arise.

When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), which is the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), is in the process of ceasing, and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), which is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), is in the process of arising, at that time it is said: "At the moment the future mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) arises, one is liberated from all obstacles."
"Should one say that the mind not yet liberated is liberated,
or should one say that the mind already liberated is liberated? Answer:
If the mind has already been liberated, it should be said that it is "liberated.
If it has already been liberated, one should not say it is "being liberated";
if it is being liberated, one should not say it has "already been liberated."
To claim that a mind already liberated is "liberated" is not consistent with correct principle.
Now one should question them as the Blessed One has said:
"If craving is severed without remainder, Like a lotus in the water..."
“A bhikṣu abandons this world and the next, Just as a snake sheds its old skin.
Do you consider this statement to be well-spoken?
Answer: [Yes.]
So it is. What do you intend? Is it that having already abandoned [a view], you abandon the statement?
If one has not yet relinquished [the precepts], can one say that they have relinquished them? Answer: One who has already relinquished them may say that they have relinquished them.
Listen to what I say:
if one has already relinquished, one should not say "relinquish";
if one is relinquishing, one should not say "has already relinquished."
To say that [defilements] have been abandoned when they have already been abandoned is not consistent with correct principle.
Furthermore,
the Blessed One said:
"Having severed pride, being well-established in self-cultivation, with a virtuous mind liberated in every way,
dwelling alone in tranquility and not indolent— one transcends death and reaches the further shore.
Do you consider this statement to be well-spoken?
Answer: It is so. What do you maintain?
Is it that one who has already arrived says they have arrived,
or does one who has not yet arrived say they have arrived? Answer:
If one has already arrived, one says "arrived. Listen to what I say:
if one has already arrived, one should not say "arrived."
If one has arrived, one should not say that one has already arrived.
To say that one has already arrived when one has indeed arrived is contrary to correct principle;
since that [latter case] conforms to principle, this [former case] should likewise be so.
Therefore, one should distinguish the meaning within the sūtras as the Blessed One said:
"Beasts return to the forest thickets; birds return to the void; the noble ones return to nirvāṇa."
"Phenomena resolve into conceptual differentiation," as the Blessed One said: "Bhikṣus,
you should know:"
"Based on revulsion, one becomes dispassionate; based on dispassion, one attains liberation; based on liberation, one attains nirvana.
What is revulsion? Answer:
If, regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one is without further training (*aśaikṣa*), feels revulsion, and opposes them, this is called "disgust" (*nirveda*).
How does one rely on disgust to become free from defilement? Answer:

If it is associated with revulsion—namely, the wholesome roots of non-greed and absence of excessive greed, non-hatred and absence of excessive hatred, and non-delusion and absence of excessive delusion—this is called "relying on revulsion to become free from defilement."
What is liberation based on detachment from defilements? Answer:

If a mind associated with detachment from defilements has already attained resolution, is currently attaining resolution, or will attain resolution, this is called liberation based on detachment from defilements.
What is meant by "relying on liberation and nirvāṇa"? Answer:
If greed is permanently severed, hatred is permanently severed, delusion is permanently severed, and all afflictions are permanently severed, this is called relying on liberation and nirvāṇa.
As the Blessed One said:
"There are three realms.
Namely:"
"The realm of abandonment, the realm of detachment, and the realm of cessation.
What is the realm of abandonment? Answer:
The abandonment of the fetter of craving and the severance of the remaining fetters is called the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*).
What is the realm of detachment (*virāgadhātu*)? Answer:
The severance of the fetter of craving is called the element of detachment (*vairāgyadhātu*).
What is the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*)? Answer:
The abandonment of all other factors conducive to bondage is called the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
Are all elements of abandonment also elements of detachment (*virāgadhātu*)? Answer:
It is so. If it is the element of detachment,
is it the element of abandonment?
Answer: It is so.
Are all elements of abandonment (prahāṇadhātu) elements of cessation (nirodhadhātu)?
Answer: It is so.
If it is the element of cessation, is it the element of abandonment?
Answer: It is so.
Are all elements of detachment (virāga-dhātu) elements of cessation (nirodha-dhātu)?
Answer: It is so.
If it is the cessation element (*nirodhadhātu*), is it the relinquishment element (*prahāṇadhātu*)?
Answer: It is so. As the Blessed One has said:
“There are three perceptions,
namely: the perception of relinquishment, the perception of detachment, and the perception of cessation.”
What is the perception of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃjñā*)? Answer:
With the exception of the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇāsaṃyojana*), the resolution that abandons all other fetters is called the perception of abandonment.
What is the dissociation from perception? Answer:
The fetter of craving, through which all perceptions are severed and resolved, is called dissociation from perception.
What is the cessation of perception? Answer:
The severance of all other perceptions associated with the fetters is called the cessation of perception.
The Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume One;
The Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Volume Two,
composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree:
Cultivation, respect, power, cessation, The ultimate of the aggregates of nirvāṇa,
Full knowledge, and the three refuges— In this chapter, may all these be fully explained.
What is craving? Answer:
All forms of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and pervasive craving, joy and pervasive joy, delight and pervasive delight—this is called craving.
What is reverence (*gaurava*)? Answer:

It is that which possesses reverence, possesses the nature of reverence; that which possesses mastery (*vaśitā*), possesses the nature of mastery; and the arising of fear toward one who possesses mastery—this is called reverence.
What is affection and respect? Answer:

It is when a certain class of person—toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, their own teachers and preceptors, or any other wise, venerable, and fellow-practitioner of the holy life—dwells with a heart of fondness and joy, maintaining reverence. Wherever there is such love and respect, this is called affection and respect.
How does one make offerings? Answer: There are two kinds.
There are two kinds of offerings: first, the offering of material wealth; second, the offering of the Dharma.
What is meant by "reverence"? Answer:
When there is respect and a nature of respect, mastery and a nature of mastery;
and when fear arises toward that which possesses mastery—this is called respect.
What is meant by "offering and honoring"? Answer:

It is when a certain class of person—toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; toward their preceptors and instructors; and toward any other wise, venerable, and fellow-practitioner of the holy life—provides offerings and dwells in a state of honoring them.
If, in this regard, there is offering and reverence, this is called "offering and reverence.
What is physical strength? Answer:
That the body is courageous, robust, agile, and capable of accomplishing tasks—this is called physical strength.
What is physical inferiority? Answer:
When the various bodies are not courageous, not fierce, not strong, not robust, not light, not agile, and incapable of accomplishing anything, this is called inferiority of body (*kāyadaurbalya*).
How many bases (*āyatana*) do bodily strength and bodily inferiority subsume?
By how many consciousnesses is it cognized? Answer:
It is comprised within one base, namely:
The sphere of tangibles is cognized by two consciousnesses, namely:
body-consciousness and mental-consciousness.
For example:
when two strong men wrestle with one another, as soon as their wrists meet, each knows the other’s relative strength. Or again:
When the strong seize the weak, the relative superiority or inferiority of their strength is likewise mutually recognized.
What is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? Answer:
All cessations are disconnections (*visamyoga*).
What is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? Answer:
Not all cessations are disjunctions.
What is impermanent cessation? Answer:
The dispersal, destruction, dissolution, and disappearance of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is called cessation through impermanence (anityatā-nirodha).
What is the difference between cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and cessation through impermanence? Answer:
As for non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*):

it is liberation from epidemics, calamities, sorrows, and various demonic activities not by the power of analytical discernment; it is the practice of worldly suffering, rather than the subduing or transcending of craving.
Regarding "cessation through impermanence":
it refers to the dispersal and disintegration of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), their destruction and disappearance, and their passing away.
This is called the distinction between the two types of cessation.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are two nirvāṇa realms, namely:
the nirvāṇa realm with remainder and the nirvāṇa realm without remainder."
"What is the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder?
Answer: It is when the outflows (āsrava) of an arhat have been eternally exhausted."
Life-span still persists;
the primary elements and derived matter continue in an uninterrupted succession.
Relying upon the body of the five sense faculties, the mental continuum proceeds.
Because the residual basis remains, all fetters are eternally exhausted;
having attained this realization,
it is called the realm of nirvana with residual basis.
What is the realm of nirvana without remainder? Answer:
It is when the arhat’s outflows are forever exhausted and his lifespan has already come to an end.
The primary elements and derived matter have ceased their continuity;
based upon the body of the five sense faculties, the mind no longer functions.
Because there is no remaining substrate, all fetters are forever extinguished.
It is called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Regarding this nirvana, should it be said to be "with training" (śaikṣa)?
Is it that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Or is it neither that of one in training nor that of one beyond training? Answer:
Nirvāṇa should be described as "neither-learner-nor-non-learner. Some, however, say:
Nirvāṇa is [sometimes] a learner, [sometimes] a non-learner, and [sometimes] neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is the state of training (*śaikṣa*)?
It refers to having attained the abandonment of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and having achieved their realization through contact.
What is the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
This refers to the attainment of the abandonment of all fetters by one beyond training (aśaikṣa), which constitutes their realization and acquisition.
What is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
This refers to the attainment of the abandonment of all fetters through contaminated (sāsrava) means, which constitutes their realization and acquisition.
Regarding this point, one should simply say that nirvāṇa is "neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Yet you claim:
"Nirvāṇa is learner, it is non-learner, and it is neither-learner-nor-non-learner"?
Answer: It is so. What do you maintain?

Regarding those who have previously, by means of the mundane path, attained the acquisition of disjunction from sensual desire and ill-will—which is neither that of a learner nor that of one beyond learning—have they, having not yet attained the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Truths, cultivated that clear realization; and having attained clear realization, realized the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), thereby becoming learners (*śaikṣa*)?
Answer: It is so. Furthermore!
What is the intended meaning?

[It is this: "The acquisitions of disjunction (visaṃyoga-prāpti) from sensual desire and ill-will that were previously attained through the mundane path—being neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa)—should, at the time of subsequently realizing the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala), be transformed into the acquisition of a learner (śaikṣa)."
If he were to become a learner (*śaikṣa*) at this present time, he would have necessarily been a learner previously, because his essence is eternally abiding.

To designate him as a learner before he has realized the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) and while he does not yet possess "attainment as a learner" (*śaikṣalābha*) is contrary to correct principle.
What is your position?

When one who is a candidate for arhatship (arhattvapratipannaka) abandons all fetters (saṃyojana) through training and realizes the fruit of arhatship, does he then become one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Answer:
"So it is. Furthermore,
what is your position?"

"When one who is a candidate for arhatship (arhattvapratipannaka) has abandoned all fetters (saṃyojana) through training and realizes the fruit of arhatship, those very same abandoned fetters should then transform into the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
If they were to become those of no-more-learning at this present time, they would have had to be so previously, because their essential nature is eternally abiding.

If one has not yet realized the fruit of arhatship, there is no "attainment of the state beyond training" (aśaikṣa-prāpti); yet to call such a person "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) would contradict correct reasoning.
What do you maintain?
When Arhats who have abandoned the fetters of those beyond training fall back from the fruit of arhatship, do they thereby become "trainees" (śaikṣa)?
Answer: It is so. Furthermore!
What is your position?
"When those Arhats who have abandoned the fetters of no-more-learning fall away from the fruit of Arhatship, those very same abandoned fetters should then become the fetters of a learner."
If he were to become a learner (*śaikṣa*) at this present time, he would have had to be a learner previously, because his essence is eternally abiding.
Since there is no "attainment of a learner" prior to the non-retrogression from the fruit of arhatship, to designate him as a learner [at that point] would be contrary to correct principle.

Furthermore, Nirvana should not be such that—having first been neither-learner-nor-non-learner—it later becomes a learner; having first been a learner, it later becomes a non-learner; or having first been a non-learner, it later again becomes a learner.
Furthermore,
Nirvana should not possess the categories of "those in training" (*śaikṣa*), "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), or "neither in training nor beyond training.
If it were so, it would result in a twofold division.
Because all phenomena are not fixed, there would necessarily be confusion;
thus, one should not posit that the intrinsic nature and characteristics of phenomena are fixed.
Furthermore, the Buddha did not speak of Nirvana as having the nature of either those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Because *nirvāṇa* is eternally "neither-learner-nor-non-learner," all dharmas are determined and free from confusion; they eternally abide in their own nature and do not abandon their own nature;
*nirvāṇa* is permanently abiding and without change.
Therefore, regarding nirvāṇa, one should simply say:
"neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

He has accomplished the aggregate of precepts of one beyond training, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
What is the aggregate of precepts of one beyond training?
Answer: The bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What is the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training?
Answer: The three samādhis of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
That is to say:
Emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
What is the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training? Answer:
The right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is wisdom (jñāna).
What is the aggregate of liberation (vimukti-skandha) of one beyond training? Answer:
The mind associated with the attention of one beyond training—having already resolved, currently resolving, or about to resolve.
What is the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training?
Answer: The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
What is the difference between the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-prajñā-skandha) and the aggregate of liberation and the vision of knowledge (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha)?
Answer: The knowledge of suffering and its origin belonging to one beyond training (aśaikṣa) constitutes the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-skandha) of one beyond training;
the knowledge of cessation and the path belonging to one beyond training constitutes the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha) of one beyond training.
Furthermore, the knowledge of suffering, its origin, and its cessation belonging to those beyond training (aśaikṣa) constitutes the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-skandha) of those beyond training;
the knowledge of the path belonging to those beyond training constitutes the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha) of those beyond training.
Furthermore, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of its origin, and the knowledge of the path belonging to one beyond training constitute the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training;
the knowledge of cessation belonging to one beyond training constitutes the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
This is what is called the distinction.
As the Blessed One said: "O Bhikṣus!"
"One should know that there is only one ultimate, and no other ultimate.
In this context, what dharma is called "ultimate"? Answer:
At times, the World-Honored One speaks of the "ultimate" (niṣṭhā) with respect to the Path;
at other times, he speaks of the "ultimate" with respect to Cessation (prahāṇa).
Regarding his speaking of the "ultimate" with respect to the Path:
As the Blessed One said:
"A certain class of people, wise yet arrogant, cannot know the ultimate;
because they have not realized the Path, they die unsubdued."
Regarding the expression "the sound of finality" in reference to "abandonment," it is as the Blessed One said:
"One who has reached the ultimate has no fear, no doubt, and no regret."
"Because they have forever uprooted the arrow of existence, they dwell in their final body;
this is the ultimate end. It is the unsurpassed path of peace, the pure path of deathlessness, for all marks have been exhausted."
Furthermore,
a sutra states:
A certain brahmin named Maudgalyāyana came to the place where the Buddha was and questioned him, saying:
"Venerable Gautama!
When you instruct and admonish the bhikṣus, once they have received your teaching, are they all able to realize the most ultimate realm of parinirvāṇa?"
