The World-Honored One replied:
"This matter is not fixed;
for some it can be realized, while for others it cannot."
As it is said in a sutra:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"There are certain non-Buddhists who, although they likewise establish the abandonment and knowledge of all grasping, are unable to establish it fully."
That is to say:

"It is only the knowledge of abandonment regarding the clinging to sensual desire, the clinging to views, and the clinging to precepts and observances that is designated, not the clinging to the doctrine of self.
What is the meaning of this?
Some might say: "This was the Blessed One preaching the Dharma impulsively. They should not say this.
Why is this? Because the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is not entirely without cause, nor is it based on a meager cause.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Regarding the statement that this reveals the partial abandonment of those [defilements], they should not say such a thing. Why is that?
Ordinary beings also possess the capacity to sever a small portion of the grasping at a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Nevertheless, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, extensively expounded the essential points of the Dharma for the great assembly of immeasurable devas and humans, revealing them without error so that each might understand according to their own kind.

There were various non-Buddhists who had secretly heard the names of the Buddha’s teachings on the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), hindrances (nīvaraṇa), applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), up to the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga); some of these were complete, while others were incomplete.
When these non-Buddhists hear that there is one who seeks to grasp at desire, they say:
"I too establish the abandonment and knowledge of grasping at desire."
If there are those who hear or see the term "clinging to views," they will say:
"I also establish the abandonment of clinging to views.
If there are those who hear or see the term "clinging to precepts," they will say:
“I also establish the abandonment and knowledge of the clinging to precepts and observances.
For instance, when many bhikṣus have gathered in one place, various non-Buddhists come and say:
“Just as Gautama proclaims the essential Dharma to his disciples, making this statement:”
“O bhikṣus, you should abandon the five hindrances. These five hindrances defile the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, harm the factors of enlightenment, and obstruct nirvāṇa.
You should well establish the mind in the four foundations of mindfulness and diligently cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.”
"We ourselves are also able to explain this essential teaching to our disciples.
In that case, what difference is there between the essential teaching spoken by Gautama and ours?
Why is it that you have returned here alone?"

"Yet those non-Buddhists cannot even recognize the names and characteristics of the five hindrances, much less can they fully comprehend—abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment?"
Nevertheless, I have spoken thus by borrowing the Buddha’s words.
One should know that the designation of "clinging" (*upādāna*) is likewise [provisional].
Furthermore:

For example, the non-Buddhist Makkhali Gosāla, failing to understand that his own body was a collection of various ailments—momentarily impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—approached the Buddha and, drumming on his belly, said:
"Since this body of mine is currently free from all diseases, you should know that it is ultimate nirvāṇa."
They do not even know the name or characteristics of "freedom from illness," much less can they realize ultimate nirvana.
Nevertheless, they have stolen the Buddha’s words and thus made such a statement.
One should know that the same applies to the conceptualization of "the abandonment of grasping."

For what reason do the non-Buddhists only establish the abandonment and knowledge of the three types of clinging (*upādāna*), but not that of "clinging to the doctrine of self" (*ātmavādopādāna*)? Answer:

Because throughout the long night, they have clung to the existence of a real self, as well as a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-principle (*jīva*), a living being (*jantu*), a nourisher (*poṣa*), and a person (*pudgala*).

Since they maintain that there is a truly existent self, how could they possibly propose the abandonment of the grasping to the doctrine of self, while claiming it is equivalent to proposing the abandonment of all forms of grasping?
What meaning does this have?
Answer: This refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, conforming to that verbal expression.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"Those non-Buddhists posit that there is a truly existent sentient being who undergoes annihilation;
however, from the perspective of ultimate truth, no such real sentient being exists—
it is merely said so in accordance with their terminology."
This case is likewise, and thus there is no fault.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are two types of thorough knowledge (parijñā), namely:"
There is thorough knowledge through wisdom and thorough knowledge through abandonment.
What is thorough knowledge through wisdom? Answer:
The various forms of knowledge, vision, clarity, awakening, and clear realization—
this is called the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*).
What is the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*)?
Answer: The permanent abandonment of all greed, the permanent abandonment of hatred and delusion, and the permanent abandonment of all afflictions—
this is called the full knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
The Blessed One sometimes uses the term "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) with reference to "knowledge," and sometimes uses the term "thorough knowledge" with reference to "abandonment.
Regarding the use of the term "thorough knowledge" with reference to "knowledge":
As a gāthā says: The noble Māṇava is tranquil, Able to benefit all beings in the world;
Possessing wisdom, he fully understands That craving gives rise to manifold sufferings.
What is wise one should do; what is not to be done, the wise one should not say.
One should thoroughly understand this: regarding that which exists but is not performed, the term "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) is used in the sense of "abandonment."
As it is said in the Sūtra:

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "I shall now explain to you the phenomena that are to be fully known (*parijñeya*), the intrinsic nature of full knowledge (*parijñā-svabhāva*), and that which is capable of full knowledge (*parijñātṛ*)."
The phenomena to be fully known are the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
The intrinsic nature of full knowledge is:
This refers to the permanent abandonment of greed, the permanent abandonment of hatred and delusion, and the permanent abandonment of all afflictions.
One who is able to fully comprehend this is an Arhat whose outflows are forever exhausted.
One does not cling to such indeterminate matters as "the Tathāgata exists after death," and so forth. For those who take refuge in the Buddha, in what do they take refuge? Answer:
If a phenomenon truly exists or is presently manifest, and is designated through conceptualization and verbal expression, it is called "Buddha."
Taking refuge in all those dharmas of one beyond training that constitute the attainment of enlightenment is called taking refuge in the Buddha.
As for those who take refuge in the Dharma, in what do they take refuge? Answer:
If a phenomenon truly exists and is presently manifest, such that it is designated by perception and conceptualization and expressed through conventional discourse, it is called *dharma*.
Taking refuge in such a nirvāṇa—the exhaustion of craving, detachment, cessation, and extinction—is called taking refuge in the Dharma.
Regarding those who take refuge in the Sangha, in what do they take refuge? Answer:
Those phenomena that truly exist, currently exist, and are designated through conceptualization and conventional expression are called the Sangha.
Taking refuge in all those qualities of the Saṅgha consisting of the trainees (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called taking refuge in the Saṅgha.
The two faculties of black and white, the mind, The hindrances of restlessness-and-regret, lethargy-and-drowsiness, and doubt,
as well as ignorance and the unshared [afflictions]— In this chapter, I pray that these shall be fully explained.
What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)? Answer:

It is all forms of being without shame, having no sense of shame, and lacking distinct shame; being without embarrassment, having no sense of embarrassment, and lacking distinct embarrassment; being without reverence, lacking the nature of reverence, and lacking self-mastery or the nature of self-mastery.
Regarding those who possess power, acting without fear is called *āhrīkya* (lack of shame).
What is *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread)? Answer:
To have no sense of shame, no cause for shame, and no distinct sense of shame; no sense of modesty, no cause for modesty, and no distinct sense of modesty;
to feel no dread, no fear, and to perceive no dread regarding various transgressions—this is called "lack of shame" (āhrīkya).
What is the difference between lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)? Answer:
The arising of fearlessness toward those who are authoritative is lack of shame.
Not perceiving fear in regard to any transgressions is shamelessness (*āhrīkya*).
Such is the distinction.
What is modesty (*hrī*)?
Answer:

There is shame (*hrī*), that which is shameful (*hrīya*), and the basis for shame; there is modesty (*apatrāpya*), that which is modest, and the basis for modesty; there is reverence (*gaurava*), the nature of reverence, mastery (*vaśitā*), and the nature of mastery.
The arising of fear toward those who are authoritative is called *hrī* (shame).
What is *apatrāpya* (dread of blame)? Answer:
To have shame, to have that which is shameful, and to have a distinct sense of shame; to have modesty, to have that which is modest, and to have a distinct sense of modesty;
to feel dread, fear, and a profound perception of dread toward all transgressions—this is called *hrī* (shame).
What is the distinction between shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*)? Answer:
That which arises as a sense of fear toward those who are authoritative is shame.
To perceive a profound sense of dread regarding all transgressions is *hrī* (moral shame).
Such is the distinction between them.
What are the predominant unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*)?
Answer:
Regarding the unwholesome roots that can sever the wholesome roots and are first abandoned at the time of detachment from sensual desire—
what are these "unwholesome roots associated with the subtle"?
Answer: Regarding the unwholesome roots, they are abandoned last at the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire.
Because of that abandonment, one is said to be "free from the defilement of desire."
What are the superior wholesome roots of the desire realm? Answer:

They are the conventional knowledge at the edge of clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of the desire realm attained when a bodhisattva enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), as well as the wholesome roots of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion of the desire realm attained when a Tathāgata attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
What are the subtle concomitant roots of goodness? Answer:
At the time when the roots of goodness are severed, these are the last to be abandoned; because they are abandoned, it is called the severance of the roots of goodness.
If all minds have passed away, have those minds undergone transformation and disintegration? Answer:
All minds that have passed away have indeed undergone transformation and disintegration.
There are minds that undergo transformation and disintegration, yet those minds are not of the past; namely,
future and present minds associated with greed and hatred.
As the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus! Suppose you were to be attacked by hostile bandits who were to saw apart your bodies or your various limbs and joints;..."
Regarding that, you should not allow your minds to become corrupted, and you must also guard your speech so as not to utter evil words.
If your minds become corrupted or if you utter evil words, it will constitute a profound obstacle to what you yourself seek.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus! You all..."
"One should not give rise to a mind of transformation and decay toward the objects of exquisite desire.
If the mind is defiled by attachment, is that mind subject to transformation and decay? Answer:
Those minds that are defiled and attached, those minds are all subject to transformation and decay.
There are minds subject to transformation and decay that are not defiled and attached.
That is to say:
The past mind dissociated from greed, as well as future and present minds associated with hatred.
As the Blessed One said: "O Bhikṣus!..."
"Suppose one is beset by hostile bandits... [as explained at length] ...it constitutes a profound obstacle to what one seeks for oneself.
What is restlessness (*auddhatya*)? Answer:
When various states of mind are not tranquil, do not cease, and are flighty and agitated—
this restless nature of the mind is called *auddhatya* (restlessness).
What is *kaukṛtya* (remorse)?
Answer: It refers to the mind’s state of being scorched, agitated, and transformed by distress;
this nature of mental regret is called *kaukṛtya* (remorse).
If various states of mind are characterized by restlessness (*auddhatya*), are those minds associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is a state of mind characterized by restlessness that is not associated with remorse;
that is to say,
there is a mind devoid of remorse that possesses a nature of agitation.
There is a state of mind characterized by remorse that is not associated with restlessness; namely,
a non-defiled state of mind possessing the nature of regret.
There is a mind that possesses restlessness and is also associated with remorse;
that is to say,
a defiled mind has the nature of regret.
There is a state of mind that is without restlessness and is also not associated with remorse;
that is to say:
excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
What is torpor? Answer:

It is the state of heaviness of body and heaviness of mind; lack of pliancy in body and lack of pliancy in mind; drowsiness of body and drowsiness of mind; and mental agitation of body and mental agitation of mind.
The state of mental dullness and heaviness is called *styāna* (torpor).
What is *middha* (drowsiness)? Answer:
When various states of mind are drowsy, they proceed in a state of dullness and subtlety;
this nature of mental obscurity and brevity is called *middha* (sleepiness).
If various states of mind possess *styāna* (sloth), are those minds associated with *middha*?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is a mind that possesses torpor (styāna) but is not associated with sleep (middha).
That is to say:
there is a state of mind that is free from sleep but possesses the nature of torpor;
there is also a state of mind that possesses sleep but is not associated with torpor.
That is to say:
there is an undefiled mind that possesses the nature of sleep;
there is also a mind that possesses lethargy (*styāna*) and is associated with sleep.
That is to say:
there is a defiled mind that possesses the nature of sleep;
there is a mind that lacks mental torpor (*styāna*) and is also not associated with sleep.
That is to say:
setting aside the aforementioned characteristics, should sleep be described as wholesome?
Is it unwholesome?
Or is it indeterminate? Answer:
Sleep should be described as either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to sleep occurring with a wholesome mind, proceeding in a state of dullness and subtlety.
What is the nature of mental dullness and brevity? How is it unwholesome?
It refers to the state where an unwholesome mind functions in a drowsy, obscure, and subtle manner.
The nature of the mind being dull and abbreviated:
what is meant by "indeterminate"?
It refers to indeterminate consciousness that functions while one is asleep, proceeding in a state of stupor and subtlety.
When the mind is dull and its nature is obscured,
as in a dream, should one say that merit increases,
or that non-merit increases?
Does non-merit increase, or does that which is neither merit nor non-merit increase? Answer:
Regarding dreams, one should say: either merit increases, or non-merit increases, or that which is neither merit nor non-merit increases.
Regarding the increase of merit:
as if in a dream one practices giving, performs meritorious deeds, observes the precepts and fasts, or engages in any other such single act of merit, it continues to evolve in succession.
Regarding the increase of non-merit:

as when, in a dream, one commits taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, intentional false speech, or drinking intoxicants, or any other such non-meritorious act—whichever it may be—the continuity of that [non-merit] persists.
Regarding "the increase of neither-meritorious-nor-non-meritorious [karma]":
it is like the continuous progression of neither-meritorious-nor-non-meritorious states within a dream.
What phenomenon is designated as a "dream"?
Answer: When one is asleep, the various minds and mental factors operate with respect to their objects.
Having awakened, one recollects them accordingly and is able to explain them to others.
"I have seen such and such things in a dream.
This is called a dream.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
“There are five hindrances.
Do the five hindrances encompass all hindrances,
or do all hindrances encompass the five hindrances?
Answer: The "hindrances" (nīvaraṇa) include the five hindrances, but the five hindrances do not include all hindrances.
What is not included?
That is to say:
the veil of ignorance.
As the Blessed One said:
"Enveloped by the veil of ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving,
both the foolish and the wise alike experience such a conscious body.
Are those veils what envelop it?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi). There are cases where there is an obscuration (nīvaraṇa) but not a concealment (paryavasthāna).
That is to say:
the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) of the past and future;
there are those that are obscuring (nivṛta) but not hindrances.
That is to say:
when other afflictions, excluding the five hindrances, manifest,
those with hindrances are likewise obscured.
That is to say:
when any one of the five hindrances (pañca-nīvaraṇa) is present,
there is that which is neither a hindrance nor a concealment.
That is to say:
excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
are all those latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) necessarily unwholesome (akuśala)?
Answer: All unwholesome latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) are bound to the desire realm.
However, there are latent tendencies of ignorance bound to the desire realm that are not unwholesome.
That is to say:
the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm.
Are all those latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) bound to the form and formless realms indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Answer: All latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) bound to the realms of form and formlessness are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
There are indeed indeterminate latent tendencies of ignorance.
It is not associated with the form realm or the formless realm;
that is to say,
it is the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity and the view of extreme adherence which are bound to the desire realm.

Are all the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) necessarily universal (*sarvatraga*)? Answer:
All universal latent tendencies of ignorance are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origination.

There is the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), which is not universal (*asarvatraga*).
That is to say:
the ignorance associated with the non-universal latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origination.
Are all the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the cessation and the path [of vision] non-universal (*asarvatraga*)? Answer:
All latent tendencies of ignorance abandoned through the cessation and the path [of vision] are non-universal.
There is a non-universal latent tendency of ignorance that is not abandoned by the vision of cessation or the path;
namely, the ignorance associated with non-universal latent tendencies that are abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin.
What is the latent tendency of non-associated ignorance? Answer:
It refers to all forms of ignorance—lack of understanding regarding suffering, and lack of understanding regarding the origin, cessation, and the path.
What is the exclusive fetter of restlessness?
Answer: There is no such thing as an exclusive fetter of restlessness.
Two or three characteristics are common to both [conditioned phenomena and unconditioned space], while aging, death, and impermanence are strong;
the three characteristics exist for a single moment.
This chapter shall fully explain the arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*): should these be called "matter" (*rūpa*)?
Is it not form? Answer: It should be said that it is not form.
Are the arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence of non-material phenomena (arūpadharma) to be described as non-material or as material? Answer:
One should say it is non-material (arūpa).
Regarding the arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence of a visible phenomenon (sanidarśana-dharma), should one say they are visible or invisible?
Answer: One should say they are invisible.
Are the arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence of invisible phenomena also to be called invisible?
Is there seeing?
Answer: One should say there is no seeing.
Regarding the arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence of a dharma that possesses resistance (*sapratigha*):
should these be said to possess resistance,
or to be without resistance (*apratigha*)?
Answer: One should say they are non-resistant (*apratigha*).
Regarding non-resistant phenomena—namely arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence—should they also be said to be non-resistant?
Is it with resistance?
Answer: It should be said that it is without resistance.

Regarding the conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*)— namely, arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence— should they be said to be with outflows or without outflows (*anāsrava*)? Answer:
One should say they are with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
As for the arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence of phenomena that are without-outflows (*anāsrava*), should they be said to be without-outflows or with-outflows?
Answer: It should be said that they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—namely arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence—should they be said to be conditioned?
Is it unconditioned?
Answer: It should be said that it is conditioned.
Regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)— namely birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), aging (*jarā*), and impermanence (*anityatā*)—
should they be called unconditioned or conditioned? Answer:
One should say that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are devoid of "arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence.
Regarding past phenomena—do their arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence belong to the past?
Is it future or present?
Answer: It should be said to be past.
Regarding future dharmas— their arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence— should they be said to be future, or past and present? Answer:
One should say they belong to the future.
As for the arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence of present phenomena, should they be said to belong to the present,
or to the past and future?
Answer: One should say they are present.
As for wholesome factors—their arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence—should these be said to be wholesome?
"Are they unwholesome or indeterminate? Answer:
"One should say that wholesome and unwholesome dharmas—namely arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence—should be called unwholesome."
Is it wholesome or indeterminate?
Answer: It should be said that it is unwholesome.
Regarding indeterminate phenomena (avyākṛta-dharma)— their arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence— should they be called indeterminate,
or wholesome (kuśala), or unwholesome (akuśala)? Answer:
It should be said that they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)— namely, arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence— should they be said to be bound to the desire realm,
or bound to the form or formless realms?
Answer: One should say they are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Regarding the phenomena bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*)—namely, arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence—should one say they are bound to the form realm?
Are they bound to the desire realm or the formless realm?
Answer: One should say they are bound to the form realm.
Regarding the factors bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)— namely arising, duration, aging, and impermanence— should they be said to be bound to the formless realm,
or bound to the desire or form realms?
Answer: One should say they are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Regarding the factors of training (*śaikṣadharma*)—their arising, duration, aging, and impermanence—should these be said to be of training?
Is it "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) or "neither training nor beyond training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa)?
Answer: It should be said to be "training" (śaikṣa).

Regarding the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—their arising, duration, aging, and impermanence—should they be said to belong to one beyond training, or to one in training (*śaikṣa*), or to neither-training-nor-beyond-training? Answer: [They are] to be said to belong to one beyond training.

One should say they belong to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). As for phenomena that are neither-of-learning-nor-of-no-more-learning (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)—namely, their arising, duration, aging, and impermanence—should these be said to be neither-of-learning-nor-of-no-more-learning?
Is it training (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Answer: It should be said that it is neither training nor beyond training.
Regarding the phenomena abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*)— namely, arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence— should they be said to be abandoned by seeing,
or abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or not abandoned at all?
Answer: It should be said that they are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).
As for the factors abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)—namely, arising, duration, aging, and impermanence—should these be said to be abandoned by cultivation?
Is it abandoned by seeing or not abandoned?
Answer: It should be said that it is abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the dharmas that are not subject to abandonment (*aprahātavya*)—namely, arising (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), aging (*jarā*), and impermanence (*anityatā*)—should they be said to be non-abandonable?
Or are they abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)? Answer:
One should say it is not severed. What is aging? Answer:
The turning away from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and their manifestation as maturation and transformation— this is called aging. What is death?

Answer: Those various sentient beings, from their respective homogeneous classes of sentient beings, undergo transition, dissolution, and disappearance; they relinquish their lifespan, heat, and life-faculty; they cast off the aggregates and their bodies perish.
This is called death.
What is impermanence? Answer:
The disintegration, destruction, disappearance, and passing away of all conditioned phenomena—
this is called impermanence.
What is the difference between death and impermanence?
Answer: All deaths are impermanent, but there are things that are impermanent which are not death.
That is to say:
Excluding death, all other formations cease.
Is the power of karma stronger,
or is the power of impermanence stronger?
Answer: The power of karma is strong, not the power of impermanence. Some say this:
The power of impermanence is strong, not the power of karma. Why is this?
Because karma, too, is impermanent.
In this context, the power of karma is strong, not the power of impermanence. Why is this so?
Karma can extinguish the formations (*saṃskāra*) of the three periods of time, whereas impermanence (*anityatā*) extinguishes only the formations of the present.
As the Blessed One said:
"There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*): the arising of the conditioned can be discerned, as can its passing away and its alteration while abiding."
"How does it arise within a single kṣaṇa?
Answer: "It arises."
What is exhaustion?
Answer: Impermanence.
What are "abiding" and "alteration"? Answer: Aging.
Mindfulness of the unconditioned and signless; knowing the turning of the Dharma wheel, the exhaustion of outflows,
having few desires, contentment, and full sustenance— may this chapter be fully explained as spoken by the World-Honored One.
"One should know that practicing various other ascetic austerities is devoid of meaning;
one gains neither profit nor peace, just like rowing a boat on dry land.
For what reason did the Blessed One speak thus?
Is there no purpose in practicing other ascetic penances? Answer:
Those practices lead toward death, approach death, and culminate in death; for it is not by such ascetic penances that one can transcend death.
Furthermore,
the World-Honored One said:
"Sit cross-legged, with the body upright and the intention set straight, dwelling in mindfulness directed toward the front."
What is meant by "dwelling in mindfulness directed toward the presence"?
Answer: For the practitioner who cultivates insight:

Fixing the mind between the eyebrows, one may contemplate it as bluish-black, or as bloated, or as festering and putrid, or as disintegrating, or as bloody, or as being devoured, or as severed and scattered, or as white bones, or as a skeleton; these are called "abiding in mindfulness directed toward the object."
Furthermore,
the World-Honored One said:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!..."
“Did the Brahmā Tiṣya not speak of the ‘one who dwells in the sixth signlessness’?
What is meant by “the one who dwells in the sixth signlessness”? Answer:
Those who follow by faith and those who follow by dharma are called the sixth dwelling in signlessness. Why is this?
These two signless states cannot be established, nor can they be designated as being "here" or "there."

Whether it be the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), or the dharma-knowledge of suffering... [as explained in detail] ...up to the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Because this signlessness (*animitta*) cannot be established and cannot be designated as being "here" or "there," it is therefore called the sixth dwelling in signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
“When the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma, the bhikṣus such as Kauṇḍinya saw the Dharma.
The Earth-dwelling Yakṣas raised their voices and proclaimed it everywhere:”
"The World-Honored One is now at the Deer Park of the Sages in Vārāṇasī, turning the Wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects.
Does that earth deity possess right knowledge and vision such that he knows, "The Buddha has turned the Wheel of Dharma, and the bhikṣus have seen the Dharma"?
Answer: There is none.
How does he know this?
Answer: Because of faith in the World-Honored One.
That is to say:
The Buddha gave rise to a conventional thought: "I have turned the wheel of Dharma; the bhikṣus have seen the Dharma. It was by this that they knew it.
Or, it was because the Buddha told others: "I have turned the wheel of Dharma; the bhikṣus have seen the Dharma."

Pūrṇa heard this, either from the great virtuous celestial sages, or because those venerable ones such as Kauṇḍinya and others had given rise to a mundane thought: "The Buddha has turned the wheel of Dharma; we have seen the Dharma."
By this means, he knows;
or he informs others, and the earth deities hear it.
Furthermore!
The Sūtra says:
"There are bhikṣus who have attained arhatship, whose outflows are exhausted.

The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven frequently assemble in the Sudharmā Hall and proclaim: 'In such-and-such a place, there is a certain venerable one, or his disciple, who has shaved off hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, left the home life with right faith, and is diligently cultivating the Noble Path.'"
With all taints exhausted, he has realized the state free from taints, with liberation through mind and wisdom.
In this very life, he has personally attained realization, dwelling in the full possession of that attainment.
Furthermore, they personally realize:
"Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished;
there will be no further existence. Do those devas possess correct knowledge and vision such that they know those bhikṣus have attained arhatship and that their outflows are exhausted?
Answer: There is none.
How does one know this?
Answer: Because of faith in the World-Honored One.
That is to say:
The Buddha gave rise to a conventional thought: "These bhikṣus have attained arhatship; their outflows are exhausted. By this means, they came to know it.
Or the Buddha informed others: "These bhikṣus have attained arhatship; their outflows are exhausted."
Thus he was able to hear it.
Or he heard it from a venerable celestial being or a rishi;
or that venerable one gave rise to a mundane thought: "I have exhausted the outflows and attained arhatship."
By this means, he knows it;
or he informs others, and the devas hear it.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Among the ministers and officials of the kingdom of Magadha, some are disciplined by the transformative Dharma, while others practice in accordance with the Dharma.
What is meant by 'disciplined by the transformative Dharma'?"
What is meant by "practice in accordance with the Dharma"? Answer:
If one perceives the Dharma while among the devas, it is called "subduing through transformational teaching."
If one perceives the Dharma while among human beings, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
Furthermore,
if one perceives the Dharma without having formally undertaken the precepts, it is called "subduing through the transformative Dharma" (dharmavineya).
If one upholds the precepts and perceives the Dharma, this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma.
What is meant by "having many desires"? Answer:
All desires, past desires, and future desires—these are called "much desire.
What is "lack of contentment"? Answer:
Whatever is not joyful, not equally joyful, not universally joyful, not already joyful, and not appropriately joyful—this is called lack of joy and contentment (*anabhirati-anasaṃtuṣṭi*).
What is the difference between having many desires (*bahukāmatā*) and lack of joy and contentment?
Answer:

To have longing for, to seek, to search for, to solicit, to yearn for, and to employ means toward objects not yet obtained—namely, desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, medicine, and other requisites—is what is called "excessive desire."

To repeatedly hope for, repeatedly desire, repeatedly delight in, and repeatedly seek after already obtained agreeable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, medicine, and other requisites—this is called lack of contentment.
Such are the distinctions.
What is "having few desires"? Answer:
That which is not desired, has not been desired, and ought not to be desired—this is called having few desires.
What is contentment? Answer:
All forms of joy—joy that is equal, pervasive, past, and future—are called "contentment.
What is the difference between fewness of desires and contentment?
Answer:

Regarding desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, as well as clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, medicine, and other requisites that have not yet been obtained—refraining from longing for them, seeking them, searching for them, soliciting them, yearning for them, or making efforts toward them is called having few desires.
Regarding those already obtained: pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, medicine, and other requisites.
That which no longer hopes, no longer desires, no longer delights in, and no longer seeks—this is called contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*).
Such are its distinctions. What is meant by being "difficult to satisfy" (*durabhisaṃbhava*)?
Answer:
To eat repeatedly, to chew repeatedly, to eat much, to chew much, to eat greatly, and to chew greatly—little is not able to satisfy this.
This is called being difficult to fill.
What is meant by "difficult to nourish"? Answer:
Those who are gluttonous, those who are excessively gluttonous.
Indulgence, extreme indulgence;
craving, extreme craving;
relishing the act of chewing, relishing the act of tasting and sipping.
To eat by being choosy and to consume by being choosy—such a course cannot provide salvation.
This is called being difficult to support.
What is the difference between being difficult to satisfy and being difficult to support?
Answer: It is precisely as previously stated; this is what is meant by "distinction.
What is meant by "easy to fill"?
Answer:
Those who do not eat repeatedly, do not consume repeatedly, do not eat much, do not consume much, do not eat excessively, and do not consume excessively, being able to sustain themselves with little.
This is called being easy to satisfy.
What is meant by being easy to support? Answer:

They are not gluttonous, nor excessively gluttonous; they do not indulge, nor excessively indulge; they do not crave, nor excessively crave; they do not delight in chewing, nor delight in tasting or sipping; they do not pick and choose what to eat, nor pick and choose what to chew, but simply obtain whatever is available and thereby sustain themselves.
This is called being easy to nourish.
What is the difference between being easy to satisfy and being easy to nourish? Answer:
This is what was previously explained; this is called the distinction.

The specific characteristics of vitarka, vicāra, auddhatya, and so forth, as well as moha, vidyā, māna, vihiṃsā, the predominance of the many [defilements], the faculties, the natures, and the perversions— I pray that these may be fully explained in this chapter.
What is volition (*cetanā*)? Answer:
All volitions, equal volitions, and increased volitions; the nature of volition, the category of volition—mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) and mental action (*manas-karman*).
This is called volition (*cetanā*).
What is deliberation (*vitarka*)? Answer:
Various forms of reflection (*vitarka*), equal reflection, and intensified reflection; weighing, deliberating, and examining—this is called reflection (*vicāra*).
What is the difference between volition (*cetanā*) and reflection?
Answer: Volition (cetanā) is karma;
deliberation (vitarka) is wisdom (prajñā).
This is called the distinction.
What is vitarka? Answer:
The various mental states that seek, discern, manifest, investigate, and construct;
which differentiate and categorize— this is called vitarka (applied thought).
What is investigation (vicāra)? Answer:
It refers to all mental states that investigate, follow along, operate in accordance with, flow together with, and are subordinate to [the mind].
This is called investigation (*vicāra*).
What is the difference between applied thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*)? Answer:
The coarse nature of the mind is called vitarka (applied thought);
the subtle nature of the mind is called vicāra (sustained thought).
This is the distinction between them.
What is restlessness? Answer:
It is the lack of tranquility and cessation in various states of mind; it is agitation, restlessness, and the inherent quality of mental agitation.
This is called restlessness.
What is mental distraction? Answer:
The various states of mental distraction, wandering, and instability— this lack of one-pointedness is called mental agitation (*citta-vikṣepa*).
What is the difference between restlessness (*auddhatya*) and mental agitation?
Answer: The characteristic of non-quiescence is called restlessness;
the characteristic of lack of one-pointedness is called mental distraction.
This is called the distinction.
What is ignorance? Answer:
There is no wisdom in the three realms.
What is meant by "lack of correct knowledge"? Answer:
"Is it not the case that you say 'lack of correct awareness (asaṃprajanya) is wisdom induced by improper reasoning'?
He replied:
So it is. What do you intend?
Are all those who speak falsely with full awareness doing so because they have lost mindfulness and lack clear comprehension?
Answer: It is so. Furthermore!
What is it that you desire?
Is it not the case that there is "lying with full awareness"? Answer:
Not so. You should listen to my words. If one says:
Regarding the statement, "Lack of correct awareness (*asamprajanya*) is wisdom induced by what is unreasonable;
those who speak falsely while possessing correct awareness do so because they have lost mindfulness and lack correct awareness," one should then say:
"There is no instance of speaking falsehood without full awareness.
If one were not to say:
"There is no instance of speaking falsehood without full awareness," [then...]
Then one should not say:
"Lack of clear comprehension (*asamprajanya*) is wisdom induced by improper reasoning;
those who speak falsely despite possessing clear comprehension do so all because they have lost mindfulness and lack clear comprehension."
To assert this is, in both cases, unreasonable.
One should challenge them by asking:
"Are all instances of ignorance associated with lack of correct knowledge (*asamprajanya*)?"
Answer: It is so. What do you intend?

Are all those who speak falsehoods while possessing right knowledge actually proceeding toward ignorance, being entangled by ignorance, and speaking falsely because they have lost mindfulness and lack right knowledge?
Answer: It is so. Furthermore!
What is it that you do not accept?
Is it not the case that there is "lying with full awareness"? Answer:
Not so. You should listen to what I say: if one says:
"If all ignorance is associated with lack of clear comprehension (*asamprajanya*),

and all instances of lying while possessing clear comprehension are directed toward ignorance, enveloped by ignorance, and result in lying due to loss of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension," then one should say:
"There is no instance of speaking falsehood without full awareness.
If one were not to say:
"There is no instance of speaking falsehood without full awareness";
Then one should not say:
"All ignorance is associated with lack of clear comprehension (*asamprajanya*).

All those who speak falsely despite possessing clear comprehension do so because they are oriented toward ignorance, enveloped by ignorance, and due to loss of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension."
To speak in such a manner is likewise unreasonable in both cases.
What is *mada* (pride-intoxication)? Answer:
All forms of *mada*—intoxication, extreme intoxication, delusion, and extreme delusion;
the mind’s arrogance and self-importance: these are called *mada*. What is *māna*?
Answer: All conceits—past, present, and future;
the uplifting of the mind, the self-exalting of the mind—this is called conceit (*māna*).
What is the distinction between *mada* (intoxication) and *māna* (pride)? Answer:
When one does not compare oneself to others but becomes attached to one's own qualities, resulting in a state of mental haughtiness and self-indulgence, it is called *mada*.
If, in comparison with others, one elevates oneself by relying on specific characteristics, this is called pride (*māna*). This is the distinction.
If one gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), thinking, "I see suffering as suffering," or "I see the origin as the origin"—what is the object-condition (*ālambana*) for this?
Answer:
Suppose there is a certain class of person who associates with virtuous friends, hears the true Dharma, and attends to it correctly.

By reason of these conditions, they attain the "patience in conformity with the truths" (satyānulomikī kṣānti)—that which pertains to the limit of the clear observation of suffering (duḥkha-abhisamaya-anta):
Regarding the patience toward suffering and the joy therein, one clearly realizes it as suffering.
Regarding the limit of the clear realization of the origin:
regarding the patience toward the origin and the joy therein, one clearly realizes it as the origin.

Because he maintains this through the mental attention of that patience, or because he does not attend to it further in the interim, views and doubt do not arise; even if they were to arise, he would not perceive them and would think:
"Regarding suffering, I see it as suffering," or "Regarding the origin, I see it as the origin."
From this, there arises conceit—past, present, or future—as well as mental exaltation and self-appropriation; this is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This has suffering (*duḥkha*) as its object, or it has origination (*samudaya*) as its object.
If one gives rise to overweening pride, thinking, "I see cessation as cessation," or "I see the path as the path," what is the object of this [pride]?
Answer:
It is like a certain person who associates with virtuous friends, hears the true Dharma, and attends to it with correct mental attention.

By means of these causes and conditions, one attains the "patience in conformity with the truths" (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*). Regarding "at the conclusion of the clear observation of cessation" (*nirodha-abhisamaya-anta*):

it is the patient acceptance of and delight in cessation, clearly manifesting that this is cessation. Regarding "at the conclusion of the clear observation of the path" (*mārga-abhisamaya-anta*): [it is the patient acceptance of and delight in the path, clearly manifesting that this is the path].
Having patience for and delight in the path, one clearly realizes this path.

Because of maintaining that mental attention through such patience, or because of not attending to it during the intermediate stage, views and doubt do not arise; even if they were to arise, one does not perceive them, and thus forms this thought:
"Regarding cessation, I see it as cessation," or "Regarding the path, I see it as the path."
From this, pride arises, has arisen, or will arise; it is the exalting and relying of the mind, the self-appropriation of the mind, which is termed overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This takes as its object those very minds and mental factors.
If one gives rise to overweening pride, thinking, "My births are exhausted," what is the object of this [thought]?
Answer: It is as when a certain class of persons forms this thought:
“This is the path, this is the practice;
by relying on this path and this practice, I have fully understood suffering, completely abandoned its origin, realized its cessation, and cultivated the path;
my birth has been exhausted.”
From this, there arises conceit—past, present, and future—as well as mental exaltation and self-importance; this is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This, moreover, has "arising" (*jāti*) as its object.
If one gives rise to overweening pride, thinking, "My holy life is established," what is its object?
Answer: It is as when a certain person thinks to themselves:
“This is the path, this is the practice;
by relying upon this path and this practice, I have fully understood suffering, have permanently abandoned its origin, have realized its cessation, and have cultivated the path;
my holy life has been established.”
From this, there arises conceit—past, present, and future;
the mind’s inflation and self-exaltation is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This takes those very minds and mental factors as its object.
If one gives rise to overweening pride, thinking, "What was to be done by me has been accomplished," what is the object of this [pride]?
Answer: It is as when a certain class of person thinks and says:
“This is the path, this is the practice;
relying upon this path and this practice, I have fully understood suffering, have forever abandoned its origin, have realized its cessation, and have cultivated the path;
I have severed the underlying tendencies, destroyed the afflictions, vomited out the fetters, exhausted the taints, and accomplished what was to be done.”
From this, there arises conceit—past, present, or future; the mind’s loftiness and self-importance, which is termed overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This, moreover, takes that very mind and its mental factors as its object.
If one gives rise to overweening pride, thinking, "I shall not undergo further existence," what is the object of this [thought]?
Answer: It is as when a certain class of person thinks and says:
“This is the path, this is the practice;
by relying on this path and this practice, I have fully understood suffering, have forever abandoned its origin, have realized its cessation, and have cultivated the path;
my birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.”
From this, there arises conceit—past, present, and future; the mind’s loftiness and self-importance.
This is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This, moreover, has existence as its object.
What is meant by "conceiving oneself as inferior while giving rise to pride"? Answer:
Suppose there is a certain person who, seeing another who is superior to himself in terms of lineage, clan, wealth and status, skills and arts, fields and houses, and so forth, forms this thought:
"He is slightly superior to me, and I am slightly inferior to him.
Yet he is inferior to others by many hundreds of thousands of times.
From this arises conceit—past, present, and future—a loftiness of mind, and a self-exaltation.
This is called "conceiving pride while considering oneself lowly.
As the Sūtra says:
"If one gives rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill-will, or thoughts of harm—whether harming oneself, harming others, or harming both."
What is self-harm through sensual desire and discursive thought? Answer:

It is when a certain class of persons, due to the arising of the fetter of greed, experiences physical and mental exhaustion, physical and mental burning, physical and mental fever, and physical and mental parching.
Furthermore, by reason of this, one shall experience for a long night results of maturation that are undesirable, unpleasant, disagreeable, and unpleasing.
Thus does one bring harm upon oneself.
What is harmful seeking through desire? Answer:
It is when a certain class of person, due to the arising of the fetter of greed, gazes upon the wife of another.
When that husband sees this, anger and resentment arise in his mind, along with grief and affliction;
thus he harms another.
How does seeking through sensual desire harm both?
Answer: For example, there is a certain class of person who, having given rise to the fetter of greed, defiles and seizes another's wife.
Once the husband has become aware of it, he then beats, binds, or takes the life of that person, or else seizes their wealth and treasures.
Thus, both are harmed.
How does the thought of ill will harm oneself? Answer:

For instance, there is a certain class of persons who, because they give rise to the obsession of hatred, experience physical and mental exhaustion, physical and mental burning, physical and mental fever, and physical and mental parching;
furthermore, by reason of this, they shall undergo for a long night the ripening fruits that are unlovely, unpleasant, disagreeable, and displeasing.
Thus is self-harm.
How does the search for malice harm others? Answer:
Suppose there is a certain class of person who, due to the arising of the obsession of hatred, takes the life of another being.
Such is the harming of another.
How, then, does one harm by means of the concomitance with thoughts of ill will?
Answer: For example, there is a certain class of persons who, because they give rise to the obsession of hatred, take the lives of others;
they are likewise taken by others to have their own lives taken.
Thus, both are harmed.
How does harmful vitarka harm oneself? Answer:

Suppose there is a certain class of person who, due to the arising of the fetter of harmfulness, experiences physical and mental exhaustion, physical and mental burning, physical and mental fever, and physical and mental scorching;
furthermore, by reason of this, they shall experience for a long night various results of maturation that are unlovely, unpleasant, disagreeable, and displeasing.
Thus is self-harm.
How does harmful thought harm others? Answer:
Suppose there is a certain person who, due to the arising of the fetter of malice, beats or binds others;
in this way, they harm others.
What is "harming accompanied by harmful thoughts"?
Answer: For example, there is a certain class of persons who, because they give rise to the fetter of malice, strike and bind others;
they, in turn, are also struck and bound by others.
In this way, both are harmed.
Is it wisdom that is more abundant,
or is it the object that is more abundant?
Answer: The objects are many, but the wisdom is not. Why is this so?
Since wisdom is also an object,
is wisdom more numerous,
or is consciousness more numerous?
Answer: It is consciousness that predominates, not wisdom. Why is this so?
All forms of knowledge (*jñāna*) are associated with consciousness (*vijñāna*), but not all forms of consciousness are associated with knowledge;
this is because consciousness associated with patience (*kṣānti*) is not associated with knowledge.
Are outflowing (*sāsrava*) formations more numerous?
Which is more numerous: uncontaminated formations or contaminated formations? Answer:
Contaminated formations are more numerous, not uncontaminated formations.

Why is this? Because contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) comprise ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of two bases, whereas uncontaminated formations (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*) comprise only a portion of two bases.
What is the perfection of formations?
Answer: For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), there is bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood.
What is the perfection of protection?
Answer: For those beyond training, it is restraint of the faculties.
What is the nature of an ordinary person?
Answer:

If there is non-acquisition, has-been-non-acquisition, or will-be-non-acquisition regarding the noble dharmas, noble warmth, noble vision, noble patience, noble desire, and noble wisdom—this is called the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Regarding this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),
should it be said to be wholesome,
unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Answer: It should be said that it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
For what reason is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not wholesome?
Answer:
Wholesome dharmas are acquired either through application (*prayoga*) or through other conditions.
One does not apply effort seeking to become an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore,
at the time when the roots of goodness are severed, all wholesome dharmas are relinquished, and one acquires the state of non-possession (*aprāpti*) regarding all wholesome dharmas;
if the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were itself wholesome by nature, then those who have severed their roots of goodness would no longer be ordinary persons.
Why is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not unwholesome? Answer:
At the time of becoming free from the defilements of desire, all unwholesome states are abandoned, and one attains the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of unwholesome dharmas.

If the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were unwholesome (*akuśala*), then ordinary persons who have become detached from the defilements of desire would no longer be ordinary persons.
Should this state of being an ordinary person be said to be bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Is it bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu)?
Or is it bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)? Answer:
One should say that it is either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm.
Why is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not exclusively bound to the desire realm?
Answer:
When one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm, all dharmas of the desire realm are abandoned, and one acquires the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of desire-realm dharmas.

If the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were exclusively bound to the desire realm, then ordinary persons who die in the desire realm and are reborn in the formless realm would no longer be ordinary persons.
Why is the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not exclusively bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)? Answer:

When one passes away from the realm of form and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all dharmas of the realm of form are abandoned, and one acquires the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the dharmas of the realm of form.

If the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were exclusively bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), then those ordinary persons who pass away from the form realm and are reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would no longer be ordinary persons.
For what reason is the state of being an ordinary person not exclusively bound to the formless realm?
Answer:

Upon entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*), one first realizes the suffering of the desire realm through direct insight (*abhisamaya*), and subsequently realizes the suffering of the form and formless realms in combination.
When the noble path arises, it first accomplishes the tasks of the desire realm, and subsequently accomplishes the tasks of the form and formless realms in combination.
Therefore, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not exclusively bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Should this state of being an ordinary person be said to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*),
or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Answer: It should be said that it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Why is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*)?
Answer: All dharmas abandoned through seeing are defiled; however, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not defiled.
Furthermore:

When the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is in the process of ceasing and the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is in the process of arising, at that moment one abandons the nature of an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the three realms and attains its state of non-possession;
it is not because of the abandonment of factors to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) at that time.
What dharma is called "the state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*)? Answer:
It is the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) within the three realms that are non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).
If various phenomena are associated with wrong view, are those phenomena also associated with wrong thought?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with wrong view but not with wrong thought; namely,
wrong thought associated with wrong view, as well as other phenomena associated with wrong view that are not associated with wrong thought.
There are phenomena associated with wrong reflection but not with wrong view; namely,
those phenomena associated with wrong view that are themselves associated with wrong reflection, as well as other phenomena associated with wrong reflection that are not associated with wrong view.
There are phenomena that are associated with wrong view and also associated with wrong intention;
that is to say,
with the exception of the wrong intention associated with wrong view and the wrong view associated with wrong intention, all other phenomena associated with both wrong view and wrong intention.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with wrong view nor with wrong intention;
namely, wrong intention that is not associated with wrong view.
Regarding wrong view that is dissociated from wrong thought,
as well as all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra):
if those phenomena are associated with wrong view, are those phenomena also associated with wrong effort?
Answer: This should be treated as a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with wrong view that are not associated with wrong effort.
That is to say:
there is wrong effort associated with wrong view;
there are also phenomena associated with wrong effort that are not associated with wrong view.
That is to say:
wrong view and other factors associated with wrong effort that are not associated with wrong view;
there are also factors associated with wrong view and also associated with wrong effort.
That is to say:
with the exception of wrong diligence associated with wrong view, there are other factors associated with wrong view;
furthermore, there are factors that are neither associated with wrong view nor associated with wrong diligence.
That is to say:

wrong effort dissociated from wrong view, as well as all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra).
As it is with wrong view in relation to wrong effort, so it is with wrong view in relation to wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration.
As it is with wrong view in relation to wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration; [so it is with the others].
The same applies to wrong thought (mithyā-saṃkalpa) in relation to wrong effort (mithyā-vīrya), wrong mindfulness (mithyā-smṛti), and wrong concentration (mithyā-samādhi).
Are those phenomena associated with wrong effort also associated with wrong mindfulness?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena that are associated with wrong effort (mithyāvīrya), but not with wrong mindfulness (mithyāsmṛti).
That is to say:
wrong mindfulness.
There are dharmas associated with wrong mindfulness that are not associated with wrong diligence.
That is to say:
wrong diligence. There are dharmas associated with wrong diligence that are also associated with wrong mindfulness.
That is to say:
factors associated with wrong effort and wrong mindfulness;
and there are factors that are neither associated with wrong effort nor with wrong mindfulness.
That is to say:
all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), matter (rūpa), the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
This is just as when wrong effort (mithyā-vīrya) is contrasted with wrong mindfulness (mithyā-smṛti).
The same applies when wrong effort is paired with wrong concentration.
Just as wrong effort is paired with wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration,
so too is wrong mindfulness paired with wrong concentration.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Two.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

The nature and maturation of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, Their abandonment, views, existence, roots, and bonds— These constitute the conditions for possession and accomplishment; In this chapter, I pray that they shall be fully explained.
There are: three fetters— namely:
The fetter of the view of a self-identity, the fetter of adherence to rules and observances,
and the fetter of doubt. The three unwholesome roots— namely:
The unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
The three outflows— namely:
The outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
The four floods (*ogha*): namely—
The flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views,
and the flood of ignorance. The four yokes— namely:
The yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views,
and the yoke of ignorance. The four graspings— namely:
The grasping at sensual desire, the grasping at views, the grasping at rules and observances,
and the grasping at a doctrine of self. The four bodily fetters— namely:

The bodily fetter of sensual desire, the bodily fetter of ill will, the bodily fetter of attachment to precepts and observances, and the bodily fetter of dogmatic adherence to "this alone is the truth.
The five hindrances— namely:
The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse,
and the hindrance of doubt. The five fetters— namely:
The fetter of greed, the fetter of hatred, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of envy,
and the fetter of stinginess. These are the five lower fetters, namely:

The fetter of sensual desire that leads downward, the fetter of ill will that leads downward, the fetter of the view of a self-identity that leads downward, the fetter of adherence to rules and observances that leads downward, and the fetter of doubt that leads downward.
The five fetters binding one to the higher realms (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are:

the fetter of attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), the fetter of attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), the fetter of restlessness (*auddhatya*), the fetter of pride (*māna*), and the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The five views— namely:

the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extreme adherence (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), the esteeming of views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
The six groups of craving—
namely: the group of craving born of eye-contact, and the groups of craving born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
The seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):

namely, the underlying tendency of sensual desire, the underlying tendency of ill will, the underlying tendency of attachment to existence, the underlying tendency of pride, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the underlying tendency of views, and the underlying tendency of doubt.
The nine fetters— namely:

the fetter of craving, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of views, the fetter of grasping, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.
There are ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): namely,
thirty-six underlying tendencies bound to the desire realm, and thirty-one underlying tendencies each bound to the form and formless realms.
Regarding the three fetters... up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
How many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Answer:
Among the three fetters:
one is indeterminate, and two should be analyzed as follows:
The fetters of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*):
they are either unwholesome (*akuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are unwholesome; in the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*), they are indeterminate.
The three unwholesome roots are exclusively unwholesome.
Among the three outflows (āsrava):
First, the indeterminate; second, that which should be analyzed.
That is to say, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*):
It is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), along with their associated factors, are unwholesome; the remainder are indeterminate.
Regarding the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*):
They are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
Those associated with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anottappa*) are unwholesome; the rest are indeterminate.
Among the four floods (*ogha*):
One is indeterminate; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*):
It is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), along with their associated factors, are unwholesome; the remainder are indeterminate.
The flood of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha*):
They are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
The three views of the desire realm are unwholesome;
the two views of the desire realm and the five views of the form and formless realms are indeterminate.
The flood of ignorance (avidyā-ogha) is either unwholesome (akuśala) or indeterminate (avyākṛta).
That which is associated with shamelessness (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya) is unwholesome; the remainder is indeterminate.
As with the four floods,
so it is with the four yokes.
Regarding the four graspings:
One is indeterminate; three should be analyzed.
That is to say, the grasping for sensual desire:
It is either unwholesome or indeterminate.

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), along with their associated factors, are unwholesome; the remainder are indeterminate. Regarding the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*):
They are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
The two views of the desire realm are unwholesome;
the two views of the desire realm and the four views of the form and formless realms are indeterminate.
The clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is either unwholesome (akuśala) or indeterminate (avyākṛta).
In the desire realm (kāmadhātu), it is unwholesome; in the form and formless realms (rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu), it is indeterminate.
Among the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*):
two are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and two should be analyzed.
That is to say:
The fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-satkāyadṛṣṭi-śarīra-bandhana*):
in the desire realm it is unwholesome; in the form and formless realms it is indeterminate. The five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*):
They are exclusively unwholesome.
Among the five fetters:
three are unwholesome; two should be analyzed.
That is to say:
the fetters of greed and pride are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
The desire realm is unwholesome; the form and formless realms are neutral.
Among the five lower fetters, two are unwholesome.
First, it is indeterminate;
second, it should be analyzed as follows:
The fetters of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*):
they are either unwholesome (*akuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are unwholesome; in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), they are indeterminate.
The five fetters binding one to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*):
exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Among the five views (*pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ*):
Two are indeterminate; three should be analyzed. Namely:
false view, adherence to views, and adherence to rites and rituals.
They are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
Those in the desire realm are unwholesome; those in the form and formless realms are indeterminate.
Among the six groups of craving:
Two are unwholesome; four should be analyzed as follows:
namely, the group of cravings produced by eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact.
It is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
That which belongs to the desire realm is unwholesome; that which belongs to the Brahma-world is indeterminate.
This refers to the aggregate of craving born from mental contact:
They are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
Those belonging to the desire realm are unwholesome; those belonging to the form and formless realms are indeterminate.
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
Two are unwholesome, one is indeterminate, and four should be analyzed as follows:
namely, the underlying tendencies of pride and doubt.
It is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
In the desire realm it is unwholesome; in the form and formless realms it is indeterminate.
Regarding the latent tendency of ignorance:
It is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
That which is associated with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) is unwholesome; the rest is indeterminate.
As for the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*):
They are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
The three views of the desire realm are unwholesome;
the two views of the desire realm and the five views of the form and formless realms are indeterminate.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*):
three are unwholesome (*akuśala*);
six should be analyzed.
That is to say:
the fetters of craving, pride, grasping,
and doubt are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
The desire realm is unwholesome; the form and formless realms are indeterminate.
As for the fetter of ignorance:
it is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
That which is associated with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) is unwholesome (*akuśala*); the rest are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
As for the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), it is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
One view in the desire realm is unwholesome;
two views in the desire realm and three views in the form and formless realms are indeterminate.
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
Thirty-three are unwholesome, sixty-four are indeterminate, and one should be analyzed.
That is to say:
the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
They are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
Those associated with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anottappa*) are unwholesome; the remainder are indeterminate.
Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*)... up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many have maturation (*savipāka*)?
How many are without maturation? Answer:
All unwholesome [dharmas] have maturation; all neutral [dharmas] are without maturation.
Regarding the three fetters... up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
How many are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)? Answer:
Among the three fetters: the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), with views as its precursor, has two possibilities:
it is either abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned by both insight and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

If there is the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is abandoned by the patience regarding suffering at the limit of clear realization for those who follow by faith or follow by dharma, this is abandoned through vision.
As for the others—if they are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are abandoned through the cultivation of what is to be abandoned;
if they are disciples of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*), they are abandoned through the vision of what is to be abandoned.
This is as with the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Among the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), it is the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*);
among the five views (*pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ*), it is likewise the view of a self-identity and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the fetters of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), with views as their precursor, there are two categories:
those abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

If the fetters of adherence to precepts and observances and doubt are bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and are abandoned by the various patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of clear observation (*abhisamaya-anta*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), they are abandoned through vision.
The remainder—namely, for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
for the disciples of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*), those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
This is as with the fetters of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*), there are the flood and yoke of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Among the four graspings (*upādāna*), there are the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭy-upādāna*) and the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*).
Among the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*), there are the fetter of precepts and observances and the fetter of dogmatic adherence to "this alone is the truth" (*parāmarśa-kāyagrantha*).

Among the five fetters binding one to the lower realms (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), there are the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Among the five views (*pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ*), there are false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the view of holding [inferior] views as supreme (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Among the seven latent tendencies (*sapta anuśayāḥ*), there are the latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*) and doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*).
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of views-attachment (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*) are likewise so.
The unwholesome root of greed (*lobha-akuśalamūla*) has cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as its precursor.
There are two categories:
either abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or abandoned by both vision and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).
