If it is the unwholesome root of greed, which is abandoned by the various knowledges of those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have seen the tracks [of the path], this is abandoned by cultivation.
As for the others—if they are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), they abandon those to be abandoned by cultivation;
if they are disciples of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*), they abandon those to be abandoned by seeing.
This is as with the unwholesome root of greed (*lobha-akuśalamūla*).
The unwholesome roots of hatred and delusion;
among the three outflows (āsrava), the outflow of sensual desire (kāma-āsrava);
among the four floods (ogha) and yokes (yoga), the flood and yoke of sensual desire (kāma-ogha and kāma-yoga).
Among the four graspings, it is the grasping for sensual desire;
among the four bodily fetters, it is the fetters of sensual lust and ill will;
among the five hindrances, it consists of the remaining hindrances with the exception of restlessness-remorse and doubt.
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is the fetter of aversion;
among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), it is the fetters of sensual desire and aversion;
and among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is the underlying tendencies of sensual greed and aversion.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) is also like this.
The outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) have views as their precursor.
There are three categories:
those abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and those abandoned by both insight and cultivation.

If there are outflows with outflows (*sāsrava*) or the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which are abandoned by the various patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of clear observation (*abhisamaya-paryanta*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), these are abandoned by insight.

If there are the outflows of the fluxes (*āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), which are abandoned by the various knowledges of those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have seen the tracks [of the path], these are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As for the remainder—if they belong to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), they are abandoned through cultivation;
if they are disciples of the World-Honored One (*bhagavat-śrāvaka*), they are abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*).
Just as with the outflow of the taints (*āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*):
among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*), there are the flood and yoke of existence (*bhava*) and the flood and yoke of ignorance;
and among the four graspings (*upādāna*), there is the grasping for self-theory (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*).
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are the fetters of greed (*rāga*) and conceit (*māna*);
among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*), there is the group of craving born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇākāya*);
and among the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are the latent tendencies of greed for existence (*bhavarāga*), conceit, and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetters of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), conceit (*māna*),
and ignorance (*avidyā*) are likewise [to be abandoned by cultivation]. The hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*) is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As with the hindrance of remorse (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*):
among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are the fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*);
and among the five higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Among the six groups of craving (ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya), it is the first five;
among the nine fetters (nava-saṃyojana), it is the fetters of envy (īrṣyā) and avarice (mātsarya)— it is likewise so.
Regarding the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*): if it belongs to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
if it belongs to a disciple of the World-Honored One (*śrāvaka*), it is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):
twenty-eight are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), and ten are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
As for the remainder—if they belong to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)—they are abandoned through cultivation.
"World-Honored One, regarding the disciples who have severed what is abandoned by vision:
among the three fetters... up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are abandoned by the vision of suffering?
...up to how many are abandoned by cultivation?"
Answer: Among the three fetters,
the fetter of the view of a self-identity is abandoned through the vision of suffering.

For example, regarding the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*): among the five lower-tier fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), there is the fetter of the view of a self-identity;
among the five views (*pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ*), there are the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
It is likewise. The fetter of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*) is of two kinds:
either abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), or abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
For example, regarding the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*): among the four graspings (*upādāna*), it is the grasping for precepts and observances;
among the four bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*), it is the bodily tie of attachment to precepts and observances.
Among the five fetters of the lower realm (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), it is the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);
among the five views (*pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ*), it is likewise the view of attachment to precepts and observances. It is the same in both cases.
The fetter of doubt is of four kinds:
it may be abandoned through the vision of suffering, and so on, up to being abandoned through the vision of the path.
As with the fetter of doubt:
Among the four floods and yokes, it is the flood and yoke of views;
among the four clingings, it is the clinging to views;
among the four bodily fetters, it is the bodily fetter of dogmatic adherence to "this is the truth."
Among the five hindrances, it is the hindrance of doubt;
among the five fetters of the lower realm, it is the fetter of doubt;
among the five views, it is wrong view and the attachment to views.
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the underlying tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*);
and among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetters of view-attachment (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—
are likewise [to be understood].
The three unwholesome roots are of five kinds:
they are either abandoned through the vision of suffering,
and so on, up to being abandoned through cultivation.
As with the three unwholesome roots, so it is with the three taints (*āsrava*);
and among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*), they consist of the remaining floods and yokes, excluding views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Among the four graspings (*upādāna*), there are the grasping for sensual pleasures (*kāma-upādāna*) and the grasping for self-identity (*ātmavāda-upādāna*).
Among the four bodily fetters (*kāya-saṃyojana*), there are the bodily fetter of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the bodily fetter of ill will (*vyāpāda*).
Among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), there are the remaining hindrances, excluding restlessness-and-remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are the fetters of greed, hatred, and pride.
Among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), there are the fetters of sensual desire and ill will.
Among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*), there is the group of craving born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇākāya*).
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), with the exception of views and doubt, the remaining underlying tendencies are likewise [to be understood].
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetters of craving, aversion, pride, and ignorance are also thus.
The hindrance of regret (kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa) is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya). As with the hindrance of regret:
among the five fetters (saṃyojana), there are the fetters of envy (īrṣyā) and avarice (mātsarya).
The five fetters binding one to the higher realms;
among the six classes of craving for the body, the first five;
and among the nine fetters, the fetters of envy and avarice—these are likewise so.
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):

twenty-eight are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), nineteen through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), nineteen through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), twenty-two through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), and ten are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Regarding the three fetters... up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
how many are views (*dṛṣṭi*), and how many are not views?
Answer: Among the three fetters,
two are views.
One is not a view.
The three unwholesome roots are not views.
Among the three outflows (āsrava):
one is not [associated with] views;
the second should be analyzed.
That is to say:
the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava) is either based on views (dṛṣṭi) or not based on views.
In the desire realm:
the five views are "view";
the remainder are not "view."
With outflows:
either views or non-views.
The realms of form and formlessness:
The five views are views;
the others are not views.
Within the four floods and yokes:
One is a view;
three are not views.
Among the four graspings and the four bodily fetters:
The two views and the two non-views;
the five hindrances and the five fetters:
both are non-views.
Among the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni):
two are views (dṛṣṭi);
three are non-views (adṛṣṭi).
The five higher fetters (pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni):
not views. The five views (pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ):
These are views.
The six bases of craving are not views.
Among the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):
one is a view (*dṛṣṭi*), and six are not views.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*):
Two are views; seventy are not views.
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), thirty-six are views and sixty-two are not views.
Regarding the three fetters... up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
how many are with vitarka and vicāra?
How many are without vitarka and with vicāra only?
How many are without vitarka and without vicāra? Answer:
Three fetters; they are of three kinds.

The three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) are accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*). This also applies to the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*),
with the exception of the flood (*ogha*), yoke (*yoga*), and clinging (*upādāna*) of desire.
The remaining floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and graspings (*upādāna*) are of three kinds:
the flood of desire, the yoke of desire, and the grasping of desire;
these are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
The remaining three graspings and the three fetters are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
The remaining two fetters are [of the same nature].
The three types of five hindrances,
the three fetters,
and [the states] with vitarka and vicāra.
The remaining two fetters and three lower-fettering bonds are of three types;
the other two lower-fettering bonds are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Among the five fetters binding one to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is without vitarka and vicāra;
the remaining four and the five views (*pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ*) belong to all three types.
The first five bases of attachment,
as well as the latent tendencies of sensual desire and aversion,
are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
The sixth is the attachment to the body (*kāmarāga*),
along with the other five latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), which are of three types.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are the fetters of aversion (*pratigha*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*).
They are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
The remaining six [factors] are of three types.
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya), thirty-six belong to the desire realm.
There are those with vitarka and vicāra;
thirty-one types in the form realm;
and thirty-one in the formless realm.
Without vitarka and without vicāra.
Regarding the three fetters... up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya):
how many are associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya)?
With how many roots of suffering (*duḥkha*), joy (*sukha*), grief (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are they associated?
Answer: Among the three fetters (*saṃyojana*):

The fetters of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are associated with three faculties, excluding the faculties of suffering (*duḥkha*) and grief (*daurmanasya*).
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*) is associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering.
Among the three unwholesome roots,
the unwholesome root of greed is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculties of pain and sorrow.
The unwholesome root of hatred is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculties of pleasure and joy.
The unwholesome root of delusion, as well as the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), are associated with five faculties.
The outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*).
Among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*):
the flood and yoke of desire (*kāma*), and the flood and yoke of ignorance (*avidyā*).
They are associated with the five faculties (*indriya*).
The flood and yoke of existence (bhava-ogha and bhava-yoga) are associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkha-indriya) and the faculty of grief (daurmanasya-indriya).
The flood and yoke of views (dṛṣṭi-ogha and dṛṣṭi-yoga) are associated with four faculties.
Excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Among the four graspings (*upādāna*):
the grasping for sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*) is associated with five faculties.
The grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
The grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the grasping at a self-theory (*ātmavādopādāna*) are associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculties of suffering and mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The bodily tie of ill-will is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculties of pleasure and joy.
The remaining three bodily ties and the hindrance of sensual desire are associated with three faculties.
Excluding the faculties of suffering and grief,
the hindrance of ill-will is associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculties of pleasure and joy.
The hindrances of sloth-torpor and restlessness are associated with five faculties.
The hindrance of sleepiness is associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculties of pleasure and pain.
The hindrances of regret and doubt are associated with two faculties:
namely, the faculty of mental distress (daurmanasya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣā).
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*):
the fetter of greed (*rāga*) and the fetter of conceit (*māna*) are associated with three faculties (*indriya*),
excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*).
The fetter of aversion is associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculties of pleasure and joy.
The fetter of envy is associated with two faculties.
That is to say:
the faculty of sorrow and the faculty of equanimity.
The fetter of stinginess is associated with these two faculties.
That is to say:
the faculty of joy and the faculty of equanimity.
Among the five lower fetters:
The fetter of ill will is associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy.
The fetter of doubt is associated with four faculties.
Excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*),
the remaining three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are associated with three faculties.
Excluding the faculties of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Among the five fetters binding one to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*):
the fetter of craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is associated with one faculty. Namely:
The faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), the remaining four fetters (saṃyojana), and the four views (dṛṣṭi) are associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) and the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasyendriya).
Wrong view is associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*):
The first five bases of craving are associated with two faculties,
namely: the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of equanimity.

The sixth, the latent tendency of attachment to the body (*kāyānuśaya*), as well as the latent tendencies of desire for existence (*bhavarāga*) and pride (*māna*), are associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculties of suffering (*duḥkha*) and mental grief (*daurmanasya*).
The latent tendency of hostility (*pratighānuśaya*) is associated with three faculties.
Excluding the faculties of pleasure and joy,
the latent tendencies of views and doubt are associated with four faculties;
excluding the faculty of pain.
The latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) is associated with five faculties.
Among the nine fetters (saṃyojana):
the fetters of craving (tṛṣṇā), pride (māna), and grasping (parigraha) are associated with three faculties.
Excluding the faculties of suffering and grief,
the fetter of ill-will is associated with three faculties;
excluding the faculties of pleasure and joy.
The fetter of ignorance is associated with five faculties.
The fetters of views and doubt are associated with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering.
The fetter of envy is associated with two faculties,
namely: the faculty of mental distress and the faculty of equanimity.
The fetter of stinginess is associated with two faculties,
namely: the faculty of joy and the faculty of equanimity.
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
the four views, pride, and the greed abandoned through the vision [of the truths] in the desire realm are associated with two faculties.
That is to say:
the faculties of joy and equanimity,
as well as hatred abandoned through the path of seeing and doubt.
It is associated with two faculties,
namely: the faculty of mental distress (daurmanasya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣā).
False views and the ignorance abandoned through seeing are associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculties of pleasure and pain.
Greed abandoned through cultivation is associated with three faculties.
Excluding the faculties of suffering and grief,
hatred is associated with three faculties;
excluding the faculties of pleasure and joy.
Ignorance (avidyā) is associated with the five faculties.
The thirty-one latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) and the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya).
The thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
[This applies to] the three fetters (*saṃyojana*)... up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies.
How many are bound to the desire realm?
How many are bound to the form realm?
How many are bound to the formless realm?
Answer: The three fetters are of three kinds.
The three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire are bound to the desire realm.
The outflows (āsrava) are of two kinds: either bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) or bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
The outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) is of three kinds.
[Likewise are] the flood of desire (kāma-ogha) and the yoke of desire (kāma-yoga).
And the desire-to-grasp [outflow],
which is bound to the desire realm;
these are the outflow of existence and the yoke of existence.
And the grasping at a theory of self (ātmavādopādāna).
These two types are either bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
Or they are bound to the formless realm;
the remaining floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*),
as well as the other two graspings (*upādāna*), are of three kinds.
Among the four bodily fetters:
sensual desire, ill will, and the five hindrances are bound to the realm of desire;
the remaining two bodily fetters are of three kinds.
Among the five fetters:
greed and conceit,
as well as three of the three lower fetters, are of three types.
The remaining three fetters,
as well as the latent tendencies of sensual desire and ill will that lead to the lower realms,
are bound to the desire realm.
Among the five fetters bound to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*):

attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*) is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*); attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
The remaining three fetters are of two kinds:
either bound to the realm of form or bound to the formless realm.
The five views and the sixth, the attachment to the body (*kāyagṛddhi*), are of three types.
The attachments to the body produced by eye-, ear-, and body-contact are of two types,
or are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Or the group of cravings born from nose-contact and tongue-contact that are bound to the form realm;
[and those] bound to the desire realm.
Among the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):
sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) are bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Greed is of two kinds:
either bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) or bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
The remaining latent dispositions (anuśaya) are of three types.
Among the nine fetters (saṃyojana):
the fetters of ill-will (pratigha), envy (īrṣyā), and avarice (mātsarya).
Those bound to the desire realm;
the remaining fetters are of three types.
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
Thirty-six are bound to the desire realm;
thirty-one are bound to the form realm;
thirty-one are bound to the formless realm.
If various fetters (*saṃyojana*) fall within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), do those fetters exist within the desire realm?
Answer: One should formulate this as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are fetters that fall within the desire realm, yet those fetters do not reside in the desire realm.
That is to say:
when one who is bound by the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) passes away from the form realm and arises as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm.
Furthermore, when Māra dwells in the Brahma-world,
because he is entangled by fetters, he reviles and rejects the Tathāgata.
There are fetters existing in the desire realm, yet those fetters do not themselves fall within the desire realm.
That is to say:
one who dies in the desire realm while bound by the *paryavasthānas* (obsessions) arises as an intermediate being (*antarābhava*) in the form realm;
or, while dwelling in the desire realm, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the form and formless realms manifest before them.
There are fetters that fall within the desire realm, and those fetters also exist within the desire realm;
namely, the envelopments and that which is enveloped by them when one passes away from the desire realm.
One gives rise to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the birth existence (*upapattibhava*) of the desire realm,
as well as abiding in the desire realm;
the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm manifest before one.
There are fetters that do not fall within the desire realm, and those fetters likewise do not exist within the desire realm;
namely, when one who is bound by the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) passes away from the form realm.
The arising of the intermediate existence and the existence at birth in the realm of form;
passing away from the realm of form to be born in the formless realm;
and passing away from the formless realm to be born in the formless realm.
When one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm, or while abiding in the form realm, the fetters of the form and formless realms manifest before one.
When abiding in the formless realm, the fetters of the formless realm manifest before one.
If various fetters (saṃyojana) fall within the form realm (rūpadhātu), do those fetters exist within the form realm?
Answer: One should formulate this in four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are fetters that fall into the form realm, yet those fetters do not reside in the form realm;
namely, when one who is bound by the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) passes away from the desire realm.

One arises in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and while abiding in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the form realm manifest before one.
There are fetters belonging to the form realm, yet those fetters do not fall within the form realm.
That is to say:
one who dies in the form realm while being bound by the active outbursts (paryavasthāna) arises as an intermediate state being (antarābhava) in the desire realm.
Furthermore, when Māra dwells in the Brahma-world, because he is bound by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
he reviles and rejects the Tathāgata;
as well as when he dwells in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the fetters manifest before him.
There are fetters that fall into the form realm, and those fetters also exist within the form realm;
namely, one who is bound by the envelopments (paryavasthāna) passes away from the form realm.
One gives rise to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the form realm, and while abiding in the form realm,
the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the form realm manifest before one.
There are fetters that neither fall into the form realm nor exist within the form realm;
namely, those by which one who is bound by the envelopments (paryavasthāna) passes away from the desire realm.
One arises in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) or the birth existence (*upapattibhava*) of the desire realm;
one passes away from the desire realm and is born in the formless realm;
or one passes away from the formless realm and is born in the formless realm.
One who passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm,
as well as one who dwells in the desire realm,
has the fetters of the desire and formless realms manifest before them.
When one dwells in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the formless realm manifest.
Are all those fetters that belong to the formless realm necessarily present in the formless realm? Answer:
Those fetters that exist in the formless realm, those fetters fall within the formless realm.
There are fetters that fall within the formless realm, yet those fetters do not exist in the formless realm.
That is to say:
One dwells in the desire realm or the form realm, and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the formless realm manifest before them.
Are those fetters not included within the desire realm? Is it not the case that those fetters do not exist in the desire realm? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). It should be understood that these are the reverse of the above.
Regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*) that do not fall within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): are those fetters not present in the form realm?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
It should be understood that these are the reverse of those mentioned above.
If various fetters do not fall within the formless realm, do those fetters not exist in the formless realm? Answer: It is so.
There are fetters that do not exist in the formless realm, yet those fetters are not such that they do not fall within the formless realm;
namely, those belonging to one who dwells in the desire or form realms.
When the fetters of the formless realm are present before one,
and that disciple of the World-Honored One who is fully possessed of vision has not yet abandoned the various forms, is he bound by those forms?
Answer: It is so.
If something is bound by form, is that form not yet abandoned?
Answer: It is so.
If feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness have not been abandoned, are those feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness bound?
Answer: It is so.
There are fetters of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; those feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness have not been abandoned.
That is to say:
one who goes from family to family (kulānkula), or one who returns once more (sakṛdāgāmin).

Or, in the case of an ekavīcika (one-interval practitioner), regarding the desire realm, the upper and middle grades of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation have already been abandoned and fully known; however,
they remain bound by the lower grade of fetters associated with those [abandoned] aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
If a disciple of the World-Honored One who possesses right view has already severed all forms, is he dissociated from those forms? Answer: It is so.
If one is liberated from a given form, has that form already been abandoned? Answer: It is so.
If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have been severed,
are that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness dissociated? Answer:
There is dissociation from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness have already been abandoned.
Yet there is feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that have been abandoned but are not dissociated.
That is to say:
one who goes from family to family (kulānkula), or a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).

Or, in the case of an ekavīcika (one-interval practitioner), regarding the upper and middle grades of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, these have already been abandoned and fully known; however,
they remain bound by the lower grade of fetters associated with those [abandoned] aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
There are five types of persons (*pudgala*), namely:

those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those liberated through resolute confidence (*śraddhādhimukta*), those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
Regarding these five types of persons, how many of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*)—up to and including the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—do they possess?
How many are not accomplished?
Answer: For one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin):
Regarding the three fetters:
as long as the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen,
one possesses them all.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has arisen:
two are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots (akuśala-mūla):
Those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire:
all are accomplished.
Those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire:
None are accomplished.
Regarding the three outflows (āsrava):
those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
All are accomplished.
For one who has already abandoned the defilement of desire:
two are accomplished, and one is not accomplished.
Regarding the four floods, yokes, and graspings:
those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire possess them all.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire:
three are accomplished, one is not accomplished.
Regarding the four bodily fetters:
Those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire:
all are accomplished.
Those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire:
Two are accomplished and two are not accomplished.
Regarding the five hindrances:
for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire—
If the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all [factors] are accomplished;
if the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path has already arisen, four are accomplished and one is not.
For one who is already free from the defilement of desire:
None are accomplished.
Regarding the five fetters:
for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of sensual desire;
All are accomplished.
Having already abandoned the defilement of desire:
two are accomplished, three are not accomplished.
Regarding the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*):
for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*) and for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all [five] are fully possessed.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, four are accomplished and one is not.
When one is already free from the defilement of desire (*vītarāga*), but the subsequent knowledge of suffering has not yet arisen, three are accomplished and two are not.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*) has arisen, two are accomplished and three are not accomplished.
Regarding the five fetters of the higher realm (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīyasaṃyojanāni*): one who is not yet free from passion for the form realm (*rūparāga*)—
All are accomplished.
Having already become free from the defilement of form:
four are accomplished, and one is not accomplished.
Regarding the five views:
as long as the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, one possesses all of them.
Once the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen, one possesses three and does not possess two.
Regarding the six groups of craving:
those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire possess them all.
Having already abandoned the defilements of desire, but not yet having abandoned the defilements of the Brahma-world:
four are accomplished, two are not accomplished.
Having already abandoned the defilements of the Brahma-world:
One is accomplished and five are not accomplished.
Regarding the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire—
All are accomplished.
Having already become free from the defilement of desire:
five are accomplished, two are not accomplished.
Regarding the nine fetters:
those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire possess all of them.
One who has already become free from the defilement of desire:
six are accomplished, three are not accomplished.
Regarding the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya):
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire and for whom the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) has not yet arisen,
all [these factors] are fully accomplished.
When the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen:
one does not possess any of the [defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm;
all others are possessed.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) has not yet arisen:
one does not possess any of the [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering in the three realms;
all others are possessed.
When the dharma-knowledge of origination has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of origination (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen:
one does not possess [the afflictions] abandoned through the vision of suffering in the three realms, nor those abandoned through the vision of origination in the desire realm.
All others are accomplished.
When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) has not yet arisen:
those [defilements] of the three realms to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin are all not accomplished.
All others are accomplished.
When the dharma-knowledge of cessation has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen:
those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the three realms, as well as those abandoned through the vision of cessation in the desire realm, are all not accomplished.
All others are accomplished.
When the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) has already arisen, but the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen:
those [defilements] of the three realms to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation are all not accomplished.
All others are accomplished.
Once the dharma-knowledge of the path has arisen,

those [defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation in the three realms, as well as those to be abandoned through the vision of the path in the desire realm, are no longer accomplished.
All others are accomplished.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire but not yet free from the defilement of form,
and for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen:
Nothing of the desire realm is accomplished;
all others are accomplished.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of origination has not yet arisen:
One does not possess all [defilements] of the desire realm, nor those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form and formless realms;
one possesses all others.
When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen:
All [factors] of the desire realm, as well as those of the form and formless realms to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin, are not accomplished.
All others are accomplished. Once the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) has arisen:
All [factors] of the desire realm, as well as those of the form and formless realms to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation, are not accomplished.
All others are accomplished. Having already become free from the defilement of the form realm:
If the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen:
all [factors] of the desire and form realms are not accomplished;
all others are accomplished.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen:

one does not possess [the defilements] of all those belonging to the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm.
The others are all accomplished.
When the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen:
[the afflictions] of the desire realm and the form realm are all [present].
Furthermore, those [factors] of the formless realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of its origin are not accomplished;
all others are accomplished.
Once the subsequent knowledge of cessation has arisen:
All [factors] of the desire and form realms, as well as those of the formless realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation, are not accomplished.
All others are accomplished. This is the same as for one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin).
The same applies to those who follow by Dharma (dharmanusārin).
As for those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta), [they are so called] with respect to the three fetters (saṃyojana).
None are accomplished.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots,
one has not yet abandoned desire-taint.
All are accomplished.
Those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire: none are accomplished.
Regarding the three outflows (āsrava):
those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire possess them all.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire accomplishes two and does not accomplish one.
Regarding the four floods and yokes, for one who is not yet free from the defilement of desire:
Three are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
Having already become free from the defilement of desire:
two are accomplished and two are not accomplished.
Regarding the four types of clinging (*upādāna*),
one who has not yet abandoned desire and passion accomplishes two and does not accomplish two.
One who has already become free from the defilement of desire:
achieves one [of these fetters] and does not achieve three.
Regarding the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*).
One who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire:
two are accomplished, two are not accomplished.
One who has already abandoned the defilement of desire:
None of these are accomplished.
Regarding the five hindrances,
one has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
Regarding the four attainments and one non-attainment:
for those who have already become free from the defilement of desire, none of these are attained.
Regarding the five fetters,
those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire possess them all.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire accomplishes two [fetters] and does not accomplish three among the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni).
One who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire accomplishes two and does not accomplish three.
One who has already abandoned the defilement of desire:
None are accomplished.
Regarding the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), one has not yet abandoned passion for the realm of form (*rūparāga*):
All are accomplished. Having already become free from the defilement of form (*rūparāga*):
four are accomplished, one is not accomplished.
Regarding these five views,
none are established; regarding the six bases of craving, [the same applies].
Those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of sensual desire: all possess [them].
Those who have already abandoned the defilement of sensual desire, but have not yet abandoned the defilement of the Brahma-world:
Four are accomplished and two are not accomplished.
Having already become free from the defilements of the Brahma-world:
one is accomplished and five are not accomplished.
Regarding the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*) accomplish five and do not accomplish two.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire accomplishes three [fetters] and does not accomplish four among the nine fetters.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire:
six are accomplished, three are not accomplished.
One who has already abandoned the defilement of desire:
Three are accomplished and six are not accomplished regarding the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire:
Ten are accomplished; eighty-eight are not accomplished.
Having already abandoned the defilement of desire but not yet abandoned the defilement of form:
six are accomplished; ninety-two are not accomplished.
One who has already become free from the defilement of form:
three are accomplished, ninety-five are not accomplished;
as in the case of one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta).
The same applies to the "attained-by-insight" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
As for the "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin), regarding the three fetters and the three unwholesome roots:
None are accomplished.
Regarding the three outflows (āsrava):
two are accomplished, and one is not accomplished.
Regarding the four floods and yokes:
two are accomplished and two are not accomplished.
Regarding the four graspings:
One is accomplished, and three are not accomplished.
Regarding the four bodily fetters and the five hindrances:
none are accomplished.
Regarding the five fetters:
two are accomplished and three are not accomplished.
Regarding the five lower fetters:
None are accomplished. Regarding the five fetters of the higher realm (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*):
four are accomplished, and one is not accomplished.
Regarding the five views:
none are established.
Regarding the six groups of craving:
One is accomplished; five are not accomplished.
Regarding the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
three are accomplished; four are not accomplished.
Regarding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*):
three are accomplished and six are not accomplished.
Regarding the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
Three are established; ninety-five are not established.
With how many conditions is the view of a self-base related to the view of a self-base?
With how many conditions is the view of a self-base related to the clinging to precepts and observances... up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm?

...up to: with how many conditions does the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm act as a condition for the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm?

With how many conditions is the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm related to the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity... up to the latent tendency of pride to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm?
Answer:
The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and [another] view of a self-identity serve as four, three, two, or one object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
What are the four?
If a view of a self-identity arises immediately after another view of a self-identity, then one contemplates that preceding birth and subsequent birth as four conditions.
What are the three?
If a view of a self-identity arises immediately after another view of a self-identity, and one does not contemplate that preceding birth and subsequent birth, they serve as three conditions.
Excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

there may be a case where, immediately after a view of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) has ceased, another mind arises, and subsequently, the view of self-existence arises again; in this case, that preceding [view] and the succeeding [view] serve as three conditions for one another.
Excluding the equal-and-immediate [condition], what are the two?

For example, when a view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises immediately after another mind, and subsequently a further view of self arises, one does not reflect upon that preceding birth and the subsequent birth; these two serve as conditions.
That is to say:
the cause-condition and the predominant-condition. What is the one?
Regarding the view of a self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in a subsequent life and the view of a self-existence in a previous life:
if it acts as an object-condition (*ālambana*), it is both an object-condition and a dominant condition (*adhipati*);
if it does not act as an object-condition, it is solely a dominant condition.
Future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* in relation to past and present *satkāyadṛṣṭi*:
if it acts as an object-condition (*ālambana*), it is both an object-condition and a predominant condition (*adhipati*);
if it does not act as an object-condition, it is solely a predominant condition.
Future and present *satkāyadṛṣṭi* in relation to past *satkāyadṛṣṭi*:
if it acts as an object-condition (*ālambana*), it is both an object-condition and a dominant condition (*adhipati*);
if it does not act as an object-condition, it is solely a dominant condition.
The view of a self-identity in the desire realm and the view of a self-identity in the form and formless realms have one another as their dominant condition (*adhipati*). Likewise,
the view of a self-identity in the form and formless realms and the view of a self-identity in the desire realm [have one another as their dominant condition].
If it acts as an equal-and-immediate condition, it is both an equal-and-immediate condition and a dominant condition;
if it does not act as an equal-and-immediate condition, it is solely a dominant condition.
The view of a self-existence belonging to the form realm [acts] with respect to the view of a self-existence belonging to the formless realm:
It serves as a single predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and the view of self-existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*):
if it acts as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it serves as both an immediately preceding condition and a predominant condition.
They do not act as equal-and-immediate conditions; they have one [condition], the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

It should be understood that the same applies to the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) with respect to other views of a self-identity, the view of a self-identity with respect to all other non-universal [factors], all other non-universal [factors] with respect to all non-universal [factors], and universal [factors] with respect to all non-universal [factors].
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) have four, three, two, or one object (*ālambana*).
What are the four?

If, immediately following the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arises, and one contemplates that former birth and subsequent birth, it serves as four conditions.
What are the three?

If, immediately following the view of a self-identity, the grasping at precepts and observances arises, but one does not contemplate that former birth and subsequent birth, it serves as three conditions.
Excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

there may be a case where, immediately after the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), another mind arises, followed by the arising of the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). In this case, one contemplates that preceding [mind] and succeeding [mind], which serve as three conditions.
Excluding the equal-and-immediate [condition], what are the two?

For example, when a view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is immediately followed by another state of mind, and subsequently a grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) arises; one does not reflect upon that preceding birth and the subsequent birth as being the two conditions.
That is to say:
the cause-condition and the dominant-condition. What is the one?
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arising later and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arising earlier:
if they function as an object of focus (*ālambana*), they constitute an object-dominance (*ālambanādhipati*);
if they do not function as an object of focus, there is one [type of] dominance.
Regarding future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and past and present *śīlavrataparāmarśa*:

if they act as an object of cognition (*ālambana*), they are both the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*); if they do not act as an object of cognition, they are only the predominant condition.
Regarding future and present views of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and past clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*):
if they act as an object-condition (*ālambana*), they are both object-condition and predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*);
if they do not act as an object-condition, they are one [predominant] condition.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the form and formless realms share one dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Likewise,
the view of a self-identity in the form and formless realms and the clinging to precepts and observances in the desire realm [share one dominant condition].

If it acts as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but not as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it serves as the object-condition and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If it acts as an immediately preceding condition but not as an object-condition, it serves as the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition.

If it acts as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it serves as the equal-and-immediate, the object, and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If it does not act as an equal-and-immediate condition and an object-condition, it is a single dominant condition.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form realm and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the formless realm have one another as their dominant condition (*adhipati*).
The view of a self-identity in the formless realm and the clinging to precepts and observances in the form realm [likewise have one another as their dominant condition].
If it acts as an object-condition but not as an immediately antecedent condition, it serves as the object-condition and the predominant condition.
If it acts as an immediately antecedent condition but not as an object-condition, it serves as the immediately antecedent condition and the predominant condition.

If it acts as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it serves as the immediately preceding, the object, and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If it does not act as an immediately preceding condition and an object-condition, it is solely the dominant condition.
As it is with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), so should one understand:

the view of a self-identity with all other universal factors (*sarvatraga*); universal factors with universal factors; and all other non-universal factors with universal factors. It is likewise in these cases.

Nine fetters (saṃyojana) are explained in this chapter: namely, the fetter of attachment to sensual pleasure (kāmarāga), the fetter of ill will (pratigha), the fetter of attachment to existence (bhavarāga), the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi), the fetter of grasping at precepts and vows (śīlavrataparāmarśa), the fetter of doubt (vicikitsā), the fetter of envy (īrṣyā), the fetter of avarice (mātsarya), and the fetter of ignorance (avidyā). These nine fetters are categorized according to their association with the realms, their nature as minor or major, their inclusion within the seven latent tendencies (anuśaya), their dependence on a basis, their connection, their path of abandonment, and their thorough knowledge (parijñā). This chapter shall explain them in full.
Regarding the fetter of attachment... up to the fetter of stinginess:
if there is the binding of the fetter of attachment toward this object, is there also the binding of the fetter of aversion?
Answer: If there is a bond of ill-will (pratigha-saṃyojana) regarding this object, there is necessarily a bond of craving (anunaya-saṃyojana).
However, there may be a bond of craving without a bond of ill-will.
That is to say:
regarding phenomena of the form and formless realms, there is a fetter of craving that has not been abandoned.
If one is bound by the fetter of craving toward these phenomena, is one also bound by the fetter of conceit?
Answer: It is so.
If one is bound by the fetter of pride, is one also bound by the fetter of craving?
Answer: It is so.
If there is a bond of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) regarding this object, is there also a bond of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: If there is bondage by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) regarding this object, there is necessarily bondage by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*).
However, there may be bondage by the fetter of ignorance without there being bondage by the fetter of craving.
That is to say:

when the knowledge of suffering has already arisen, but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen, there remains the fetter of ignorance to be abandoned by the vision of the origin regarding those phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
If one is bound by the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) regarding this object, is one also bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of craving but not bound by the fetter of views;
that is, when the knowledge of origination has arisen, but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen.

Regarding those phenomena dissociated from the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, as well as regarding those phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned.
When the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen:

regarding those phenomena dissociated from the fetter of views to be abandoned by the vision of the path, as well as regarding those phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation, the fetter of craving has not yet been abandoned.
Among the disciples who possess right view:
regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are those for whom the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) has not yet been severed;
or there are those who are bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of craving.
That is to say:
when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen;
regarding those phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, there remains the fetter of views to be abandoned by the vision of the origin that has not yet been severed.
Or there may be those bound by both:
namely, those who are fully fettered.
Regarding the phenomena abandoned through seeing and cultivation, there are two fetters that bind.
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen:
regarding the phenomena abandoned through seeing origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation, there are two fetters that bind.
When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen:
regarding those phenomena associated with the fetters of views to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, there are two fetters that bind.
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:
Regarding the phenomena associated with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), there are two types of bondage by the fetters.
Or, there may be cases where neither of the two is bound.
That is to say:
When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen:
regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination, there is no bondage by the two fetters.
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:
Regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation, there is no bondage by the two fetters.
A disciple of the Blessed One who possesses vision:
regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through vision, there is no bondage by the two fetters.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire has no bondage by the two fetters regarding the phenomena of the desire realm.
One who is already free from the defilement of form:
Regarding the phenomena of the desire and form realms, there are no two fetters that bind one.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm:
regarding the phenomena of all three realms, there are no two fetters that bind one.
As it is with the fetter of views,
so it is with the fetter of doubt.
If there is a binding by the fetter of craving toward a certain object, is there also a binding by the fetter of grasping toward that same object?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of craving (anunaya-saṃyojana), but not bound by the fetter of grasping (parāmarśa-saṃyojana).
That is to say:
the knowledge of origination has already arisen, but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen;
regarding phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation, the fetter of craving for them has not yet been severed.
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:
regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation, the fetter of craving has not been severed.
This refers to a disciple of the Blessed One who possesses vision.
Regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) that has not yet been abandoned;
or there may be the binding of the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) without the binding of the fetter of craving.
That is to say:
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen:
regarding those phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, there exists the fetter of grasping to be abandoned by the vision of the origin that has not yet been severed;
or, in some cases, both [fetters] bind one.
That is to say:
one who is bound by all fetters has two types of bonds regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen:
regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, cessation, and the path, there are two fetters that bind.
When the knowledge of the origin has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen:
Regarding the phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, there are two fetters that bind.
When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:
regarding the phenomena abandoned through the vision of the path, there are two fetters that bind.
Or there may be those who are unbound by both;
that is to say,
when the knowledge of origination has already arisen, but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen.
Regarding phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, there is no bondage by the two fetters.
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:
regarding phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering, its origin, and its cessation, there is no bondage by the two fetters.
A disciple of the World-Honored One who possesses right view has no two fetters bound to them regarding the phenomena to be abandoned by seeing.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire:
Regarding the phenomena of the desire realm, there are no two fetters that bind.
Having already become free from the defilement of the form realm: regarding the phenomena of the desire and form realms, there are no two fetters that bind.
One who is already free from the defilements of the formless realm has no bondage by the two fetters regarding the phenomena of the three realms.
If there is bondage by the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) toward a certain object, is there also bondage by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) toward that same object?
Answer: If one is bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) with respect to a certain object, one is necessarily bound by the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*).
However, there may be cases where one is bound by the fetter of attachment but not by the fetter of envy.
That is to say:
regarding the factors abandoned through vision in the desire realm, as well as the factors of the form and formless realms, the fetter of craving has not been abandoned;
this is as in the case of the fetter of envy.
The same applies to the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).
Just as the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) forms one category with respect to what follows;
so too does the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) form one category with respect to what follows.
If one is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) with respect to this object, is one also bound by the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*)? Answer:
If one is bound by the fetter of ill-will with respect to this object, one is necessarily bound by the fetter of conceit.
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of pride but not by the fetter of ill-will;
that is to say,
regarding phenomena of the form and formless realms, the fetter of pride has not yet been abandoned.
If there is a bond of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) regarding this matter, is there also a bond of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*)? Answer:
If there is a bond of ill-will regarding this matter, there must necessarily be a bond of ignorance.
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) but not bound by the fetter of ill-will (pratigha-saṃyojana).

This refers to one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire (kāmarāga), for whom the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen;

such a person has not yet abandoned the fetter of ignorance regarding the phenomena of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, though they have abandoned that which is to be abandoned through the vision of origin.
Regarding phenomena of the form and formless realms, there is the fetter of ignorance that has not yet been abandoned.
If one is bound to these phenomena by the fetter of aversion, is one also bound by the fetter of views?
Answer: This should be treated as four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of malice (pratigha-saṃyojana), but not bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana).
That is to say:
for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire— having already produced the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) but not yet produced the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)—

there remains unabandoned fetter of malice (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*) with respect to those factors in the desire realm dissociated from the views to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, as well as with respect to those factors in the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen, but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:

regarding those factors in the desire realm associated with the fetter of views to be abandoned by the vision of the path, as well as regarding those factors in the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation, the fetter of ill-will remains unsevered.
Among the disciples of the World-Honored One who possess right view but have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire:
regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation, they have not yet severed the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).
Alternatively, they may be bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of ill-will.

That is to say, for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire— when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen—
there remains the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the vision of origin with respect to those phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
Regarding the phenomena of the form and formless realms, there is the fetter of views that has not yet been abandoned;
or, there may be bondage by both.
That is to say:

Regarding those who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*): for those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire (*kāmarāga*), and for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*) binding them to the phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.

Regarding the phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation, there are two fetters that bind them.
When the knowledge of origin has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen:
regarding the phenomena associated with the fetter of views that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path in the desire realm, there are two fetters that bind them.
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen, but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:
regarding those factors associated with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the vision of the path within the desire realm, there are two fetters that bind [the individual];
or, in some cases, neither of the two binds.
That is to say:
when the knowledge of origination has already arisen, but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen;
[this refers to] those phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination.

Furthermore, regarding those factors dissociated from the fetters of views that are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path within the form and formless realms, as well as those factors abandoned through cultivation within the form and formless realms, there is no bondage by the two types of fetters.
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:
regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation;

and regarding those phenomena associated with the fetters of views to be abandoned through the vision of the path within the form and formless realms; as well as regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation within the form and formless realms—there is no bondage by two fetters.
A disciple of the World-Honored One who possesses right view,
but has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire,
is bound by no two fetters with respect to the dharmas to be abandoned by seeing, nor with respect to the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation in the realms of form and formlessness.
Having already become free from the defilement of desire:
regarding the phenomena of the desire realm, there are no two fetters that bind them.
Having already become free from the defilement of form:
Regarding the phenomena of the desire and form realms, there are no two fetters that bind.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm:
regarding the phenomena of the three realms, there are no two fetters that bind.
As it is with the fetter of views;
so it is with the fetter of doubt.
If one is bound to this object by the fetter of ill-will, is one also bound by the fetter of grasping?
Answer: This should be treated as four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of ill-will (pratigha-saṃyojana), yet not bound by the fetter of grasping (parigraha-saṃyojana).
That is to say:
one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of sensual desire,
for whom the knowledge of origination has already arisen, but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen;
Regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation, there is the fetter of ill-will that has not yet been abandoned.
When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:
regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation, there is the fetter of ill-will that has not yet been abandoned.
Among the disciples of the World-Honored One who possess right view but have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire:
regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation, there are those for whom the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) has not been severed;
or there are those who are bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) but are not bound by the fetter of ill-will.
That is to say:
one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, for whom the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen;

regarding the phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, there remains the fetter of grasping (parāmarśa-saṃyojana) to be abandoned by the vision of origin that has not yet been severed.
Regarding the phenomena of the form and formless realms, there are fetters of grasping that have not yet been abandoned;
or there may be those bound by both.
That is to say:

Regarding those who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*): for those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, there are two types of fettering bonds (*saṃyojana-bandhana*) with respect to the phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen:
regarding the phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation, there are two fetters that bind.
When the knowledge of the origin has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen:
Regarding the factors abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path within the desire realm, there are two fetters (saṃyojana) that bind;
when the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
there are two fetters that bind the factors abandoned through the vision of the path within the desire realm.
Or there may be those who are unbound by both;
that is to say,
those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen:

regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination, as well as those phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms, there is no bondage by the two fetters.
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen:

regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation, as well as those phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms, there are no two fetters that bind.
A disciple of the World-Honored One who possesses right view,
but has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire,
is bound by no more than two fetters with respect to the factors abandoned through vision, as well as the factors abandoned through cultivation belonging to the realms of form and formlessness.
One who has already become free from the defilement of desire:
regarding the phenomena of the desire realm, there are no two fetters that bind them.
One who has already become free from the defilement of form:
Regarding the phenomena of the desire and form realms, there are no two fetters that bind.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm:
regarding the phenomena of the three realms, there are no two fetters that bind.
If one is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) regarding this object, is one also bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)? Answer:
If one is bound by the fetter of envy regarding this object, one is necessarily bound by the fetter of ill-will.
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of ill-will but not by the fetter of envy.
That is to say:
regarding those phenomena in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by insight, the fetter of ill-will has not yet been severed.
As it is with the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*);
so too it is with the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*)!
