The same applies to the fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Just as the fetter of craving (*rāga*) forms the "small seven" in relation to the subsequent ones,
this continues up to the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*) in relation to the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya*).
According to what is appropriate,
the same applies to the "small sevenfold" [sets]. As with the small sevenfold, so it is here.
The same applies to the seven great [kalpas].
The difference is that two are paired with one.
...up to eight [factors] paired with one.
Just as there are seven [factors] beginning with past craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
so too there are those beginning with past, future, and present craving.
Each of these likewise has seven;
thus it should be understood that there are forty-nine phrases in total.
Regarding the three fetters up to the ninety-eight proclivities:
within these ninety-eight proclivities,
how many proclivities are subsumed by each one?
Answer: All should be analyzed as follows:
Among the three fetters: the fetter of the view of a self-body subsumes three;
the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances subsumes six;
and the fetter of doubt subsumes twelve.
Among the three unwholesome roots— the unwholesome roots of greed and hatred each comprise five [factors],
while the unwholesome root of delusion comprises four.
A small portion of one [aggregate].
Among the three outflows (āsrava): thirty-one are subsumed under the outflow of sensual desire (kāma-āsrava), and fifty-two are subsumed under the outflow of existence (bhava-āsrava).
The outflow of ignorance comprises fifteen [factors].
Among the four floods: the flood of sensual desire comprises nineteen;
the flood of existence comprises twenty-eight.
The flood of views comprises thirty-six [factors];
the flood of ignorance comprises fifteen.
This is as with the four floods.
The four yokes are likewise.
Among the four graspings—desire-grasping comprises twenty-four;
view-grasping comprises thirty.
The clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) comprises six [factors]. The clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*) comprises thirty-eight.
Among the four fetters of the body (*kāyagrantha*), there are the fetter of sensual desire (*abhidhyākāyagrantha*) and the fetter of ill will (*vyāpādakāyagrantha*).
Each [of the former] comprises five;
the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances comprises six;
and the fetter of adherence to this as real comprises twelve.
Among the five hindrances— the hindrance of sensual desire and the hindrance of ill will—
each comprises five [factors].
The hindrance of doubt comprises four.
The remaining hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are not included therein.
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of greed (*rāga*) and the fetter of pride (*māna*) each include fifteen [of the ninety-eight proclivities].
The fetter of aversion (pratigha-saṃyojana) comprises five [of the ten fetters]. The fetters of envy (īrṣyā) and avarice (mātsarya) are not comprised by any [of the ten].
Among the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni), the fetters of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and aversion (vyāpāda) each comprise five.
The fetter of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) comprises three;
the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana) comprises six;
and the fetter of doubt (vicikitsā-saṃyojana) comprises twelve.
Among the five fetters conducive to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*): the fetter of desire for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) comprises a small portion of one;
the fetter of desire for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) comprises a small portion of another;
and the fetter of restlessness (*auddhatya*) is not comprised by any [of these].
The fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) subsumes two [of the nine types of pride] in part; the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) subsumes two [of the nine types of ignorance] in part.
Among the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) each subsume three [of the nine types of views].
Wrong view and the grasping at views each comprise twelve [factors].
The grasping at precepts and observances comprises six.
Among the six groups of craving—craving born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact each comprise two minor portions.
The groups of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact each comprise a small portion of one [aggregate].
The group of craving born of mind-contact comprises thirteen [aggregates] and a small portion of two.
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): the underlying tendencies of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and hostility (*pratigha*) each comprise five;
the underlying tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) comprises ten;
and the underlying tendencies of pride (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) each comprise fifteen.
The latent tendency of views comprises thirty-six [factors];
the latent tendency of doubt comprises twelve.
Among the nine fetters—those of craving, conceit, and ignorance—each comprises fifteen.
The fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) comprises five [factors]; the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and grasping (*parāmarśa*) each comprise eighteen;
and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*) comprises twelve.
The fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are not included [in the ninefold classification].
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): the view of a self-entity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) of the desire realm is subsumed under the view of a self-entity of the desire realm;
and so on, up to the ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm, which is subsumed under the ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the three fetters up to the ninety-eight proclivities:
does the former subsume the latter,
or does the latter subsume the former?
Answer: The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) do not mutually include one another.
The three fetters and the three outflows (*āsrava*)—the three fetters and a portion of two outflows mutually include one another, while the remainder do not mutually include one another.
Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the four floods (*ogha*): the three fetters and a portion of the three floods mutually include one another;
the remainder do not include one another.
As it is with respect to the four floods, so it is with respect to the four yokes (*yoga*).
Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the four graspings (*upādāna*): the three fetters and one portion of one grasping mutually include one another;
the remainder do not mutually include one another.
Regarding the three fetters and the four bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*): one fetter and one bodily tie mutually include one another.
The others are not mutually inclusive.
Among the three fetters and the five hindrances, one fetter and a portion of one hindrance are mutually inclusive;
the others are not mutually inclusive.
The three fetters (saṃyojana) and the five fetters do not mutually include one another.
The three fetters and the five lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana)—the three fetters and three of the lower fetters—mutually include one another.
The others are not mutually inclusive.
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the five higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are not mutually inclusive.
The three fetters and the five views (*dṛṣṭi*): two of the fetters and two of the views are mutually inclusive.
The others are not mutually inclusive.
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the six bases of craving (*taṇhākāya*) are mutually non-inclusive.
The three fetters and the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—specifically, the three fetters and one portion of one underlying tendency—are mutually inclusive.
The remaining ones do not mutually include one another.
Regarding the three fetters and the nine fetters—the three fetters and one of the nine fetters mutually include two parts [of each other].
The remaining ones do not mutually include one another.
Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): the three fetters and twenty-one underlying tendencies mutually include one another;
the remainder do not mutually include one another.
… And so on, up to … the nine fetters and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies: seven fetters and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies mutually include one another.
The remaining factors are not mutually inclusive.
Among the three fetters up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many cause the continuity of the desire realm existence (*kāmadhātu-bhava*)?
How many cause the continuity of the form realm existence (*rūpadhātu-bhava*)?
How many [factors] cause the continuity of the formless realm?
Answer: All [of these] should be analyzed.
That is to say:
the three fetters cause the continuity of the three realms of existence (*bhava*).
The three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) cause the continuity of the realm of desire (*kāma-bhava*).
The outflow of sensual desire (kāmāsrava) causes the continuity of existence in the realms of form and formlessness.
The outflow of ignorance (avidyāsrava) causes the continuity of the three realms of existence.
Among the four floods (ogha) and yokes (yoga):
The flood and yoke of sensual desire cause the continuity of sensual existence (*kāma-bhava*).
The flood and yoke of existence cause the continuity of form and formless existence (*rūpa- and ārūpya-bhava*).
The floods and yokes of views and ignorance cause the continuity of the three existences (*tri-bhava*).
Among the four graspings (*upādāna*):
the grasping for sense-pleasures (*kāmopādāna*) causes the continuity of the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu*);
the graspings for views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) and for rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*) cause the continuity of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
The grasping at a theory of self (ātmavādopādāna) causes the continuity of existence in the realms of form and formlessness.
Among the four fetters of the body (kāyagrantha),
the first two cause the continuity of existence in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
The latter two [fetters] cause the continuity of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
The five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) cause the continuity of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Among the five fetters (*pañca-saṃyojana*):
The fetters of greed and conceit cause the continuity of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
The remaining three fetters cause the continuity of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Among the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*):
The first two [fetters] cause the continuity of the realm of desire;
the latter three cause the continuity of the three realms of existence.
Among the five fetters pertaining to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*):
Attachment to form causes the continuity of existence in the realm of form;
attachment to the formless causes the continuity of existence in the formless realm;
the remaining three [types of attachment] cause the continuity of existence in both the realm of form and the formless realm.
The five views cause the continuity of the three realms of existence.
Among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*),
the groups of craving born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact cause the continuity of the realms of desire and form.
The group of cravings born of nose-contact and tongue-contact causes the continuity of sensual existence (*kāmadhātu*).
The group of cravings born of mind-contact causes the continuity of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) cause the continuity of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Desire for existence (*bhavarāga*) causes the continuity of the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The remaining four [fetters] cause the continuity of the three realms of existence (*bhava*).
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*):
the fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*), ill-will (*pratigha*), and avarice (*mātsarya*) cause the continuity of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The remaining six fetters cause the continuity of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Among the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*):
thirty-six belong to the desire realm and cause the continuity of the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Thirty-one [factors] of the form realm—causing the continuity of existence in the form realm.
Thirty-one [factors] of the formless realm—causing the continuity of existence in the formless realm.
The three fetters up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies.
By means of which meditative concentration are the three fetters abandoned? Answer:
Three [fetters]—or four—are abandoned by means of [the four foundations of mindfulness].
Alternatively, they are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya* [attainment]:
the three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya*;
the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) are abandoned by relying on either [the *anāgamya*] or the seven [stages].
Alternatively, they are abandoned by the stage of *anāgamya* (the threshold concentration).
Among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*):
the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) and the yoke of desire (*kāma-yoga*) are abandoned by the stage of *anāgamya*.
The flood and yoke of existence and the flood and yoke of ignorance— these depend either on seven [bases] or on the cessation of the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The flood and yoke of views— these depend on four [bases].
Alternatively, they are extinguished by relying on the *anāgamya* [attainment].
Among the four graspings (*upādāna*),
the grasping of sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*) is extinguished by relying on the *anāgamya*.
The clinging to views and the clinging to precepts and observances— either depend on four [bases] or depend on the *anāgamya* for their cessation.
The clinging to the doctrine of self— either depends on seven [bases].
Alternatively, they may be abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya* stage.
Among the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*),
the first three are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya* stage.
The latter two— either based on the four [dhyānas] or based on the *anāgamya* for cessation.
The five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*)— based on the *anāgamya* for cessation.
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*):
the fetters of greed (*rāga*) and conceit (*māna*)— either depend on seven [stages] or are extinguished by depending on the *anāgamya* [stage].
The remaining three fetters are abandoned based on the *anāgamya* stage.
Among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*),
the first two are abandoned based on the *anāgamya* stage.
The latter three— either based on the four [dhyānas] or based on the *anāgamya*— are extinguished.
Among the five fetters pertaining to the higher realms (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*),
attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*) is either based on the four [dhyānas].
Alternatively, they may depend on the *anāgamya* [attainment] for cessation;
the remaining four— alternatively, they may depend on seven,
or they may depend on the *anāgamya* for cessation.
Regarding the five views: they either depend on the four [dhyānas] or depend on the threshold concentration (anāgamya) for their cessation.
Among the six groups of craving (ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya):
The group of cravings born of nose-contact and tongue-contact are abandoned based on the *anāgamya* stage.
The groups of cravings born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact are either abandoned based on the *anāgamya* or the first dhyāna.
Alternatively, it relies on the *anāgamya* [dhyāna] for the cessation of the group of cravings born of mental contact— or alternatively, it relies on seven [stages],
or relies on the *anāgamya* for their cessation.
Among the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):
sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya* [attainment].
Existential greed (*bhavarāga*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) are abandoned by relying on any of the seven [stages].
Or, for the abandonment of views and doubt, it relies on the *anāgamya* stage— or it relies on four [stages]. Or, for the abandonment [of these],
it relies on the *anāgamya* stage.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*):
craving, pride, and ignorance— either depend on seven [stages] or are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage.
Ill-will, envy, and avarice are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya* [preliminary] stage.
Views, grasping, and doubt are either abandoned by relying on the four [dhyānas] or by relying on the *anāgamya* stage.
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):
thirty-six of the desire realm are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya* [attainment];
thirty-one of the form realm and those of the formless realm to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are abandoned by relying on either the four [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya*.
Or, for those abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, it is based on the *anāgamya* [attainment] or the cessation [attainment]; or it is based on seven [stages],
or based on the *anāgamya* and the cessation [attainments].
If various fetters are past, have those fetters already bound [the individual]? Answer:
Various fetters are past.
Those fetters are already bound;
the fetter of existence is already bound;
those fetters are not of the past.
That is to say:
the fetters of the future and present have already bound one.
As for those fetters of the future, will those fetters bind one in the future?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There may be a fetter (saṃyojana) that is future, yet that fetter is not one that will bind.
That is to say:
the fetters of the future have already been abandoned, already fully understood, already ceased, and already vomited out;
one will certainly never fall back from them.
There are fetters that ought to bind, yet those fetters do not belong to the future;
that is to say,
they are fetters of the past that have already been abandoned, already fully understood, already ceased, and already vomited out.
He will certainly fall away.
There are fetters in the future, and he will also be bound by those fetters. Namely:
The fetters of the future have already been abandoned, fully understood, extinguished, and vomited out;
one will certainly fall away from them.
There are fetters that do not belong to the future, and those fetters likewise shall not bind one in the future.
That is to say:
the fetters of the past have already been abandoned, fully understood, extinguished, and vomited out;
one will certainly not fall back from them.
Regarding present fetters:
if various fetters are present,
are those fetters currently binding?
Answer: Those fetters that are present—
those fetters bind one now.
There are fetters that bind at present,
yet those fetters are not of the present;
that is to say:
One binds the fetters of the past, future,
and present. By means of this path,
one abandons the fetters of the desire realm.
When one falls back from this path,
does one again become bound by those fetters? Answer:
Furthermore, those who employ this path to sever the fetters of the form and formless realms will still be bound by those very fetters.
When one retreats from this path,
does one again become bound by those fetters? Answer:
One again becomes bound by those fetters.
There are nine thorough knowledges (parijñā), namely:
The exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin in the desire realm is the first full knowledge (parijñā).
The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin in the form and formless realms is the second full knowledge.
The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of cessation in the desire realm is the third thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of cessation in the form and formless realms is the fourth thorough knowledge.
The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm is the fifth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the form and formless realms is the sixth thorough knowledge.
The exhaustion of the five lower fetters—the seventh thorough knowledge.
The exhaustion of the attachment to the realm of form—the eighth thorough knowledge.
The exhaustion of all fetters—the ninth thorough knowledge.
Are all types of full knowledge subsumed within the nine types of full knowledge,
or are the nine types of full knowledge subsumed within all types of full knowledge? Answer:
All nine are subsumed [by the first], but the nine do not subsume all.
What is not subsumed? Namely:
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen—the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the three realms are exhausted.
These are not comprised within the nine [categories].
For a disciple of the Blessed One who possesses right view but has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire—the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm are exhausted.
It is not comprised within the nine [fetters].
Having abandoned the defilement of desire but not yet having abandoned the defilement of form—the fetters of the form realm to be abandoned by cultivation are exhausted.
It is not comprised within the nine.

One who is already free from the defilements of the form realm but not yet free from the defilements of the formless realm— [in whom] the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm are exhausted—
is not included among the nine [categories].
There are eight types of individuals (pudgala):
1. The candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka).
2. The fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala).
3. The candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka).
4. The fruit of once-returning;
5. the candidate for non-returning;
6. the fruit of non-returning.
7. The candidate for arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka).
8. The fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).
These eight persons (pudgala) [are established] with respect to the nine thorough knowledges (parijñā).
How many are accomplished?
How many are not accomplished? Answer:
For one entering the stream (srotāpanna-pratipannaka)—
either they do not possess [any], or they possess one, two, three, four, or five [of the faculties].
That is to say:

In the stages from the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) up to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), [the practitioner] does not possess [it].

In the stage of the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), one [knowledge] is possessed.
At the stage of the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) and the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), one accomplishes two.
At the stage of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), one accomplishes three.
At the stage of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), one accomplishes four.
At the stage of the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), one accomplishes five.
The fruit of stream-entry—achieves six.

One proceeding toward the fruit of once-returning—if, having further abandoned desire and defilement, they enter into rightness and the state beyond birth—it is as in the case of one proceeding toward stream-entry.
If one proceeds from the fruit of stream-entry toward the fruit of once-returning, as well as those established in the fruit of once-returning—they achieve six.

As for those proceeding toward the fruit of non-returning who, having already become free from the defilement of desire, enter into rightness and the state beyond birth—they are like those proceeding toward the fruit of stream-entry.
If one proceeds from the fruit of once-returner toward the fruit of non-returner—one accomplishes six.
As for the fruit of non-returner—one accomplishes one.
That is to say:
Regarding the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya):
one who is a candidate for arhatship (arhattva-pratipannaka) either accomplishes one or accomplishes two.
That is to say:
one who has not yet abandoned attachment to the realm of form accomplishes one;
one who has already abandoned attachment to the realm of form accomplishes two.
The fruit of arhatship— accomplishes one,
namely: the exhaustion of all fetters.
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Four.
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Volume Five.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree:
Sudden and gradual, bound and liberated, Fruits, inclusion, the seven [categories], and the three;
Death and birth, not sixfold— I pray that this chapter may explain them all.
In each of the three realms, there are two categories of fetters, namely:

those abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Regarding the two categories of fetters abandoned through vision and cultivation in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), is it possible to be simultaneously bound by them?
Answer: There is. That is to say:

When an ordinary person who has already become detached from the defilements of desire falls away from that detachment, or when they die in the form or formless realms and are reborn in the desire realm—
does there ever occur a simultaneous severance of fetters?
Answer: There are. Namely:
When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) becomes free from the defilements of desire,
is there any instance where they gradually attain bondage? Answer:
No. Is there any gradual liberation from bondage? Answer:
There are. That is to say:
a disciple of the Blessed One first abandons those fetters to be abandoned by insight, and subsequently abandons those fetters to be abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the two categories of fetters—those to be abandoned by vision and those to be abandoned by cultivation—in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), is it possible for one to be simultaneously bound by them? Answer: Yes.
That is to say:

when an ordinary person who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm falls away from that detachment, and when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire or form realms.
Is there any case where one is simultaneously liberated from the fetters?
Answer: There is. Namely:
When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) becomes detached from the defilements of the form realm (rūpa-rāga), is there any instance where they gradually attain bondage? Answer:
No. Is there any gradual liberation from bondage? Answer:
There is. That is to say:
a disciple of the Blessed One first abandons those fetters to be abandoned by insight, and subsequently abandons those fetters to be abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding the two categories of fetters to be abandoned through vision and cultivation in the formless realm, is it possible to acquire their bondage all at once? Answer: No.
Is there any case of simultaneous liberation from the fetters? Answer: No.
Is there any case where one is bound gradually? Answer: No.
Is there gradual disentanglement from the fetters?
Answer: There is.
That is to say:
a disciple of the World-Honored One first abandons those fetters to be abandoned by insight, and subsequently abandons those fetters to be abandoned by cultivation.
When the fetters of the desire realm to be abandoned by insight are exhausted, in which fruit are they included?
Answer: There are four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or there may be no [fruit].
To which fruit does the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm belong?
Answer: [They are included in] the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) or the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala), or they have no location.
As for the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) in the form realm (rūpadhātu), in which fruit is it subsumed?
Answer: There are four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or there may be none.
To which fruit does the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through cultivation in the form realm belong?
Answer: It is the fruit of arhatship, or it belongs to no [fruit].
To which fruit does the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned by insight in the formless realm belong?
Answer: There are four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
To which fruit does the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm belong?
Answer: The fruit of arhatship.
There are five categories of fetters, namely:
Regarding the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering... up to the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation:
In what fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering included? Answer:
Regarding the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or where they do not exist:
If one asks, "To which fruit does the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] belong?
The answer is:
Regarding the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or [the case where] there is no [fruit]:
the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation—into which fruit is it included? Answer:
Regarding the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or [the case where] there is no [fruit]:
the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the path of seeing—into which fruit is this included? Answer:
Regarding the four fruits of śrāmaṇya:
to which fruit does the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through cultivation belong? Answer:
Regarding the fruit of arhatship,
there are nine categories of fetters, namely:
Regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), up to those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
when the fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering are exhausted, in which fruit (*phala*) are they included? Answer:
Regarding the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or [the case where] there is no [fruit]:

when the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) up to the dharma-knowledge of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna) are exhausted, in which fruit are they included? Answer:
Regarding the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or the case where there is no [fruit]:
when the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) are exhausted, in which fruit are they included? Answer:
Regarding the four fruits of śrāmaṇya:
to which fruit does the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through cultivation belong? Answer:
Regarding the fruit of arhatship:
there are fifteen classes of fetters (*saṃyojana*), namely five classes for each of the three realms:
the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)... up to the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
When the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path within the desire realm are exhausted, in which fruit are they included?
Answer: They are included in the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or there is no specific location.
In what fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm included?
Answer: It is included in the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of arhatship; or there is no such place.
The exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path within the form realm (rūpadhātu)—in which fruit is this comprised?
Answer: It is comprised in the four fruits of śramaṇaship, or it may be in no [fruit].
In what fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the form realm included?
Answer: It is included in the fruit of Arhatship, or there is no specific location.
The exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)—in which fruition (phala) is this comprised?
Answer: It is comprised in the four fruits of the śramaṇa, or it is not comprised in any [fruit].
Question: To which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—within which fruition is it subsumed?
Answer: It is the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding the exhaustion of each of the three fetters up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), in which fruit are they included? Answer:
Among the three fetters, the exhaustion of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is included in four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it is not included in any.
Just as it should be understood that among the three fetters, the destruction of the view of a self-identity [is required],
so too it is for the destruction of the view of a self-identity among the five lower fetters, and for the destruction of the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes among the five views.
The exhaustion of the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) is subsumed within the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
As it was explained regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), so should one understand the exhaustion of the clinging to rules and observances and doubt here.

Likewise, among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*), it is the flood and yoke of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha/yoga*); among the four graspings (*upādāna*), it is the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭy-upādāna*) and the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); among the four bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*), it is the clinging to rules and observances and the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence (*parāmarśakāyagrantha*); among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), it is the clinging to rules and observances and doubt; among the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), it is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the grasping for views, and the clinging to rules and observances; among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is the underlying tendencies of views and doubt; and among the nine fetters (*grantha*), the exhaustion of the fetters of views, grasping, and doubt is likewise to be understood.
The exhaustion of the three unwholesome roots is subsumed within the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of arhatship, or it has no fixed location.
As with the exhaustion of the three unwholesome roots, so should it be understood for [the other cases]:

Among the three outflows (*āsrava*): the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*). Among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*): the flood and yoke of sensual desire. Among the four graspings (*upādāna*): the grasping for sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*). Among the four bodily ties (*kāya-grantha*): covetousness and ill will. Among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*): the first four hindrances. Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*): the fetters of ill will, envy, and avarice. Among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*): covetousness and ill will. Among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*): the group of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact. Among the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*): sensual greed and ill will. Among the nine fetters (*navasaṃyojana*): the fetters of resentment, envy, and avarice—the exhaustion [of these] is likewise so!
The exhaustion of the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsava*) and ignorance (*avijjā-āsava*) is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.

Just as with the exhaustion of the outflows of existence and ignorance, one should understand that among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*), it is the floods and yokes of existence and ignorance; among the four graspings (*upādāna*), it is the grasping at self-theory (*attavāda-upādāna*); among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is the fetters of greed and conceit; and among the five higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), it consists of the remaining four, excluding the greed for the form realm (*rūparāga*).

Among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), it is the group of craving born of mental contact; among the seven underlying tendencies (*sapta-anuśaya*), it is the tendencies of existence, sensual desire, ignorance, and pride; and among the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*), it is the fetters of craving, pride, and ignorance—it is the same for all these.
The exhaustion of the hindrance of doubt is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or there is no specific location [for its inclusion].
The exhaustion of the fetter of lust for the form realm (*rūparāga-anuśaya*) is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship, or there is no specific location.
Just as it should be understood that the craving-body born of eye-contact, ear-contact,
and body-contact is exhausted when the fetters conducive to the higher realms (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana) are exhausted, so too is it for the others!
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):

the exhaustion of those latent dispositions in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path is comprised within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or else there is no [specific] location.

The exhaustion of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm is subsumed within the fruits of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and arhat (*arhat*), or it has no fixed location.

The exhaustion of the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path in the form realm is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no fixed location.

The exhaustion of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*), or there is no such place [where it is not].

The exhaustion of the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), and cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is subsumed under the four fruits of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), or there is no such place.
The exhaustion of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the formless realm is subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
the exhaustion of the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the formless realm is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding the exhaustion of all fetters within the stage of one entering the stream (srotāpattipratipanna), by which fruit is it subsumed? Answer: Nowhere.
Question: Among the various fetters (saṃyojana) that are exhausted within the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala), by which fruit are they subsumed? Answer:
By the fruit of stream-entry.
When all fetters (*saṃyojana*) within the stage of one heading toward the first fruit are exhausted, by which fruit are they subsumed?
Answer: By the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), or there is no [specific] location.
Question: Among the various fetters (saṃyojana) that are exhausted in the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala), by which fruit are they subsumed?
Answer: They are subsumed by the fruit of once-returning.
Question: Among those who are candidates for the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmipratipannaka), when all fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted, by which fruit are they subsumed?
Answer: They are subsumed under the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala), or there is no such case.
Question: Among the various fetters (saṃyojana) that are exhausted within the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), by which fruit are they subsumed? Answer:
By the fruit of non-returning.
Regarding the exhaustion of all fetters within the stage of the candidate for arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka), by which fruit is it subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed by the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), or there is no specific location.
Question: Among the fruits of arhatship, the exhaustion of all fetters (saṃyojana)—in which fruit is this included?
Answer: It is included in the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding a disciple of the Blessed One who possesses right view:
if they have not yet abandoned the defilements of sensual desire, but have exhausted all fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the realm of desire, in which fruit are they included? Answer:
Regarding the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), or perhaps there is no such case:

if one has already become free from the defilements of desire (*kāmarāga*) but is not yet free from the defilements of the form realm (*rūparāga*), and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the form realm are exhausted—into which fruit is this subsumed?
Answer: There is no such case.

For one who is already detached from the defilements of form (*rūpa-rāga*) but not yet detached from the defilements of the formless (*ārūpya-rāga*), and for whom all fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm have been exhausted—into which fruit is this included?
Answer: There is no such case.
Are the factors of training (śaikṣadharma) accomplished by those who have attained the stream-entry (srotāpanna) included within the fruit of stream-entry?
Answer: It is sometimes included and sometimes not included.
In what way is it included?
Answer: There is the conditioned fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) which has already been attained and not lost.
How could it not be included?
Answer: Regarding the conditioned phenomena, such as the superior and progressive untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) attained by those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna)—
even if these phenomena are included within the fruit of stream-entry— are they considered "dharmas of training" (śaikṣadharma)?
Answer: It is either training (śaikṣa) or neither-training-nor-non-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa). What is training?
Answer: It is the conditioned fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
Why is it neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Answer: The unconditioned fruit of stream-entry.
Are the factors of training (śaikṣadharma) accomplished by those who are once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin) subsumed under the fruit of once-returning?
Answer: Sometimes it is included, and sometimes it is not.
How is it included?
Answer: There is the conditioned fruit of a once-returner, which has already been attained and not lost.
Why is it not included?
Answer: Regarding the conditioned phenomena, such as the superior, further-advanced untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) attained by those who are once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin)—
even if these phenomena are subsumed within the fruit of once-returning— are they the dharmas of training (śaikṣa-dharma)?
Answer: It is either training (śaikṣa) or neither-training-nor-non-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa). What is training?
Answer: It is the conditioned fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).
Why is it neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Answer: It is the unconditioned once-returner fruit.
Are the trainee dharmas accomplished by those who are non-returners included within the fruit of non-returning?
Answer: It is sometimes included and sometimes not included.
In what way is it included?
Answer: There is the conditioned fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) which has already been attained and not lost.
Why is it not included?
Answer: Regarding the conditioned phenomena, such as the superior and progressive untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) attained by those who are non-returners (anāgāmin)—
even if these phenomena are subsumed under the fruit of non-returning— are they considered "dharmas of training" (śaikṣadharma)?
Answer: It is either training (śaikṣa) or neither-training-nor-non-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa). What is training?
Answer: It is the conditioned fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Why is it neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa)?
Answer: It is the unconditioned fruit of non-returning.
Regarding the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) accomplished by all Arhats, are these dharmas included within the fruit of Arhatship?
Answer: It is so.
If a dharma is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship, is this an asaikṣa dharma?
Answer: It is either *aśaikṣa* (beyond training) or neither *śaikṣa* nor *aśaikṣa*. What is *aśaikṣa*?
Answer: It is the conditioned fruit of arhatship.
Why is it neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: The unconditioned fruit of arhatship.
Are the untainted dharmas accomplished by those who are stream-enterers subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry?
Answer: It is sometimes included and sometimes not included.
In what way is it included?
Answer: The conditioned and unconditioned fruits of stream-entry have already been attained and are not lost.
Why, then, are they not included?
Answer:

It consists of the conditioned dharmas, such as the superior and further-advanced untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) attained by those who have entered the stream (srotāpanna), as well as the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana-kṣaya) realized by them, and the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) accomplished by those who have entered the stream.
If a dharma is included within the fruit of stream-entry, is this an outflow-free (anāsrava) dharma? Answer: It is so.
Regarding the untainted dharmas accomplished by those who are once-returners: are these dharmas subsumed within the fruit of once-returning? Answer:
Some are subsumed; some are not.
What is included? Answer:
The conditioned and unconditioned fruits of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), already attained and not lost.
What is not included? Answer:

The conditioned dharmas, such as the superior and further-advanced untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) attained by those who are once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin), as well as the destruction of the fetters (saṃyojana-kṣaya) realized by them, and the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) accomplished by those once-returners.
If one posits that the fruit of the once-returner is included therein, is this an untainted (anāsrava) dharma? Answer: It is so.
Regarding the untainted dharmas accomplished by those who are non-returners (anāgāmin), are these dharmas subsumed within the fruit of non-returning?
Answer: Some are subsumed, while others are not.
What is included? Answer:
The conditioned and unconditioned fruits of non-returning, already attained and not lost.
What is not included? Answer:

The conditioned phenomena, such as the superior and progressive untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) obtained by those who are non-returners (anāgāmin), as well as the exhaustion of all fetters (saṃyojana) realized by them, and the non-analytical cessations (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) accomplished by those non-returners.
If a dharma is subsumed under the fruit of non-returning, is this an untainted (anāsrava) dharma? Answer: It is so.
Regarding the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) accomplished by the various Arhats: are these dharmas subsumed within the fruit of Arhatship?
Answer: Some are subsumed, while others are not.
What is included? Answer:
The conditioned and unconditioned fruits of arhatship, already attained and not lost.
What is not included? Answer:
The non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) accomplished by an Arhat.
If a phenomenon is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship, is this an untainted (anāsrava) phenomenon? Answer: It is so.
Regarding those dharmas accomplished by a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), are these dharmas included within the fruit of stream-entry?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are dharmas that are accomplished by a stream-enterer but are not included within the fruit of stream-entry. These are:

the conditioned dharmas such as the superior, untainted faculties attained by a stream-enterer; the exhaustion of the fetters realized by them; and the non-analytical cessations (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and tainted dharmas accomplished by a stream-enterer.
There are dharmas subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry that are not possessed by one who is a stream-enterer;
namely, those dharmas of the fruit of stream-entry which have not yet been attained or have already been lost.
There are dharmas that are accomplished by a stream-enterer and are also subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry;
namely, the fruit of stream-entry that has already been attained and not lost.
There are dharmas that are neither accomplished by a stream-enterer nor subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry.
That is to say: with the exception of the aforementioned characteristics.
If one accomplishes the dharmas of a once-returner, are these dharmas subsumed within the fruit of once-returning?
Answer: One should formulate this in four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are dharmas that are accomplished by a once-returner, yet are not subsumed under the fruit of once-returning. These are:

the conditioned dharmas such as the superior, further-advanced untainted faculties attained by a once-returner; the exhaustion of the various fetters realized by him; and the tainted dharmas of non-analytical cessation accomplished by a once-returner.
There are dharmas subsumed under the fruit of once-returning that are not accomplished by one who is a once-returner;
namely, those dharmas of the fruit of once-returning which have not yet been attained or have already been lost.
There are dharmas that are accomplished by a once-returner and are also subsumed under the fruit of once-returning;
namely, those dharmas of the fruit of once-returning that have already been attained and not lost.
There are dharmas that are not accomplished by a once-returner, nor are they subsumed within the fruit of a once-returner;
namely, those other than the aforementioned characteristics.
If one accomplishes the non-returning of all dharmas, is this dharma subsumed under the fruit of non-returning?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are dharmas that are accomplished by a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) but are not included within the fruit of non-returning.

These are: the conditioned dharmas such as the superior, further-advanced untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) attained by the non-returner; the exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) realized by him; and the non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and tainted dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*) accomplished by the non-returner.
There are dharmas subsumed under the fruit of non-returning that are not accomplished by one who is a non-returner;
namely, those dharmas of the fruit of non-returning that have not yet been attained or have already been lost.
There are dharmas that are accomplished by one who is a non-returner (anāgāmin) and are also subsumed under the fruit of non-returning;
namely, those dharmas of the fruit of non-returning that have already been attained and not lost.
There are dharmas that are neither accomplished by one who is not a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), nor are they subsumed under the fruit of non-returning.
That is to say: with the exception of the aforementioned characteristics.
Regarding those dharmas accomplished by an arhat: are these dharmas subsumed within the fruit of arhatship?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are dharmas that an Arhat possesses which are not included within the fruit of Arhatship;
namely, the non-analytical cessations (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and contaminated (sāsrava) dharmas possessed by an Arhat.
There are dharmas subsumed under the fruit of arhatship that are not accomplished by an arhat;
namely, those which have not yet been attained or have already been lost.
There are dharmas that are accomplished by an arhat and are also subsumed under the fruit of arhatship;
namely, those dharmas of the fruit of arhatship which have already been attained and not lost.
There are dharmas that are neither accomplished by an Arhat nor subsumed within the fruit of Arhatship;
namely, those other than the aforementioned characteristics.
Do all those who die and are born within the desire realm necessarily undergo existence in the desire realm?
Answer: This should be treated as four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are those who die and are reborn in the desire realm, yet do not undergo existence within the desire realm;
that is to say,
passing away from the desire realm, they arise as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) in the form realm.
There is an existence involving desire that does not involve dying and being born within the desire realm;
namely, when one passes away from the form realm and arises as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm.
There are those who die and are born within the desire realm, and likewise undergo existence in the desire realm;
that is to say,
passing away from the desire realm, they arise as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the desire realm.
There are those who do not die or take birth in the desire realm, nor do they undergo existence within the desire realm;
that is to say:
passing away from the form realm, they are born in the form or formless realms.
When one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the formless or form realms,
do all those who die and are born in the form realm undergo existence in the form realm (*rūpabhava*)? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There are cases where one dies and is reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), yet does not undergo existence in the form realm (*rūpabhava*).
That is to say:
Passing away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one arises as an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This constitutes the acquisition of a form-existence (*rūpabhava*), yet it does not mean that one dies and is reborn within the form realm itself.
That is to say:
Passing away from the desire realm, one arises as an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm.
There are also those who die and are born within the form realm, and they likewise experience the existence of form (*rūpabhava*).
That is to say:
Dying in the form realm, one arises in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the form realm.
This existence does not consist of dying or being born within the form realm itself, nor does it involve receiving a form-realm existence (*rūpabhava*).
That is to say:
One dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the desire or formless realms;
one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the formless or desire realms.
Are all those who die and are reborn in the formless realm necessarily subject to existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*)?
Answer: All those who die and are reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) receive a formless existence (ārūpyabhava).
However, there are those who receive a formless existence who do not die in the formless realm but are born in the formless realm.
That is to say:
passing away from the desire realm or the form realm and being reborn in the formless realm.
How many are there who die and are reborn within the desire realm?
Answer: Four. Namely:
Ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire and form realms.
How many are there who die and are born in the form realm? Answer:
Three: namely,
ordinary beings of the desire realm, ordinary beings of the form realm, and noble ones of the form realm.
How many are there who die and are born in the formless realm? Answer: Two.
That is to say:
ordinary beings and noble ones in the formless realm.
Are all those who do not die or take birth in the desire realm necessarily not experiencing existence in the desire realm?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are cases where one neither dies nor is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet it is not that one does not undergo rebirth in the desire existence (*kāmabhava*).
That is to say:
one passes away from the form realm and arises as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm.
There is no such thing as not experiencing the existence of desire, nor is there any death or birth that does not occur within the desire realm.
That is to say:
passing away from the desire realm, one arises as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) of the form realm.
This existence does not consist of dying and being born within the desire realm, nor does it involve receiving a birth in the desire realm.
That is to say:
passing away from the realm of form, one is reborn in the realm of form or the formless realm;
passing away from the formless realm, one is reborn in the formless realm.
There are cases where one dies and is reborn not outside the desire realm, yet does not fail to undergo existence within the desire realm;
that is to say:
passing away from the desire realm, one arises in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the desire realm.
Are all those who do not die or take birth in the form realm necessarily not experiencing existence in the form realm?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations.
There are cases where one does not die or take birth in the form realm, yet it is not that one does not undergo existence in the form realm.
That is to say:
passing away from the desire realm and arising as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) of the form realm.
There is a non-sensuous form existence (arūpya-rūpa-bhava) that is not such that one does not die and take birth within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
That is to say:
passing away from the realm of form, one arises as an intermediate state being (antarābhava) in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
There are those who do not die or take birth in the form realm, nor do they undergo existence in the form realm;
that is to say:
passing away from the desire realm, they are born in the desire or formless realms.
One who passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the formless or desire realms:
there is one who does not die in the form realm nor is reborn there, yet it is not the case that they do not undergo existence in the form realm.
That is to say:
One passes away from the form realm and arises in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the form realm.
Are all those who do not die or take birth in the formless realm necessarily not receiving a formless existence?
Answer: Those who do not die or are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) all do not undergo existence in the formless realm (ārūpyabhava).
However, there are those who undergo existence in the formless realm who do not die in the formless realm, yet are not born in the formless realm.
That is to say:
dying in the formless realm and being born in the desire or form realms.
How many are there who do not die and are not born in the desire realm?
Answer: Five. Namely:
Regarding those who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the desire realm, ordinary beings in the form and formless realms, and noble ones (*ārya*):
how many are there who do not die or take birth in the form realm?
Answer: Six. Namely:
Regarding ordinary beings and noble ones within the three realms:
how many are there who do not die or take birth in the formless realm? Answer:
The four are:
ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire realm and the form realm.
Is there anyone who dies in the desire realm and is not reborn in the desire realm? Answer: There is.
That is to say:
one who has arisen as an intermediate being (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm or the form realm may be reborn in the formless realm or attain parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible for one to die in the desire realm and not be reborn in the form realm?
Answer: There are. Namely:

One who arises in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) may be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or may attain parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible, however, for one to die in the desire realm and not be reborn in the formless realm?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
One arises in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm or the form realm, or attains parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible for one to die in the form realm and not be reborn in the form realm?
Answer: Yes.
There is. That is to say:
when one arises as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm or the form realm, or is born into the formless realm, or attains parinirvāṇa.
Is there anyone who dies in the form realm and is not reborn in the desire realm? Answer: There is.
That is to say:
arising as an intermediate being (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm or the form realm, one is born in the formless realm or attains parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible that one dies in the form realm and is not born in the formless realm?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
One may arise in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or attain parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible to die in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and not be reborn in the formless realm?
Answer: Yes.
There are. That is to say:
those who arise as intermediate beings (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm or the form realm, or those who attain parinirvāṇa.
Is there anyone who dies in the formless realm and is not reborn in the desire realm? Answer: There is.
That is to say:
one who has arisen in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm or the form realm may be born in the formless realm, or attain parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible for one to die in the formless realm and not be born in the form realm?
Answer: There is. Namely:
Those who arise in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire or form realms and are then reborn in the formless realm, or attain parinirvāṇa—
how many are there among those who die in the desire realm and are not reborn in the desire realm?
Answer: Six. That is to say:
Regarding ordinary beings and noble ones within the three realms:

how many are there who die in the desire realm and are not reborn in the form realm? Answer: *Note: This is the opening of a formal Abhidharma inquiry. The full answer would typically follow with a detailed enumeration based on the specific categories of beings and their rebirth destinies.*
Sixth: namely, ordinary beings and noble ones within the three realms.
How many are those who die in the various desire realms and are not reborn in the formless realm? Answer: Four.
That is to say:
ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire and form realms.
Among those who die in the form realm and are not reborn in the form realm, how many are there?
Answer: Five. Namely:
Regarding ordinary beings of the desire realm, ordinary beings of the form and formless realms, and noble ones:
how many are there who die in the form realm and are not reborn in the desire realm?
Answer: Five. Namely:
Regarding ordinary beings of the desire realm, ordinary beings of the form and formless realms, and noble ones:
how many are there who die in the form realm but are not reborn in the formless realm?
Answer: Three. Namely:
Regarding those born as ordinary beings in the desire realm, and ordinary beings and noble ones in the form realm:
how many are there who, upon dying in the formless realm, are not reborn in the formless realm?
Answer: Two. Namely:

Regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): how many are there who die in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and are not reborn in the desire realm? Answer: [There are none].
The four are:
ordinary beings and noble ones in the formless realm, and ordinary beings in the desire and form realms.
How many are those who die in the formless realm and are not reborn in the form realm? Answer: Four.
That is to say:
ordinary beings and noble ones in the formless realm, and ordinary beings in the desire and form realms.
Is it possible for one to die in the desire realm and not be reborn within the three realms?
Answer: There is. Namely:
One may arise in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or attain parinirvāṇa.
Is it possible for one who dies in the form realm not to be reborn within the three realms?
Answer: Yes.
There are. That is to say:

Third: namely, ordinary beings in the desire realm.
How many are those who, having been born as ordinary beings or noble ones in the form realm, die in the formless realms and are not reborn in the three realms? Answer:
The second refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Is there anyone who, without having abandoned the defilement of desire, passes away and is not reborn in the desire realm? Answer: There is.
That is to say:
one arises as an intermediate being (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm.
Is it possible for one who has not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm to die and not be reborn in either the desire or form realms?
Answer: There is. Namely:
There are intermediate existences (*antarābhava*) arising in the desire and form realms.
Is it possible that one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm, at the end of life, is not reborn within the three realms?
Answer: Yes.
There are. That is to say: the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
How many are those who, without having abandoned the defilements of sensual desire, do not take birth in the desire realm at the end of their lives?
Answer: Two.
That is to say:
ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire realm.
Among these, how many are there who, having not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm, do not take birth in the desire or form realms at the end of their lives?
Answer: Four. That is to say:

Regarding ordinary beings and noble ones in the desire and form realms who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm, and who, at the end of their lives, are not reborn within the three realms— how many such individuals are there? Answer:
The four are:
ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire realm and the form realm.
In this regard, regarding the desire realm— how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*),
and how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) bind them? Answer:
In ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase and nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) bind.
In noble ones (*ārya*), ten underlying tendencies increase and six fetters bind.
Regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): how many underlying tendencies increase for both ordinary beings and noble ones?
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) are they bound? Answer:
For ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), sixty-two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase, and they are bound by six fetters.
In the noble ones (*ārya*), six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase and three fetters (*saṃyojana*) bind.
Regarding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones, how many underlying tendencies increase, and how many fetters bind?
Answer: In ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase, and they are bound by six fetters (*saṃyojana*).
In noble ones (*ārya*), three underlying tendencies increase, and they are bound by three fetters.
Forty-two [factors] increase accordingly; two [factors] arise through conditions and immediate succession;
there are those who possess faculties yet do not know or realize. In this chapter, I wish to explain fully the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*),

and from the eye faculty up to the proclivity of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm— among these ninety-eight proclivities, how many proclivities increase (*anuśerate*) in each one?

Answer: The eye faculty is associated with the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation. It is increased by these latent dispositions.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
As for the female faculty, it is pervasive throughout the desire realm and is increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation.
The male faculty (*puruṣendriya*)—is also like this.

The life faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—is subject to the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are omnipresent throughout the three realms as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi-pañcendriya*)—are also like this.
Regarding the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*): all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with it.
The same applies to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Regarding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*): [the latent dispositions] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and all pervasive [dispositions] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) increase in accordance with it.

Furthermore, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in relation to] the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya)— namely, those of the form realm and all [those] of the desire realm,
excluding doubt (vicikitsā) that takes the untainted as its object and the ignorance (avidyā) associated with it.
All other latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with it.
Regarding the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasyendriya), all latent dispositions of the desire realm increase in association with it.
Regarding the three untainted faculties (anāsravendriya), no latent dispositions increase in association with them.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, and tangibles; and the elements of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and body-consciousness—these are pervasive throughout the desire realm and the form realm.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase [in relation to these].

The same applies to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the spheres of visible form, sound, and tangibles; the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the aggregate of appropriated form (*rūpôpādāna-skandha*), and the first five elements; as well as to phenomena that are material, visible, and resistant (*sapratigha*).

The odor, flavor, nose, tongue, and consciousness elements are pervasive throughout the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and are increased by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The same applies to the odor and flavor bases (*gandha- and rasa-āyatana*).
Regarding the mind-base (*manāyatana*), the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*)—all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

The same applies to the mind-base, the phenomena-base, the last four aggregates (*skandha*), the last four clinging-aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), the consciousness-element, formless phenomena, invisible phenomena, non-resistant phenomena, contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena, past, future, and present phenomena, and phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
In untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas—no latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase.
It is the same for dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and dharmas not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
For wholesome (*kuśala*) and dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), [the latent dispositions] are the universal [defilements] of the three realms.
Furthermore, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation increase in relation to them.
As for unwholesome states and those states bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), all latent dispositions of the desire realm increase in relation to them.
As for neutral states (*avyākṛta-dharma*), [the latent dispositions] of all [categories] in the form and formless realms, as well as two classes of the desire realm, increase in relation to them.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] increase therein.
As for phenomena pertaining to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), all latent dispositions of the realm of form increase therein.
As for phenomena pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all latent dispositions of the formless realm increase therein.
Regarding phenomena abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*): all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned by seeing increase with respect to them.
Regarding the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and origin (*samudaya-satya*): all latent dispositions increase with respect to them.
Regarding the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*): no latent dispositions increase with respect to them.
The same applies to the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the three samādhis.
Regarding the four dhyānas, all latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the form realm increase therein.
The four immeasurables are increased by the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The same applies to the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the first eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding the four formless [attainments], all underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the formless realm increase therein.

Regarding the last five liberations and the last two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana), the underlying tendencies that are omnipresent in the formless realm as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

Regarding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*): with the exception of those views that take the untainted as their object, all other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association with it.
Regarding the threefold samādhi: the universal latent dispositions of the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with it.

Regarding the fetter of the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*): all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), increase therein.
The same applies to the lower-fetter of the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-augha-nīvaraṇa*), the view of a self-existent body itself, and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*): all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), the universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) increase [in association with it].

The same applies to the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśasaṃyojana*), and the lower-tier fetter (*avarabhāgīyasaṃyojana*) that is the adherence to precepts and observances.

Regarding the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsāsaṃyojana*): it increases through the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*) associated with doubt, which has as its object outflows (*sāsrava*) abandoned by vision (*darśanaprahātavya*), as well as that which has as its object the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The same applies to the fetter of doubt among the lower-tier fetters (*ānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of doubt (*anuśaya*), and the fetter of doubt.
As for the unwholesome roots of greed and hatred, the underlying tendencies with outflow (*sāsrava*) that have the desire realm as their object increase [in relation to them].

The same applies to the first two bodily fetters, the first two hindrances, the fetter of ill-will, the first two lower-tier fetters, the first two underlying tendencies, and the fetter of resentment.

Regarding the unwholesome root of delusion: all other latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase [in association] with it, except for those types of ignorance (avidyā) that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.
Regarding the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava): all latent dispositions belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) increase [in association] with it.
The same applies to the flood, yoke, and clinging of sensual desire; and to the hindrances of torpor-and-drowsiness and restlessness.
As for the outflows: all underlying tendencies of the form and formless realms increase in accordance with them.
The flood and yoke of existence, and the clinging to the doctrine of self—these are likewise.
Regarding the outflow of ignorance: with the exception of that ignorance which takes the untainted as its object, all other underlying tendencies increase in association with it.
The same applies to the flood and yoke of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*, *vidhā*), the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*), and the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*).

Regarding the flood and yoke of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*, *vidhā*): the latent tendency of ignorance associated with views increases in relation to both those [states] that have outflow as their object and are to be abandoned by vision, as well as those that are without outflow and have views as their associated object.
The same applies to the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), and the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*).
