Regarding this bond of clinging to what is real (*satkāyadṛṣṭiparāmarśa-bandhana*), the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that have outflows (*sāsrava*) and take [conditioned] objects as their referent increase through being abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
The same applies to the view-grasping (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) and the grasping-fetters (parāmarśa-saṃyojana).

Regarding the remorse-hindrance (kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa), the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are omnipresent in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) increase [in association with it].

The envy-fetter (īrṣyā-saṃyojana), the stinginess-fetter (mātsarya-saṃyojana), and the group of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact—the same applies to these envy- and stinginess-fetters as well.

Regarding the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*): the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) associated with doubt that takes untainted objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), increase therein.

Regarding the fetters of greed (*rāga-saṃyojana*) and pride (*māna-saṃyojana*): the latent tendencies of the outflow-tainted objects in all three realms (*traidhātuka-sāsrava-ālambana*) increase therein.
The same applies to the group of craving born of mental contact, the latent tendencies of pride, and the fetters of craving and pride.
Regarding sensual desire for the form realm—there is the increase of the pervasive latent tendencies of the form realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding the craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*): the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm increase therein.

Regarding the latter three fetters leading to higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*): the pervasive and cultivation-abandoned latent dispositions of both the form and formless realms increase therein.

Regarding the group of cravings born of eye, ear, and body-contact—the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that are omnipresent throughout the desire and form realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase [in relation to them].
Regarding the underlying tendency of sensual greed—the underlying tendencies pertaining to the outflows of the form and formless realms increase [in relation to them].

Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm: all such dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm, as well as the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), increase [in association with them].

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm: all such dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), increase [in association with them].

Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the desire realm—all such [dispositions] to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, with the exception of those taking the untainted as their object and uncommon ignorance—along with all pervasive latent dispositions, increase in association.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the desire realm— excluding those with pure objects (*anāsravālambana*) and non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*)— are [to be abandoned] by the path of seeing within the desire realm.
All other [defilements] and the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [in association with it].
Regarding the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm— all those to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as the universal latent dispositions, increase [in association with it].
The same applies in detail to the five categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms.

The distinction is that one should speak of "one's own realm" (*svadhātu*), from the eye faculty up to the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, as well as the consciousness that takes these as objects and the consciousness that takes those objects as its objects. Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions, how many latent dispositions increase (*anuśerate*) for each of these?
Answer: The eye faculty conditions consciousness belonging to the three categories of the desire realm and the form realm.
The universal [afflictions] of the formless realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation are the objects of the consciousness that takes them as its object.
The four categories of the three realms are likewise for the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The female faculty is conditioned by consciousness.
The three categories of the desire realm,
the universal [defilements] of the form realm,
and those abandoned through cultivation.
The object-condition consciousness consists of four categories from the desire realm and three categories from the form realm.
The universal [factors] of the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation are likewise [not associated] with the male faculty and the faculty of suffering.
The life-faculty conditions consciousness belonging to the three realms and three categories;
it also conditions the object-conditioned consciousness.
The four categories within the three realms:
the mind-faculty, the consciousness that takes [them] as its object, and the consciousness that takes the object of that object as its object.
The conditioned object-condition is likewise for the faculty of equanimity. As for the faculty of pleasure, it is the condition for consciousness.
The four categories of the desire realm;
those conditioned by the form realm;
and two categories of the formless realm.
And the universal [factors],
the object-condition consciousness,
and the four categories of the desire and formless realms.
The conditioned objects of the form realm are the objects of the faculty of joy; they are the objects of consciousness associated with the desire and form realms that have conditioned objects.
The two categories [of afflictions] of the formless realm,
as well as the universal [afflictions], are the objects of the object-conditioning consciousness.
The desire and form realms have conditioned objects as their conditions;
the four divisions of the formless realm [have them as well].
The faculty of grief has consciousness as its condition.
The outflow-conditions (sāsrava-ālambana) of the desire realm,
the universal [defilements] of the form realm,
and those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The object-condition consciousness (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna) has conditioned phenomena of the desire realm as its objects,
and the three categories [of defiled phenomena] of the form realm.
The universal factors of the formless realm,
those to be abandoned by cultivation,
and the five faculties beginning with faith.
Conditioned by consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and conditioned by the object of consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*). These pertain to the four categories within the three realms.
Three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) take consciousness as their object.
The two categories of the three realms,
as well as the universal [factors],
are the object-conditioned consciousnesses.
The three realms and four categories consist of the consciousnesses conditioned by the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, and tangibles.
These belong to the three categories within the desire realm and the form realm.
The universal [defilements] of the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation are the objects of the consciousness that takes them as its object.
The three realms and four categories:
the sense bases of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, and tangibility; the aggregate of form-clinging (*rūpôpādāna-skandha*);
and the first five elements—these are likewise both visible and resistant (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*).
The elements of odor, taste, nose, tongue, and consciousness have consciousness as their condition;
they consist of the three categories of the desire realm and the universal [defilements] of the form realm.
And those abandoned by cultivation;
the consciousnesses that take these as objects;
and the four categories of the desire realm.
The three categories of the form realm,
the universal [defilements] of the formless realm,
and those abandoned through cultivation.
The same applies to the spheres of odor and taste.
The consciousness-elements of eye, ear, and body take as their objects the three categories of the desire and form realms.
The object-condition consciousness consists of the four categories of the desire realm and the form realm,
the two categories of the formless realm,
and the universal [defilements].

The mind element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are consciousness conditioned by objects (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and consciousness conditioned by the conditions of objects (*ālambanapratyaya-vijñāna*). They have conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their object. The mind base (*mana-āyatana*) is likewise.
The same applies to the last four aggregates, to conditioned phenomena,
and to phenomena of the past, future, and present. This also applies to consciousness that takes the dharma-element as its object.
All [factors] of the three realms;
consciousness that takes objects as its object; and conditioned objects.

The same applies to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), as well as to formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and wholesome phenomena. Furthermore, the consciousness that takes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as its object [is also included].
The four categories of the desire realm and the form realm;
the two categories of the formless realm;
and the universal [factors].
The object-condition consciousness consists of the four categories within the three realms;
the same applies to material phenomena.
The latter four aggregates of clinging have consciousness as their object and are with outflows.
The object-condition consciousness (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna) has conditioned phenomena as its object; it is the element of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu).

The same applies to contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) and phenomena to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaprahātavyadharma*). As for uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*), they are the objects of consciousness.
The three realms, the three categories,
as well as the universal [mental factors], and the consciousness that takes objects as its objects.
The conditioned object-condition and the non-abandonable phenomena are likewise.
The consciousness that takes unconditioned phenomena as its object consists of two categories from each of the three realms,
as well as the universal [mental factors].
Consciousness conditioned by objects has conditioned things as its object; consciousness conditioned by unwholesome phenomena has unwholesome phenomena as its object.

The objects of consciousness in the desire realm that have outflows (sāsrava) as their conditions, the universal factors (sarvatraga) of the form realm, and those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) are the objects of the object-conditioning consciousness (ālambanālambana-vijñāna).
The conditioned factors of the desire realm;
the three categories of the form realm;
and the universal factors of the formless realm.
The same applies to the factors bound to the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation.
Consciousness conditioned by indeterminate dharmas consists of the three categories of the desire realm and those with outflows (sāsrava) conditioned by the form and formless realms.
The object-condition consciousness consists of the four categories of the desire realm and those with conditioned objects from the form and formless realms.
The consciousness that takes as its object the dharmas associated with the form realm consists of the three categories of the desire realm and the outflow-tainted objects of the form realm.
The universal [defilements] of the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation are the objects of the consciousness that takes them as its object.
The three categories of the desire realm;
the conditioned objects of the form realm;
and the four categories of the formless realm.
The consciousness that takes as its object the phenomena associated with the formless realm consists of the three categories of the desire and form realms,
and the outflow-tainted objects of the formless realm.
The object-condition consciousness consists of three categories of the desire realm and four categories of the form realm.
The consciousness that takes conditioned phenomena of the formless realm as its object, and the consciousness that takes the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training as its object,
consists of two categories within the three realms.
And the universal [factors],
the object-conditioned consciousness,
and those belonging to the four categories of the three realms.
The consciousness that takes as its object dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner consists of four categories from the three realms,
as well as those with outflows that are abandoned through the path of vision.
The object-condition consciousness has conditioned phenomena as its object;
it is the consciousness that takes the phenomena abandoned by cultivation as its object.

The three realms and three categories [of objects] are the objects of the consciousness that takes objects as its objects. The three realms and four categories [of objects] are the objects of the consciousness that takes consciousness as its object.
The truths of suffering and origination are consciousnesses with outflow as their object.
They are consciousnesses that take objects as their objects.
The conditioned object-condition is likewise for conventional knowledge.
As for the consciousness that takes the truth of cessation as its object:
The two categories of the three realms,
as well as the universal [factors], are the consciousnesses that take objects as their objects.
Conditioned by the conditioned,
consciousness conditioned by the truth of the path pertains to two categories within the three realms.
And the universal [factors], as well as the object-condition consciousness,
consist of four categories across the three realms.
The same applies to the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation,
and the path, as well as the three samādhis.
The consciousnesses that take the four dhyānas as their object consist of the four categories of the desire realm and the conditioned objects of the form realm.
The two categories [of afflictions] of the formless realm,
as well as the universal [afflictions], are the objects of the consciousness that takes them as its objective condition.
The four categories of the desire realm and the formless realm;
the conditioned objects of the form realm;
and the consciousnesses that take the immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, and equanimity as their objects.
The three categories of the desire and form realms,
the universal [defilements] of the formless realm,
and those abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*):
it consists of three categories from the desire realm and four categories from the form and formless realms.
The pure liberation,
the latter four bases of mastery,
and the first eight totalities.

The same applies to the immeasurable of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which takes as its object the consciousnesses belonging to the three categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*): there are three categories in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and four categories in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The two categories of the formless realm,
as well as the universal [defilements],
and the first two liberations.
The same applies to the first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Regarding the three lower formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they take consciousness as their object and take the object-of-consciousness as their object.
The three categories of the desire realm,
the four categories of the form realm,
and the conditioned objects of the formless realm.
The consciousness that takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object consists of the three categories of the desire and form realms,
and the outflow-tainted objects of the formless realm.
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*): it consists of three categories from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and four categories from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The conditioned objects of the formless realm are the consciousness that is the object of the liberations of the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness, as well as the consciousness that is the object of the object-condition.
These are the three categories of the desire realm.
The four categories of the form and formless realms;
the last two liberations and the last two bases of mastery, which take consciousness as their object;
and the three categories of the three realms.
The object-condition consciousness consists of three categories from the desire realm and four categories from the form and formless realms.
Dharma-knowledge takes as its object the two categories [of afflictions] of the desire realm,
as well as the universal [afflictions].
The universal [defilements] of the form realm,
as well as those abandoned through cultivation,
take consciousness as their object-condition.
The four categories of the desire realm,
the three categories of the form realm,
and the universal [defilements] of the formless realm.
And those abandoned through cultivation:
the consciousness that takes subsequent knowledge as its object consists of the two categories of the form and formless realms.
And the universal [factors],
the desire-realm universal [factors],
and those abandoned through cultivation.
The object-condition consciousness consists of three categories from the desire realm and four categories from the form and formless realms.
The knowledge of others' minds takes as its object the consciousnesses of four categories of the desire realm, four categories of the form realm,
and two categories of the formless realm.
And the universal [mental factors],
as well as the object-condition consciousness,
consist of four categories across the three realms.

The consciousness that takes the threefold samādhi as its object consists of the three realms and the three categories; the consciousness that takes that [first] consciousness as its object likewise consists of the three realms and the three categories.

The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the object-condition for consciousness in four categories within the three realms; it is also [the object-condition] for three categories within the three realms.
The object-condition consciousness consists of four categories within the three realms.
The same applies to the view of a self-identity, the fetters conducive to the lower realms, the view of a self-identity, and the view of extremes.
The fetter of adherence to rules and observances takes as its object consciousness pertaining to the three realms and three categories,
as well as that which is associated with outflows and abandoned through the path of vision.
The object-condition consciousness consists of four categories within the three realms.

The same applies to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the fetter of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśasaṃyojana*), the lower-fetter of clinging to precepts and observances (*avarabhāgīya-śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*), and clinging to precepts and observances itself.
The fetter of doubt has outflows as its object;
the object-condition consciousness [also] has outflows as its object.

The conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya*) are as follows: the outflows (*āsrava*) of ignorance, the floods (*ogha*), the yokes (*yoga*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), the fetter of adherence to this as real (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the fetters of greed and pride (*rāga-māna-saṃyojana*), the lower-fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), the group of cravings born of mental contact (*manaḥ-saṃsparśa-ja-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of pride, ignorance, views, and doubt; likewise for the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of craving, pride, ignorance, views, grasping, and doubt.
The three unwholesome roots, the consciousness conditioned by the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*),
the objects of the outflows of the desire realm,
and those [factors] of the form realm that are universal (*sarvatraga*) and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The object-condition consciousness consists of the conditioned factors of the desire realm and the three categories of the form realm.
The universal [defilements] of the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation;

the flood, yoke, and grasp of desire; the first two bodily fetters; the hindrances other than remorse; the fetter of aversion; the first two lower-tier fetters; the latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion; and the fetter of ill will.
The same applies to the consciousnesses that have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana):
those belonging to the three categories of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The outflow-tainted objects of the form and formless realms are the object-condition for the consciousness that takes them as its object;
these are the three categories of the desire realm.

The outflows (*āsrava*), yokes (*yoga*), grasping at a self-identity (*ātmavādopādāna*), and the underlying tendency of craving for existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*) that have conditioned phenomena of the form and formless realms as their object are likewise so.
The objects of the hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*) are the three categories of the desire realm,
the universal [defilements] of the form realm, and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The objects of the objects of that consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) are the four categories of the desire realm.
The three categories of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
the universal [defilements] and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
and the fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*), as well as the group of cravings born of the nose, tongue, and touch, together with the fetters of envy and avarice.
It is likewise.
The form-attachment-favorable-to-the-higher-bonds (rūparāga-ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana) takes as its object the consciousness of the three categories of the desire realm and the form realm.
The universal [defilements] of the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation are the object-condition for the consciousness that takes them as its object;
these pertain to the three categories of the desire realm.
The four categories of the form and formless realms;
the objects of the final four fetters leading to higher rebirth (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*);
and the three categories of the three realms.

Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*): it consists of three categories from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and four categories from the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).

The consciousness that conditions the group of cravings born of eye, ear, and body-contact has as its objects the three categories of the desire and form realms. The consciousness that conditions those objects likewise has as its objects the three categories of the desire and form realms.
The four categories of the desire and form realms,
as well as the universal and cultivation-abandoned [defilements] of the formless realm—
these are the latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and those abandoned through cultivation, which take consciousness as their object.
The three categories of the desire realm,
the universal [defilements] of the form realm, and those abandoned through cultivation are the object-conditioned consciousnesses.
The four categories of the desire realm,
the three categories of the form realm,
and the universal and cultivation-abandoned [defilements] of the formless realm.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) that take consciousness as their object consist of the three categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those with outflows (*sāsrava*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The universal [afflictions] of the form realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation,
which take consciousness as their object-condition, have conditioned phenomena of the desire realm as their objective support.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the desire realm take as their object the consciousness [associated with] the three categories of the form realm, the universal [defilements] of the formless realm, and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
The three categories of the desire realm,
those with outflows conditioned by the objects of the path of seeing,
the universal [defilements] of the form realm, and those abandoned through cultivation.
The object-condition consciousness consists of four categories of the desire realm and three categories of the form realm.
The pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm,
as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation,
and the latent dispositions of the form realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as through cultivation, take consciousness as their object-condition.
The three categories of the desire and form realms,
as well as the universal [defilements] and those abandoned through cultivation of the formless realm,
are the objects of the object-condition consciousness.
The three categories of the desire realm and the four categories of the form and formless realms:
these are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation that take consciousness as their object within the form realm.
The three categories of the desire and form realms;
the outflow-tainted objects of the form realm abandoned through the vision of cessation;
and the universal [defilements] of the formless realm as well as those abandoned through cultivation.
The object-condition consciousness consists of the three categories of the desire realm and the conditioned objects of the form realm.
The four categories of the formless realm;
the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the form realm that take consciousness as their object;
and the three categories of the desire and form realms.
And those with outflows conditioned by [objects] abandoned through the path of seeing in the form realm;
and those universal [defilements] of the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation, which take the object-conditioning consciousness as their object.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, belonging to the three categories of the desire realm and the four categories of the form and formless realms, take consciousness as their object-condition.
The three divisions of the three realms are the objects of the object-conditioning consciousness;
[these consist of] the three divisions of the desire realm.
The four categories of the form and formless realms.

The consciousness that serves as the object-condition for the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation in the formless realm consists of three categories from all three realms.
And the contaminated objects to be abandoned by the vision of cessation within the formless realm;
the object-condition consciousness consists of the three categories of the desire realm.
The four categories of the form realm;
the conditioned-object-conditioned [defilements] of the formless realm;
and the consciousness that conditions the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of vision in the formless realm.
The three realms and three divisions,
as well as the formless realm,
[include] those factors with outflows that are objects of the path of seeing and are to be abandoned by it.
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*):
it consists of three categories from the desire realm and four categories from the form and formless realms.
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Fascicle Five.
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Fascicle Six.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

In the second section on the Aggregates of Bondage (*saṃyojana-skandha*), within the fourth sub-section on the Ten Gates of Compendium (*daśamukha-saṃgraha*), part two: Regarding the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) … up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm—within the fifteen categories (*pakṣa*) of mind across the three realms, how many minds arise immediately after (*samanantara*) each one?
Answer: The mind-faculty (manas-indriya) gives rise to fifteen types of consciousness by way of equal-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
The same applies to the faculty of equanimity (upekṣā-indriya) and the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā-indriya).
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)—as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)—gives rise to eleven minds.
The faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*)—as an immediately preceding condition—gives rise to five minds.
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is likewise.
The faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*) gives rise to ten minds through immediate succession (*samanantara*).
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) does not give rise to any mind through immediate succession.
The faculties of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) and "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) give rise to three minds through immediate succession.
The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousness elements arise immediately after ten types of mind.
The olfactory and gustatory consciousness elements arise immediately after five types of mind.
The same applies to unwholesome dharmas.
From the mind, dharma, and mental-consciousness elements (*dhātu*), fifteen minds arise in immediate succession (*anantara*).
These consist of the mind and dharma bases (*āyatana*).
The last four aggregates,
the last four grasping aggregates,
and the consciousness element.
It is formless, invisible, and non-obstructive.
It is a contaminated, conditioned phenomenon.
It is present, wholesome, or indeterminate.
The factors bound to the three realms that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner—
namely, those abandoned through seeing and cultivation— are also like this.
Uncontaminated factors give rise to three types of mind as their equal-and-immediate [successors].
The same applies to the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those not to be abandoned (*aprahāya*).
Past dharmas give rise to two types of mind by way of equal and immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
future dharmas do not give rise to mind.
The truths of suffering and origination—by way of equal and immediate succession—give rise to fifteen minds.
The same applies to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and conventional knowledge.
The Truth of the Path—by way of equal immediacy—gives rise to three types of consciousness:
the knowledge of the subsequent (anvaya-jñāna), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
The same applies to the three samādhis.
The four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the immediately preceding [condition], give rise to six minds:
the first, second, fourth, and fifth liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
The knowledge of others' minds is also like this.
The third, sixth, and seventh liberations, as well as their immediately succeeding states, give rise to five types of consciousness.
The latter four bases of mastery and the ten totalities are also like this.
The eighth liberation—non-arising consciousness.
Dharma-knowledge—immediately following—gives rise to two types of consciousness.
The three fetters—immediately following—give rise to fifteen types of consciousness.

The same applies to: existence and the outflow of ignorance; the floods and yokes of existence, views, and ignorance; the last three graspings; the last two bodily fetters; the fetters of greed and pride; the last three lower fetters; the last four higher fetters; the five views; the group of craving born of mental contact; the last five latent tendencies; and the six fetters beginning with craving. It is likewise so for these.
The three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*)—through the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—give rise to five types of consciousness.

The same applies to the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the yoke of desire (*kāma-yoga*), the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*), the first two fetters (*saṃyojana*), the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the knots of aversion (*pratigha*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and stinginess (*mātsarya*), the first two fetters conducive to the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the group of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact (*ghrāṇa-jihvā-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), the underlying tendencies of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*) and aversion (*pratigha-anuśaya*), and the knots of resentment (*āghāta*), envy, and stinginess.
The fetters of attachment to the realm of form and the formless realm (*rūpa-ārūpya-rāga ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*)—as immediate antecedents (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—give rise to ten minds.
The latter four fetters of the higher realms—as immediate antecedents—give rise to three minds.
The same applies to the groups of craving born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact.
The thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm produce five types of mind through immediate succession (*samanantara*).
The thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as immediate antecedents (*samanantara-pratyaya*), give rise to ten minds.
The thirty-one underlying tendencies of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as immediate antecedents, give rise to fifteen minds.

Regarding the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—each of these increased latent tendencies should be said to be "with vitarka and with vicāra"?
"Is it 'without vitarka and with vicāra only,' or is it 'without vitarka and without vicāra'? Answer:
It should be said:
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the eye-faculty possess all three [natures].
The same applies to those increased by the ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, pleasure, joy, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) predominant in the female faculty (*strīndriya*) are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
The same applies to those predominant in the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*), the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), and the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

The latent dispositions predominant in the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the objects of form, sound, and touch; and the elements of mind, mental phenomena, and mental consciousness possess all three [characteristics].

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body; visible forms, sounds, and tangibles; the mind and mental objects; the five aggregates, the five aggregates of clinging, and the six elements; that which is material and immaterial, that which is visible and invisible, that which is resistant and non-resistant, and all outflowing conditioned phenomena.

The same applies to the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that increase in relation to dharmas of the past, future, and present; those that are wholesome or indeterminate; those bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu); those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa); and those abandoned through vision (darśana-prahātavya) or cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
Regarding the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness, the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that increase therein are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding the bases of odor and taste, the unwholesome factors bound to the desire realm, the underlying tendencies that increase therein are likewise so.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in the spheres of visual, auditory, and tactile consciousness— some are with vitarka and vicāra,
some are without vitarka and with vicāra only;
the latent dispositions that increase in the factors associated with the formless realm are without vitarka and without vicāra.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the truths of suffering and its origin possess all three [types].

The same applies to the four immeasurables, the first two liberations, the first four bases of mastery, the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, and the latent dispositions increased by the threefold samādhis.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in the first dhyāna are either with vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and with vicāra alone;
those that increase in the [last] three dhyānas are without vitarka and without vicāra.
The same applies to the latent dispositions increased by the four formless attainments, the latter six liberations, the latter four bases of mastery, and the ten totalities.
Regarding the latent dispositions increased by the three fetters—these possess all three [types].

The existence-taint (*bhava-āsava*) and the ignorance-taint (*avijjā-āsava*); the last three floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and clingings (*upādāna*); the last two fetters (*saṃyojana*); the craving-fetter (*rāga-saṃyojana*) and the conceit-fetter (*māna-saṃyojana*); the last three lower-fettering bonds (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); the remaining four higher-fettering bonds (*uddhambhāgīya-saṃyojana*) excluding sensual desire for the formless realm; the five views (*diṭṭhi*); the sixth [clinging], the clinging to the body (*kāyupādāna*); the last five underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); and the underlying tendencies augmented by the six fetters beginning with craving—these are likewise [to be abandoned].
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) augmented by the three unwholesome roots—those accompanied by vitarka and vicāra;

the outflows of desire (kāma-āsava), the floods (ogha), the yokes (yoga), and the clingings (upādāna); the first two bonds (saṃyojana); the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa); the fetters of ill-will, envy, and avarice; the first two fetters conducive to the lower realms; the group of cravings born of nose-contact and tongue-contact; the first two latent dispositions; and the latent dispositions augmented by the fetters of ill-will, envy, and avarice—are likewise [accompanied by vitarka and vicāra].
The latent tendencies increased by craving for the formless realm are without applied thought and without sustained thought.

The latent tendencies increased by the group of cravings born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact are either with applied thought and sustained thought, or without applied thought and with sustained thought.
Alternatively, there are those with no vitarka and only vicāra;
these are the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the thirty-six latent dispositions of the desire realm— possessing both vitarka and vicāra—
and the latent dispositions increased by the thirty-one latent dispositions of the form realm— possessing all three.

Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the thirty-one latent dispositions of the formless realm—which are without vitarka and without vicāra—and each of the latent dispositions increased by the faculties from the eye-faculty up to the ignorance-latent disposition abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm: should these be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, or the faculty of equanimity?
Answer: It should be stated that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) predominant in the eye faculty are associated with four faculties.
Excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*),

the same applies to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, life, pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
The latent tendencies increased by the female faculty (*strī-indriya*) are associated with three faculties,
excluding the pleasure and pain faculties.
The same applies to those increased by the male, joy, and grief faculties.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) predominant in the mind-faculty (manas-indriya) are associated with five faculties.
The latent dispositions predominant in the faculty of suffering (duḥkha-indriya) are associated with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of pleasure (sukha-indriya).
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in the spheres of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the mental consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu) are associated with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya).
The same applies to the latent dispositions that increase in the objects of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body which are abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya-dharma).

Regarding form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibles; eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness; and the mental faculty and the sphere of mental objects—the underlying tendencies that increase therein are associated with the five faculties.

The same applies to: visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*); the five aggregates (*skandha*), the five clinging-aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), and the six elements (*dhātu*); the material and the immaterial; the visible and the invisible; the resistant and the non-resistant; outflowing (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena; the past, future, and present; the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; those bound to the desire realm; those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*); phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*); and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase therein. All are likewise.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in relation to phenomena associated with the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma) are associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) and the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya).
The latent dispositions that increase in relation to phenomena associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma) are associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the truths of suffering and its origin are associated with five faculties.
Those increased by conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) are likewise.
The latent dispositions increased by the first dhyāna are associated with three faculties.
Excluding the faculties of suffering and sorrow,
the same applies to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, and equanimity, as well as by the knowledge of others' minds.
The latent dispositions increased by the second dhyāna are associated with the faculties of joy and equanimity.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) augmented by the immeasurable joy (*muditā*), the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are likewise [associated with the faculty of pleasure].
The latent dispositions augmented by the third dhyāna are associated with the faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
The latent tendencies (anuśaya) increased in the fourth dhyāna are associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).

The same applies to those increased in the four formless attainments (ārūpya), the latter six liberations (vimokṣa), the latter four bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana).
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the threefold samādhi are associated with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya).
The latent dispositions increased by the three fetters (saṃyojana) are associated with four faculties.

Excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). [These are: the unwholesome root of greed (*lobha-akuśalamūla*); the flood (*ogha*), yoke (*yoga*), and grasping (*upādāna*) of views; the grasping of rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); the fetter of the body consisting of the grasping of rules and observances and the adherence to "this is the truth" (*parāmarśa-kāyagrantha*); the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*); the fetters of greed and conceit (*rāga-māna-saṃyojana*); and the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) of sensual desire, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping of rules and observances, and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

The five views, the six bases of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*), the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire, pride, views, and doubt, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of craving, pride, views, grasping, and doubt, and the latent tendencies that are increased—these are also thus.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the unwholesome root of hatred (dveṣa) are associated with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).

The same applies to the fetter of hatred (pratighasaṃyojana), the hindrance of hatred (pratighanīvaraṇa), the knot of hatred (pratighagrantha), the lower-fetter of hatred (pratighāvarabhāgīyasaṃyojana), the latent disposition of hatred, and the latent dispositions increased by the knot of hatred.
The underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increased by the unwholesome root of delusion are associated with five faculties.

The same applies to those increased by the outflows (āsrava) of desire and ignorance, the floods (ogha), the yokes (yoga), the grasping of desire (kāma-upādāna), the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) of torpor and restlessness, and the underlying tendencies and fetters (saṃyojana) of ignorance.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the outflows with leakage (sāsrava)— which are associated with three faculties,

excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkha) and the faculty of grief (daurmanasya)— are likewise [increased] by the flood of existence (bhava-ogha), the yoke of existence (bhava-yoga), the grasping for the doctrine of self (ātma-vādopādāna), sensual desire for the form realm (rūpa-rāga), restlessness (auddhatya), pride (māna), the fetters conducive to higher rebirth (ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana), and the latent disposition of attachment to existence (bhavarāgānuśaya). These are the latent dispositions increased by them.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) of torpor, restlessness, and doubt are associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculties of pleasure and pain.
The fetters (saṃyojana) of envy and avarice, as well as the fetters of envy and avarice among the nine fetters, increase latent dispositions in the same manner.
The latent tendencies increased by attachment to the formless realm are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

All latent tendencies abandoned through vision and those abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, as well as the latent tendency of pride (*māna*), which increase these [tendencies], are associated with three faculties.
Excluding the faculties of pleasure and pain:
the latent tendencies of attachment to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm increase in association with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of pain.

The latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm that are associated with the latent tendency of aversion (dveṣa-anuśaya) are associated with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
The latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm that are associated with the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) are associated with five faculties.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) augmented by the thirty-one latent dispositions of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are associated with three faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) and the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya).
The latent dispositions augmented by the thirty-one latent dispositions of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
Who possesses the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm?
Who does not achieve it? Answer:
Regarding the eye faculty—those in the form realm and those in the desire realm who have already obtained it and have not lost it achieve it.
In the formless realm and in the desire realm—when not yet obtained or already lost—one does not possess [the faculties].
The same applies to the ear, nose, and tongue faculties.
The body faculty is possessed in the desire and form realms.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)—it is not accomplished.
As for the female and male faculties (strī- and puruṣendriya)—in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), if they have been obtained and not lost—they are accomplished;
in the form and formless realms, as well as in the desire realm if they have not yet been obtained or have already been lost—they are not accomplished.
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), and the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*)—all sentient beings possess these.
The pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*)—those from the Śubhakṛtsna heaven downward, as well as noble ones born in higher realms, possess this.
Ordinary beings born in the higher realms do not possess it.
As for the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*): they possess it in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but they do not possess it in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
The faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*) is accomplished by those from the Ābhāsvara heaven downward,
as well as by noble ones (*ārya*) born in higher realms;
it is not accomplished by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born in higher realms.
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is possessed by those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire;
it is not possessed by those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire.
The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi-pañcendriya*) are possessed by those who have not severed their roots of goodness (*akuśalamūla*).
Those who have severed the roots of goodness do not possess them.
Regarding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*): those who have already obtained them and not lost them possess them;
those who have not yet obtained them or have already lost them do not possess them.
The elements of eye, ear, nose, and tongue are accomplished when they have been obtained and not lost in the form realm and the desire realm;
they are not accomplished when they have not yet been obtained or have already been lost in the formless realm and the desire realm.
The same applies to the bases of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue.
The elements of body, visible form, sound, and tangibility are accomplished in the desire realm and the form realm.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), [these] are not accomplished.

The same applies to the bases of body, visible form, sound, and tangibility; the aggregate of form-grasping (rūpōpādānaskandha); the first five elements (dhātu); phenomena that are visible and possess resistance (sanidarśana-sapratigha-dharma); and phenomena bound to the desire and form realms (kāma-rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma).
The elements of odor, flavor, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness are accomplished in the desire realm;
they are not accomplished in the form or formless realms.
The same applies to the bases of odor and flavor.

The eye, ear, and body-consciousness elements are accomplished when they are present below the Brahma-world, as well as when one is born in the three higher dhyānas and these consciousnesses are currently manifest; they are not accomplished when they are not currently manifest or in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are all possessed by every sentient being.

These consist of the mind base (*manāyatana*), the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*), the last four aggregates (*skandha*), the four clinging-aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), and the consciousness element.

The same applies to formless phenomena, those that are invisible and non-resistant, outflowing and non-outflowing phenomena, conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, past, future, and present phenomena, indeterminate phenomena, those bound to the formless realm, phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, and phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation as well as those not to be abandoned.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is possessed by those in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the form realm (rūpadhātu), and by noble ones (ārya) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
It is not possessed by ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) in the formless realm.
The same applies to material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).
Regarding wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*): those who have not severed their roots of goodness possess them;
those who have severed their roots of goodness do not possess them.
Unwholesome dharmas: one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire possesses them;
one who has already abandoned the defilement of desire does not possess them.
Dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): one who has attained them and not lost them possesses them.
Not yet obtained or already lost—non-possession (*aprāpti*).
Regarding factors abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*): if the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen—one possesses them;
if it has already arisen—one does not possess them.
The truths of suffering and its origin are accomplished by all sentient beings.
The same applies to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and conventional knowledge.
Regarding the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya): if it has been attained and not lost, one possesses it;
if it has not yet been attained or has already been lost, one does not possess it.

The same applies to the four immeasurables (apramāṇa), the eight liberations (vimokṣa), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana), and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
Regarding the Truth of the Path: if already attained, it is possessed;
if not yet attained, it is not possessed.

The same applies to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), as well as to the three samādhis and the triple samādhis.
Regarding the first dhyāna: those below the Brahma-world and noble ones born in higher realms possess it;
ordinary beings born in higher realms do not possess it.
Regarding the second dhyāna— up to the Ābhāsvara heaven—
the noble ones born in higher realms possess it,
whereas ordinary beings born in higher realms do not possess it.
Regarding the third dhyāna— up to the Śubhakṛtsna heaven—
it is accomplished by noble ones born in higher realms,
but not accomplished by ordinary beings born in higher realms.
Regarding the fourth dhyāna: those below the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) heaven, as well as noble ones born in higher realms, possess it;
ordinary beings born in higher realms do not possess it.
Regarding the sphere of infinite space: those below the sphere of infinite space [possess it];
as for noble ones born in higher realms, they possess it;
as for ordinary beings born in higher realms, they do not possess it.
Regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*): those below the sphere of infinite consciousness possess it;
as for noble ones (*ārya*) born in higher realms, they possess it;
as for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born in higher realms, they do not possess it.
Regarding the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana): those below the sphere of nothingness [possess it];
as for noble ones born in higher realms, they possess it;
as for ordinary beings born in higher realms, they do not possess it.
Regarding the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*): one who has not yet produced the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) possesses it;
once it has been produced, one does not possess it.
The same applies to the lower-tier fetter of the view of a self-identity, the view of a self-identity itself, and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*): as long as the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, one possesses them;
once it has arisen, one does not possess them.

The same applies to the flood (*ogha*) and yoke (*yoga*) of views, the grasping (*upādāna*) of views, the grasping of precepts and observances, the last two of the bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*), the last two of the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) consisting of the grasping of precepts and observances and doubt, the last three of the views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of views and doubt, as well as the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of views, grasping, and doubt.
The three unwholesome roots are accomplished by one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of sensual desire, but are not accomplished by one who has already abandoned it.

The same applies to the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the flood (*ogha*), the yoke (*yoga*), and the clinging (*upādāna*); the first two fetters (*saṃyojana*); the first four hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); the fetters of aversion (*pratigha*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*); the first two fetters conducive to the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); the group of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact; the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*vyāpāda*); and the fetters of resentment (*krodha*), envy, and avarice.
The existence-outflow (*bhava-āsrava*) and the ignorance-outflow (*avidyā-āsrava*): one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*) possesses them;
one who has already abandoned the defilement of the formless realm does not possess them.

The same applies to the existence-flood (*bhava-ogha*), the ignorance-flood (*avidyā-ogha*), the existence-yoke (*bhava-yoga*), the yoke of ignorance (*avidyā-yoga*), the grasping at a self-theory (*ātma-vādopādāna*), the fetters of greed (*rāga*) and pride (*māna*), the four subsequent fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the group of craving produced by mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed for existence, pride, and ignorance, and the fetters of craving, pride, and ignorance.
The hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) is possessed by ordinary persons who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
as well as by noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire and for whom the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen.
It is not possessed by ordinary beings who have already abandoned the defilements of desire,
nor by noble ones who have already abandoned the defilements of desire— provided that the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path has already arisen.
The fetter of attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga-ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) is possessed by one who has not yet abandoned passion for the realm of form;
it is not possessed by one who has already abandoned passion for the realm of form.
The group of cravings born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact is possessed by one who has not yet abandoned passion for the Brahma-world.
One who has already become free from the defilements of the Brahma-world does not possess them.
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has not yet become free from the defilements of the desire realm,

as well as a noble one (*ārya*) who has not yet become free from the defilements of the desire realm and for whom the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, do possess the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already abandoned the defilements of desire, noble ones (*ārya*),
and noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire— provided that the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) has already arisen—

are not possessed of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm. Ordinary beings who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire [are possessed of them].
It is also accomplished by noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire— specifically those for whom the dharma-knowledge of origination has not yet arisen—
as well as by ordinary beings and noble ones who have already abandoned the defilements of desire.
Furthermore, noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire—once the dharma-knowledge of origination has arisen—do not possess them.
Nor do ordinary beings who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire possess the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] in the desire realm.
It is also accomplished by noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire— specifically those for whom the dharma-knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen—
as well as by ordinary beings and noble ones who have already abandoned the defilement of desire.
Furthermore, noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire—once the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) has arisen—do not possess [the latent dispositions].

Nor do ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire possess the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) pertaining to the desire realm.
It is also accomplished by noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire— provided that the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen—
as well as by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones who have already abandoned the defilement of desire.

Furthermore, noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire—provided that the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) has already arisen—do not possess [them].
As for those who have not abandoned the defilements of desire, they do possess the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Those who have already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm do not possess them.
As for the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm:

ordinary beings who have not yet become detached from the form realm, as well as noble ones who have not yet become detached from the form realm and in whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, possess them.
It is not possessed by ordinary beings or noble ones who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm,
nor by noble ones who have not yet become detached from the defilements of the form realm but for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has already arisen.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*):

they are possessed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm, as well as by noble ones (*ārya*) who have not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm and for whom the subsequent knowledge of the origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.
It is not possessed by ordinary beings or noble ones who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm,
nor by noble ones who have not yet become detached from the defilements of the form realm but for whom the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm to be abandoned through the vision of cessation are accomplished by: (1) ordinary beings who have not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm;
and (2) noble ones who have not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm, provided that the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.
It is not possessed by ordinary beings who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm,
nor by noble ones who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm— provided that the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodhānvayajñāna) has already arisen.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the form realm are possessed by: (1) ordinary beings who have not yet become free from the defilements of the form realm;
and (2) noble ones who have not yet become free from the defilements of the form realm, provided that the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen.
It is not possessed by ordinary beings or noble ones who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm,
nor by noble ones who have not yet become detached from the defilements of the form realm but for whom the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) has already arisen.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm to be abandoned by cultivation are possessed by one who has not yet become free from attachment to the form realm;
they are not possessed by one who has already become free from attachment to the form realm.
The latent dispositions of the formless realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering are possessed by one in whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.
Regarding those that have already arisen—one does not possess them.

Regarding the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)—if the subsequent knowledge of the origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen—one possesses them.
Regarding those already arisen: one does not possess them.

Regarding the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation in the formless realm: one possesses them as long as the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen.
Regarding those that have already arisen—one does not possess them.

Regarding the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the formless realm—one possesses them as long as the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) has not yet arisen.
Regarding those already arisen—one does not possess them.
Regarding the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—if one has not yet become free from the defilements of the formless realm—one possesses them;
if one has already become free from the defilements of the formless realm—one does not possess them.

When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of each factor, from the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm— at that time,
among the ninety-eight latent tendencies, how many latent tendencies attain full knowledge?
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are exhausted?
Answer: When the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*) is fully known (*parijñāta*), craving for forms (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (pṛthagjana): thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known, but no fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
For a noble one (ārya): three underlying tendencies are fully known, but no fetters are exhausted.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Regarding the female and male faculties: when they are fully known (*parijñāta*), sensual craving is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known, the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For the Noble One—the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known (*parijñāta*), and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
It is the same for the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*): at the time it is fully known—
With the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm,
three underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known and three fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
The same applies to the faculties of mind, equanimity, faith, and so forth.
Regarding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*): at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm is exhausted. That is to say:
when the faculty of pleasure attains full knowledge, no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
Regarding the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*): at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), craving for the Ābhāsvara realm is exhausted.
That is to say:
when the faculty of joy attains full knowledge, there is no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the spheres of visible form, sound, and tangibility—when these are fully known (*parijñā*), craving for form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*) is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known, yet no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For the Noble One—there is full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), but no exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The same applies to the bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, and tangibles; to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of grasping at form (*rūpopādānaskandha*); to the first five elements; and to those phenomena that are material, visible, and resistant, as well as those phenomena bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-saṃprayukta*).

Regarding the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness—at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*) of these, craving for the realm of desire (*kāmarāga*) is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For the Noble One—there is full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The same applies to the spheres of odor and taste, as well as to unwholesome phenomena and those phenomena bound to the desire realm.
Regarding the eye, ear, and body-consciousness elements: when their full knowledge (*parijñā*) is attained, craving for the Brahma world is exhausted.
That is to say:
upon the attainment of full knowledge of the eye, ear, and body-consciousness elements, there is no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Regarding the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*): when full knowledge (*parijñā*) is attained, craving for the formless (*ārūpyarāga*) is exhausted;
three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known, and three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are destroyed.

The same applies to the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*); the last four aggregates (*skandha*), the four grasping-aggregates (*upādānaskandha*); the consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*); formless, invisible, non-obstructive, contaminated (*sāsrava*), and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*); those of the past, future, and present; the wholesome, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātupratisaṃyukta*); those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*); and phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*). It is likewise so.
Regarding the phenomena to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*): at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*),
for one who has not yet abandoned craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*), when the knowledge of the path-type (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) is present,
fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known and three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For one who has already become detached from the craving for form— when the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of the path) is present—
one attains full comprehension (*parijñā*) of seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
This occurs at the time of attaining full comprehension of the truths of suffering and its origin.
With the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm,
three underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully understood (parijñā), and three fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
The same applies to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the latter two liberations (vimokṣa), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the threefold samādhi.
Regarding the first dhyāna—at the time of attaining full knowledge (parijñā), craving for the Brahma-world is exhausted. That is:
when full knowledge of the first dhyāna is attained, there is no exhaustion of fetters (saṃyojana).
Regarding the second dhyāna— at the time of attaining full knowledge (parijñā)—
the craving for the Ābhāsvara realm is exhausted.
That is to say:
In the second dhyāna, one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*), yet there is no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The same applies to the immeasurable joy (*pramuditā-apramāṇa*), the first liberation (*vimokṣa*), and the first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
In the third dhyāna—at the time of attaining full knowledge—the craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm is exhausted.
That is to say: in the third dhyāna, full knowledge is attained, yet there is no exhaustion of fetters.
In the fourth dhyāna—at the time of attaining full knowledge—there is the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*).
For an ordinary person (pṛthagjana): thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known, but no fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
For a noble one (ārya): three underlying tendencies are fully known, but no fetters are exhausted.
The same applies to the three immeasurables, the pure liberation, the latter four spheres of mastery, the first eight spheres of totality, and the knowledge of others' minds.
At the time of attaining full knowledge of the sphere of infinite space, craving for the sphere of infinite space is exhausted.
That is: one attains full knowledge of the sphere of infinite space, yet there is no exhaustion of fetters.
The same applies to the liberation of the sphere of infinite space and its corresponding base of totality.
Regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*): when full knowledge (*parijñā*) is attained, craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness is exhausted.
That is to say:
at the attainment of full knowledge of the sphere of infinite consciousness, there is no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The same applies to the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness and its corresponding base.
Regarding the sphere of nothingness—when full comprehension is attained, craving for the sphere of nothingness is exhausted.
That is: one attains full knowledge of the sphere of nothingness, yet there is no exhaustion of fetters.
The same applies to liberation from the sphere of nothingness.

Regarding the fetter of the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*): at the moment of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is present—for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm—eighteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known, but no fetters are exhausted.

For one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm (rūparāga), there is the full comprehension (parijñā) of nine underlying tendencies (anuśaya), but no exhaustion of fetters (saṃyojana).
The same applies to the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as a lower-fetter (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana), as well as to the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
Regarding the fetters of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*):

at the moment of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is present for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm, fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known and these three fetters are exhausted.

For one who has already become detached from the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*), there is the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the exhaustion of three fetters (*saṃyojana*), and likewise for the flood (*ogha*), yoke (*yoga*), and grasping (*upādāna*) of views;

the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); the last two of the bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*); the last two of the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); the last three of the views (*dṛṣṭi*); and the underlying tendencies of views and doubt (*dṛṣṭi- and vicikitsā-anuśaya*); as well as the fetters of views, grasping, and doubt (*dṛṣṭi-, parāmarśa-, and vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).
