When full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is attained, craving for the realm of desire (*kāmarāga*) is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully comprehended, the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
The Noble One—having attained full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), has exhausted the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The same applies to the flood, yoke, and clinging of sensual desire; the first two of the bodily ties (*bandhana*); the first four hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); the fetters of ill-will, envy, and avarice; the first two lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); the group of cravings born of nose-contact and tongue-contact; the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and ill-will; and the fetters of resentment, envy, and avarice.

Regarding the outflow of sensual desire (*āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*): at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), there is the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*), the attainment of full knowledge of three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the exhaustion of three fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The same applies to the flood (*ogha*) and yoke (*yoga*) of existence and ignorance, the grasping at a self-theory (*ātma-vādopādāna*), the fetters of greed and pride (*rāga-māna-saṃyojana*), the last four higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the group of craving born of mental contact (*mano-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), the underlying tendencies of greed for existence, pride, and ignorance (*bhavarāga-māna-avidyā-anuśaya*), and the fetters of craving, pride, and ignorance (*tṛṣṇā-māna-avidyā-saṃyojana*).
Regarding the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*):

at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has exhausted desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*), thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
When the noble path of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) is present, eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known (parijñā), yet no fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
At the time when the full knowledge of the desire for the form realm (rūparāga) is attained, the craving for the form realm (rūpatṛṣṇā) is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (pṛthagjana): thirty-one latent dispositions (anuśaya) are fully known (parijñāta), but no fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
For a noble one (ārya): three latent dispositions are fully known, but no fetters are exhausted.
When the category of craving born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact is fully understood, craving for the Brahma-world is exhausted.
That is: when these three categories of craving are fully understood, no fetters are yet exhausted.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*):

at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has exhausted craving for the desire realm, thirty-six latent dispositions attain full knowledge and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.

When the Noble One brings the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) into manifestation: there is full comprehension (*parijñā*) of ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), but no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).

At the time of attaining full comprehension of the underlying tendencies to be abandoned by the vision of the Origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the Desire Realm: it is the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has exhausted craving for the Desire Realm.
When thirty-six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known (parijñāta), three fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
When a noble one brings the knowledge of phenomena regarding the aggregates (dharmajñāna) into manifestation, seven underlying tendencies are fully known, but no fetters are exhausted.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation— at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*):
for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has exhausted craving for the desire realm,
thirty-six latent dispositions attain full knowledge and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.

When the Noble One brings the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) into manifestation—one fully knows (*parijñā*) seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), but no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
At the time of fully knowing the underlying tendencies to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) in the desire realm:
it is the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) whose craving for the desire realm is exhausted.
When the thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known (*parijñāta*), the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
When the noble path of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is present, eight underlying tendencies are fully known, but no fetters are exhausted.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm— at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*):
for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when desire is exhausted, thirty-six latent dispositions are fully known and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
The Noble One—attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
This occurs at the time of attaining full knowledge of the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when the craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted: thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known (*parijñāta*), but no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For a noble one (*ārya*), when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) is present before them.
Regarding the eighteen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) for which full knowledge (*parijñā*) is attained but no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted:
at the moment when full knowledge of the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm is attained,
the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has exhausted craving for the form realm.
—Thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known (parijñāta), yet no fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
For the noble one, the subsequent knowledge of the aggregates (anvaya-jñāna) is present before them.
—Twelve underlying tendencies are fully known, yet no fetters are exhausted.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*):

at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has exhausted craving for the form realm, thirty-one latent dispositions attain full knowledge, yet no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
When the noble one brings the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) into manifestation—
there is full comprehension (parijñā) of twelve underlying tendencies (anuśaya), but no exhaustion of fetters (saṃyojana).
This occurs at the time of attaining full comprehension of the underlying tendencies of the form realm (rūpadhātu) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted:
thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known (*parijñāta*), but no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For a noble one (*ārya*), when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is present.
—At the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.

Regarding the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the form realm: at the time of attaining full knowledge, craving for the form realm (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (pṛthagjana): there is full knowledge (parijñā) of thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya), but no exhaustion of fetters (saṃyojana).
For a noble one (ārya): there is full knowledge of three underlying tendencies, but no exhaustion of fetters.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*): at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*),
when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is present,
eighteen latent dispositions are fully known for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm.
There is no exhaustion of fetters.
For one who has already become detached from the defilement of form—nine underlying tendencies are fully known;
there is no exhaustion of fetters.

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*): at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*),
when the subsequent knowledge of the origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) is present,
for one who has not yet become detached from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*), twelve latent dispositions attain full knowledge, but no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.

For one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm—there is the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), but no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).

At the time of attaining full comprehension of the underlying tendencies of the formless realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) manifests.
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm, twelve underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known (*parijñāta*), but no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For one who has already abandoned the defilements of the form realm—six underlying tendencies are fully known, but no fetters are exhausted.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*),
when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is present,
for one who has not yet become free from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), fourteen latent dispositions attain full knowledge and the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm— seven underlying tendencies are fully known and three fetters are exhausted—
at the time when the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm are fully known.
With the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm,
three underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known and three fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.

This occurs at the time of realizing the cessation of each individual factor, from the eye faculty up to the underlying tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are realized through cessation?
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are exhausted? Answer:
When the eye-faculty is realized as ceasing,
craving for forms is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are realized as ceasing, but no fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
The Noble One—having realized the cessation of the three underlying tendencies (anuśaya), has no remaining fetters (saṃyojana).
Up to the Arhat—having realized the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies, has exhausted the nine fetters.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
When the female and male faculties are realized through cessation, craving for the realm of desire is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), when thirty-six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are realized through cessation, the three fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
When a noble one attains the fruit of non-returning—there is the realization of the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of six fetters.
Upon reaching arhatship—there is the realization of the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of nine fetters.
The same applies to the faculties of suffering and sorrow.
When the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is realized through its cessation:
one attains the fruit of Arhatship—the realization of the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The same applies to the faculties of mind, equanimity, faith, and so forth.
When the faculty of pleasure is realized through cessation, craving for the realm of Universal Purity is exhausted. That is to say:
The realization of the cessation of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) results in the exhaustion of no fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Up to the stage of Arhat:
the realization of the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) results in the exhaustion of nine fetters.
When the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) is realized through cessation:
craving for the Ābhāsvara realm is exhausted.
That is to say:
Realizing the cessation of the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*), there is the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Up to the stage of Arhat:
realizing the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there is the exhaustion of the nine fetters.
When one realizes the cessation of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, and the element of tangibles, craving for form is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), when thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are realized as ceased, there is no exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana).
The Noble One—having realized the cessation of the three underlying tendencies (anuśaya), has no remaining fetters (saṃyojana).
Up to the Arhat—having realized the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies, has exhausted the nine fetters.

The same applies to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, and tangible objects; the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the aggregate of appropriated form (*rūpopādānaskandha*), the first five elements, phenomena that possess form (*rūpin*), that are visible (*sanidarśana*), that are resistant (*sapratigha*), and phenomena bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātupratisaṃyukta*).
When the cessation of the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness is realized, craving for the realm of desire is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when the cessation of the thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is realized, the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
The noble one— having attained the fruit of non-returning—
realized the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and exhausted six fetters.
He reached the state of an arhat.
The cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is realized, and the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
The same applies to the spheres of odor and taste, as well as to unwholesome phenomena bound to the desire realm.
This is also the case when the cessation of the visual, auditory, and tactile consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*) is realized.
With the exhaustion of craving for the Brahma-world,
one realizes the cessation of the three elements of consciousness; there is no further fetter to be exhausted.
Upon reaching arhatship,
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
This occurs at the time of realizing the cessation of the mind-base (manāyatana), the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu).
One attains the fruit of arhatship;
there is the realization of the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The same applies to the sense bases of mind and mental objects, the last four aggregates, the four clinging-aggregates, the element of consciousness, formless phenomena, invisible phenomena, non-obstructive phenomena, tainted phenomena, conditioned phenomena, past, future, and present phenomena, wholesome and indeterminate phenomena, phenomena bound to the formless realm, phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, and phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation.
When one realizes the cessation of the phenomena to be abandoned by insight,
one attains the fruit of stream-entry;
one realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.
The same applies up to the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning,
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings the six fetters to an end.
Upon reaching arhatship,

one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight latent tendencies (anuśaya) and brings the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana) to realization at the time of realizing the cessation of the truths of suffering and its origin.
One attains the fruit of arhatship.
One realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The same applies to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the last two liberations, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the threefold triple samādhi.
When one realizes the cessation of the first dhyāna—
the exhaustion of craving for the Brahma-world—
one realizes the cessation of the first dhyāna itself, yet there is no exhaustion of fetters.
Up to the stage of Arhat,
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
This occurs at the time of realizing the cessation of the second dhyāna.
In the Ābhāsvara Heaven, craving is exhausted;
one then realizes the cessation of the second dhyāna, with the exhaustion of fetters.
This continues until the stage of Arhatship.
The realization of the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The same applies to the immeasurable joy (*muditā*), the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
When one realizes the cessation of the third dhyāna,
craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm is exhausted;
that is, upon realizing the cessation of the third dhyāna, there is no further exhaustion of fetters.
Upon reaching arhatship,
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
This occurs at the time of realizing the cessation of the fourth dhyāna.

Regarding the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*): for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is the realization of the cessation of thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), but no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For a noble one (*ārya*), there is the realization of the cessation of three underlying tendencies, but no exhaustion of fetters.
Up to the stage of Arhat—there is the realization of the extinction of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The same applies to the three immeasurables, the pure liberations, the latter four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the first eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the knowledge of others' minds.
When one realizes the cessation of the base of infinite space,
craving for the base of infinite space is exhausted.
That is to say:
He realizes the cessation [of those defilements], and with the exhaustion of the fetters,
he reaches the stage of Arhat.
He realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
The same applies to the liberation of the sphere of infinite space and its corresponding bases of totality.
When one realizes the cessation of the sphere of infinite consciousness,
craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness is exhausted.
That is: he realizes that cessation, with the exhaustion of the fetters,
up to the stage of Arhatship.
One realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and brings the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana) to completion.
The same applies to the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness and its corresponding bases of mastery (kṛtsnāyatana).
When one realizes the cessation of the sphere of nothingness, [the same occurs].
The exhaustion of craving for the sphere of nothingness: that is,
the realization of its cessation, which is the exhaustion of the fetters.
Up to the stage of Arhat,
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and brings the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) to an end.
The same applies to the liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*).
When the fetter of the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) is abandoned and realized,
the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) is present;
eighteen underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are abandoned and realized, yet there is no exhaustion of all fetters.
Upon reaching the fruit of stream-entry,
one realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.
Upon reaching the fruit of once-returning, it is likewise.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*),

one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and brings six fetters (*saṃyojana*) to an end. Upon reaching arhatship (*arhattva*), [the remaining defilements are likewise extinguished].
One realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
The same applies to the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), which is a lower-tier fetter, as well as to the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
When one realizes the cessation of the fetters of adherence to precepts and observances and doubt,
one attains the fruit of stream-entry—
realizing the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and exhausting the three fetters.
It is the same for the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning,
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings the exhaustion of the six fetters to completion.
Up to the stage of Arhat:
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and brings the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) to an end.

The same applies to the flood (*ogha*), yoke (*yoga*), and grasping (*upādāna*) of views; the grasping of rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); the last two bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*); the lower-fettering factors (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) consisting of the grasping of rules and observances and doubt; the last three views; and the underlying tendencies of view and doubt; as well as the fetters of view, grasping, and doubt.
When one realizes the cessation of the three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*),

an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has exhausted desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmāvacara-rāga*) realizes the cessation of thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The noble one— having attained the fruit of non-returning—
realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings the six fetters to an end.
He proceeds to the state of an arhat.
The cessation and realization of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) constitutes the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).

This also applies to the flood (*ogha*), yoke (*yoga*), and clinging (*upādāna*) of sensual desire; the first two of the bodily ties (*bandhana*); the first four hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); the fetters of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and stinginess (*mātsarya*); the first two lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); the group of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact; the underlying tendencies of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*pratigha*); and the fetters of resentment (*krodha*), envy, and stinginess. It is the same for these as well.
When one realizes the cessation of the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*),
one attains the fruit of arhatship.
One realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and brings the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) to an end.

The flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the yoke of ignorance (*avidyā-yoga*), the grasping at a self-theory (*ātma-vādopādāna*), the fetters of greed (*rāga*) and conceit (*māna*), the last four fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the group of craving born of mental contact (*mano-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), the underlying tendencies of greed for existence (*bhavarāga-anuśaya*), conceit, and ignorance, as well as the fetters of craving, conceit, and ignorance—these are also likewise [to be abandoned].
When one realizes the cessation of the hindrance of doubt,
an ordinary person who has exhausted sensual desire realizes the cessation of thirty-six underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.

When the Noble One brings the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) into presence, he realizes the cessation of eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), though no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are yet exhausted;
this constitutes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
He then realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.
The same applies to the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning,
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings six fetters to an end.
Upon reaching arhatship,
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and brings the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana) to witness.
This occurs at the moment of realizing the cessation of sensual desire for the form realm (rūparāga).

Regarding the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*): for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is the realization of the cessation of thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), but no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For a noble one (*ārya*), there is the realization of the cessation of three underlying tendencies, but no exhaustion of fetters.
Upon reaching arhatship— when one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana)—
and when one realizes the cessation of the group of cravings born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact.
The exhaustion of craving for the Brahma-world is the realization of the cessation of the three bodies of craving; it is the absence of fetters and the exhaustion of craving.
Upon reaching arhatship—there is the realization of the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
This occurs at the time of realizing the cessation of the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the desire realm.
An ordinary person who has exhausted desire for the realm of sensuality realizes the cessation of thirty-six underlying tendencies and exhausts the three fetters.
A noble person, when the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering is present before them, realizes the cessation of ten underlying tendencies, but does not exhaust any fetters.
Upon reaching the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*),
one realizes the cessation of the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Upon reaching the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), it is likewise.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala),
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and brings six fetters (saṃyojana) to an end.
Upon reaching the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala)...
When one realizes the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*),
it is at the time of realizing the cessation of the underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm. At that moment,
an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has exhausted sensual craving realizes the cessation of thirty-six underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of three fetters.

When the noble one brings the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaye-dharmajñāna*) into presence, seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned and realized, though no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
This constitutes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
Eighty-eight underlying tendencies are abandoned and realized, and three fetters are exhausted.
The same applies up to the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning,
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings the six fetters to an end.
Upon reaching the fruit of arhatship,
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and brings the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana) to realization.
This occurs at the moment of realizing the cessation of the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] within the desire realm.
An ordinary person who has exhausted desire for the realm of sensuality realizes the cessation of thirty-six underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.

A noble person, when the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (nirodha-dharma-jñāna) is present before them, realizes the cessation of seven underlying tendencies, though no fetters are yet exhausted.
Upon reaching the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala),
one realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the three fetters (saṃyojana).
Upon reaching the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala), it is likewise.
Upon reaching the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala),
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and brings six fetters (saṃyojana) to an end.
Upon reaching Arhatship (Arhattva)...
The cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is realized, and the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
At the time when the cessation of the underlying tendencies to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the desire realm is realized:
for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has exhausted sensual craving, thirty-six underlying tendencies are realized as ceased, and three fetters are exhausted.

When the noble one brings the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) into presence, he realizes the cessation of eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), though no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are yet exhausted.
This constitutes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
He realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.
The same applies up to the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning,
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings the six fetters to an end.
Up to the stage of Arhat,
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
This occurs at the time of realizing the cessation of the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) within the desire realm.
An ordinary person who has exhausted sensual desire realizes the cessation of thirty-six underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters;
such a noble one attains the fruit of non-returning.
The realization of the cessation of ninety-two latent dispositions (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of six fetters (saṃyojana) constitutes the stage of Arhatship.
The realization of the cessation of ninety-eight latent dispositions and the exhaustion of nine fetters [constitutes the same].
When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm,
an ordinary person who has exhausted craving for the form realm realizes the cessation of thirty-one latent dispositions, but there is no exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana).

When the Noble One brings the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) into manifestation, he realizes the cessation of eighteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), though no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are yet exhausted.
Upon reaching the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), he realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.
The same applies up to the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning—one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and exhausts six fetters (saṃyojana).
Upon reaching arhatship—one realizes the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies and exhausts nine fetters.
When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the form realm,
an ordinary person who has exhausted craving for the form realm realizes the cessation of thirty-one latent dispositions, but there is no exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana).

When the noble one brings the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaye anvayajñāna*) into manifestation, he realizes the cessation of twelve underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), though no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are yet exhausted.
Upon reaching the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), he realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and exhausts the three fetters.
It is the same for the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning—one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and brings six fetters (*saṃyojana*) to an end.
Upon reaching arhatship—one realizes the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies and brings nine fetters to an end.
When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has exhausted craving for the form realm realizes the cessation of thirty-one latent dispositions, but there is no exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

When the noble one brings the knowledge of the subsequent destruction (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) into manifestation, he realizes the cessation of twelve underlying tendencies (anuśaya), though no fetters (saṃyojana) are yet exhausted.
Upon reaching the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), he realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and exhausts the three fetters.
The same applies up to the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning—one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings six fetters to an end.
Upon reaching arhatship—one realizes the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies and brings nine fetters to an end.
When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the form realm,
an ordinary person who has exhausted craving for the form realm realizes the cessation of thirty-one latent dispositions, but there is no exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The Noble One who has attained the fruit of Stream-entry realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.
It is the same up to the fruit of Once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of Non-returner—one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings six fetters to an end.
Upon reaching Arhatship—one realizes the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies and brings nine fetters to an end.
When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the form realm,
craving for the form realm is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), this involves realizing the cessation of thirty-one latent dispositions, yet there is no exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The Noble One—having realized the cessation of the three underlying tendencies (anuśaya), has no remaining fetters (saṃyojana).
Up to the Arhat—having realized the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies, nine fetters are exhausted.

When the cessation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the formless realm is realized and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is present, eighteen latent dispositions are realized as ceased, yet no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
Upon reaching the fruit of stream-entry—
one realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.
It is the same upon reaching the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of Non-returning—
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings the six fetters to an end.
Upon reaching the fruit of Arhatship— [the same applies].
When one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*),

it is at the moment when the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are realized as ceased; at that time,
the subsequent knowledge of the origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) is present, whereby twelve underlying tendencies are realized as ceased, but no fetters are exhausted.
Upon reaching the fruit of stream-entry—
one realizes the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.
Upon reaching the fruit of once-returning, it is likewise.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning—
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings six fetters to an end.
Upon reaching arhatship— [the same applies].
When one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana),
at the moment of realizing the cessation of the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the formless realm,
the knowledge of the category of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) manifests.
— By realizing the cessation of the twelve underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there is no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*);
this constitutes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).—
By realizing the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies, there is the exhaustion of the three fetters.
The same applies up to the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning—
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings the six fetters to an end.
Up to the stage of Arhat:
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
This occurs at the time of realizing the cessation of the underlying tendencies to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
One attains the fruit of stream-entry—
realizing the cessation of eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the three fetters.
It is the same for the fruit of once-returning.
Upon reaching the fruit of non-returning—
one realizes the cessation of ninety-two underlying tendencies and brings six fetters to an end.
Upon reaching arhatship— [the same applies].
When one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*),
at the moment of realizing the cessation of the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
one attains the fruit of arhatship.
The realization of the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Volume 6; *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Volume 7.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The eight learners and ten non-learners; the three paths of vision, cultivation, and realization.
Worldly and untainted views and knowledge—this chapter shall explain them in full.
As the Blessed One has said:
"The learner who has seen the path is endowed with the eight factors of training."
How many does he accomplish in the past?
How many in the future?
How many in the present?
Answer: If one relies on the concentration with directed thought and sustained investigation (*savitarka-savicāra*),
the vision of a beginner manifests before them.
—There is none in the past;
there are eight in the future and the present.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
Furthermore, if one relies on the concentration with directed thought and sustained investigation (savitarka-savicāra),
and the training in vision (śaikṣa-darśana) manifests before them—
there are eight [knowledges] in the past, future, and present.
— That [attainment] is not lost once it has ceased.
If one relies on a concentration without vitarka and without vicāra,
the vision of training manifests in the present.
—Eight in the past and future;
seven in the present.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one relies on the formless attainments—
when the vision of a trainee (śaikṣa) is present—
there are eight [factors] of the past and future.
There are four present [factors].
Once they have ceased, they are not lost, provided one has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
— — Or when a mundane mind (*laukika-citta*) is present,
there are eight [dharmas] in the past and future,
and none in the present.
If one relies on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra—
when the vision of a beginner manifests before them—
it does not exist in the past.
There are eight in the future and seven in the present;
once they have ceased, they are not lost.
Furthermore, if one relies on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra,
and the training in vision manifests before one—
there are seven [factors] in the past and seven in the present.
The eight future [dharmas]—
once they have ceased, they are not lost—
if one relies on the formless attainments.
The learning-insight (śaikṣa-darśana) manifests before one.
There are seven past [factors] and eight future [factors].
There are four present [factors].
Once they have ceased, they are not lost,
provided one enters the meditative attainment of cessation.
— Or when a mundane mind is present:
seven from the past,
eight from the future.
It does not exist at present;
yet, once it has ceased, it is not lost.
This is with reference to the meditative concentration accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
When the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) manifests:
seven [knowledges] are past;
eight are future and present.
If one relies on the formless attainments—
when the vision of a beginner manifests before them—
it does not exist in the past.
Eight [factors] are future;
four are present;
having ceased, they are not lost.
If, moreover, based on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti),
the vision of one in training (śaikṣa) manifests in the present,
then four [factors] are past and four are present.
The eight future [factors]—
once they have ceased, they are not lost— if one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
— Or when a mundane mind is present:
four from the past and eight from the future.
It does not exist in the present;
once it has ceased, it is not lost,
provided one relies on a meditative concentration accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
When the knowledge of seeing (*dṛṣṭi-jñāna*) is present before one,
four [knowledges] pertain to the past;
eight pertain to the future and the present.
— That [attainment] having ceased, it is not lost.
If one relies on a meditative concentration without vitarka and without vicāra,
the vision of training manifests in the present.
— Four in the past, eight in the future,
and seven in the present.
As the Blessed One said:
"The Arhat whose outflows are exhausted is endowed with the ten factors of one beyond training.
How many of these does he possess in the past?
How many are future?
How many are present? Answer:
If one relies on the concentration with vitarka and vicāra—
when the first knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is present—
there is none in the past.
Ten in the future and nine in the present;
once they have ceased, they are not lost.
Furthermore, if one relies on a meditative concentration with vitarka and vicāra,
and the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests—
there are nine [knowledges] in the past and present.
The ten future [dharmas]—
once they have ceased, they are not lost—
if one relies on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra.
When the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is present,
there are nine in the past and ten in the future.
There are eight present [factors].
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
This applies if one relies on the formless attainments.
When the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is present,
nine [knowledges] are past and ten are future.
There are five present;
once they have ceased, they are not lost,
provided one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
— — Either a mundane mind manifests.— — Nine in the past;
ten in the future.
It does not exist in the present;
once it has ceased, it is not lost.
This is in dependence upon the meditative concentration with vitarka and vicāra.
— At the initial manifestation of the knowledge and vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñānadarśana)—
nine [factors] are past and present; ten are future.
— That [attainment] is not lost once it has ceased.
Furthermore, if one relies on a meditative concentration with vitarka and vicāra,
the wisdom or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests in the present.
Ten [factors] are past and future;
nine are present.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one relies on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra—
when either wisdom or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is present—
there are ten [factors] in the past and ten in the future.
There are eight present [factors].
Those, having ceased, are not lost.
This is if one relies on the formless attainments.
When the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is present,
ten [factors] are past and future,
and five are present.
— That [attainment] is not lost once it has ceased.
Whether one enters the attainment of cessation,
or a mundane mind manifests before one—
—Ten [factors] in the past and future;
none in the present.
This is according to the concentration that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
—At first, the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests in the present.
There is none in the past;
there are ten in the future.
There are eight present [factors].
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
Furthermore, if one relies on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra.
When the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is present,
there are eight [knowledges] in the past and present,
and ten in the future.
— That which has ceased is not lost.
If one relies on the formless attainments,
the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests before them.
— Eight in the past, ten in the future,
and five in the present.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
If one enters the attainment of cessation—
or if a mundane mind manifests— [the attainment remains].
— Eight in the past, ten in the future,
and none in the present.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
If one relies on a meditative concentration with applied and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra),
the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests before them.
— Eight in the past, ten in the future,
and nine in the present.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
If one relies on a meditative absorption free from applied and sustained thought—
the first [moment] of the vision of one beyond training manifests in the present.
—Eight in the past and present;
ten in the future.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
Furthermore, if one relies on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra,
when either the knowledge or the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests,
nine [factors] are past.
Ten in the future and eight in the present;
once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one relies on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti),
when either knowledge (jñāna) or vision (darśana) of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests,
nine [factors] are past.
Ten [factors] are future;
five are present;
having ceased, they are not lost.
If one enters the attainment of cessation—
whether it be the conventional mind that manifests before one—
there are nine past [minds].
There are ten in the future;
there are none in the present.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one relies on the concentration with vitarka and vicāra—
when either the knowledge or the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is present—
there are nine [factors] in the past and nine in the present.
Regarding the future ten:
if one relies on the formless attainments,
the first knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests in the present.
—In the past, there are none;
in the future, ten;
in the present, five.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
If one again relies on the formless attainments,
the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests before them.
—Five in the past and present; ten in the future.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one enters the attainment of cessation—
either with a mundane mind manifesting before one—
there are five past [dharmas].
There are ten in the future;
there are none in the present.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one relies on the concentration with vitarka and vicāra—
when the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is present—
there are five past [factors].
Ten in the future,
nine in the present;
once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one relies on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra—
when the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is present—
there are five past [factors].
Ten in the future and eight in the present;
once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one relies on the formless attainments—
when the first fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) vision manifests—
there are five past and present [factors].
The ten future [factors]—
once they have ceased, they are not lost—
if one further relies upon the formless absorptions.
When the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is present,
six [factors] are past and ten are future.
There are five present [factors];
once they have ceased, they are not lost, provided one has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
— Or when a mundane mind manifests: six past [dharmas],
ten future [dharmas].
It does not exist at present;
yet, once it has ceased, it is not lost.
This is in dependence upon a meditative concentration characterized by both vitarka and vicāra.
When the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is present,
six [factors] are past and ten are future.
There are nine present [factors].
Once they have ceased, they are not lost,
provided one relies on a meditative concentration that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
When the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is present,
six [factors] belong to the past and ten belong to the future.
There are eight present [factors].
What is "view" (*dṛṣṭi*)? Answer:
The eye-faculty, the five views, mundane right view, and the views of those in training and those beyond training.
What is knowledge? Answer:
The wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses;
the wisdom associated with the mental consciousness, excluding the untainted forbearances (*anāsrava-kṣānti*). What is wisdom?
Answer: It is the wisdom associated with the six consciousnesses.
Are all views knowledge?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is that which is vision but not knowledge.
That is to say, the eye faculty and the untainted receptivities (anāsrava-kṣānti).
There is wisdom that is not vision,
namely, the discernment associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

With the exception of the five views and mundane right view, all other outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is both "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
That is to say: the five views;

mundane right view; and, excluding the untainted forbearances (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), the remaining untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
There is also that which is neither view nor knowledge.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics: Are all views wisdom? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is that which is vision but not wisdom,
namely, the eye-faculty.
There is wisdom that is not vision;
namely, the wisdom associated with the five groups of consciousness,
as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Excluding the five views and mundane right view,
the remaining outflow-tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness is both a view and wisdom.

This refers to all untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) other than the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), as well as the five views (pañcadṛṣṭi) and mundane right view (laukikasamyagdṛṣṭi).
There are also instances that are neither views nor wisdom.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Are all forms of knowledge (jñāna) also wisdom (prajñā)? Answer:
All forms of knowledge (*jñāna*) are wisdom (*prajñā*).
However, there is wisdom that is not knowledge, namely, the untainted forbearances (*anāsravakṣānti*).
Is knowledge subsumed under vision (*darśana*)?
Is wisdom subsumed by view?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are instances that are vision but not included within knowledge,
namely the eye-faculty and the untainted forbearances (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
There are instances that are knowledge but not included within vision.
This refers to the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses;
the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising;
and, excluding the five views and mundane right view, the remaining outflow-tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness.
There are views that are also subsumed under wisdom (*jñāna*);
namely, the five views, conventional right view,
and all other untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) except for the untainted patiences (*kṣānti*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
There are those that are neither included within vision nor within knowledge;
this refers to all cases except for the characteristics mentioned above.
What is wisdom that is included within vision?
Does wisdom encompass views?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are instances of vision not subsumed under wisdom,
namely the eye-faculty.
There are instances of wisdom not subsumed under vision.
This refers to the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising;
and, excluding the five views and mundane right view, it refers to all other impure wisdom associated with the mental consciousness.
There are views that are also subsumed under wisdom;
namely, the five views, conventional right view,
and all untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā) other than the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
There are those that are neither views nor subsumed under wisdom;
these are cases other than those previously mentioned.
Is wisdom subsumed under knowledge?
Does wisdom (prajñā) include knowledge (jñāna)? Answer:
Wisdom includes knowledge, but knowledge does not include wisdom.
What is not included? It refers to untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
Are all those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭi*) also possessed of knowledge (*jñāna*)?
Answer: It is so.
If one has accomplished knowledge, does that person possess vision?
Answer: It is so.
Is one who possesses view also possessed of wisdom?
Answer: It is so.
If one is endowed with wisdom, does that person possess vision?
Answer: It is so.
Are all those who possess knowledge (jñāna) also possessed of wisdom (prajñā)?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes wisdom (prajñā), does one also possess knowledge (jñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
Are those views which have been abandoned and fully understood also [the objects of] that knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If wisdom has already abandoned and already fully known [a certain object], has that [object] been seen?
Answer: It is so.
Are those views which have been abandoned and fully understood also [the objects of] wisdom?
Answer: It is so.
If wisdom has already abandoned and already fully known [a certain object], has that [object] also been seen?
Answer: It is so.
Are those wisdoms which have already been abandoned and already fully known also [instances of] discernment?
Answer: It is so.
If wisdom has already been abandoned and has already been fully known, is that [wisdom] also knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
Are all right views the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions.
There is right view that is not the factor-of-enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
That is to say, there is mundane right view;
and there are factors of enlightenment consisting of the investigation of phenomena that are not right view,
namely, the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
There is that which is both right view and the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena;
this refers to all untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
There is also that which is neither right view nor the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Are all forms of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is right knowledge that is not the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena;
this refers to conventional right knowledge.
There are factors of enlightenment consisting of the investigation of phenomena that are not right knowledge;
these refer to the untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
There are also factors of enlightenment consisting of the investigation of phenomena that are right knowledge.
This refers to all other untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) excluding untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).

There is that which is neither correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) nor the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*); this refers to everything except the aforementioned characteristics.

When each of the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) and the eight factors of the path (maggaṅga) manifests, how many factors of enlightenment and how many factors of the path manifest?
Answer: If, based on the threshold concentration (anāgāmyasamādhi), the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga) manifests:
For one in training—six factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present.
For one beyond training—six factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path are present.
This is when relying on the first dhyāna.
When the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (satisambojjhaṅga) is present:
for one in training (sekha), seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path (maggaṅga) are present;
for one beyond training (asekha), seven factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path are present.
If, based on the intermediate dhyāna,
the awakening factor of mindfulness is present:
for one in training (śaikṣa), six awakening factors and seven path factors are present.
For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.
It is the same when relying on the third or fourth dhyāna.
If relying on the second dhyāna:
When the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (satisambojjhaṅga) is present:
for one in training (sekha), seven factors of enlightenment and seven factors of the path (maggaṅga) are present;
for one beyond training (asekha), seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present.
If, relying on the formless attainments,
the awakening factor of mindfulness manifests:
for one in training, six awakening factors and four path factors manifest.
For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and five factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.

These are the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya), energy (vīrya), tranquility (praśrabdhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekṣā); likewise, the path factors of right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), right effort (samyagvyāyāma), right mindfulness (samyaksmṛti), and right concentration (samyaksamādhi).
If, based on the first dhyāna, the enlightenment factor of joy (prītisambodhyaṅga) is present:
for one in training (śaikṣa), seven enlightenment factors and eight path factors (mārgāṅga) are present;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven enlightenment factors and nine path factors are present.
If, based on the second dhyāna,
the enlightenment factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present:
for one in training (*śaikṣa*), seven factors of enlightenment and seven factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are present.
For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and the eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.
If, based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna), right intention (samyak-saṃkalpa) is present:
for one in training (śaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present.
For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and nine factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.
If, relying on the first dhyāna, right thought (samyaksaṃkalpa) is present:
for one in training (śaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present.
For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and nine factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.
If, based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna), right speech (samyagvāc) is present:
for one in training (śaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present.
For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and nine factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.
If, relying on the first dhyāna, right speech (samyagvāc) is present:
for one in training (śaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present.
For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and nine factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.
If, based on the intermediate dhyāna, right speech (samyagvāk) is present:
for one in training (śaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment and seven factors of the path are present.
For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.
It is the same when relying on the third or fourth dhyāna.
If, relying on the second dhyāna, right speech (samyagvāc) is present:
For those in training (śaikṣa), the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and the seven factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.
For those beyond training (aśaikṣa), the seven factors of enlightenment and the eight factors of the path are present.
This is likewise true for right action (samyak-karmānta) and right livelihood (samyag-ājīva).
If a phenomenon is associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, is that phenomenon also associated with the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with mindfulness that are not the investigation of phenomena;
namely, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). There are phenomena associated with the investigation of phenomena that are not mindfulness.

That is to say, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga). There are factors associated with the mindfulness of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) that are also the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya);
these refer to the factors associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with mindfulness nor are they the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).

These are: all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), form (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*). This is as in the case of the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The same applies to the enlightenment factors of energy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, as well as to right effort and right concentration.
Regarding those phenomena that are associated with the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, are those phenomena also associated with the enlightenment factor of joy?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena that are associated with mindfulness but not with joy.

This refers to the factor of enlightenment that is joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), as well as those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) which are not associated with joy.
There are also factors associated with joy that are not associated with mindfulness;
these refer to the mindfulness that is associated with the factor of enlightenment that is joy.
There are phenomena that are associated with mindfulness and also associated with joy; namely, those phenomena associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with mindfulness nor associated with joy.

This refers to the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness dissociated from joy, as well as other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitasika), matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
As it is with regard to the factor of enlightenment of joy,
so it is with regard to right view and right thought.
If a phenomenon is associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, is that phenomenon also associated with right mindfulness? Answer: It is so.
If various phenomena are associated with right mindfulness, are those phenomena also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness? Answer: Yes.

If a phenomenon is associated with the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), is that phenomenon also associated with the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are factors associated with the investigation of phenomena (dharma-pravicaya) but not with diligence (vīrya),
namely, the awakening factor of diligence (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
There are factors associated with diligence but not with the investigation of phenomena.

This refers to the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmavicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga). There are factors that are associated with the investigation of phenomena and are also associated with diligence;
these refer to the factors associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with the investigation of dharmas nor associated with diligence;
namely, other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
As it is with the awakening factor of energy,
so it is with the awakening factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, as well as right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

If a phenomenon is associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), is that phenomenon also associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are factors associated with the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) but not with joy (prīti);
namely, the factor of awakening that is joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga), as well as those factors associated with the investigation of phenomena that are not associated with joy.
There are factors associated with joy but not with the investigation of phenomena.

This refers to the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) associated with the factor of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga). There are also phenomena that are associated with both the investigation of phenomena and joy;
these refer to those factors associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with the investigation-of-phenomena awakening factor (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) nor associated with joy (*prīti*).

These include: the investigation-of-phenomena awakening factor when it is not associated with joy; all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); form (*rūpa*); unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*); and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
As it is with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), so it is with right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
Are those phenomena that are associated with the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) also associated with right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: All phenomena associated with right view are also associated with the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
However, there are phenomena associated with the investigation of phenomena that are not associated with right view.
This refers to those factors associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that are not included within right view.
Are all those factors associated with the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) also associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with diligence (vīrya) but not with joy (prīti).

This refers to the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), as well as those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that are not associated with joy.

There are also factors associated with joy that are not associated with energy; these refer to the factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy that are themselves associated with energy.
There are phenomena associated with both diligence and joy,
namely those phenomena associated with both.
There are phenomena associated neither with diligence nor with joy.

This refers to the factor of enlightenment of energy dissociated from joy, as well as other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
As it is with the factor of enlightenment of joy, so it is with right view and right thought.

If various dharmas are associated with the enlightenment factor of diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*), are those dharmas also associated with the enlightenment factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sambodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena associated with diligence but not with pliancy;
namely, the factor of enlightenment that is pliancy.
There are phenomena associated with pliancy but not with diligence.
This refers to the factor of enlightenment that is diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*). There are factors that are associated with diligence and also associated with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*);
namely, those factors associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with diligence nor with pliancy;
namely, all other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
As it is with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*),
so it is with the factors of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Are those phenomena that are associated with the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) also associated with right effort (*samyag-vīrya*)?
Answer: It is so.
If a phenomenon is associated with right effort, is that phenomenon also associated with the factor of enlightenment of effort?
Answer: It is so.
Are those phenomena that are associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy also associated with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with joy (prīti) that are not associated with pliancy (praśrabdhi).
This refers to the factor of enlightenment of pliancy associated with joy.
There are factors associated with pliancy that are not associated with joy;
namely, the factor of enlightenment of joy itself, as well as those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy that are not associated with joy.
There are phenomena associated with joy and also associated with pliancy;
namely, those phenomena associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with joy nor associated with pliancy.

This refers to the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) dissociated from joy, as well as other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*). As it is with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy,

so it is with the factors of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Regarding those phenomena associated with the factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), are they also associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: This should be treated in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There are phenomena associated with joy that are not associated with right view;

namely, those phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy that are associated with right view, as well as those phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy that are not associated with right view.
There are phenomena associated with right view but not with joy;
namely, the factor of enlightenment that is joy and is associated with right view, as well as those factors associated with right view but not associated with the factor of enlightenment that is joy.
There are phenomena associated with joy and also associated with right view;
namely, those phenomena associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with joy nor associated with right view.

This refers to right view not associated with the factor of joy, the factor of joy not associated with right view, as well as other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
As it is with right view,
so it is with right intention.
Regarding those phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy, are they necessarily associated with the factor of enlightenment of investigation?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with pliancy (praśrabdhi) that are not associated with meditative concentration (samādhi).
That is to say, there are factors that are associated with concentration but are not pliancy;
namely, the factor of awakening that is pliancy.
There are phenomena that are associated with both pliancy and concentration;
namely, those phenomena associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with pliancy nor with concentration.

This refers to the remaining mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), form (rūpa), the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra). As it is with the factor of enlightenment of investigation (dharma-vicaya-sambodhyaṅga),
so it is also with the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekṣā-sambodhyaṅga), right effort (samyag-vyāyāma), right mindfulness (samyak-smṛti), and right concentration (samyak-samādhi).
If various phenomena are associated with the awakening factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), are those phenomena also associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena associated with pliancy but not with right view;
namely, right view itself, and those factors associated with the awakening factor of pliancy that are not associated with right view.
There are phenomena associated with right view but not with pliancy.
This refers to the factor of enlightenment of pliancy associated with right view.
There are factors that are both associated with pliancy and associated with right view;
namely, those factors associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with pliancy nor with right view;

namely, the factor of enlightenment of pliancy when it is not associated with right view, as well as other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
As it is with right view,
so it is with right intention.
Are those factors that are associated with the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena also associated with the enlightenment factor of equanimity?
