Answer: One should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are factors that are associated with the dharma but are not abandoned.

That is to say, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga) is associated with equanimity but not with concentration; whereas the factor of enlightenment of concentration (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) is associated with concentration but not with equanimity.
There are factors associated with meditative concentration (samādhi) and also associated with equanimity (upekṣā), namely those factors associated with both.
There are also factors that are neither associated with meditative concentration nor associated with equanimity.
This refers to other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), matter (rūpa), the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
As it is with the factor of equanimity (upekṣā-sambodhyaṅga),
so it is also with right effort (samyag-vyāyāma) and right mindfulness (samyak-smṛti).
If various dharmas are associated with the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), are those dharmas also associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There are factors that are associated with concentration but not with right view;
namely, right view itself, and those factors associated with the awakening factor of concentration that are not associated with right view.
There are factors that are associated with right view but not with concentration.
This refers to the factor of enlightenment of concentration associated with right view.
There are factors that are both associated with concentration and associated with right view;
namely, those factors associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with concentration nor associated with right view;

namely, the factors of enlightenment consisting of concentration that are dissociated from right view, as well as other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
As it is with right view,
so it is with right intention.
Are those phenomena that are associated with the factor of enlightenment of investigation into phenomena also associated with right concentration?
Answer: It is so.
If a dharma is associated with right concentration, is that dharma necessarily associated with the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena?
Answer: It is so.
Are those phenomena that are associated with the enlightenment factor of equanimity also associated with right view?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena that are associated with equanimity (upekṣā) but are not right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
That is to say: right view, as well as those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of equanimity that are not associated with right view.
There are factors associated with right view but not with equanimity; namely, those factors associated with right view that are associated with the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
There are phenomena that are associated with equanimity and are also right view;
namely, those phenomena associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with equanimity nor are they right view.

This refers to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity that is dissociated from right view, as well as other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
As it is with respect to right view,
so it is with respect to right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).
If a phenomenon is associated with the enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*), is that phenomenon also associated with right effort (*samyag-vīrya*)?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena associated with equanimity but not with right effort;
that is to say, right effort itself.
There are phenomena associated with right effort but not with equanimity.
This refers to the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). There are factors that are associated with equanimity and also associated with right effort;
these refer to the factors associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with relinquishment nor with right effort;
namely, other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
As it is with right effort,
so it is with right mindfulness and right concentration.
Are those phenomena that are associated with right view also associated with right thought?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena that are associated with right view but not with right thought.
This refers to right intention associated with right view, as well as those factors associated with right view but not associated with right intention.
There are also factors associated with right intention but not associated with right view.
This refers to right view associated with right thought, as well as those factors associated with right thought that are not associated with right view.
There are factors that are associated with both right view and right thought.
This refers to those factors associated with both.
There are factors that are neither associated with right view nor associated with right intention;

namely, right intention not associated with right view, right view not associated with right intention, and all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), as well as matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra).
If all phenomena are associated with right view, are those phenomena also associated with right effort?
Answer: This should be analyzed in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with right view but not with right effort;
that is to say, right effort associated with right view.
There are phenomena associated with right effort but not with right view.
This refers to right view, as well as those factors associated with right effort that are not associated with right view.
There are also factors associated with both right view and right effort;
these refer to the factors associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with right view nor with right effort;
namely, right effort that is not associated with right view, as well as other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
As it is with right effort,
so it is with right mindfulness and right concentration.
Are those phenomena that are associated with right thought also associated with right effort?
Answer: This should be treated as a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena that are associated with right attention (samyak-smṛti) but not with right effort (samyak-vīrya).
This refers to right effort associated with right thought.
There are also phenomena associated with right effort but not associated with right thought;
namely, right thought itself, as well as those phenomena associated with right effort that are not associated with right thought.
There are phenomena that are associated with both right attention and right effort;
namely, those phenomena associated with both.
There are also phenomena that are associated with neither right attention nor right effort.

This refers to right effort that is dissociated from right thought, as well as other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
As it is with respect to right effort,
so it is with respect to right mindfulness and right concentration.
If all phenomena are associated with right effort, are those phenomena also associated with right mindfulness?
Answer: This should be analyzed by way of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with right effort but not with right mindfulness;
namely, right mindfulness itself.
There are phenomena associated with right mindfulness but not with right effort.
This refers to right effort.
There are factors that are associated with both right effort and right mindfulness;
namely, those factors associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with right effort nor with right mindfulness;
namely, other mental states and mental factors, form, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
As it is with right mindfulness,
so it is with right concentration.
Are those phenomena that are associated with right mindfulness also associated with right concentration?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are dharmas that are associated with right mindfulness but are not associated with right concentration.
That is to say, right concentration.
There are factors associated with right concentration that are not right mindfulness;
that is to say, right mindfulness.
There are phenomena associated with right mindfulness and also with right concentration;
namely, those phenomena associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with right mindfulness nor with right concentration.
That is to say: other mental states and mental factors, form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.

Regarding the wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses and the wholesome, out-flowing (sāsrava) wisdom associated with the mental consciousness:
are all these mundane right views also mundane right knowledge?
Answer: All mundane right view is mundane right knowledge.
However, there is mundane right knowledge that is not mundane right view.
That is to say, regarding the wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses:
does mundane right view subsume mundane right knowledge,
or does mundane right knowledge subsume mundane right view?
Answer:
Conventional right knowledge (samyagjñāna) subsumes conventional right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), but conventional right view does not subsume conventional right knowledge.
What is not subsumed?
This refers to the wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses.
Are all those who possess mundane right view also possessed of mundane right knowledge? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one achieves mundane right knowledge, does one possess mundane right view?
Answer:
Thus it is.
If mundane right view has been abandoned and fully understood, has that mundane right knowledge also been abandoned and fully understood? Answer:
Thus it is.
If mundane right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) has been abandoned and fully understood, is that mundane right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) also [abandoned and fully understood]? Answer:
Thus it is. What is untainted vision (*anāsravadṛṣṭi*)? Answer:
It is the untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) other than the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
What is untainted knowledge (anāsravajñāna)? Answer:
Excluding the untainted forbearances (*anāsrava-kṣānti*), it is the remaining untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
Are all untainted views (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*) untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*)? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is uncontaminated vision that is not uncontaminated knowledge;
namely, uncontaminated receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
There is untainted knowledge that is not untainted vision, namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
There is also untainted vision that is likewise untainted knowledge.

This refers to the remaining untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*), excluding the untainted receptivities (*kṣānti*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
There is that which is neither untainted vision nor untainted knowledge; this refers to everything except the aforementioned characteristics.
Does untainted vision (anāsravā dṛṣṭi) subsume untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna),
or does untainted knowledge subsume untainted vision? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is that which is untainted vision but is not subsumed under untainted knowledge;
namely, untainted patience (*anāsravakṣānti*).
There is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that is not subsumed under untainted vision (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*),
namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). There is also untainted vision that is likewise subsumed under untainted knowledge.

This refers to the remaining untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*), excluding the untainted patiences (*kṣānti*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
There are cases that are neither included within untainted vision (*anāsravā dṛṣṭi*) nor untainted knowledge; these refer to everything other than the aforementioned characteristics.
If one possesses any untainted view (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*), does that person possess untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*)? Answer:
Those who possess untainted knowledge also possess untainted view.

There is the accomplishment of untainted view (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*) without the accomplishment of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), namely, at the time when the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) is present.
Regarding the five [categories] of false and correct views and knowledges: The left-hand [group] consists of wisdom (*prajñā*), the three trainings (*śikṣā*), and so forth;
the Brahma-receptivities (*brahmakṣānti*) consist of five; and there are the five wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). I pray that this chapter may be fully explained.
What is wrong view? Answer:
If they are not established [as distinct categories], then all five views are termed wrong view.

If it is established, then it is simply the view that there is no giving, no affection, no sacrifice, no wholesome conduct, no unwholesome conduct, and no ripening of the results of wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions; this is called wrong view.
What is wrong wisdom?
Answer: It is defiled discernment associated with the six consciousnesses.
Are all wrong views wrong knowledge? Answer:
All wrong views are wrong knowledge.
There is faulty wisdom that is not faulty view;
namely, afflicted prajñā associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as afflicted prajñā associated with the mental consciousness, excluding the five views.
Is wrong view subsumed by wrong knowledge,
or is wrong knowledge subsumed by wrong view? Answer:
Wrong knowledge subsumes wrong view,
but wrong view does not subsume wrong knowledge.
What is not so subsumed?
This refers to the defiled wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as the defiled wisdom associated with the mental consciousness, excluding the five views.
Are all those who possess wrong view also possessed of wrong knowledge?
Answer: All those who possess wrong view also possess wrong knowledge.
However, there are those who possess wrong knowledge but not wrong view, namely, those in training who have seen the tracks.
If various wrong views have been abandoned and fully understood, are they also wrong knowledge? Answer:
Those various wrong knowledges that have been abandoned and fully understood are also wrong views.
There is wrong view that has been abandoned and fully understood, yet it is not wrong knowledge;
this refers to those in training who have seen the path. What is right view?
Answer: It is wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)?

Answer: It is wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is not subsumed under the untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
Are all right views (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions.
There is right view that is not right knowledge.
This refers to untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
There is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) that is not right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), namely:

wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-saṃprayukta-kuśala-prajñā*), as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
There is that which is both right view and right knowledge;

this refers to untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*), as well as wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
There is that which is neither right view nor right knowledge.
That is to say, setting aside the aforementioned characteristics:
does right view encompass right knowledge,
or does right knowledge encompass right view?
Answer: This should be treated as four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is right view that is not subsumed under right knowledge.
This refers to untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
There is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) that is not subsumed under right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*);
namely, wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
There is right view that is also subsumed under right knowledge;

this refers to untainted receptivities (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) and wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
There are those that are neither subsumed under right view nor subsumed under right knowledge;
namely, all cases other than those previously mentioned.
Are all those who possess right view also possessed of right knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If one is endowed with right knowledge, is one also possessed of right view?
Answer: It is so.
Are those right views that have been abandoned and fully understood also right knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If right knowledge has already been abandoned and fully understood, is that right view?
Answer: It is so.
Are all instances of wrong wisdom (mithyā-prajñā) fetters (saṃyojana)?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is wisdom that is not a fetter (saṃyojana).
This refers to the remaining defiled wisdom, excluding the two fetters (*saṃyojana*).
There are fetters that are not wrong wisdom;
namely, the seven fetters.
There is that which is both wrong wisdom and a fetter;
namely, the two fetters.
There is that which is neither wrong wisdom nor a fetter.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
What is the vision of one in training? Answer:
Training in wisdom.
What is training in knowledge? Answer:
One trains in the eight knowledges.
What is the wisdom of training? Answer:
The vision of one in training (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi*) and the knowledge of one in training (*śaikṣa-jñāna*) are collectively termed the wisdom of one in training (*śaikṣa-prajñā*).
Are all visions of one in training instances of the knowledge of one in training? Answer:

All knowledge (*jñāna*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) is also vision (*darśana*) of those in training. However, there is vision of those in training that is not knowledge of those in training, namely, the untainted forbearances (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
Is all vision of those in training wisdom (*prajñā*) of those in training?
Answer: It is so.
If it is wisdom in training, is it also vision in training?
Answer: It is so.
Is all knowledge of training (śaikṣa-jñāna) wisdom of training (śaikṣa-prajñā)?
Answer: All knowledge of training (śaikṣajñāna) is also wisdom of training (śaikṣaprajñā).
However, there is wisdom of training that is not knowledge of training, namely, untainted forbearance (anāsravakṣānti).
Does the training in vision encompass the training in knowledge?
Or does the training in knowledge encompass the training in vision? Answer:

The vision of one in training (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi) subsumes the knowledge of one in training (śaikṣa-jñāna), but the knowledge of one in training does not subsume the vision of one in training. What is not subsumed?
Namely, the untainted forbearances (anāsrava-kṣānti).
Does the training in view encompass the training in wisdom?
Or does the training in wisdom encompass the training in view? Answer:
They encompass one another in turn.
Does the training in wisdom encompass the training in knowledge?
Or does the training in knowledge encompass the training in wisdom?
Answer: Learner’s wisdom (śaikṣī prajñā) includes learner’s knowledge (śaikṣī vidyā), but learner’s knowledge does not include learner’s wisdom. What is not included?
That is to say, untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
Regarding those who have attained the vision of training (*śaikṣa-darśana*), do they also possess the knowledge of training (*śaikṣa-jñāna*)? Answer:
All those who possess the wisdom of training (śaikṣa-jñāna) also possess the vision of training (śaikṣa-darśana).

However, there are those who possess the vision of training but do not possess the wisdom of training—namely, at the moment when the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti) is present.
Are all those who possess the vision of training also possessed of the wisdom of training?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses the wisdom of training (śaikṣa-prajñā), does that person possess the vision of training (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi)?
Answer: It is so.
Those who possess the knowledge of one in training (śaikṣajñāna), do they also possess the wisdom of one in training (śaikṣaprajñā)?
Answer: Those who possess the knowledge of training (śaikṣa-jñāna) also possess the wisdom of training (śaikṣa-prajñā).

However, there are those who possess the wisdom of training but do not possess the knowledge of training; this refers to the time when the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) is manifest.
What is the vision of one beyond training? Answer:
It is the wisdom of one beyond training that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
What is the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna)?
Answer: It consists of the eight knowledges of one beyond training.
What is the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣaprajñā)? Answer:
The vision of one beyond training and the knowledge of one beyond training are collectively termed the wisdom of one beyond training.
Are all those that are the vision of one beyond training also the knowledge of one beyond training?
Answer: All those that are the vision of one beyond training are also the knowledge of one beyond training.

There is knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) that is not vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi), namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Are all visions of one beyond training wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣaprajñā)?
Answer: Yes.
All views of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are also wisdom of those beyond training.
However, there is wisdom of those beyond training that is not a view of those beyond training; namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
Are all knowledges of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) wisdoms of those beyond training? Answer: Yes.
If it is the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-prajñā), is it the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna)? Answer: It is so.

Is the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi) subsumed by the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna), or is the knowledge of one beyond training subsumed by the vision of one beyond training? Answer:

The knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) subsumes the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi), but the vision of one beyond training does not subsume the knowledge of one beyond training.
What is not subsumed? Namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Is the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi) subsumed by the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣaprajñā)?
Or is the wisdom of one beyond training subsumed by the vision of one beyond training? Answer:
The wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna) subsumes the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-dṛṣṭi), but the vision of one beyond training does not subsume the wisdom of one beyond training.
What is not subsumed? Namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
Does the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) include the insight of one beyond training (aśaikṣaprajñā)?
Or does the insight of one beyond training include the wisdom of one beyond training? Answer:
They are mutually inclusive.
Are all those who have achieved the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-dṛṣṭi) also possessed of the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna)? Answer:
Thus it is. If one has accomplished the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna), does that person possess the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi)? Answer:
Thus it is. Are those who have achieved the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-dṛṣṭi) also possessed of the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-prajñā)? Answer:
Thus it is. If one has accomplished the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna), does that person possess the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-darśana)? Answer:
Thus it is. Those who have attained the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna), do they possess the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣaprajñā)? Answer:
Thus it is. If one has accomplished the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-prajñā), does that person possess the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna)? Answer:
Thus it is. What is the view that is neither of one in training nor of one beyond training? Answer:
The eye faculty, the five views, and mundane right view.
What is knowledge that is neither of the trainee nor of the one beyond training? Answer:
The wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as the contaminated wisdom associated with the mental consciousness.
What is wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer:
Regarding the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses and the tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness:
are all those views that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner also knowledges that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner vision (dṛṣṭi) but is not non-learner-nor-non-learner knowledge (jñāna).
This refers to the eye faculty.
There is knowledge that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa), but it is not the view that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
This refers to the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as the remaining tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness, excluding the five views and mundane right view.
There is that which is neither the vision of one in training nor of one beyond training, and is also neither the knowledge of one in training nor of one beyond training;
namely, the five views and mundane right view.
There is that which is neither the non-vision of one in training nor of one beyond training, and is also neither the non-knowledge of one in training nor of one beyond training.
That is to say, setting aside the aforementioned characteristics:
Are all views that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner also wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner vision but not non-learner-nor-non-learner wisdom;
namely, the eye-faculty.
There is wisdom that is neither of the learner nor of the non-learner, yet is not the view that is neither of the learner nor of the non-learner;
namely, wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as worldly right view, excluding the five views.
Other outflow-tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness includes both views that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner as well as wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
namely, the five views and mundane right view.
There is that which is neither non-learner-nor-non-learner view (*na-śaikṣa-na-aśaikṣa-dṛṣṭi*) and also not non-learner-nor-non-learner wisdom (*na-śaikṣa-na-aśaikṣa-prajñā*).
This refers to everything except the aforementioned characteristics. Are all non-learner-nor-non-learner cognitions (*jñāna*) non-learner-nor-non-learner wisdom?
Answer: It is so.
If it is wisdom that is neither of the trainee nor of the non-trainee, is it knowledge that is neither of the trainee nor of the non-trainee?
Answer: It is so.
Is that which is comprised by neither-learner-nor-non-learner view also comprised by neither-learner-nor-non-learner knowledge?
Is that which is comprised by knowledge that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner also comprised by view that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations.
There is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner view but is not subsumed under neither-learner-nor-non-learner knowledge;
namely, the eye-faculty.
There is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner knowledge but is not subsumed under neither-learner-nor-non-learner view.
This refers to the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as all other contaminated wisdom associated with the mental consciousness— excluding the five views and mundane right view.
This includes that which is categorized as neither-learner-nor-non-learner vision (*dṛṣṭi*) and is also subsumed under neither-learner-nor-non-learner knowledge (*jñāna*).
This refers to the five views and mundane right view.
There are those that are neither included within the views that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, nor within the knowledge that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
these are cases other than those previously described.
Is non-learner and non-non-learner vision subsumed by non-learner and non-non-learner wisdom?
Or is non-learner and non-non-learner wisdom subsumed by non-learner and non-non-learner vision?
Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner vision (*dṛṣṭi*) but is not subsumed under neither-learner-nor-non-learner wisdom (*prajñā*);
namely, the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
There is wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner which is not subsumed under non-learner-nor-non-learner view;
namely, wisdom associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, as well as worldly right view, excluding the five views.
Other contaminated wisdom associated with the mental consciousness is comprised of neither-training-nor-non-training views as well as neither-training-nor-non-training wisdom;
that is to say, the five views and mundane right view.
There are cases that are neither non-learner nor non-non-learner views, yet are not subsumed under non-learner nor non-non-learner wisdom;
namely, those excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Are non-learner nor non-non-learner knowledges subsumed under non-learner nor non-non-learner wisdom?
Is non-learner and non-non-learner wisdom subsumed by non-learner and non-non-learner knowledge?
Answer: They are mutually subsumed.
Regarding those who have achieved views that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner:
are they also possessed of knowledge that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer:
It is so. Even if one accomplishes knowledge that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
that [knowledge] is not learner-knowledge.
Is it not the vision of one beyond training? Answer: It is so.
Regarding those accomplished views that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner: are they wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer: Yes.
If one achieves wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, is that [wisdom] also vision that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer: It is so.
Are all those that are accomplished as neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee knowledge (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣajñāna) also neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee wisdom (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣaprajñā)? Answer: Yes.
If one possesses non-learner and non-non-learner wisdom (*prajñā*), does one possess non-learner and non-non-learner knowledge (*jñāna*)? Answer: Yes.
If those views that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner have already been abandoned and fully understood, are they also knowledges that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer: It is so.
If non-learner and non-non-learner knowledge has been abandoned and fully understood, is that non-learner and non-non-learner view? Answer: It is so.
If all views that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner have already been abandoned and fully understood, are they [also] wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer: It is so.
If non-learner and non-non-learner wisdom has been abandoned and fully known, is that non-learner and non-non-learner view? Answer: It is so.

If various forms of knowledge that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner have already been abandoned and fully understood, are those forms of wisdom also neither-learner-nor-non-learner? Answer: It is so.
If non-learner and non-non-learner wisdom has been abandoned and fully understood, is that non-learner and non-non-learner knowledge? Answer: It is so.
As the Great Brahmā has declared: "I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Sovereign.
In this world, I am the creator and the progenitor; I am the Father of all."
"Among the five views, under which view is this subsumed?
By perceiving which truth is this view abandoned? Answer:
"To claim, 'I am Brahmā, I am the Great Brahmā, I have attained mastery' is to grasp inferior phenomena as superior;
it is subsumed under the grasping of views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) and is abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya)."
"To say, 'I am the creator and progenitor of the world; I am its father,' is to conceive of what is not a cause as a cause.
It is subsumed under the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)."
As the gods of the Brahmakāyika heaven say:
"This is Brahmā; this is Mahābrahmā."
Having attained mastery,
one is able to create and transform within this world.
"He is able to bring us forth; he is our father.
Among the five views, under which view is this subsumed?
Through the vision of which truth is this view abandoned?
Answer: To say, "This is Brahmā; he is the Great Brahmā; he has attained mastery," is to grasp inferior phenomena as superior.
This is subsumed under the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
To think, "In this world, he is the creator and the progenitor; he is our father," is to misapprehend what is not a cause as being a cause (*ahetāv ahetudṛṣṭi*).
It is comprised within the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
Regarding those who give rise to this view:
"I tolerate everything.
Among the five views, under which view is this subsumed?
By perceiving which truth is this view abandoned?

Answer: Among the views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), it is subsumed under the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). It is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding those who give rise to this view:
"I do not tolerate anything at all"—
among the five views, by which view is this subsumed?
Through the vision of which truth is this view abandoned?
Answer: Among the views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), it is subsumed under the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
This view is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). It arises as follows:
"I tolerate one part, but I do not tolerate another part."
Regarding these [views], under which of the five views are they subsumed?
By perceiving which truth are these views abandoned? Answer:
One portion of those who tolerate [the view] is subsumed under the eternalist view within the view of extremes;
one portion of those who do not tolerate it is likewise so subsumed.
Among the views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), it is subsumed under the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Both are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Those who give rise to this view:
"There are Arhats who, being tormented by celestial Māras, discharge impurities.
Among the five views, under which view is this subsumed?
By perceiving which truth is this view abandoned?
Answer: It is the misapprehension of what is not a cause as being a cause;
it is subsumed under the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This is abandoned by seeing suffering.
It refers to those who give rise to this view:
"There is still ignorance regarding one's own liberation in an Arhat."
"Among the five views, under which view is this subsumed?
By perceiving which truth is this view abandoned? Answer:
The untainted knowledge and vision of all arhats is comprised within wrong view and is to be abandoned by the path of seeing.
Regarding those who give rise to this view:
"There is doubt concerning the liberation of an Arhat regarding his own liberation"—
within the five views, by which view is this subsumed?
By seeing which truth is this view abandoned?
Answer: All Arhats have transcended doubt.
It is subsumed under wrong view and is to be abandoned by the path of vision.
Those who give rise to this view:
"There are Arhats who are liberated solely through others.
Among the five views, under which view is this subsumed?
By perceiving which truth is this view abandoned?
Answer: All Arhats are without obstruction and without turning away; they possess the eye of wisdom of direct perception and have realized mastery through bodily witness.
[This state] is subsumed under the category of right view.
Abandoned by the path of seeing,
those who give rise to this view [think]:
"The path and the factors of the path are what is designated by the term 'suffering'."
"Among the five views, under which view is this subsumed?
By perceiving which truth is this view abandoned? Answer:
To regard what is not a cause as a cause is subsumed under the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Fascicle Seven.
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Fascicle Eight.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

The two types of wisdom and the two liberations; Clear wisdom, the three forms of verified confidence, The cultivation of meditative absorption regarding inversions— In this chapter, may all these be fully explained.
What is the knowledge of others' minds? Answer:

It is that wisdom which is produced by cultivation, is the fruit of cultivation, relies upon cultivation, has been attained and not lost, and is able to know the present mental states and mental factors of the desire and form realms, or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mental states and mental factors within the mental continuums of others; this is called [the knowledge of others' minds].
The knowledge of others' minds.
What is the knowledge of recollecting past lives? Answer:

If wisdom is produced through cultivation, is the fruit of cultivation, and relies upon cultivation such that, once attained, it is not lost, one is able to recollect and know various past lives, their diverse characteristics, and the speech uttered therein.
This is called the knowledge of recollecting past abodes.
Do all knowledges of others' minds directly know the minds and mental factors of others?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the knowledge of others' minds, yet it does not directly know the mental states and mental factors of others.
That is to say:
there is knowledge of others' minds regarding the past and future;
however, there is present knowledge of others' minds and mental factors that is not "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna).
That is to say:
there is someone who, either by observing signs, or by hearing words, or by attaining such "knowledge acquired at birth," is able to directly know the minds and mental factors of others.
There is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), which also directly knows the minds and mental factors (*cittacaittadharma*) of others.
That is to say:

if this knowledge is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), is the fruit of cultivation, relies upon cultivation, has been attained and not lost, it can directly know the present minds and mental factors of others within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or their untainted (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors.
There is that which is neither the knowledge of others' minds nor the direct cognition of others' minds and mental factors;
that is to say:
excluding the aforementioned cases.
Do all knowledges of recollecting former abodes necessarily involve the present recollection and knowledge of the events of those former abodes?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations.
There is knowledge of recollecting past lives that does not involve the direct recollection of past events;
namely, knowledge of recollecting past lives regarding the past and the future.
There are those who currently recollect and know various past lives, yet this is not the "knowledge of recollecting past abodes" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
That is to say:

for example, there may be one who has attained the knowledge of birth through intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyutpādajñāna*), or who has attained such knowledge acquired at the place of birth (*upapattipratilambhikajñāna*), and is thus able to currently recollect and know various past lives.
There is the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), by which one also currently recollects and knows various matters of past lives.
That is to say:

if this knowledge is produced through cultivation, is the fruit of cultivation, relies upon cultivation, has been attained and not lost, it is able to currently recollect and know the various characteristics and modes of past lives.
Furthermore, there are those whose speech is such that they possess neither the knowledge of recollecting past lives nor the present recollection and cognition of various past events.
That is to say:
Excluding the aforementioned cases, does all knowledge of recollecting past abodes know the mental continuum of others' past aggregates, bases, and elements?
Answer: No.
One should formulate four permutations.

There is the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) that does not know the mental continuum of another’s past aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
That is to say:

If this knowledge is produced through cultivation, is the fruit of cultivation, and is based upon cultivation—having been attained and not lost—it knows the mental continuum of its own past aggregates, bases, and elements from previous lives.
There is knowledge of the mental continuum of another’s past aggregates, bases, and elements that is not the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
That is to say:

it is a knowledge produced by cultivation, which is the fruit of cultivation, which relies upon cultivation, which has been attained and not lost, and which knows the mental continuum of another’s past aggregates, bases, and elements in this very life.

There is the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), which also knows the mental continuity of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) of others in the past.
That is to say:

if a knowledge is produced through cultivation, is the fruit of cultivation, relies upon cultivation, has been attained and not lost, it knows the mental continuity of the aggregates, bases, and elements of others in previous lives.

There is a knowledge that is neither the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) nor the knowledge of the mental continuity of others' past aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
That is to say:

it is a knowledge produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), which is the fruit of cultivation, based upon cultivation, already attained and not lost, and which knows the mental continuity of the aggregates, bases, and elements from this life back into the past.
What is the liberation of mind through desirelessness (*akopya-cetovimukti*)? Answer:

It is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) of an Arhat who is liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimukta*), or the resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*), the state of having attained resolute confidence, or the state of about to attain resolute confidence, of a mind associated with the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
What is the immovable liberation of mind? Answer:

It is the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising of an Arhat of immovable nature; or it is the mental resolve, the resolved state, or the future resolve associated with the right view of one beyond training.
Are all instances of liberation through loving-kindness at various times associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Sometimes there is liberation through loving-kindness that is not associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
That is to say:
the liberation of mind of an Arhat liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), which is the resolve, has resolved, or will resolve, in association with the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
There is a liberation through resolve associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), which is not occasional and is free from passion.
This refers to the mental resolve, the resolved state, and the future resolve of an Arhat of immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*) associated with the knowledge of exhaustion.
Sometimes the liberation through loving-kindness is also associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
That is to say:
the mental resolve (*adhimokṣa*) associated with the knowledge of exhaustion of an Arhat liberated by time (*samayavimukta*), whether it has already resolved, is currently resolving, or will resolve.
There is a non-timely liberation of mind through desire that is also not associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
That is to say:

the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) of an Arhat of immovable dharma, or the mental resolve, the resolved state, or the future resolve associated with the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Are all immovable mental liberations associated with the knowledge of non-arising? Answer:
All that are associated with the knowledge of non-arising are immovable mental liberations.
There is the liberation through the immovable mind, which is not associated with the knowledge of non-arising.

This refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) of an Arhat of the immovable type, or the resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*)— whether already resolved, currently resolving, or about to resolve— of a mind associated with the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
For what reason is the "timely liberation of mind" (samayavimukti) called "love" (preman)? Answer:
Because an Arhat of timely liberation constantly and earnestly guards this dharma, cherishing and preserving it as a treasure, lest he encounter conditions that cause him to fall away from it.

It is like a person with only one eye, who—along with his own relatives and friends—diligently guards, cherishes, and treasures that eye, ensuring it does not encounter conditions such as cold, heat, dust, or obscuration, lest this single eye be further ruined or destroyed.
That is also like this; therefore, it is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
What is the training in clear knowledge (*vidyā*)? Answer:
Training in wisdom.
What is training in knowledge? Answer:
One studies the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
What is the clear knowledge (*vidyā*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)? Answer:
Regarding "the wisdom of one beyond training" (aśaikṣaprajñā): what is the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna)? Answer:
Regarding the eight knowledges of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
at the time of the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), which of them is first realized as verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*)?
Is it that of the Buddha?
Is it the Dharma?
Or the Sangha? Answer:
At the time of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, its origin, and its cessation, one first attains verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*) in the Dharma.
At the time of the clear observation of the path, one first attains verified confidence in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Regarding those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), how many of the four perversions (*viparyāsa*) have they already abandoned,
and how many have they not yet abandoned? Answer:
All [defilements] have been severed.
For those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna), how many of the three samādhis—emptiness (śūnyatā), wishlessness (apranihita), and signlessness (animitta)—are accomplished in the past?
How many are accomplished in the future?
How many are present? Answer: Future:
All [factors] of the past:
those that have already ceased but have not been lost.
Present: If it is present before one,
are all past paths already cultivated and already stilled?
Answer: All paths that are past have already been cultivated and already ceased.
There are paths that have already been cultivated and already ceased, yet are not past; [namely, those that are present].
That is to say:
regarding the future path, it has already been cultivated and already stilled.
Are all paths that are "future" necessarily "not yet cultivated and not yet stilled"?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is that which is "future" but is not "unpracticed and unceased."
That is to say:
the path that is future has already been cultivated and already stilled.
There is a path that is "not yet cultivated and not yet stilled," which is not "future."
That is to say:
the path never before attained now first manifests.
There is a "future" path that is also "neither yet cultivated nor yet stilled."
That is to say:
there is the path that is "future," which has not yet been cultivated and has not yet ceased.
There is also a path that is neither "future" nor "not yet cultivated and not yet ceased."
That is to say:
the Path that has passed away;
and the Path previously attained which is now present before one.
Question: Are all paths that are present being correctly cultivated? Answer:
All paths that are present are being correctly cultivated.
There is the correct cultivation of the Path that is not present;
this refers to when the Path, never before attained, first manifests in the present.
That which is cultivated in the future is the path of that same category.

It is comprised of eight knowledges and constitutes cultivation. Through the knowledge of the realization of cessation, which takes characteristics as its object, one knows the seven wholesome mental applications (*saṃjñā*). May this chapter be fully explained.
There are eight knowledges;
namely, from the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) up to the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)? Answer:

It is all untainted knowledge regarding the conditioned phenomena of the desire realm—namely, the causes of those phenomena, the cessation of those phenomena, and the path capable of abandoning those phenomena.
Furthermore,
all untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) pertaining to the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the stage of the knowledge of phenomena is called "knowledge of phenomena" (dharma-jñāna).
What is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)? Answer:

It is all untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) regarding the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the form and formless realms—namely, the causes of those conditioned phenomena, the cessation of those conditioned phenomena, and the path that can sever those conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore,
all untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) pertaining to subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) and the stage of subsequent knowledge is called subsequent knowledge.
What is the knowledge of others' minds? Answer:
It is that wisdom which, as a fruit of cultivation, knows the present minds and mental factors of others.
What is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
Answer: It is the outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) of the three realms.
What is the knowledge of suffering? Answer:
It is the knowledge that operates with the mental aspects of suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self regarding all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
What is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*)? Answer:
It is the knowledge that functions with the aspects of cause, origination, production, and condition with respect to the causes of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What is the knowledge of cessation? Answer:
It is the knowledge that functions with the aspects of cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation regarding the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What is the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)? Answer:

It is the knowledge that arises by way of the aspects of being a path, being suchness, being practice, and being an outlet, directed toward the path that serves as the antidote to all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
Regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), how many among the eight knowledges does each one subsume?
Answer: The knowledge of phenomena subsumes the knowledge of phenomena—the partial portions of five knowledges.
That is to say:
the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
The subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) subsumes the subsequent knowledge itself and a portion of five knowledges.
That is to say:
the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
The knowledge of others' minds subsumes the knowledge of others' minds.
A small portion of four knowledges,
namely: the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
Conventional knowledge comprises conventional knowledge and a portion of the knowledge of others' minds.
Knowledge of suffering comprises knowledge of suffering and a portion of two other knowledges.
That is to say:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna). The knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna) subsumes the knowledge of origin—namely, a portion of two knowledges.
That is to say:

the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna). The knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) subsumes the knowledge of cessation and a small portion of two other knowledges.
That is to say:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna). The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) subsumes the knowledge of the path and a portion of three other knowledges.
That is to say:

the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna). If one possesses the knowledge of phenomena, how many of these eight knowledges does one possess?
How many are not accomplished? Answer:
Either three, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
That is to say:

at the time of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti)— if there is no knowledge of others' minds— one accomplishes three.
When one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes four [knowledges].
At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*):
if one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes four [knowledges].
When one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, five are accomplished.
At the time of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation:
when one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, five are accomplished.
When one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, six [knowledges] are accomplished.
At the moment of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path:
when one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, six [knowledges] are accomplished.
When possessing the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven.
At the time of the knowledge of the dharma of the path up to the subsequent knowledge of the path:
when not possessing the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes eight [knowledges].
If one accomplishes the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), among these eight knowledges, how many does one accomplish and how many does one not accomplish?
Answer: Either four, five, six, seven, or eight.
That is to say:
At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) and the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of origin (samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti): there is no knowledge of others' minds;
one accomplishes four [knowledges].
When possessing the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes five [knowledges].
At the time of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation,
there is no knowledge of others' minds.
One who possesses the knowledge of others' minds accomplishes six.
At the moment of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation, up to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path:
If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds,
one accomplishes six;
if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven.
At the time of the knowledge of the dharma of the path up to the subsequent knowledge of the path:
there is no knowledge of others' minds;
one accomplishes seven.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes eight [knowledges].
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds, among these eight knowledges, how many are accomplished and how many are not accomplished?
Answer: There may be two, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
That is to say, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
At the time of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti): one accomplishes two.
At the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) and the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti):
— At the time of attaining the four:
during the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), one possesses five.
At the time of the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation:
one accomplishes six.
At the time of the dharma-knowledge of cessation up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path:
When one accomplishes the seven [knowledges],
from the time of the dharma-knowledge of the path up until the subsequent knowledge of the path:
one accomplishes eight.
If one achieves conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), how many of these eight knowledges does one achieve,
and how many does one not achieve? Answer:
Or one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight;
namely, for ordinary beings and noble ones at the moment of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes one;
if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes two.
At the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering and the patience regarding subsequent knowledge of suffering:
If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes three;
if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes four.
At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*):
If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes four;
if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes five.
This applies from the time of the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation.
When one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, five [knowledges] are accomplished.
When one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, six are accomplished.
This applies from the moment of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation up until the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path.
If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes six.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven.
At the time of the dharma-knowledge of the path up to the subsequent knowledge of the path:
If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven [knowledges].
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes eight.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), how many of these eight knowledges does one accomplish?
How many are not accomplished? Answer:
Either three, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
That is to say:

at the time of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti)— if there is no knowledge of others' minds— one accomplishes three.
When one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, four [knowledges] are accomplished.
At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*):
if one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, four [knowledges] are accomplished.
When one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, five [knowledges] are accomplished.
At the time of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation:
when one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, five [knowledges] are accomplished.
When one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, six [knowledges] are accomplished.
At the moment of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path:
when one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, six [knowledges] are accomplished.
When possessing the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven [knowledges].
At the time of the knowledge of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna) up to the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna):
when not possessing the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven [knowledges].
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes eight [knowledges].
If one accomplishes the knowledge of the origin [of suffering], among these eight knowledges, how many are accomplished and how many are not accomplished?
Answer: There are five, six, seven, or eight. Namely:
At the time of the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation:
if there is no knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes five;
if there is knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes six.
At the time of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation up to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path:
if there is no knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes six;
if there is knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven.
At the time of the knowledge of the dharma regarding the Path (mārga-dharmajñāna) up to the subsequent knowledge of the Path (mārgānvayajñāna):
if there is no knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), one accomplishes seven;
if there is knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes eight.
If one has attained the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), how many of these eight knowledges are attained and how many are not attained? Answer:
Or six, seven, or eight; that is to say,
at the time of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of cessation, up to the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of the path:
If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes six.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven.
This applies at the time of the dharma-knowledge of the path up to the subsequent knowledge of the path.
If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes eight.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of the path, how many of these eight knowledges does one accomplish?
How many are not accomplished? Answer:
Either seven or eight.
That is to say:
if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven;
if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes eight.
If one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also cultivate the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate this as four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the dharma-knowledge but not the subsequent knowledge;
that is to say,
at the time of entering the clear realization of the dharma-knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
When those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (śrotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), or arhat, bring the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) into manifestation,
there is cultivation of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) that is not [simultaneously] the knowledge of phenomena.
That is to say:
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation;
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings the already attained subsequent knowledge into manifestation—
there is simultaneous cultivation (*ubhaya-bhāvanā*).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) within the clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭa-pada*) or an arhat has not yet brought an untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) into manifestation.
When one has not yet attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) such that it is present before one, and is thus able to cultivate both simultaneously,
there are cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
When a learner (śaikṣa), one who has seen the tracks (dṛṣṭiprāpta), or an arhat, has already attained mundane knowledge (lokasamvṛtijñāna) which is present before them;
or when they have not yet attained mundane knowledge which is present before them, and in both cases it is not being cultivated.

For all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), at the time of a defiled mind, an indeterminate mind, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual heaven (*asaṃjñika*), or during the moment of untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
If one is cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), is one also cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*)?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions.
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), but not the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
and for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, at the time of entering the clear realization of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).

When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) has the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) present before them, it is not at a time when the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is present.
When they have not yet attained the outflow-free knowledge (anāsravajñāna) present before them, they are not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds.
When mundane knowledge has not yet been brought into presence, one cultivates dharma-knowledge but not the knowledge of others' minds.
There is also the case where one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds but not dharma-knowledge; namely:
When an ordinary person brings to presence the knowledge of others' minds— whether already attained or not yet attained—
and when they bring to presence the conventional knowledge not yet attained while cultivating the knowledge of others' minds.

For one who has attained the vision of the path (śaikṣa-darśana-mārga) or is an arhat, when the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) is present before them, it is not at a time of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).
There is simultaneous cultivation [of both].
That is to say:
When one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire enters the path of clear realization (abhisamaya) at the stage of subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna);

or when a trainee (śaikṣa), a "seer of the tracks" (dṛṣṭiprāpta), or an Arhat brings to presence the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) that they have already attained, which is at that time the knowledge of another's mind (paracitta-jñāna).
When one has not yet attained the manifestation of untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) but is cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna);
when one has not yet attained the manifestation of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) but is able to cultivate both simultaneously;
and there are cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
when entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation;

and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has attained the manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), but it is not the time of dharma-knowledge or knowledge of others' minds.
When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has already been attained and is present before one, but the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is not;
when conventional knowledge has not yet been attained and is present before one, and neither is being cultivated;
or when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds.

At all times of defiled minds, indeterminate minds, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the realm of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), and during moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), does one also cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)?
Answer: This should be analyzed in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) but not conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings the already attained dharma-knowledge into manifestation.
When the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet arisen before one, and one is not cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna),
there is cultivation of conventional knowledge that is not dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna).
That is to say:
When ordinary beings bring to presence mundane knowledge already acquired or not yet acquired;

when those who have entered the path of vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and arhats bring to presence mundane knowledge already acquired; and when they enter into the subsequent knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation within the process of clear realization (abhisamaya).
When mundane knowledge has not yet arisen and is not present, and one is not cultivating dharma-knowledge,
there is simultaneous cultivation.
That is to say:

When one who has attained the vision of the path (śaikṣa-darśana-mārga) or an arhat has not yet brought the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) into manifestation, but is cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna);
or when they have not yet brought conventional knowledge into manifestation, but are cultivating dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna).
There is that which is neither cultivated; namely,

when a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat has attained an outflow-free knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) that is present before them, but it is not at the time of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).

At all times of defiled minds, indeterminate minds, the attainment of non-conception, the attainment of cessation, the realm of non-conception, and during the moment of untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), does one also cultivate the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), but not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding origination, cessation, and the path;
or when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has attained the present manifestation of the knowledge of phenomena, but not the knowledge of suffering.
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering that is not the knowledge of phenomena;
namely, at the time of entering the clear realization of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).

For those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (śrotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), or arhat, when the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) has already been acquired and is present before them, it is not the time for the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).
There is simultaneous cultivation [of both].
That is to say:
At the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada-śaikṣa*) or an arhat brings the already attained dharma-knowledge of suffering into manifestation.
When untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet arisen before one,
and when mundane knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has not yet arisen before one, there are instances where both are cultivated together,
and instances where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*);

and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has attained the manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), but it is not the untainted knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) or the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).

When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has already been attained is present, when conventional knowledge not yet attained is present, and when one is not cultivating the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*);

at all times for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), during states of afflicted mind (*kliṣṭacitta*), indeterminate mind (*avyākṛtacitta*), the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the realm of non-conception (*asaṃjñideva*), and during the moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also cultivate the knowledge of aggregation (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is that which is the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) but not the cultivation of knowledge (jñāna).
This refers to the time when one enters into the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the dharma-knowledges regarding suffering, cessation, and the path.

For one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (śrotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), or arhat, when the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already been attained and is present before them, it is not the time for the knowledge of origination (samudayajñāna).
There are cases where one cultivates the knowledge of origination but not the knowledge of phenomena.
That is to say:
When entering the clear realization of the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*),

for a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat, the subsequently attained knowledge of origin (*anuprāpta-samudaya-jñāna*) is present, but it is not at the time of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
There is simultaneous cultivation [of both].
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada-śaikṣa*) or an arhat brings the dharma-knowledge of origin already attained into manifestation.
When untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has not yet arisen in the present,

and when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has not yet arisen in the present, during the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*),
there is a case where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of the cessation of suffering (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*);

when a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings forth the already attained untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) into the present, but it is not the time of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) or the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*).
