When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has already been attained is present, conventional knowledge not yet attained is not present; nor is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*) cultivated.

This occurs for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) during moments of afflicted or neutral minds, during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), in the realm of non-conception (*asaṃjñideva*), and during moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also cultivate the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) but not the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna); namely,
when entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the dharmajñānas regarding suffering, its origin, and the path.

For one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (śrotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), or arhat, when the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already been attained and is present before them, it is not at a time of the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna).
There are cases where one cultivates the knowledge of cessation but not the knowledge of phenomena; namely:

When entering the realization of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), for a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or for an Arhat, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them; it is not the time of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*). At that time, there is the simultaneous cultivation [of both].
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization of the knowledge of the dharma of cessation; at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path;
and when a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat brings the already attained knowledge of the dharma of cessation into manifestation.
When untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has not yet arisen in the present,
and when mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has not yet arisen in the present, there are instances where both are cultivated together,
and instances where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin;

or when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has attained the manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), but it is not the dharma-knowledge or the knowledge of cessation.
When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has already been attained is present,
when conventional knowledge not yet attained is present, and when neither is being cultivated; at all times for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),

during defiled or neutral states of mind, during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual gods (*asaṃjñisattva*), and during the moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also cultivate the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) that is not the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
This refers to the time when one enters into the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation.

For one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (śrotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), or arhat, when the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has already been acquired and is present, but it is not at a time of path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna):
there is cultivation of path-knowledge, but not of dharma-knowledge.
That is to say:

For one who has attained the vision of the tracks (śaikṣa-darśana-mārga) or an Arhat, when the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) has already arisen and is present, it is not the time of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
There is simultaneous cultivation [of both].
That is to say:
At the time of entering the path of clear realization through the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*);
when a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings the already attained knowledge of the dharma regarding the path into manifestation;
and at the time when an untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) not yet attained is brought into manifestation.
When one has not yet attained mundane knowledge (*lokasamvṛtijñāna*) such that it is present before one, and is able to cultivate both [knowledges] simultaneously,
there is a case where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation,

for a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat, the already attained untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) is present; this is not the case when the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is present.
When one who has already attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) brings it into manifestation,
or when one who has not yet attained conventional knowledge brings it into manifestation, or when neither is being cultivated; at all times for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),

during afflicted or neutral states of mind, during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual heaven (*asaṃjñika*), and during moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
If one cultivates subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), does one also cultivate knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is cultivation of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the subsequent knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation.
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, it is at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna).

For a learner (śaikṣa) who has seen the tracks [of the noble ones] or an arhat, it is when the subsequently attained knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has already been acquired and is present before them, but not at a time when the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) is present.
When untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet arisen before one, and one is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna);
or when mundane knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has not yet arisen before one, and one is cultivating subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), but not the knowledge of others' minds.
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds that is not conventional knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
This refers to when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), whether having already attained it or not yet attained it, brings the knowledge of others' minds into manifestation.
When mundane knowledge has not yet arisen and one is cultivating the knowledge of others' minds;
or when a learner who has seen the path or an arhat has already attained the knowledge of others' minds and it is present before them, but it is not at a time of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
There is simultaneous cultivation; namely,
when one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire enters the path of clear observation at the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the categories (mārgānvaya-jñāna).

When a learner who has seen the tracks (a *śaikṣa* who has attained the vision of the truths) has the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) present before them, which is the knowledge of others' minds;
or when they have not yet attained the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) present before them, and are cultivating the knowledge of others' minds.

When mundane knowledge (*lokasamvṛtijñāna*) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, it is possible to cultivate both [knowledges] simultaneously; however, there are also cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path, the learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or the arhat has already attained the manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*).
When one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has already been attained is present;
when one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge that has not yet been attained is present; and when neither is being cultivated, both are present.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);

at all times of defiled mind (*kliṣṭacitta*) or neutral mind (*avyākṛtacitta*); during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the state of the non-conceptual heavens (*asaṃjñideva*); and at the time of the uncontaminated receptivities (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), does one also cultivate conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is cultivation of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that is not conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna);
namely, at the time of entering the path of subsequent knowledge during the clear realization (abhisamaya).
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat has the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) present before them;
or when they have not yet attained the outflow-free knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) present before them, and are not cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
There is the cultivation of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) that is not inferential knowledge (anvayajñāna).
This refers to when conventional knowledge— whether already attained or not yet attained— is present before an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat brings conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) into manifestation;
or when one has not yet attained conventional knowledge and does not cultivate subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) while it is being manifested.
There is simultaneous cultivation;
that is to say,
when one enters the clear realization of the subsequent knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation.
When one who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-darśana-pratipannaka) or an arhat, before the manifestation of untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna), cultivates mundane knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna);
or when, before the manifestation of mundane knowledge, they cultivate subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).

There is that which is neither cultivated in both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation]. This refers to the time when one enters the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

For those in training (*śaikṣa*), those who have seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*), and Arhats, when untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has already arisen and is present before them, it is not at the time of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

This also applies during all defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*), neutral minds (*avyākṛta-citta*), the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñika*), and at the time of the untainted receptivities (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
If one cultivates subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), is it also suffering knowledge (*duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Answer: One should formulate this as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are cases where one cultivates the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) but not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna); namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the subsequent knowledge of origination (samudaya) and cessation (nirodha).

For one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (śrotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), or arhat, when the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present before them, it is not at a time when the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) is present.
There are cases where one cultivates the knowledge of suffering but not the subsequent knowledge; namely:

When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), for those in training who have seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) and for Arhats, the previously attained knowledge of suffering is present before them; this is not the time of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). There is simultaneous cultivation (*ubhaya-bhāvanā*) at that time.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada-śaikṣa*) or an arhat brings the already attained subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) into manifestation.
When the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has not yet arisen before one,
and when the mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has not yet arisen before one, there are instances where both are cultivated together,
and instances where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding origination, cessation, and the path;

and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has attained and brought to presence an untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), but it is not yet the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) or the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).

When one has already attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and it is present, yet has not yet attained [another instance of] mundane knowledge that is present, and during the time when neither is being cultivated;

for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) when their minds are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñideva*), and during the moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), does one also cultivate the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna)?
Answer: This should be treated as four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha) and cessation (nirodha).

For those who have studied and seen the tracks—the stream-enterers and arhats—when conventional knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen and is present before them, it is not at the time of the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
There are cases where one cultivates the knowledge of origination but not conventional knowledge; namely:
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*),

for a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or for an arhat, the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) that has already been attained is present, but it is not at the time of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). In this case, there is the simultaneous cultivation (*ubhaya-bhāvanā*) of both.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*);
and when a trainee who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings the already attained subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*) into manifestation.
When untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet arisen before one,
and when mundane knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has not yet arisen before one, there are times when both can be cultivated together,
and times when neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) regarding suffering, cessation, and the path;

and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or an arhat has attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) present before them, but it is not the time of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*).
When one has already attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and it is present,
yet has not yet attained mundane knowledge that is currently manifesting— during both these states when neither is being cultivated—

it is as follows: for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), during moments of afflicted or neutral minds, during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual gods (*asaṃjñideva*), and during the moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of subsequent realization (anvaya-jñāna), does one also cultivate the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of subsequent knowledge regarding suffering and its origin.

For those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (śrotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), or arhat, when the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has arisen and is present, it is not at a time when the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) is present.
There are cases where one cultivates the knowledge of cessation but not the subsequent knowledge; namely:

When entering the clear realization of the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), for a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or for an arhat, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) has already been attained and is present; this is not the time of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). At that time, there is the simultaneous cultivation [of both].
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings the subsequently attained knowledge of cessation (*prāpta-nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) into manifestation.
When untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has not yet arisen in the present,
and when mundane wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has not yet arisen in the present, there are times when both are cultivated together,
and times when neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
when entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering, its origin, and the path;

and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has attained untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) that is present before them, but it is not the time of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) or the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has already been attained is present;
when conventional knowledge not yet attained is present; when neither is being cultivated;

during all stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); during afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds; during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñideva*), and during the moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), does one also cultivate the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that is not path knowledge (mārga-jñāna); namely,
at the time of entering the clear observation (abhisamaya) of the subsequent knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation.
For one who has studied and seen the tracks and is an Arhat, when conventional knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen and is present, it is not at a time of path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*).
There are cases where path-knowledge is present but conventional knowledge is not.
That is to say:
When entering the path of clear realization through the dharma-knowledge of the path,

for a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat, the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) has already been attained and is present, but it is not at the time of the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
There is simultaneous cultivation [of both].
That is to say:
at the time of entering the path of subsequent knowledge (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) during the clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings the already attained subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) into manifestation.
When untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has not yet arisen before one,
and when mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has not yet arisen before one, there are instances where both are cultivated together,
and instances where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation;

or when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has attained the manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), but it is not yet the time for the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
When conventional knowledge already attained is present;
when conventional knowledge not yet attained is present; when neither is being cultivated;

during all instances of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), with afflicted or neutral minds, during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual heaven (*asaṃjñideva*), and during moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds, is it also conventional knowledge?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds that is not conventional knowledge; namely,
when one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire enters the path of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) during the realization (*abhisamaya*).

For those who have studied and seen the tracks [of the path] and for Arhats, when the knowledge of others' minds has already been attained and is present before them, it is not at a time of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

When the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has not yet been attained and is present before them while they cultivate the knowledge of others' minds, it is not at a time of conventional knowledge.
There is the cultivation of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) that is not the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
This refers to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who lack the knowledge of others' minds, at the time when conventional knowledge— whether already attained or not yet attained— is present before them.

There is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) possessing the knowledge of others' minds who, at a time when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has been attained and is present before him, is not at that time possessing the knowledge of others' minds;
or one who, at a time when conventional knowledge has not yet been attained and is present before him, is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds.
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation;
when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) to presence, but not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
When mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, and one is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
When untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, and one is cultivating mundane knowledge but not the knowledge of others' minds.
There is simultaneous cultivation.
That is to say:
when an ordinary person brings to presence a knowledge of others' minds that has already been attained or not yet attained.
When one has not yet attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and is currently cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);
or when a trainee who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings already-attained mundane and knowledge of others' minds into manifestation.
When one has not yet attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) manifesting before one, yet is cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);
or when one has not yet attained untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) manifesting before one, yet is able to cultivate both simultaneously;
there are also cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
and for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, at the time of entering the clear realization of the subsequent-knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding the path.

For one who has entered the path of seeing (śaikṣa-darśana-mārga) or for an arhat, when untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has already arisen and is present before them, but it is not the time of the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna);
or when untainted knowledge has not yet arisen and is not present before them—during these times, neither [of the two knowledges] is cultivated.

At all times of defiled minds, indeterminate minds, the attainment of non-conception, the attainment of cessation, the realm of non-conception, and during the moment of untainted receptivity (anāsrava-kṣānti).
If one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds, is it also the knowledge of suffering?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) that is not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
That is to say:
when an ordinary person brings to presence the knowledge of others' minds—whether already attained or not yet attained;
or when they bring to presence the conventional knowledge not yet attained while cultivating the knowledge of others' minds.
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat brings the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) into manifestation,
there is cultivation of the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) that is not the knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say:
At the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering;
for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, at the time of entering the clear realization of the path-subsequent knowledge (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*);
and for a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the noble ones] or an arhat, when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them.
When untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, at a time when one is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna);

or when mundane knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, at a time when one is cultivating the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), but not the knowledge of others' minds.
There is simultaneous cultivation; namely,
when one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire enters the path of the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) within the clear realization (abhisamaya).

When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat has not yet brought forth untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) into the present, but is cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna);
or when, having not yet brought forth conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) into the present, they are able to cultivate both simultaneously.
There is a case where neither is cultivated: namely,

at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding origination and cessation, and during the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) regarding the path.

For one who has attained the stage of a learner (śaikṣa), a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), or an arhat, when untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has already been attained and is present before them— specifically at a time other than that of the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) or the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)—

and when conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has already been attained and is present before them— specifically at a time other than that of the knowledge of others' minds— [these knowledges are not simultaneous].
When mundane knowledge (*loka-jñāna*) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, and both [knowledges] are not being cultivated;
when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*);

during all defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states of mind; during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñi-deva*), and during the moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds, does one also cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds that is not the knowledge of origination; namely,
when an ordinary person has already attained or has not yet attained the knowledge of others' minds, and it is present before them.
When mundane knowledge has not yet been attained and is being manifested while one is cultivating the knowledge of others' minds;
and when a trainee who has seen the tracks or an arhat manifests the already-attained knowledge of others' minds.
There is cultivation of the knowledge of origination, but not the knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge of origination.
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
at the time of entering the path of clear observation (*abhisamaya*) through the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*);
and for a trainee (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the truths] or an arhat, when the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them.
When untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, and one is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna).

When worldly knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, and one is cultivating the knowledge of destruction (kṣaya-jñāna), but not the knowledge of others' minds.
There is simultaneous cultivation; namely,
when one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire enters the path of the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the clear observation (abhisamaya).

When one who has attained the vision of the path (śaikṣa-darśana-mārga) or an Arhat, while the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet manifested, cultivates the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna);
or when, while the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has not yet manifested, they are able to cultivate both simultaneously.
There is the case where neither is cultivated: namely,

at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering and cessation, and the dharma-knowledge regarding the path.

For those who have studied and seen the tracks [of the path] and for Arhats, when untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has already been attained and is present before them, it is not at the time of the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) or the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna).
When conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has already been attained and is present before them, it is not at the time of the knowledge of others' minds.
When mundane knowledge (*lokajñāna*) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, and both [knowledges] are not being cultivated;
when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);

during all defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*) states of mind; when entering the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or the state of non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñideva*); and during the moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds, is it also the knowledge of cessation?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations.
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds that is not the knowledge of cessation; namely,
when an ordinary person has either already attained or not yet attained the knowledge of others' minds, and it is present before them.
When mundane knowledge has not yet been attained and is being brought into presence while cultivating the knowledge of others' minds;
and when a trainee who has seen the path or an arhat brings the already attained knowledge of others' minds into presence.
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of cessation that is not the knowledge of others' minds; namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge of cessation.

For one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, it is at the time of entering the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) through the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).

For a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the truth] and for an Arhat, it is at the time when the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them.
When untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet arisen in the present, and one is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna);
or when worldly knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has not yet arisen in the present, and one is cultivating the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), but not the knowledge of others' minds.
There is simultaneous cultivation; namely,
when one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire enters the path of clear observation at the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the categories (*dharmajñānānvayajñāna*).

When a learner (śaikṣa) who has seen the tracks (dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat, while the untainted knowledge (anāsravajñāna) has not yet manifested before them, cultivates the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna);
or when they have not yet attained mundane knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) manifesting before them, and are able to cultivate both simultaneously.
There is that which is neither cultivated:

namely, when one enters the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin, and at the time of the dharma-knowledge regarding the path.

For those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or arhat, when untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them— excluding the moments of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)—
and when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them— excluding the moment of the knowledge of others' minds— [the following applies].
When mundane knowledge (*lokajñāna*) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, and both [knowledges] are not being cultivated;
when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);

during all defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) states of mind; during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñideva*), and during the moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds, is it also the knowledge of the path?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds that is not the knowledge of the path; namely,
when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), whether having already attained it or not yet attained it, brings the knowledge of others' minds into manifestation.
When mundane knowledge has not yet arisen and present, and one is cultivating the knowledge of others' minds;
or when a learner who has seen the tracks (the noble ones) or an arhat has already attained the knowledge of others' minds which is present, but it is not the time for the knowledge of the path.
There is the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) cultivated on the path of cultivation, but it is not the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) regarding the path.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire enters the path of clear realization (abhisamaya) at the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna);

or when a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada) or an arhat brings the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) to presence, provided it is not at a time when the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) is present.
When untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, and one is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna);

or when mundane knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, and one is cultivating the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), but not the knowledge of others' minds.
There is simultaneous cultivation.
That is to say:
when one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire enters the path of the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) within the clear realization (abhisamaya).

When a learner who has seen the tracks (a *śaikṣa* who has attained the fruit of stream-entry) or an arhat brings the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) into manifestation;
or when, while yet to have attained the outflow-free knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), one brings the knowledge of others' minds into cultivation.
When mundane knowledge (*lokasamvṛtijñāna*) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, it is possible to cultivate both [knowledges] simultaneously;
there are also cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation;

when a trainee (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks or an arhat has attained and brought to presence an untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), but it is not at a time of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has already been attained and is present, but the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is not;
when conventional knowledge has not yet been attained and is not present, and neither is being cultivated;
or when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds.

At all times of defiled minds, indeterminate minds, the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation, the realm of non-perception, and the moment of untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
If one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), does one also cultivate the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) that is not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
That is to say:
when an ordinary person brings to presence mundane knowledge already acquired or not yet acquired;
and when entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the subsequent knowledge of origin and the subsequent knowledge of cessation.
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat brings conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) into manifestation;
or when one has not yet attained conventional knowledge into manifestation and is not cultivating the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering that is not conventional knowledge; namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization of the dharma-knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of the path.
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat brings the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) into manifestation,
and while that untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet been attained, they are not cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
There is simultaneous cultivation;
namely, at the time of entering the clear realization of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna).

When one who has attained the vision of the path (śaikṣa-darśana-mārga) or an arhat, while the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet manifested before them, cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna);
or when, while conventional knowledge has not yet manifested before them, they cultivate the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
There is a case where neither is cultivated:
namely, at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge regarding origination, cessation, and the path.

For those in training who have seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) and for arhats, when untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has already arisen and is present before them, it is not at the time of the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).

Furthermore, it is not during any defiled mind (kliṣṭa-citta), neutral mind (avyākṛta-citta), the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), the state of the non-percipient gods (asaṃjñi-deva), or at the time of the forbearances (kṣānti) that are untainted.
If one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), does one also cultivate knowledge of accumulation (*samudaya-jñāna*)?
Answer: This should be treated as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), but not of the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*).
That is to say:
when conventional knowledge—whether already attained or not yet attained—is present before an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*);
when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada-śaikṣa*) or an arhat brings conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) already acquired into manifestation;
and when one does not cultivate the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) because conventional knowledge not yet acquired is being brought into manifestation.
There is cultivation of the knowledge of origin, but not conventional knowledge; namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization of the dharma-knowledge of origin and the subsequent knowledge of the path.
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat has already attained the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) such that it is present before them;
or when they have not yet attained the outflow-free knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) such that it is present before them, and are not cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
There is simultaneous cultivation;
namely, at the time of entering the clear realization of the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*).

When a learner (śaikṣa), a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), or an arhat has not yet brought the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) into presence, but is cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna);
or when they have not yet brought conventional knowledge into presence, but are cultivating the knowledge of accumulation (samudaya-jñāna).
There is that which is neither cultivated;
namely, at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering, cessation, and the path.

For those in training (śaikṣa), those who have seen the tracks (dṛṣṭiprāpta), and arhats, when untainted knowledge (anāsravajñāna) has already arisen and is present before them, it is not at the time of the knowledge of origination (samudayajñāna).

Furthermore, [it does not arise] during all defiled minds (kliṣṭacitta), neutral minds (avyākṛtacitta), the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñisamāpatti), the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), the state of non-conceptual beings (asaṃjñideva), and at the time of the untainted forbearances (anāsravakṣānti).
If one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), does one also cultivate the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), but not the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
That is to say:
when conventional knowledge—whether already attained or not yet attained—is present before an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*);
when a learner (*śaikṣa*), one who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*), or an arhat brings conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) already acquired into manifestation;
and when, while not yet having acquired conventional knowledge brought into manifestation, one does not cultivate the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of cessation, but not conventional knowledge; namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization of the knowledge of the dharma of cessation and the subsequent knowledge of the path.
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat has already attained the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) such that it is present before them;
and when they have not yet attained the outflow-free knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) such that it is present before them, nor are they cultivating conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
There is simultaneous cultivation;
that is, at the time of entering the clear realization of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*).
When one who has seen the tracks (a learner) or an Arhat, while the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet manifested before them, cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna);
or when, while conventional knowledge has not yet manifested before them, they cultivate the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna).
There is that which is neither cultivated;
namely, at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, and the path.

For those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (śrotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), or arhat, when untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has already arisen and is present before them, it is not at the time of the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna).

Furthermore, it does not occur during any defiled mind (kliṣṭa-citta), any neutral mind (avyākṛta-citta), the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), the state of the heaven of non-conception (asaṃjñi-deva), or at the time of the untainted forbearances (anāsrava-kṣānti).
If one cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), does one also cultivate the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that is not path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*.
This refers to:
when conventional knowledge—whether already attained or not yet attained—is present before an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of suffering, origin, and cessation;
when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) already acquired into manifestation;
and when one does not cultivate path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*) while bringing conventional knowledge not yet acquired into manifestation.
There is knowledge of the path that is not conventional knowledge;
namely, at the time of entering the clear realization of the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat has the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) present before them;
or when, having not yet attained the outflow-free knowledge (anāsravajñāna), they do not cultivate conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
There is simultaneous cultivation.
That is to say:

when a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada) or an arhat brings forth an already attained untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) into the present and cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
When mundane knowledge has not yet arisen and is present before one, and at the time of cultivating path-knowledge,
there is a case where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:

When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation, for a learner (*śaikṣa*), one who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*), or an arhat, untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them; this is not, however, at the time of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

At all times when the mind is defiled, indeterminate, or during the attainment of non-conception, the attainment of cessation, the state of non-conceptual beings, or the moment of untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).

Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree. Section Three:

The Aggregate of Wisdom (Jñānaskandha), Sub-section Four: The Chapter on Cultivating Wisdom (Bhāvanājñāna-varga), Part Two. If one cultivates the wisdom of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), does one also cultivate the wisdom of origination (samudaya-jñāna)?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering;
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) to presence after it has already been attained.
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna); namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge regarding origin.
When the learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or the arhat brings the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) into manifestation,
there is simultaneous cultivation of both.
That is to say:
When entering the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) through the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*);
when a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the truths] or an arhat does not yet have an untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) present before them;
and when they are able to cultivate both [kinds of knowledge] while an untainted conventional knowledge (*sāṃvṛtajñāna*) that they have not yet attained is present before them.
There is a case where neither is cultivated:

namely, at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding cessation, and the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*).

For those who have attained the vision of the tracks—the learners (śaikṣa) and arhats—when untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has already been realized and is present before them, this is not at the time of the knowledge of suffering or its origin;
rather, it is when conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has already been realized and is present before them.
When mundane knowledge (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*) has not yet been attained and is not present, and neither [of the two knowledges] is being cultivated;

at all times for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), during states of afflicted or neutral minds, during the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual heaven (*asaṃjñideva*), and during moments of untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
If one cultivates the knowledge of suffering, does one also cultivate the knowledge of cessation?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding suffering.
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat brings the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) into manifestation,
there is the cultivation of the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of suffering.
That is to say:
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
and when a trainee who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an Arhat brings the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) to presence— there is simultaneous cultivation (*ubhaya-bhāvanā*).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the path of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) during the clear realization (abhisamaya);
and for those who have seen the tracks—the learners (śaikṣa)—and Arhats, when untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) has not yet manifested before them.
When one has not yet attained mundane knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) such that it is present before one, and is able to cultivate both [knowledges] simultaneously,
there are cases where neither is being cultivated.
That is to say:

At the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-anvaya-jñāna*), and the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*);

and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings forth an already attained untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that is neither the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
When the already-acquired conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is present,
when the not-yet-acquired conventional knowledge is present, and during both states when neither is being cultivated;
as well as during all defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The attainment of non-conception, the attainment of cessation,
the heaven of non-conception,
and the moment of untainted patience.
If one cultivates the knowledge of suffering, does one also cultivate the knowledge of the path?
Answer: One should formulate this as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of suffering that is not the knowledge of the path; namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge of suffering.
When the learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or the arhat brings the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) into manifestation,
there is the cultivation of the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of suffering.
That is to say:
When entering the path of clear realization through the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
for a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or for an arhat, when the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them,
there is simultaneous cultivation (*ubhayabhāvanā*).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) within the clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
and for those who have seen the tracks—the trainees (*śaikṣa*) and Arhats—at the time when untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has not yet manifested before them.

When mundane knowledge (*lokasamvṛtijñāna*) has not yet been attained and is being brought into presence, it is possible to cultivate both [knowledges] simultaneously; however, there are also cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
At the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding origination and cessation;

and when the learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or the arhat has already attained the manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*), but it is not the knowledge of suffering or the knowledge of the path.
When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has already been attained is present,
when conventional knowledge not yet attained is present, and when neither is being cultivated;
as well as all the defiled and neutral minds of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
The attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation,
the realm of non-perception,
and the moment of untainted receptivity.
If one cultivates the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), does one also cultivate the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of origination but not the knowledge of cessation; that is,
when one enters the clear realization of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge regarding origination.
When a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat brings the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) into manifestation,
there is cultivation of the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of origination.
That is to say:
When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) to presence— there is simultaneous cultivation (*ubhaya-bhāvanā*).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) within the clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has not yet brought forth the manifest presence of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

When mundane knowledge (*lokasamvṛtijñāna*) has not yet been attained and is being brought into presence, it is possible to cultivate both simultaneously; however, there are also cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:

It occurs at the time of entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering, and at the time of the dharma-knowledge regarding the path;

it also occurs for a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) and an arhat when uncontaminated knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them, but not at the time of the knowledge regarding origin or cessation.
When the already-acquired conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is present,
when the not-yet-acquired conventional knowledge is present, and during the time when neither is being cultivated;
as well as during all defiled or neutral states of mind of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
The attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation,
the realm of non-perception,
and the moment of untainted receptivity.
If one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), does one also cultivate the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna); namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding origination.
When a learner who has seen the tracks or an arhat brings the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) into manifestation,
there is the cultivation of the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of origination.
That is to say:
When entering the path of clear realization through the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna),
for a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) and for an arhat, when the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) has already been attained and is present before them,
there is simultaneous cultivation (ubhaya-bhāvanā).
That is to say:
at the time of entering the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) during the clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has not yet brought forth the present manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
When the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has not yet been attained is present before one and can be cultivated simultaneously [with other knowledges],
there are cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:

When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering and cessation, for those in training who have seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) and for arhats, uncontaminated knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has already been attained and is present before them; this is not the case at the time of the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
When already-acquired conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is present,
when unacquired conventional knowledge is present, and during the time when neither is being cultivated;
as well as during all defiled or neutral minds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation,
the realm of non-perception,
and the moment of untainted receptivity.
If one cultivates the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), does one also cultivate the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the knowledge of cessation that is not the knowledge of the path; namely,
at the time of entering the clear realization of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge of cessation.
When the learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi-pratipannaka) or the arhat brings the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) into manifestation,
there is the cultivation of the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) that is not the knowledge of cessation.
That is to say:
When entering the path of clear realization through the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna),
for a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) and an arhat, when the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) has already been attained and is present before them,
there is simultaneous cultivation of both.
That is to say:
at the time of entering the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) during the clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
and when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭa-pada*) or an arhat has not yet brought forth the present manifestation of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

When mundane knowledge (*lokasamvṛtijñāna*) has not yet been attained and is not present before one, it is possible to cultivate both [knowledges] simultaneously; however, there are also cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:

When entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin, for those in training who have seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) and for Arhats, untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has already arisen and is present before them; this is not the case at the time of the knowledge of cessation or the knowledge of the path.
When the already-acquired conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is present,
when the not-yet-acquired conventional knowledge is present, and during both states when neither is being cultivated;
as well as all the defiled and neutral minds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation,
the heaven of non-perception,
and the moment of untainted receptivity.
Regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), among these eight knowledges, how many knowledges does each one take as its object?
Answer: The knowledge of phenomena takes seven knowledges as its object, excluding the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) takes seven knowledges as its object, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).
Knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) both take eight knowledges as their objects.
Knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and knowledge of the origin (samudaya-jñāna) both take two knowledges as their objects.
That is to say:
the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge.
The knowledge of cessation does not take knowledge as its object.
Path-knowledge (maggañāṇa) takes seven knowledges as its object, excluding conventional knowledge (sammutiñāṇa).
Regarding the question of how many conditions exist between each of these—from Dhamma-knowledge up to Path-knowledge—when they are viewed in relation to themselves and to one another: Answer:
Dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) acts as four conditions for dharma-knowledge;
it acts as three conditions for subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), excluding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
and it acts as four conditions for the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
If it acts as their cause or immediate antecedent, it is not their object-condition;
if it acts as their object-condition, it is neither their cause nor their immediate antecedent.
With conventional knowledge—it acts as three conditions, excluding the causal condition.
With the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—it acts as three conditions, excluding the object-condition.
Path-knowledge is a condition for path-knowledge by way of four conditions.
Subsequent knowledge is a condition for subsequent knowledge by way of four conditions.
It is a condition for the knowledge of others' minds by way of four conditions.
If it acts as their cause or immediate antecedent (samanantara), it is not their object-condition (ālambana).
If it acts as their object-condition, it is neither their cause nor their immediate antecedent.
With conventional knowledge—it acts as three conditions, excluding the causal condition.
With the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—it acts as three conditions, excluding the object-condition.
With path-knowledge—it is a condition in four ways.
With dharma-knowledge—it is a condition in three ways, excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
With other-mind-knowledge and other-mind-knowledge—it is a condition in four ways.
If it acts as their cause or as their equal-and-immediate condition, it is not their object-condition;
if it acts as their object-condition, it is neither their cause nor their equal-and-immediate condition.
With respect to conventional knowledge—it acts as four conditions.
With respect to the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin—it acts as four conditions.
If it acts as their cause—it is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
If it serves as an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for that [knowledge], it is not a cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya).
For the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), it serves as three conditions, excluding the object-condition.
For the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), it serves as four conditions.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) acts as four conditions for conventional knowledge;
it acts as three conditions for the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) and the knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna), excluding the causal condition;
and it acts as two conditions for the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
That is to say:
they are the equal-and-immediate condition and the dominant condition.
With respect to the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), they serve as three conditions, excluding the causal condition.
The knowledge of others' minds serves as four conditions:
if it acts as its cause or its equal-and-immediate condition, it is not its object-condition;
if it acts as its object-condition, it is not its cause or its equal-and-immediate condition.

Suffering-knowledge (duḥkha-jñāna) acts as three conditions for suffering-knowledge, as well as for origin-knowledge (samudaya-jñāna) and cessation-knowledge (nirodha-jñāna)—excluding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
It acts as four conditions for path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna), dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), and subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
The knowledge of others' minds serves as four conditions:
if it acts as its cause or its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), it is not its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
if it acts as its object-condition, it is not its cause or its immediately preceding condition.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) acts as three conditions for itself, excluding the causal condition (hetupratyaya).

Knowledge of origination (samudayajñāna) and knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) act as three conditions for knowledge of origination and knowledge of cessation, excluding the object condition (ālambanapratyaya).
With respect to the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of phenomena, and the subsequent knowledge, it serves as four conditions.
With respect to the knowledge of others' minds, it serves as four conditions.
If it acts as their cause or immediate condition, it is not an object-condition.
If it serves as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for that [knowledge], it is not a cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) nor an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
For conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), it serves as three conditions, excluding the cause-condition.
For the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), it serves as three conditions, excluding the object-condition.
Cessation-knowledge (nirodha-ñāṇa) with respect to cessation-knowledge serves as three conditions, excluding the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya).
With respect to path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), dharma-knowledge (dhamma-ñāṇa), and subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-ñāṇa), it serves as four conditions.
With respect to knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-ñāṇa), it serves as four conditions.
If it acts as their cause or immediate antecedent condition, it is not their object-condition;
if it acts as their object-condition, it is neither their cause nor their immediate antecedent condition.
With conventional knowledge—it acts as three conditions, excluding the causal condition.
With the knowledges of suffering and origin—it acts as three conditions, excluding the object-condition.
With the knowledge of the path, and with the knowledges of phenomena and inference—it acts as four conditions.
With respect to the knowledge of others' minds—it serves as four conditions.
If it acts as its cause or its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), it is not its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
If it acts as its object-condition, it is not its cause or its immediately preceding condition.
With conventional knowledge—it acts as three conditions, excluding the causal condition.
With the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation—it acts as three conditions, excluding the object-condition.
Regarding those fetters bound to the desire realm, are those fetters abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are fetters bound to the desire realm that are not abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).
That is to say:
the fetters of the desire realm that are abandoned by patience (kṣānti).
Some are abandoned by subsequent knowledge,
some are not abandoned;
there are fetters that are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but are not bound to the desire realm.
That is to say:
the fetters of the form and formless realms are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
There are also fetters bound to the desire realm that are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena.
That is to say:
the fetters of the desire realm are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
There are also fetters that are not bound to the desire realm and are not abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena.
That is to say:
the fetters of the form and formless realms are either abandoned through patience (*kṣānti*) or abandoned through other types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Or [are there] fetters that are not abandoned? Regarding those fetters bound to the realms of form and formlessness, are they abandoned by the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)? Answer:
Those fetters abandoned by subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are bound to the realms of form and formlessness.
There are, however, fetters bound to the realms of form and formlessness that are not abandoned by subsequent knowledge; namely:
The fetters of the form and formless realms are either abandoned through patience,
or abandoned through other types of knowledge,
or are not abandoned at all.
Regarding those fetters that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), are those fetters abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)? Answer:
Those fetters that are abandoned through the vision of suffering are not abandoned by the knowledge of suffering; rather, they are abandoned by patience (*kṣānti*).
Are they abandoned by other types of knowledge,
or are they not abandoned at all?
Furthermore, if a fetter is abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), is that fetter abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)?

Answer: Regarding those fetters (*saṃyojana*) that are abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), their corresponding bonds (*bandhana*) are not abandoned by the vision of suffering; rather, they are abandoned through both vision and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).
Are those fetters that are abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*) abandoned by the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path?
Answer:

Those fetters that are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, cessation, and path are not abandoned by the knowledge of the origin, cessation, or path; rather, they are abandoned either by patience (*kṣānti*) or by other forms of knowledge.
Or [it is] not abandoned.
If it is abandoned by the knowledge of the origin, cessation, or path, is that fetter abandoned by the vision of the origin, cessation, or path?
Answer:

Regarding those fetters abandoned by the knowledge of the origin, cessation, and the path: are those fetters not abandoned by the vision of the origin, cessation, and the path, but rather abandoned by cultivation?
Regarding those fetters abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*): upon the abandonment of those fetters, is their cessation realized through the knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: Those fetters that are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), their cessation is realized through the knowledge of phenomena.
There are, however, fetters whose cessation is realized through the knowledge of phenomena, yet which are not abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena.
That is to say:
either abandoned by patience (kṣānti) or abandoned by other forms of knowledge (jñāna).
If those fetters are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), is their cessation realized by the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
Answer: No.
Those fetters that are abandoned by subsequent knowledge—
those fetters are realized as ceased through subsequent knowledge.
There are fetters whose cessation is realized through subsequent knowledge.
Those fetters are not abandoned by subsequent knowledge;
that is to say,
they are either abandoned by patience.
Or, when those fetters are abandoned by other types of knowledge, is the cessation of those fetters realized by subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)? Furthermore,
when those fetters are abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), is the cessation of those fetters realized by the knowledge of suffering?
Answer: There are fetters that are abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), and for those fetters, the cessation is realized through the knowledge of suffering.
There are also fetters whose cessation is realized through the knowledge of suffering, yet those fetters are not abandoned by the knowledge of suffering.
That is to say:
