either abandoned by patience (kṣānti) or abandoned by other forms of knowledge (jñāna).

When one realizes the knowledge of the cessation of those fetters through the knowledge of suffering, is it the case that one realizes the cessation of those fetters through the knowledge of origination, cessation, and the path?
Answer:
Those fetters that are abandoned by the knowledge of origination, cessation, and the path are realized through the knowledge of the cessation [of those respective truths].

There are, however, fetters whose cessation is realized through the knowledge of origination, cessation, and the path, yet which are not abandoned by the knowledge of origination, cessation, and the path.
That is to say: either abandoned by means of patience (kṣānti),
or abandoned by means of other types of knowledge (jñāna).
One realizes the knowledge of the cessation of those fetters (the truths of origin, cessation, and the path).
Regarding the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation, from the eye faculty up to the formless realm—among the ten knowledges, how many know it?
Answer: The eye-faculty is known by seven knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). As for the female faculty (*strīndriya*),

it is known by six knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of types (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The male faculty— likewise.
The mind faculty— is known by nine knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of cessation.
The same applies to the five faculties of pleasure, joy, equanimity, faith, and so forth.
The faculty of suffering is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
The faculty of sorrow is likewise.
The three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are known by seven knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, and tangible-object elements are known by seven types of knowledge,
excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.

The same applies to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, and the sphere of tangibles; the aggregate of form-clinging (*rūpôpādānaskandha*), the first five elements (*dhātu*), and phenomena that are both visible and resistant (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*).
The odor and flavor elements are known by six types of knowledge,
excluding the knowledge of categories (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*),
and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). The same applies to the bases of odor and flavor.
The eye, ear, body, and consciousness elements are known by eight knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
The same applies to the last four aggregates of clinging, the consciousness element, contaminated phenomena, indeterminate phenomena, and phenomena abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
The nose-consciousness element and the tongue-consciousness element are known by seven knowledges—
excluding the knowledge of types, the knowledge of cessation,
and the knowledge of the path. Unwholesome states and those states bound to the desire realm are likewise.
The mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu) are known by nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna).
The same applies to the mind-base (manāyatana), the last four aggregates (skandha), conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma), and past, future, and present phenomena.
The dharma-element is known by ten knowledges.
The same applies to the dharma-base, to formless, invisible, and non-obstructive dharmas, and to wholesome dharmas.
The aggregate of form is known by eight knowledges.
The same applies to material phenomena (*rūpadharma*)— excluding those known by the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of cessation—
and to untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*): they are known by eight knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin.
The same applies to the non-abandonable dharmas (*aprahātavya*).
As for unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta*), they are known by six knowledges:
excluding the knowledge of others' minds, [they are known by] the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path.

Dharmas pertaining to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
Dharmas pertaining to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) are known by six knowledges.
Excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-ñāṇa*), knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-ñāṇa*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-ñāṇa*), and knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*).

Learner (*sekha*) and non-learner (*asekha*) phenomena are known by seven knowledges; excluding the knowledge of suffering (*dukkha-ñāṇa*), knowledge of origination (*samudaya-ñāṇa*), and knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-ñāṇa*).
Dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner are known by nine knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of the path.
The truths of suffering and its origin are known by eight knowledges.
The knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
The same applies to conventional knowledge and the threefold samādhis.
The truth of cessation is known by six knowledges.
Excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path.
The truth of the path is known by seven knowledges;
excluding the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation.
The knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the three samādhis, are likewise.
The four dhyānas are known by nine knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of cessation.
The knowledge of others' minds is also like this.
The four immeasurables are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The first three liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the first eight bases of totality are likewise.

The [remaining] three lower formless attainments are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
The fourth, fifth, and sixth liberations are also like this. The fourth formless attainment is known by six types of knowledge,
excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
The seventh and eighth liberations, as well as the latter two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana), are likewise [known by six knowledges].

Dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) is known by six knowledges, excluding subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), the knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna), and the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna).
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is known by six knowledges,

excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna), and the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna). The three fetters (saṃyojana) are known by eight knowledges.

The same applies to the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*); the flood and yoke of views and ignorance (*dṛṣṭi-avidyā-ogha-yoga*); the grasping at views and adherence to precepts and observances (*dṛṣṭi-śīlavrataparāmarśa*); the last two of the bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*); the fetters of greed and conceit (*rāga-māna-saṃyojana*); the last three of the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); the five views (*dṛṣṭi*); the groups of craving born of eye-contact, ear-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact (*sparśaja-tṛṣṇākāya*); the last four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); and the fetters of craving, conceit, ignorance, adherence to views, and doubt (*rāga-māna-avidyā-dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-vicikitsā-saṃyojana*). It is likewise so.
The three unwholesome roots are known by seven knowledges— excluding the knowledge of subsequent realization, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.

They include the outflows of desire, the floods, the yokes, the graspings, the first two of the bodily fetters, the five hindrances, the fetters of ill will, envy, and avarice, and the first two of the lower fetters.
The group of cravings born of nose-contact and tongue-contact, the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and ill-will, and the fetters of ill-will, envy, and avarice—these are also thus.
The outflowing states are known by seven knowledges.
Excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

The same applies to the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the yoke of existence (*bhava-yoga*), the grasping at the doctrine of self (*ātma-vādopādāna*), the four higher fetters (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) excluding attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*), and the latent tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāga-anuśaya*).
The craving for the formless realm is known by six knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*),
and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). The thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm are known by seven knowledges.

Excluding the knowledge of categories (*dhamma-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*). Regarding the thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): they are known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of categories, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
The thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the formless realm are known by six knowledges—

excluding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna). As it is said:

If the perception of impermanence is practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed, it can eliminate all sensual desire, desire for form, desire for the formless, restlessness, conceit, and ignorance.
With how many types of knowledge (*jñāna*) should this perception (*saṃjñā*) be said to be associated?
Answer: It should be said:
That which can eliminate desire and greed is associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).
That which can eliminate greed for the realm of form and the formless realm is associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering.

That which can eliminate restlessness, conceit, and ignorance—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)—is associated with these:
should this perception be said to be with vitarka and with vicāra?
Is it without vitarka and with only vicāra?
Or is it without both vitarka and vicāra? Answer:
It should be said:
that which can eliminate desire and greed possesses both vitarka and vicāra;
that which can eliminate greed for the realm of form and the formless realm, as well as restlessness, pride, and ignorance, may possess either vitarka and vicāra.
Whether it be with no vitarka and only vicāra,
or with neither vitarka nor vicāra—
how many faculties (indriya) should this perception (saṃjñā) be said to be associated with?
Answer: It should be said that that which can eliminate desire and greed is associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).

That which is able to eliminate craving for the realm of form and the formless realm, as well as restlessness, conceit, and ignorance— being associated with the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity—
is this perception to be called "empty"?
Are they associated with wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)? Are they associated with signlessness (*animitta*)? Answer:
One should say: it is associated with the wishless (apraṇihita).
To what realm’s bondage should this perception be said to be related?
Answer: It should be said:
that which is able to eliminate desire-attachment takes what is bound to the desire realm as its object.
That which can eliminate craving for the realm of form takes the objects bound to the realm of form as its condition;
that which can eliminate craving for the formless realm takes the objects bound to the formless realm as its condition;
that which can eliminate restlessness, conceit, and ignorance takes the objects bound to all three realms as its condition.
As it is said:
"One who is skilled in the seven points and possesses the threefold contemplation of meaning can swiftly exhaust all outflows within this Dharma and Vinaya. What are the seven?"
That is to say:
knowing as they truly are form, the origin of form, the cessation of form, the practice leading to the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these seven are also thus.
Should this wisdom be called dharma-knowledge, or even path-knowledge?
Answer: It should be said:
To know form as it truly is— this consists of four knowledges, namely:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
To know the origination of form as it truly is— this consists of four knowledges, namely:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna).
To know the cessation of form as it truly is— this consists of four knowledges, namely:
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
To know, as it truly is, the practice that leads to the cessation of form constitutes four types of knowledge:
namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
To know the gratification of form as it truly is— this consists of four types of knowledge, namely:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna).
To know the peril of form as it truly is— this consists of four knowledges, namely:
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
To know the emergence of form as it truly is— this consists of four knowledges, namely:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna).
The same applies to the sevenfold [analysis] of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as it does for form.
What is the difference between the cessation of form up to consciousness, and the emergence of form up to consciousness?
Answer: If, by means of this craving, various forms arise, the cessation of that [craving] is called the cessation of form.
If other cravings take form as their condition and increase, the abandonment of those is called the transcendence of form.
Furthermore!
If, through these karmic afflictions, various forms arise, the cessation of those is called the cessation of form.
If—through other karmic afflictions—form increases and expands, the cessation of those is called the transcendence of form.
Furthermore, if through this craving, karma, and afflictions various forms arise, the cessation of those is called the cessation of form.
If other cravings, karmas, and afflictions cause form to increase and expand, the abandonment of those is called the transcendence of form.
The same applies to the cessation and emergence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
this is what constitutes the distinction.
Regarding the seven noble ones and the five virtues: two are accomplished in the present, while three manifest in the present.
The Four Gates of Corresponding Matters: In this chapter, it is intended to explain in detail—
from the faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*) up to the one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)— how many of the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) they possess and how many they do not possess.
Answer:
A follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) may achieve one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or all eight knowledges (jñāna).
That is to say:

At the time of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*)—if there is no knowledge of others' minds, there is one; if there is knowledge of others' minds, there are two.

At the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) and the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*)—if there is no knowledge of others' minds, there are three; if there is knowledge of others' minds, there are four.

At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*): if there is no knowledge of others' minds, there are four; if there is knowledge of others' minds, there are five.

From the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*): if there is no knowledge of others' minds, there are five; if there is knowledge of others' minds, there are six.

At the time of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) up to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñānakṣānti*): there are six [knowledges] if there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and seven if there is knowledge of others' minds.

At the time of the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*): there are seven if there is no knowledge of others' minds, and eight if there is knowledge of others' minds.
The same applies to the follower by dharma (dharmanusārin).
Regarding the eight knowledges, one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) either accomplishes seven or eight;
that is to say:
Those who lack the knowledge of others' minds possess seven; those who possess the knowledge of others' minds possess eight.
It is the same for those who have attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
The body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*), the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), and the one doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) are all endowed with all eight knowledges.
For those ranging from the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) to the one liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), how many of the eight knowledges (jñāna) do they possess in the past,
how many in the future,
and how many in the present?
Answer: For one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin), regarding the eight knowledges,
at the time of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti):
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds: for one who lacks it, there is one [knowledge] in the past and future, but none in the present.
For one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds: there are two in the past and future, but none in the present.

At the time of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*): If there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there is one past, three future, and two present [knowledges].
If there is knowledge of others' minds, there are two past, four future, and two present [knowledges].
At the time of the *duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*:
if one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), there are three [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are four [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.

At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*): If there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), there are three past [knowledges], four future, and two present.
If there is knowledge of others' minds, there are four past, five future, and two present.

At the moment of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of the collection (*samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*): If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are four [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are five [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.
At the time of attaining the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*):
If there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are four past [knowledges], five future, and two present.
If there is the knowledge of others' minds, there are five past, six future, and two present.
At the time of the *dharmajñānakṣānti* of the category of collection (*samudaya*):
if there is no knowledge of others' minds, five [knowledges] exist in the past and future, and none in the present;
if there is knowledge of others' minds, six [knowledges] exist in the past and future, and none in the present.

At the time of the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*): If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*), there are five [knowledges] in the past and future, and two in the present.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are six in the past and future, and two in the present.

At the moment of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñānakṣānti*): if there is no knowledge of others' minds, five [knowledges] exist in the past and future, and none in the present.
If there is knowledge of others' minds, six [knowledges] exist in the past and future, and none in the present.

At the moment of the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*): If there is no knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*), there are five past, six future, and two present knowledges.
If there is knowledge of others' minds, there are six past, seven future, and two present knowledges.

At the moment of the patience of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*): If one lacks the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), there are six [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, there are seven [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.

At the moment of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*): If there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), there are six [knowledges] in the past and future, and two in the present.
If there is knowledge of others' minds, there are seven in the past and future, and two in the present.
At the stage of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path (mārga-dharmajñāna-kṣānti):
if there is no knowledge of others' minds, there are six [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.
If there is knowledge of others' minds, there are seven [knowledges] in the past and future, and none in the present.

At the time of the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*): If there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are six past, seven future, and two present knowledges.
If there is knowledge of others' minds, there are seven past, eight future, and two present knowledges.
At the time of the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*):
if there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), seven [knowledges] exist in the past and future, and none in the present;
if there is knowledge of others' minds, eight [knowledges] exist in the past and future, and none in the present.
The same applies to the follower by dharma (dharmanusārin).
For one resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta), regarding the eight knowledges:
excluding the knowledge of others' minds, there are seven in the future.

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds—there are eight in the future; as for the past, it exists if it has already ceased and has not been lost; as for the present, it exists if it is currently manifest.
It is the same for the "attained-by-insight" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) practitioner.
Regarding the body-witness, the one liberated by wisdom, and the one liberated in both ways, they possess eight knowledges:
all are future; as for the past, they exist if they have already ceased and have not been lost; as for the present, they exist if they are currently manifest.

When the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) manifests for those ranging from the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) to the one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), how many knowledges manifest?
Answer: For the follower by faith:
When the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is present, two knowledges are present, namely:

the pair consisting of the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*); the pair consisting of the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*); the pair consisting of the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); and the pair consisting of the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
When subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present, two knowledges are present:

namely, the pair of subsequent and suffering knowledge (duḥkha-jñāna), the pair of subsequent and origination knowledge (samudaya-jñāna), and the pair of subsequent and cessation knowledge (nirodha-jñāna).
When the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) is present, two knowledges are present, namely:
the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), or the knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
When the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) is present, two knowledges are present, namely:

When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) is present, two knowledges are present: either the knowledge of origination and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), or the knowledge of origination and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). When the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is present, two knowledges are present:
namely, the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of phenomena, or the knowledge of cessation and the subsequent knowledge.
When the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is present, two knowledges are present, namely:
the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). The same applies to one who practices in accordance with the Dharma (*anvayadharmavihārin*).

For those with conviction through resolute belief (*śraddhādhimukta*): when the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is present, either two or three knowledges are present—namely, the pair of *dharmajñāna* and *duḥkhajñāna*;

the pair of *dharmajñāna* and *samudayajñāna*; the pair of *dharmajñāna* and *nirodhajñāna*; or the pair of *dharmajñāna* and *mārgajñāna*. When it is not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are two; when it is the knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
When subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is present, either two or three knowledges are present: namely, the pair of subsequent and suffering knowledge;

the pair of subsequent and origin knowledge; the pair of subsequent and cessation knowledge; the pair of subsequent and path knowledge—[this is] two [knowledges] when it is not the knowledge of others' minds, and three [knowledges] when it is the knowledge of others' minds.
When the knowledge of others' minds is present, either two or three knowledges are present: namely, the two consisting of the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge;

or the three consisting of the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of the path, and the knowledge of phenomena; or the three consisting of the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of the path, and the subsequent knowledge.
When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is present, either one or two knowledges are present; namely:
conventional knowledge alone constitutes one, while conventional knowledge together with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) constitutes two.
When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) is present, two knowledges are present, namely:

either the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), or the knowledge of suffering and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). When the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) is present, two knowledges are present, namely: [the knowledge of origin and the knowledge of phenomena, or the knowledge of origin and subsequent knowledge].

When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) is present, two knowledges are present: either the knowledge of origination and the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), or the knowledge of origination and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). When the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is present, two knowledges are present:
namely, the knowledge of cessation and the dharma-knowledge, or the knowledge of cessation and the subsequent knowledge.
When the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is present, either two or three knowledges are present: namely, the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
If it is not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are two; if it is the knowledge of others' minds, there are three.

Regarding the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): for those who do not possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), there are two; for those who possess the knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
The same applies to those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and those who are bodily witnesses (*kāyasākṣin*). As for those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*):
When the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is present, either two or three knowledges are present. That is to say:

the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*). These are two [knowledges] when they are neither the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) nor the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); they are three [knowledges] when they are either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.

Dharma-knowledge and knowledge of origination—these two are not the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising; [if they are] the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, there are three.

Dharma-knowledge and knowledge of cessation—these two are not the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising; [if they are] the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, there are three.

Regarding dharma-knowledge and path-knowledge: they are either two—namely, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of others' minds—or three, which include the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds.
When conventional knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present, either two or three knowledges are present; namely:

The dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) together with the knowledge of categories (anvaya-jñāna) constitutes two [knowledges] when they are neither the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) nor the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna); it constitutes three [knowledges] when they are either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.

The dharma-knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) together with the knowledge of categories constitutes two [knowledges] when they are neither the knowledge of exhaustion nor the knowledge of non-arising; it constitutes three [knowledges] when they are either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.

The knowledge of the subsequent (anvaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna)—these two are not the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) or the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna); they are either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, making three.

The knowledge of the subsequent and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)—these two are not the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna); they are either the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds, making three.
When the knowledge of others' minds is present, two or three knowledges may be present simultaneously: namely, the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge (two);

or the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of the path, and the knowledge of phenomena (three); or the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of the path, and the subsequent knowledge (three).
When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is present, either one or two knowledges are present; namely:
conventional knowledge alone constitutes one [knowledge], while conventional knowledge together with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) constitutes two.
When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) is present, either two or three knowledges are present.

[Specifically,] when it is the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), there are two if they are not the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); there are three if they are the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.

Regarding the knowledge of suffering and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): there are two when they are neither the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and three when they are either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.
When the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) is present, there are either two or three knowledges present;

that is, the knowledge of origin and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)—there are two when they are neither the knowledge of exhaustion nor the knowledge of non-arising, and three when they are either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.

When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are present, there are two knowledges—neither the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)—or three knowledges, which include either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.
When the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is manifested, there are either two or three knowledges manifested; that is to say:

when the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) are present, there are two knowledges—neither the knowledge of exhaustion nor the knowledge of non-arising—or three knowledges, which include either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.

When the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) or subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is present, there are two knowledges—neither the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) nor the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)—or three knowledges, which are either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.
When the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) is manifested, there are either two or three knowledges manifested;

that is, when the knowledge of the path or the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) is present, there are two knowledges—neither the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, nor the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
These are three: either the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), or the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
The knowledges of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are two: they are not the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds.
These are three: either the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds.
The same applies to those liberated by both [wisdom and concentration].
Regarding the three samādhis, how many do those ranging from the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) up to the one liberated by both achieve,
and how many do they not achieve?
Answer:
For one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin), regarding the three samādhis, when the dharma-knowledge-acceptance of cessation (nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) has not yet arisen, they possess two;
once it has arisen, they possess three.
The same applies to the Dharma-follower (dharmanusārin).
Those with conviction through understanding (śraddhādhimukta) up to those liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) are all accomplished in the three samādhis.
Regarding the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) up to those liberated both ways, how many of the three samādhis do they accomplish in the past?
How many are future?
How many are present? Answer:
For one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin) regarding the three samādhis, if they enter the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on emptiness:
at the moment of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti), there is none in the past, two in the future, and one in the present.

At the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna* to *samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*), there is one in the past, two in the future, and one in the present.

At the time of the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna* to *samudaya-anvayajñāna*), there is one in the past and future, and one in the present.
At the moment of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñānakṣānti*): two are past, three are future, and one is present.
From the dharma-knowledge of cessation up to the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*): three are past and future, and one is present.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the wishless (*apraṇihita*):
at the moment of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), there is none in the past, two in the future, and one in the present.
At the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering up to the subsequent knowledge of origination: one past, two future, and one present.
At the time of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation: one past, three future, and one present.

At the time of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of cessation up to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path, there are two past, three future, and one present [knowledges].
It is the same for the follower by dharma.

For those with faith-resolve up to those liberated through both [wisdom and concentration], regarding the three samādhis, all are future; as for the past, they exist if they have already ceased and have not been lost; as for the present, they exist if they are currently manifest.

When the three samādhis—emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—are present before those ranging from the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) to the one liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), how many knowledges (jñāna) are present?
Answer:
When the samādhi of emptiness according to the follower-by-faith (śraddhānusārin) manifests before one, there are either two or none.
That is to say:
There are two [factors] during the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering; there are two during the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering;
and there are none during the three patiences. When the wishless samādhi is present, there are either two or none.
That is to say:
two [moments] for the dharma-knowledge of suffering, two for the subsequent knowledge of suffering, two for the dharma-knowledge of origin, two for the subsequent knowledge of origin;
and two for the dharma-knowledge of the path. There are none during the six moments of patience (*kṣānti*).
When the signless samādhi manifests, there are either two or none.
That is to say:
[the pair of] cessation and dharma-knowledge; [the pair of] cessation and subsequent knowledge; and there are none at the time of the two patiences.
The same applies to those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmanusārin).

When the concentration on the emptiness of those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) manifests, two knowledges manifest: namely, the two consisting of the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of phenomena (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna), or the two consisting of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna).
When the wishless samādhi manifests, there are either two or three [knowledges].
That is to say:

the two consisting of the knowledge of dharma and the knowledge of suffering; the two consisting of the subsequent knowledge and the knowledge of suffering; the two consisting of the knowledge of dharma and the knowledge of origin; and the two consisting of the subsequent knowledge and the knowledge of origin.
Regarding the path and dharma-knowledge: if it is not knowledge of others' minds, there are two; if it is knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
Regarding the path and subsequent knowledge: if it is not knowledge of others' minds, there are two; if it is knowledge of others' minds, there are three.

When the signless samādhi manifests, two knowledges manifest: namely, the pair consisting of the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of phenomena (nirodha-dharma-jñāna), and the pair consisting of the subsequent knowledge of cessation and the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna).
The same applies to the "attained-by-seeing" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and the "bodily-witness" (kāyasākṣin).
When the emptiness-samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi) of liberation through wisdom (prajñāvimukti) manifests before one, two knowledges manifest:

namely, either the two consisting of the knowledge of suffering and the dharma-knowledge (duḥkha-dharmajñāna), or the two consisting of the knowledge of suffering and the subsequent-knowledge (duḥkha-anvayajñāna).
When the wishless samādhi is present, there are either two or three [knowledges].
That is to say:
the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) is [either] the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) or the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), making two.

These are three: either the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). [In the case of] the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), they are two: neither the knowledge of exhaustion nor the knowledge of non-arising. These are three:
either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.

Regarding the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna): they are either two—excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna)—or three, including either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising.
Regarding the knowledge of origin and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna): they are two, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) together with the three [knowledges]; the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)—these two are not the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds;
the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising or the knowledge of others' minds—these three.

Regarding the path and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): they are not associated with the two [knowledges] of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). They are associated with three [knowledges]: either the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds.
When the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*) is present, there are either two or three [knowledges].
That is to say:
the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation is not both the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising;
it is either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, making three [types].
The knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are not the two—knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
They are either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, making three.
The same applies to those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

When the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)—ranging from those of the faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*) up to those who are liberated-in-both-ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)—manifest according to their respective applications, how many types of knowledge (*jñāna*) manifest?
Answer: For one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin),
when the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is present, there are either two [faculties] or none.
That is to say:
two [moments] for the dharma-knowledge of suffering, two for the subsequent knowledge of suffering, two for the dharma-knowledge of origin, two for the subsequent knowledge of origin;
two for the dharma-knowledge of cessation, two for the subsequent knowledge of cessation, and two for the dharma-knowledge of the path; these do not exist at the time of the eight patiences.
The same applies when the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) or the eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present.
As it is for those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin), so it is for those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
When the faculty of "I have known" (ājñendriya) is present for those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta), there are either two or three [faculties].
That is to say:

two [knowledges] regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering, two regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering, two regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination, two regarding the subsequent knowledge of origination, two regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation, and two regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation.
Regarding the path and dharma-knowledge: if it is not mind-reading knowledge, there are two; if it is mind-reading knowledge, there are three.
Regarding the path and subsequent-knowledge: if it is not mind-reading knowledge, there are two; if it is mind-reading knowledge, there are three.
It is the same when the seven factors of enlightenment and the eight factors of the path are present.
As it is for one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), so it is for one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and for one who has realized through the body (kāyasākṣin).
When the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya) is present for one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), there are either two or three [faculties].
That is to say:
the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) consists of two—namely, neither the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) nor the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
It is the knowledge of exhaustion, or sometimes the knowledge of non-arising, thus consisting of three.

Regarding the knowledge of suffering and subsequent knowledge (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*): they are not both the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), thus [possessing] two. They are either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, thus [possessing] three.
Regarding the knowledge of origin and dharma-knowledge (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*): they are not both the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, thus [possessing] two.

This is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); or, together with the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), there are three. Regarding the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*): if they are not the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, there are two;
if they are the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, there are three.

Regarding the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-dharma-jñāna): it consists of two [knowledges], namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), excluding the other two. It is either the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, thus consisting of three.
Regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna): it consists of two [knowledges], namely, the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, excluding the other two.

This is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), or the three [knowledges] including the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Regarding the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*): they are not the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds; thus there are two.
This is the knowledge of exhaustion, or the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds; thus there are three.

The path and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are associated with two [knowledges]: neither the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), nor the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), nor the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna).
They are associated with three [knowledges] when they are either the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds.
The seven factors of enlightenment and the seven factors of the path are likewise.
When right view is present, there are either two or three [factors]:

two when it is the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering; two when it is the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering; two when it is the knowledge of dharma regarding origination; two when it is the subsequent knowledge regarding origination; two when it is the knowledge of dharma regarding cessation; and two when it is the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.
Regarding the path and dharma-knowledge: if it is not the knowledge of others' minds, there are two; if it is the knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
Regarding the path and subsequent-knowledge: if it is not the knowledge of others' minds, there are two; if it is the knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
As it is with those liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*), so it is with those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

Not so. If it is associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), is it also associated with the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (anvaya-dharma-jñāna)? It is not so. It is likewise with respect to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Are those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) also associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are dharmas that are associated with dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) but are not associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*).
That is to say:
those phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not subsumed under the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).
There are also phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not the knowledge of phenomena.
That is to say:

there are factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not subsumed under the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), yet which are both associated with the knowledge of phenomena and associated with the knowledge of others' minds. Namely:
There are phenomena included within the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) that are associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
There are also phenomena that are neither associated with the knowledge of phenomena nor with the knowledge of others' minds; namely:

Dharma-knowledge and knowledge of others' minds; and all other remaining mental states and mental factors not included in or associated with dharma-knowledge and knowledge of others' minds, as well as matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
The same applies to the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as to right view.
Are those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) also associated with the concentration on emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi)?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) but are not empty.
That is to say:
the emptiness associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), as well as those factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena that are not themselves associated with emptiness;
and there are factors associated with emptiness that are not the knowledge of phenomena.
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge associated with emptiness, as well as dharmas associated with emptiness that are not associated with dharma-knowledge;
there are also dharmas that are both associated with dharma-knowledge and associated with emptiness.
That is to say:
there are two types of associated dharmas;
there are dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of what is dharma and what is non-dharma, yet are not associated with emptiness.
That is to say:

emptiness not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the knowledge of phenomena not associated with emptiness, and all other remaining mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), as well as form (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra), which are neither included within nor associated with both the knowledge of phenomena and emptiness.
The same applies to the wishless, the signless, the factor of enlightenment of joy, and right intention.

Regarding all phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), are those phenomena also associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions.
There are dharmas that are associated with dharma-knowledge but are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
That is to say:
those factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) that are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya);
and there are factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena.
That is to say:

the dharma-knowledge comprised within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," as well as those dharmas associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are neither comprised within nor dissociated from dharma-knowledge.
There are phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and also associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
That is to say:
those phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena which are subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
There are phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of the dharma but are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown. These are:

the knowledge of the dharma not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) that are neither included in nor associated with either the knowledge of the dharma or the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; as well as matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
The same applies to the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) and the faculty of final knowledge (*ājñendriya*).
Regarding all phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), are those phenomena also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*)? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but are not associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*). Namely:

The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) exists; there is also the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that is not associated with the knowledge of phenomena, namely:
The dharma-knowledge itself, as well as those factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are not associated with dharma-knowledge.
There are also factors that are both associated with dharma-knowledge and associated with mindfulness; namely:

Second, the factors associated with both [knowledge and mindfulness]. There are factors that are associated with the knowledge of what is and what is not, yet are not associated with mindfulness. Namely:
The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness dissociated from dharma-knowledge,
as well as other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind,
are likewise [dissociated] from the enlightenment factors of energy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, as well as right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

If various phenomena are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), are those phenomena also associated with the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena are also associated with the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena.

There are phenomena associated with the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) that are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna); namely,
those phenomena associated with the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena that are not subsumed within the knowledge of phenomena.
As it is for the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) in relation to what follows, so it is for the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) in relation to what follows.
*Abhidharmajñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Nine. *Abhidharmajñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree. Section Three:

The Aggregate of Wisdom (Jñānaskandha), Part Five: The Sub-section on the Seven Noble Persons (Saptāryapudgala), Part Two. Regarding all phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), are those phenomena also associated with conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of others' minds but are not conventional knowledge.
That is to say:
those mental factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
There are also factors associated with conventional knowledge that are not associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say:
those factors associated with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that are not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
There are factors that are both associated with the knowledge of others' minds and associated with conventional knowledge.
That is to say:
those phenomena subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds that are associated with conventional knowledge.
There are also phenomena that are neither associated with the knowledge of others' minds nor with conventional knowledge.
That is to say:

the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge; and all other remaining mind-elements, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind that are not included within or associated with the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge.
The same applies to path-knowledge (mārgajñāna), the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmavicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga), and right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
Are those factors that are associated with the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) also associated with the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
Answer: Not so.
Suppose a dharma is associated with the knowledge of suffering; is that dharma also associated with the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: It is not so. In relation to the knowledge of origination and cessation, the samādhis of emptiness and signlessness, and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," it is likewise.
Regarding those phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds, are those phenomena also associated with the *samādhi* of wishlessness?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not associated with the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita*). These are:

phenomena associated with both the knowledge of others' minds and the wishless concentration, as well as phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not associated with the wishless concentration.
There are phenomena that are associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) but are not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). These are:
the knowledge of others' minds associated with the wishless, and those phenomena associated with the wishless that are not associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
There are dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of others' minds and are also associated with the wishless (apraṇihita).
That is to say:
the dharmas associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with the knowledge of others' minds nor with the wishless concentration;
namely, those factors that are dissociated from the knowledge of others' minds and are not associated with the wishless concentration.

The knowledge of others' minds that is dissociated from the wishless (apraṇihita), as well as all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra)—

the same applies to these in relation to the factors of enlightenment consisting of mindfulness, diligence, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity, as well as right thought, right diligence, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
If various dharmas are associated with the knowledge of others' minds, are those dharmas also associated with the faculty of "already-known" (ājñātendriya)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not associated with the faculty of "already known.
That is to say:
those phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not subsumed within the faculty of "already known."
There are phenomena associated with the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya) that are not the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
That is to say:

the knowledge of others' minds subsumed under the faculty of "already known," as well as those phenomena associated with the faculty of "already known" that are neither subsumed by nor associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
There are dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of others' minds and are also the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya).
That is to say:
those dharmas associated with the knowledge of others' minds which are subsumed under the faculty of "already known."
There are dharmas that are neither associated with the knowledge of others' minds nor associated with the faculty of having known (*ājñātendriya*). These are:

the knowledge of others' minds not subsumed under the faculty of having known; all other mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*), as well as matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), which are neither associated with the knowledge of others' minds nor with the faculty of having known.
The same applies to the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Regarding those phenomena associated with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), are those phenomena also associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) up to right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)? Answer:

Not so. Suppose a dharma is associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) up to right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*); is that dharma also associated with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)? Answer:
Not so. If those dharmas are associated with the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), are those dharmas also associated with the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna)? Answer:
Not so. If a dharma is associated with the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), is that dharma also associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)? Answer:
It is not so. The same applies to the signless samādhi (animitta-samādhi) in relation to the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
Are those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) also associated with the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi)?
Answer: One should formulate this as four propositions.
There are dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) but are not empty (śūnya).
That is to say:
the emptiness associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), as well as those factors associated with the knowledge of suffering that are not associated with emptiness;
and there are factors associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) that are not associated with the knowledge of suffering.
That is to say:
the knowledge of suffering associated with emptiness, as well as those dharmas associated with emptiness that are not associated with the knowledge of suffering.
There are also dharmas that are both associated with the knowledge of suffering and associated with emptiness.
That is to say:
there are two types of associated dharmas;
there are dharmas that are neither associated with the knowledge of suffering nor associated with emptiness.
That is to say:
emptiness not associated with the knowledge of suffering;
the knowledge of suffering not associated with emptiness; and all other remaining mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
The same applies to the wishless (*apranihita*).

Regarding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyanga*), and the eight factors of the path (*mārgānga*), it is as explained for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
Are those factors associated with the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*) also associated with the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*)?
Answer: No.
Suppose a dharma is associated with the knowledge of cessation; is that dharma also associated with the knowledge of origination?
Answer: No.
The same applies to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*).
If various dharmas are associated with the knowledge of accumulation (*saṃbhāra-jñāna*), are those dharmas also associated with the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of origination but not with the wishless concentration; namely,
the wishless concentration associated with the knowledge of origination.
There are phenomena that are associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) but are not the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*).
That is to say:
the knowledge of origination itself, and those phenomena associated with the wishless that are not associated with the knowledge of origination.
There are dharmas that are associated with both the knowledge of accumulation (saṃbhāra-jñāna) and wishlessness (apraṇihita); namely,
those dharmas associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) nor are they the wishless (*apraṇihita*). These are:
the wishless not associated with the knowledge of origination, as well as all other mind and mental factors, form, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.

Regarding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), it is as explained for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
Are those factors associated with the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) also associated with the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
Answer: Not so.
If a dharma is associated with the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), is that dharma also associated with the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna)?
Answer: It is not so. The same applies to the samādhis of emptiness and wishlessness.
If a phenomenon is associated with the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), is that phenomenon also associated with the concentration on signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena associated with the knowledge of cessation but not with the signless;
namely, the signless [state] associated with the knowledge of cessation.
There are phenomena associated with the concentration on signlessness that are not associated with the knowledge of cessation; namely,
the knowledge of cessation itself and those phenomena associated with signlessness that are not associated with the knowledge of cessation.
There are dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of cessation and are also signless; namely,
the two types of associated dharmas.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with the knowledge of cessation nor are they signless.
That is to say:
the signless [state] dissociated from the knowledge of cessation, as well as all other mind and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.

Regarding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), it is as explained for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
Are those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) also associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)?
Answer: Not so.
Even if a dharma is associated with the concentration on the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmasūnyatā-samādhi*), is that dharma necessarily associated with the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
Answer: It is not so. The same applies in relation to the signless samādhi.
If various phenomena are associated with the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), are those phenomena also associated with the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihitasamādhi*)?
Answer: One should formulate this as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of the path but not with the wishless concentration;
namely, those wishless concentrations that are associated with the knowledge of the path.
There are phenomena associated with the wishless that are not path-knowledge; namely,
path-knowledge itself and those phenomena associated with the wishless that are not associated with path-knowledge.
There are dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of the path and also with the wishless; namely,
those dharmas associated with both.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with the knowledge of the path nor with the wishless concentration. These are:
the wishless concentration not associated with the knowledge of the path; all other mental states and mental factors; matter; unconditioned phenomena; and formations dissociated from mind.

Regarding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), it is as explained for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
If various phenomena are associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), are those phenomena also associated with the concentration on wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*)?
Answer: Not so.
If a phenomenon is associated with the wishless (apraṇihita) samādhi, is that phenomenon also associated with the emptiness (śūnyatā) samādhi?
Answer: It is not so. The same applies to the signless (*animitta*).

If a phenomenon is associated with the concentration on the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā-samādhi*), is that phenomenon also associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvyājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are dharmas associated with emptiness that are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
That is to say:
those dharmas associated with emptiness that are not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
There are phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not associated with emptiness. Namely:

those phenomena subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are themselves emptiness; and those phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are neither subsumed by nor associated with emptiness.
There are dharmas that are associated with emptiness and are also the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*); namely,
those dharmas associated with emptiness that are subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
There are phenomena that are neither associated with emptiness nor associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.

These are: the emptiness not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta) that are neither subsumed under emptiness nor the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and are dissociated from them; as well as matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma), and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
The same applies to the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya).
Regarding those phenomena associated with the concentration on emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi), are they also associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga)? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There are phenomena that are associated with emptiness but are not the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
That is to say:
The awakening factor of mindfulness associated with emptiness;
there is also the awakening factor of mindfulness associated with phenomena that is not associated with emptiness, namely:
The element of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and those factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that are not associated with emptiness;
as well as those factors that are both associated with emptiness and associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness. Namely:
Second, regarding factors associated with [the mind]:
there are factors that are neither associated with emptiness nor associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
That is to say:

The mindfulness factor of enlightenment dissociated from emptiness, as well as all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra)—

these relate to the factors of enlightenment of investigation of dharmas (dharmapravicaya), diligence (vīrya), tranquility (praśrabdhi), and equanimity (upekṣā), as well as right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), right diligence (samyagvīrya), and right mindfulness (samyaksmṛti), in the same manner.
If a dharma is associated with the emptiness samādhi, is that dharma also associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with emptiness but not with joy; namely,
the factor of enlightenment of joy associated with emptiness, and those phenomena associated with emptiness but not associated with joy.
There are phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy that are not associated with emptiness; namely,
phenomena associated with both emptiness and the factor of enlightenment of joy, as well as phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy that are not associated with emptiness.
There are dharmas that are associated with emptiness and also accompanied by joy; namely,
the two types of associated dharmas.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with emptiness nor with joy;
namely, the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not associated with emptiness.

The enlightenment factor of joy is dissociated from emptiness, as well as from all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The same applies to right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).

If various phenomena are associated with the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), are those phenomena necessarily associated with the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:
