Whatever phenomena are associated with emptiness, those phenomena are also associated with the awakening factor of concentration.
There are factors associated with the awakening factor of concentration that are not associated with emptiness; namely,
those factors associated with the awakening factor of concentration that are not subsumed under emptiness.
The same applies to right concentration.
Just as emptiness relates to what follows it,
so too do the wishless and the signless relate to what follows them.
As for the distinctions:

just as emptiness corresponds to the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), so too do right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) and wishlessness (*apranihita*) correspond to the factor of enlightenment of joy; and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right intention likewise correspond [to the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena].

If various dharmas are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), are those dharmas also associated with the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya)? Answer: No.

If a phenomenon is associated with the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātendriya), is that phenomenon also associated with the faculty of one who will come to know the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)? Answer: No.
The same applies to the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Regarding those phenomena that are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), are those phenomena also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There are dharmas that are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) but are not associated with mindfulness (smṛti).
That is to say:
Regarding the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya),
there are factors that are associated with the mindfulness factor of enlightenment but are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown. Namely:
There are factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
There are also factors that are likewise associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," namely:
Regarding the factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that are subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown":
there are factors that are neither associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor are they mindfulness. Namely:

The factors not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) are: the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), as well as all other mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).

The same applies to the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena (*dharma-vicaya*), energy (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*), as well as to right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), right effort (*samyag-vīrya*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Are those phenomena that are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) also associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are dharmas that are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) but are not associated with joy (prīti).
That is to say:

the factor of enlightenment of joy included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," as well as those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not included within the factor of enlightenment of joy and are not associated with it.
There are factors associated with the awakening factor of joy,
which are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
That is to say:
Regarding those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy that are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown":
there are factors that are both associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and associated with joy. Namely:
Regarding the factors associated with the factor of joy that are subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya),
there are factors that are neither associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor are they the factor of joy. Namely:

The factor of joy of awakening not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," as well as all other mental states and mental concomitants—whether associated or dissociated—that are not included within either the factor of joy of awakening or the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," along with matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.

If various phenomena are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), are those phenomena also associated with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not associated with pliancy; namely,
the factor of enlightenment of pliancy associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
There are phenomena associated with pliancy that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
That is to say:
those phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
There are dharmas that are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and are also pliancy (praśrabdhi).
That is to say:
those dharmas associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are also associated with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga).
There are phenomena that are neither associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) nor are they pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). These are:

the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) when it is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," as well as all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The same applies to the enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Regarding those phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), are those phenomena also associated with right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*)? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There are dharmas that are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) but are not right reflection (samyak-saṃkalpa).
That is to say:
There are right thoughts associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), as well as those not associated with right thought.
There are also phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
Furthermore, there are phenomena associated with right thought that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
That is to say:
those factors associated with right reflection that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
There are also factors that are both associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and associated with right reflection.
That is to say:
those dharmas associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) and associated with right intention (samyak-saṃkalpa).
There are also dharmas that are neither associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor associated with right intention.
That is to say:

right thought dissociated from the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," as well as all other mental states and mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind that are dissociated from the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."

Just as it is for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) in relation to what follows; so too is it for the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya) and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya) in relation to what follows.
The difference is as follows:
Regarding the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) in relation to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established:
there are factors associated with the faculty of one who has already known that are not right view. Namely:

There are factors comprised within the faculty of one who has final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) that are right view; and there are factors associated with the faculty of one who has final knowledge that are neither comprised within nor dissociated from right view.
Furthermore, there are factors associated with right view that are not the faculty of one who has final knowledge.
That is to say:
those factors associated with right view that are not subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya).
There are factors that are both associated with the faculty of one who has already known and associated with right view.
That is to say:
those phenomena associated with right view that are subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known.
There are also phenomena that are neither associated with the faculty of one who has already known nor associated with right view.
That is to say:

right view not included within the faculty of one who has already known; and all other mental states and mental factors, as well as matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind, that are not associated with right view or the faculty of one who has already known.
From the awakening factor of mindfulness up to right mindfulness, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Factors of Awakening" (*Bodhyanga-nirdeśa*).
As it is said:
"O Bhikṣus!"
I shall now explain to you forty-four matters concerning knowledge; you should listen attentively and apply your mind with great care.
What are these forty-four matters concerning knowledge? They are as follows:
Knowledge of aging and death; knowledge of the origin of aging and death; knowledge of the cessation of aging and death; and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death.

Likewise, there is knowledge of birth, becoming, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations; knowledge of the origin of volitional formations; knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations; and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations.
These are called the forty-four matters of knowledge.

Among these, regarding the forty-four matters of knowledge beginning with the knowledge of aging and death, should they be described as dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) up to path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*)?
Answer: It should be said that the knowledge of old age and death consists of four knowledges. Namely:

The knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)—these four knowledges constitute the knowledge of the origin of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa-samudaya-jñāna*).
That is to say:

the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*). The knowledge of the cessation of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa-nirodha-jñāna*) consists of these same four knowledges.
That is to say:

the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna). These four knowledges constitute the knowledge that understands the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death.
That is to say:
The same applies to the four knowledges—dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge—as they arise and so forth, up to their activity.
As it is said: "O Bhikṣus!"
"I shall explain to you the seventy-seven matters of knowledge.
You should listen attentively and apply your mind thoroughly.
What are the seventy-seven matters of knowledge?
That is to say:
the knowledge that birth is the condition for old age and death;
and the knowledge that it is not the case that there is no birth as a condition for old age and death.
The knowledge that past birth is the condition for old age and death;
the knowledge that it is not the case that old age and death arise without that [birth] as their condition;
and the knowledge that future birth is the condition for old age and death.
He knows that this is not the knowledge that aging and death do not arise from conditions, but rather the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa).
He thoroughly understands this as impermanent, conditioned, produced by the mind, arisen from causes, subject to exhaustion, subject to cessation, subject to fading away, and subject to destruction.
Thus one knows the knowledge that formations are conditioned by ignorance regarding existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and formations;
one knows that it is not the case that there is no knowledge that formations are conditioned by ignorance.
He knows the wisdom that [past] formations are conditioned by ignorance;
he knows the wisdom that they are not unconditioned by ignorance;
he knows the wisdom that future formations are conditioned by ignorance.
It is not the case that there is no knowledge of the conditionality of volitional formations through ignorance, nor of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).

One thoroughly understands this matter as impermanent, conditioned, produced by the mind, arisen from conditions, subject to exhaustion, subject to cessation, subject to detachment, and subject to extinction.
Regarding these seventy-seven instances of knowledge, such as the knowledge that aging and death have birth as their condition,
should they be described as ranging from dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) up to path-knowledge (mārgajñāna)? Answer:
It should be stated that the first six knowledges—namely, the knowledge of birth conditioned by aging and death, and so forth—are all four knowledges.
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge, the subsequent-knowledge, the conventional-knowledge, and the origin-knowledge.
The seventh dharma-abiding knowledge is a single conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
It is like the seven knowledges that understand aging-and-death conditioned by birth;
likewise, it is the same for the seven knowledges up to those that understand volitional formations conditioned by ignorance.
If one has accomplished dharma-knowledge,
does one also have subsequent knowledge? Answer:
If one has attained it,
and if one has accomplished the knowledge of types (anvaya-jñāna), does one possess that knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
Is that the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: If it has been attained and not lost.
If one achieves the knowledge of others' minds,
does one also possess that dharma-knowledge? Answer:
If one has attained it,
or if one has accomplished the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna),
does one also possess conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
Even if one has accomplished conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Is that dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has been attained.
If one has accomplished the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna),
does one also possess the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)? Answer:
It is so. If one has accomplished the knowledge of suffering,
does one possess the knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
Is that the knowledge of origination? Answer:
If it is attained.
If one has attained the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna),
has one also attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)? Answer:
Thus it is. If one has attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), has one also attained the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna)?
Answer: If one has attained it;
even if one has accomplished the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna).
Is that dharma-knowledge? Answer: It is so.
If one has accomplished dharma-knowledge,
does one have path-knowledge? Answer:
If one has attained it—
specifically, if one has accomplished the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)— does that person possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the knowledge of categories (anvaya-jñāna).
Is that the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: If it has been attained and not lost.
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds,
does one also possess the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)? Answer:
If one has attained or accomplished the knowledge of subsequent realization (anvaya-jñāna),
has that person also attained conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
Even if one has attained conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Is that subsequent knowledge?
Answer: If it is attained.
If one has accomplished the knowledge of categories (anvaya-jñāna),
does one possess the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)? Answer:
It is so. If one has accomplished the knowledge of suffering,
does that person also possess the subsequent knowledge?
Answer: If it is attained; if one has accomplished the knowledge of subsequent realization (anvaya-jñāna).
Is that the knowledge of accumulation?
Answer: It is, if it has been attained.
If one has attained the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna),
has one also attained the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)? Answer:
It is so. If one is accomplished in the knowledge of types (anvaya-jñāna), is one also accomplished in the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna)?
Answer: If one has attained it;
even if one has accomplished the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna).
Is that subsequent knowledge? Answer: It is so.
If one has accomplished the knowledge of categories (anvaya-jñāna), has that person also accomplished the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)? Answer:
If one has attained it,
and if one has accomplished path-knowledge (mārgajñāna),
does that person also possess class-knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds.
Is that mundane knowledge? Answer: It is so.
If one has attained conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna),
does one also possess the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)? Answer:
If one has attained it and does not lose it,
and if one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds,
is that the knowledge of suffering?
Answer: If it is attained; even if one has accomplished the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
Is that the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: If it has been attained and not lost.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds,
does one also possess the knowledge of origination? Answer:
If one has attained it—
specifically, if one has accomplished the knowledge of origination—
is that the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: If it has been attained and not lost;
and if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
Is that the knowledge of cessation?
Answer: If it has been attained.
If one has attained the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna),
does one possess the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna)? Answer:
If it is attained and not lost,
and if one has accomplished the knowledge of others' minds,
is that the knowledge of the path?
Answer: If one has attained it;
even if one has accomplished the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
Is that the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: If it has been attained and not lost.
If one accomplishes conventional knowledge,
does one also possess the knowledge of suffering? Answer:
If it is attained— specifically, if one has accomplished the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)—
does one also possess conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Is that the knowledge of origination? Answer:
If it is attained.
If one has attained the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna),
does one also possess conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)? Answer:
Thus it is. If one is endowed with conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), is one also endowed with the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna)?
Answer: If it is attained; even if one has accomplished the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna).
Is that mundane knowledge? Answer: It is so.
If one has accomplished conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna),
does one also have path knowledge (mārgajñāna)? Answer:
If one has attained it—
specifically, if one has accomplished path-knowledge (mārgajñāna)—
does one also possess conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
Is that the knowledge of origination? Answer:
If it is attained.
If one has attained the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna),
has one also attained the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna)? Answer:
It is so. If one is accomplished in the knowledge of suffering,
is one also accomplished in the knowledge of cessation?
Answer: If one has attained it;
even if one has accomplished the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna).
Is that the knowledge of suffering? Answer: It is so.
If one has accomplished the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna),
does one possess the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)? Answer:
If one has attained it—
suppose one has accomplished the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna); does that person possess the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna).
Is that the knowledge of cessation?
Answer: If it has been attained.
If one has attained the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna),
has one also attained the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna)? Answer:
It is so. If one has accomplished the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna),
does one possess the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)?
Answer: If one has attained it;
even if one has accomplished the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
Is that the knowledge of origination? Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna),
does one also have the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)? Answer:
If one has attained it—
specifically, if one has accomplished the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)— does one also possess the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
Is it in the future? Answer: It is so.
If one achieves the future [attainment],
does one also possess the past? Answer:
If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it;
if it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
This applies if one possesses the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
Is it present? Answer: If it is manifest before one.
If one possesses [the dharma] in the present, does one possess it in the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) in the future, is it also present?
Answer: If it is present before one,
and if one possesses it in the present, does one also possess it in the future?
Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
Is it also [achieved] in the future and the present? Answer:
It is definitely achieved in the future; as for the present, it is achieved if it manifests before one.
If one accomplishes [the dharma] in the future and the present, does one accomplish it in the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one accomplishes it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished and subsequently lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena regarding the future, does one also accomplish it regarding the past and the present?
Answer: There are [factors] that are future but neither past nor present. Namely:
Those that have already been acquired but not yet extinguished; or those that, having been extinguished, have already been lost and do not manifest before one.
There are also those that exist in the future and the past, but not in the present.
That is to say:
That which has already ceased and is not lost, yet does not manifest before one,
exists in the future and the present, but not in the past.
That is to say:
That which is present has not yet ceased; even if it has ceased, it is lost.
There is that which is future as well as past and present.
That is to say:
That which has already ceased is not lost, and it also manifests in the present.
If one is endowed with [the dharma] of the past and the present, is one also endowed with that of the future? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one is endowed with present *dharmajñāna*, is one also endowed with it in the past and future? Answer:
The future [dharmas] are necessarily accomplished.
Regarding the past, if they have already ceased but have not been lost, then they are accomplished;
if they have not yet ceased, or if they have ceased but have been lost, then they are not accomplished.
If one has accomplished [the attainment] in the past and the future, does one have it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifest in the present.
As it is with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), so it is for the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
If one possesses past knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess it in the future?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes it in the future, does one also accomplish it in the past?
Answer: If it has already been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it was extinguished but subsequently lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds in the past, does one possess it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifest at present.
If one achieves [the attainment] in the present, does one achieve it in the past? Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds in the future, does one possess it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifest in the present.
If one achieves [the attainment] in the present, does one also achieve it in the future? Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) in the past, does one also possess it in the future and the present?
Answer: One certainly possesses it in the future; as for the present, one possesses it if it is currently manifest.
If one accomplishes the future and the present, does one accomplish the past? Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds in the future, does one also possess it in the past and present?
Answer: There are cases where one possesses it in the future but not in the past or present.
That is to say:
it has been attained and not lost, and has not yet ceased; or, even if it has ceased and been lost, it does not manifest before one.
It exists in the future and the past, but not in the present.
That is to say:
that which has already ceased but has not been lost does not manifest before one;
yet there exists [it] in the future, as well as in the past and present.
That is to say:
when that [state] is present before one,
if it is accomplished in the past and the present, is it also [accomplished] in the future?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds in the present, does one also possess it in the past and the future?
Answer: It is so.
If one is accomplished in the past and the future, is one also accomplished in the present?
Answer: If it is present before one.
If one has attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past, does one also possess it in the future?
Answer: It is so.
If one achieves it in the future, does one achieve it in the past?
Answer: It is so.
If one has accomplished conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past, does one possess it in the present?
Answer: If it is present before one,
and if one possesses it in the present, does one also possess it in the past?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses future conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), does one possess it in the present?
Answer: If it is present before one,
and if one possesses it in the present, does one also possess it in the future?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past, does one possess it of the future and the present as well?
Answer: One is necessarily endowed with it in the future; as for the present, it is so if it is currently manifest.
If one is endowed with it in the future and the present, is one also endowed with it in the past?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses future conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Does that [attainment] belong to the past or the present? Answer:
It is definitely accomplished in the past; as for the present, it is so if it is currently manifest.
If one has accomplished [the attainment] in the past and the present, has one also accomplished it in the future? Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes present conventional knowledge, does one also accomplish it in the past and future? Answer: Yes.
If one achieves [the attainment] of the past and the future, does one also achieve it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifest in the present.
If one has attained past dharma-knowledge, has one also attained past subsequent knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished and subsequently lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one has accomplished past *anvaya-jñāna*, has one also accomplished past *dharma-jñāna*? Answer:
If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess the future subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: If it is attained.
Suppose one accomplishes future anvaya-jñāna; does that person also possess past dharma-jñāna?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained past dharma-knowledge, has one also attained present subsequent knowledge?
Answer: If it is manifest at present.
If one has attained present subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), has one also attained past dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge,
does one also possess past and present anvaya-knowledge?
Answer: There are past dharma-knowledges that are neither past nor present inferential knowledges. Namely:
The dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost; the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest.
Thus, there is past dharma-knowledge and past subsequent knowledge, but no present [subsequent knowledge].
That is to say:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) have already ceased but have not been lost;
yet, subsequent knowledge is not currently manifest.
There are cases where one possesses past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and present subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), but not past [subsequent knowledge].
That is to say:
dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost; subsequent knowledge is present and has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has not been lost.
There is past dharma-knowledge as well as past and present subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
That is to say:
when dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have already ceased but have not been lost, and subsequent knowledge is presently manifest.
If one has attained past and present *anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge), has one also attained past *dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of phenomena)?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished and subsequently lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge, does one also accomplish future and present category-knowledge?
Answer: There are past dharma-knowledges that are neither future nor present inferential knowledges. Namely:
The dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost, yet the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet been attained.
There is past dharma-knowledge and future subsequent knowledge, but not present [subsequent knowledge].
That is to say:
The dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost; the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has already been attained but is not present before one.
There is past dharma-knowledge, as well as future and present subsequent knowledge.
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost, and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present before one.
If one possesses the future and present subsequent knowledge, does one also possess that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer:
If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it; if it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess past and future anvaya-knowledge?
Answer: There are past dharma-knowledges that are neither past nor future category-knowledges. Namely:
The dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost, yet the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet been attained.
There is past dharma-knowledge and future subsequent knowledge that is not past.
That is to say:
Dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost; anvaya-knowledge has already been attained but has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost.
There is past dharma-knowledge, as well as past and future anvaya-knowledge.
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have already ceased but have not been lost.
If one possesses past and future subsequent knowledge, does one also possess past dharma-knowledge?
Answer:
If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it; if it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess past, future, and present category-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Answer: There are past dharma-knowledges that are neither past, future, nor present category-knowledges. Namely:
The dharma-knowledge has already been extinguished but not lost, yet the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet been attained.
There is past dharma-knowledge and future subsequent knowledge that is neither past nor present.
That is to say:

The dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has already ceased but is not lost; the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has been attained but has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
There is past dharma-knowledge together with future and present subsequent knowledge, but no past [subsequent knowledge].
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but has not been lost; the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present but has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost.
There is past dharma-knowledge, as well as past and future subsequent knowledge, but not the present.
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have already ceased but have not been lost, while the subsequent knowledge is not currently manifest.
There is past dharma-knowledge, as well as past, future, and present subsequent knowledge.
That is to say:
when the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have already ceased but are not lost, and the subsequent knowledge is present before one.
If one possesses past, future, and present subsequent knowledge, does one also possess past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
Just as with the knowledge of similarity (*anvaya-jñāna*), it is likewise for the knowledges of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
If one possesses past dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), does one also possess past knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*)?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained past knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess past knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished and subsequently lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess the future knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: If it has already been attained and not lost.
Suppose one possesses future knowledge of others' minds; does that person also possess past knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one possess present knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: If it is presently manifest.
If one has attained present knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not been extinguished, or if it was extinguished and then lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess past and present knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: There are past dharma-knowledges that are neither past nor present other-mind knowledges. Namely:
The dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost; the knowledge of others' minds has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
Thus, there is past dharma-knowledge and past knowledge of others' minds, but not present ones.
That is to say:
the knowledge of dharmas and the knowledge of others' minds have already ceased but are not lost, yet the knowledge of others' minds is not present before one.
There is past knowledge of dharmas, as well as past and present knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost, and the knowledge of others' minds is present before one.
If one possesses past and present knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess future and present knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: There are cases where one possesses past knowledge of phenomena but not future or present knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say:

the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased but is not lost; the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) has not yet been attained, or if it was attained, it has already been lost.
There is past knowledge of phenomena and future knowledge of others' minds, but not present [knowledge].
That is to say:

the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased but is not lost; the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) has already been attained but is not lost, yet it does not manifest before one.
There exists past knowledge of phenomena, as well as future and present knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but has not been lost, and the knowledge of others' minds is present before one.
If one possesses the future and present knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess the past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished past *dharmajñāna*, does one also possess past and future *paracittajñāna*?
Answer: There are cases where one possesses past *dharmajñāna* but does not possess past and future *paracittajñāna*.
That is to say:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased but has not been lost;
the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) has not yet been attained, or, having been attained, it has already been lost.
There are cases where one possesses past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and future knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), but not past [knowledge of others' minds].
That is to say:
the knowledge of phenomena has already ceased but has not been lost.
The knowledge of others' minds that has already been attained is not lost, though it may have ceased; even if it has ceased, it is not lost.
There is past dharma-knowledge, as well as past and future knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds have already ceased but have not been lost.
If one possesses past and future knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained past *dharmajñāna*, does one also possess past, future, and present *paracittajñāna*?
Answer: There are cases where one possesses past *dharmajñāna* but does not possess past, future, or present *paracittajñāna*.
That is to say:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased but has not been lost;
the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) has not yet been attained.
Even if it has been attained, it may be lost.
There are cases where one possesses past *dharmajñāna* and future *paracittajñāna*, but not past or present [paracittajñāna].
That is to say:

The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) has already ceased but is not lost; the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) has already been attained and is not lost, though it has not yet ceased; even if it has ceased, it is lost and does not manifest before one.
There is past *dharmajñāna* as well as past and future *paracittajñāna*, but no present [knowledge of others' minds].
That is to say:
the dharma-knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds have already ceased but have not been lost, yet the knowledge of others' minds is not currently manifest.
There is past dharma-knowledge, as well as past, future, and present knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say:
when the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) has already ceased but is not lost, and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is present before one.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds of the past, future, and present, does one also possess that past knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, has that person also accomplished conventional knowledge of the past? Answer: Yes.
If one has attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past, does one also possess dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) of the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess future conventional knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses future conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), does one also possess past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess present conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: If it is manifest at present.
If one possesses present conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), does one also possess past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess past and present conventional knowledge?
Answer: One necessarily possesses [the knowledge] of the past; as for the present, it is possessed if it is currently manifest.
If one possesses conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past and present, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) of the past?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one necessarily possess the future and present conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: One certainly possesses it in the future; as for the present, it is possessed if it is currently manifest.
If one has attained future and present conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), does one also possess past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), does one also possess past and future conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses past and future conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), does one possess past dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: If [the defilement] has already been extinguished and has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but subsequently lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one necessarily possess the past, future, and present conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: One certainly possesses it in the past and future; as for the present, it is possessed if it is currently manifest.
If one has attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past, future, and present, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) of the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not been extinguished, or if it was extinguished but has since been lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one possess past knowledge of suffering? Answer:
If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses past knowledge of suffering, does one also possess past knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: If it has already been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), has one also accomplished the future knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)? Answer: Yes.
If one has attained the future knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), has one also attained the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished and subsequently lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one has accomplished the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) of the past, does one possess the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) of the present? Answer:
If it is present before one,
and if one has attained the present knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), has one also attained the past knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)? Answer:
If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then it is accomplished.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) of the past, does one also possess the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) of the past and the present?
Answer: There are past dharma-knowledges that are not past or present suffering-knowledges. Namely:
Dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost; Suffering-knowledge has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
Thus, there is past Dharma-knowledge and past Suffering-knowledge, but no present [Suffering-knowledge].
That is to say:
the knowledge of the suffering of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) has already ceased but is not lost, while the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) is not present before one.
There is past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), but not [knowledge of suffering] that is past.
That is to say:

the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased but is not lost; the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) is present and has not yet ceased, or, even if it has ceased, it has not been lost.
There is past knowledge of phenomena, as well as past and present knowledge of suffering.
That is to say:
when the knowledge of the suffering of phenomena (*dharma-duḥkha-jñāna*) has already ceased but is not lost, and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) is present before one.
If one possesses the past and present knowledge of suffering, does one also possess the past knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), has one also attained the future and present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
Answer: One definitely attains it in the future; as for the present, one attains it if it is currently manifest.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) regarding the future and the present, has one also attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) regarding the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not been extinguished, or if, having been extinguished, it has been lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) of the past, does one also possess the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) of the past and the future?
Answer: One is necessarily endowed with the future [attainment].
As for the past, if it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one is endowed with it.
If it has not been extinguished, or if, having been extinguished, it has been lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one has accomplished past and future knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), has one also accomplished past knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished past *dharmajñāna*, does one also possess past, future, and present *duḥkhajñāna*?
Answer: There is [the case where] one possesses past *dharmajñāna* and future *duḥkhajñāna*, but not the past or present [instances thereof].
That is to say:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) has already ceased but is not lost; the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) has not yet ceased.
Or, even if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
There are cases where one possesses past *dharma-jñāna* as well as future and present *duḥkha-jñāna*, but not past [duḥkha-jñāna].
This refers to:
when *dharma-jñāna* has already ceased but is not lost; *duḥkha-jñāna* is present before one and has not yet ceased; or even if it has ceased, it has already been lost.
There are cases where there is past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) as well as past and future knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), but not present [knowledge of suffering].
That is to say:
when the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of suffering have already ceased but have not been lost, yet the knowledge of suffering does not manifest before one.
There is past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) together with past, future, and present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).
That is to say:
the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of suffering have already ceased but have not been lost, and the knowledge of suffering is presently manifest.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) regarding the past, future, and present, has that person also attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) regarding the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then they have attained it.
If [the knowledge] has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then it is not accomplished.

Just as with *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena) in relation to the subsequent [knowledges], forming seven small groups (*sapta-kṣudraka*), so too, up to *nirodhajñāna* (knowledge of cessation) in relation to *mārgajñāna* (knowledge of the path), one should form seven small groups accordingly, in the same manner.
As it is with the "small seven," so it is with the "great seven.
The difference is that two or more [factors] are paired with one.
Or, one may pair them two by two or more;
for example, there are seven beginning with the past, and likewise there are seven each beginning with the future, and so on, up to those beginning with the past, future, and present.
Thus it should be understood.

The three karmas in relation to the ten paths; the inclusion of the characteristics of karma within the nine gates;
the four propositions regarding the body and mind and their experiences;
and the nature of the three obstacles—what constitutes the greatest sin and its greatest fruit: I pray that this chapter may explain these in full detail.
Regarding the three types of misconduct and the three unwholesome roots:
does the former subsume the latter, or does the latter subsume the former? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There are unwholesome actions that are not unwholesome roots; namely:
There are unwholesome roots that are not unwholesome courses of action, namely: bodily and vocal misconduct, and unwholesome volition associated with wrong view.
Delusion is an unwholesome root.
There are also unwholesome roots that are unwholesome courses of action; namely:
Greed, desire, and ill will.
There are those which are neither unwholesome actions nor unwholesome roots, namely:
Excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
regarding the three types of sublime conduct and the three roots of goodness: does the former encompass the latter,
or does the latter encompass the former?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions.
There is wholesome conduct that is not a root of goodness.
That is to say:
wholesome conduct of body, speech, and volition.
There are roots of goodness that are not conduct.
That is to say:
there are roots of non-delusion not subsumed under right view;
furthermore, there are wholesome conducts that are also roots of goodness.
That is to say:
non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view.
There are also unwholesome courses of action that are not roots of goodness.
That is to say:
excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Regarding the three types of unwholesome conduct and the ten unwholesome courses of action, do the three encompass the ten?
Question: Do the ten subsume the three? Answer:
The three subsume the ten; the ten do not subsume the three.
What is not included?
It refers to those remaining misdeeds of body, speech, and mind, excluding those misdeeds of body, speech, and mind that are subsumed under the courses of action (*karmapatha*).
Regarding the three types of wholesome conduct and the ten paths of wholesome action:
do the three encompass the ten, or do the ten encompass the three? Answer:
The three encompass the ten, but the ten do not encompass the three.
What is it that is not encompassed?
It is as follows:
Excluding those excellent deeds of body, speech, and mind that are subsumed under the paths of action (*karmapatha*), there remain other excellent deeds of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding the three types of action and the ten paths of action: do the three subsume the ten?
What are the ten that encompass the three?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is karma that is not a path of action (karmapatha), namely:
mental karma, as well as bodily and vocal karma not subsumed under the paths of action.
There are courses of action that are not karma; namely,
the last three courses of action.
There are actions that are also paths of action; namely,
the first seven paths of action.
There are those that are neither karma nor paths of karma;
namely, excluding the aforementioned cases.
The three types of action refer to:
bodily, verbal, and mental action.
The four types of action refer to:

There is karma that is black with black ripening, white with white ripening, black-and-white with black-and-white ripening, and neither-black-nor-white with no ripening, which can bring all karmas to an end.
Does the triad subsume the tetrad?
Which of the four [means of integration] subsumes the three? Answer:
The three subsume the four, but the four do not subsume the three.
What is not included?
It refers to:

with the exception of the volition of training that is capable of severing all karma, the remaining untainted (anāsrava) karma, the wholesome karma bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), and all indeterminate (avyākṛta) karma.
The three types of action refer to:
body, speech, and mind.

does the former subsume the latter,
or does the latter subsume the former?
Answer: The former includes the latter, but the latter does not include the former.
What is it that is not included?
That is to say:
indeterminate karma, neutral karma, and untainted karma.
These are the three types of karma.
Body, speech, and mind.

bodily, verbal, and mental.

karma to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and karma that is not to be abandoned (*aheya*).

Does the latter include the former?
Answer: It depends on the specific case.

karma bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

The former includes the latter, but the latter does not include the former.
What is not included?
It refers to uncontaminated (anāsrava) karma.
The four types of karma are as previously explained.

One should formulate four propositions.
There are four that are not three, namely:

wholesome karma bound to the formless realm that is determinate.

There are cases that belong neither to four nor to three; namely:

there are further categories of the three types of karma, namely: wholesome and so forth,
those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, and those to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and so forth.
Does the former include the latter,
or does the latter include the former? Answer:
According to their respective functions, they mutually encompass one another in succession.
The three types of action refer to those of the past and so forth.
Furthermore, there are three types of karma, namely:
those bound to the desire realm and so forth.
Does the former subsume the latter?
Does the latter include the former? Answer:
The former includes the latter, but the latter does not include the former.
What is not included? It refers to uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
Regarding the three types of karma—
namely, wholesome and so forth— there are further three types of karma,
namely those bound to the desire realm and so on. Does the former subsume the latter?
Does the latter subsume the former? Answer:
The former subsumes the latter, but the latter does not subsume the former.
What is not included?
It refers to untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
The three types of action refer to the wholesome and so forth; furthermore, there are other sets of three types of action, namely:
Regarding the trainings and so forth, and those abandoned by vision and so forth:
does the former subsume the latter,
or does the latter subsume the former?
Answer: Depending on the specific case, they encompass one another in succession.
The three types of action (trikarma) are as follows:
Furthermore, there are various triads of karma pertaining to the desire realm and so forth,
namely: those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and others, and those to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and others.
Does the former include the latter,
or does the latter include the former? Answer:
The latter subsumes the former; the former does not subsume the latter.
What is not subsumed? It is as follows:
Untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
The three types of karma refer to those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, there are three types of karma, namely:
those to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and so forth. Does the former subsume the latter?
Does the latter include the former? Answer:
It depends on the specific case; they include one another through mutual inclusion.
Is there any karma that results in the experience of the body but not of the mind?
Answer: There is.
That is to say:
unwholesome karma.
Is there any karma that results in mental feeling but not bodily feeling?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Regarding wholesome karma that is without vitarka (applied thought):
Is there any karma that brings about feeling (vedanā) in both body and mind? Answer:
There is. Namely: wholesome karma accompanied by vitarka.
Is there any karma that does not induce feeling in body or mind, yet induces a karmic maturation?
Answer: There is.
That is to say:
the maturation of various karmas consists of matter (*rūpa*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
As it is said regarding the three obstructions (*trīṇy āvaraṇāni*): [namely...]
The affliction-obstruction, the karma-obstruction, and the maturation-obstruction.
What is the affliction-obstruction?
It is as follows:

Suppose there is one whose nature is fully possessed of the burning afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion; because of this, it is difficult for them to give rise to weary detachment, difficult to instruct, difficult to awaken, difficult to escape, and difficult to attain liberation.
What is the obstruction of karma?
It refers to the five deeds of immediate retribution.
What is the obstacle of maturation?

It refers to the states in which sentient beings dwell: the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the northern continent of Uttarakuru, and the station of the non-conceptual gods (asaṃjñisattva).
Among the three types of unwholesome conduct, which constitutes the greatest offense?
It is the false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha; this karma brings about the fruit of a lifespan of one kalpa in the Avīci Hell.
Among the three types of wholesome conduct (*sucarita*), which yields the greatest fruit?

It is the volition (*cetanā*) within the meditative attainment of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); this karma can take as its fruit an eighty-thousand-eon lifespan in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The three categories of the false and the correct, and their identity or difference;
The inclusion of the three types of misconduct—crookedness, etc.—within the characteristics of the sublime, the pure, and silence;

The acquisition of results by karma through six phrases such as "unreasonably," and its existence across the three periods of time; And the eight phrases concerning the ripening result (*vipākaphala*).
The five karmas are neither prior nor posterior. In this chapter, I wish to explain in full detail:
Are all those that are wrong speech also wrong livelihood?
Or, if they are wrong livelihood, are they also wrong speech?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is that which is wrong speech but not wrong livelihood.
That is to say:
excluding the four types of verbal misconduct arising from greed, there are other forms of verbal misconduct.
There is that which constitutes wrong livelihood but is not wrong speech.
That is to say:
the three unwholesome actions of body arising from greed include wrong speech and also wrong livelihood.
That is to say:
Regarding the four types of verbal misconduct arising from greed,
there are those that are neither wrong speech nor wrong livelihood, namely:
Excluding those bodily unwholesome actions arising from greed, are all other bodily unwholesome actions and all wrong occupations necessarily wrong livelihood? Conversely,
if something is wrong livelihood, is it necessarily a wrong occupation?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions.
There is that which is wrong action but not wrong livelihood.
That is to say:
with the exception of the three types of bodily misconduct arising from greed, all other forms of bodily misconduct.
There is that which is wrong livelihood but not wrong action.
That is to say:
the four types of verbal misconduct arising from greed;
there is also unwholesome action that constitutes wrong livelihood.
That is to say:
the three types of unwholesome bodily conduct arising from greed;
there are those which are neither wrong action nor wrong livelihood.
That is to say:
with the exception of the four types of verbal misconduct arising from greed, all other forms of verbal misconduct.
Are all instances of right speech also right livelihood?
If one possesses right livelihood, does one possess right speech?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is right speech that is not right livelihood; namely,
all other types of excellent verbal conduct apart from the four types of excellent verbal conduct arising from non-greed.
There is right livelihood that is not right speech; namely,
the three types of sublime bodily conduct arising from non-greed.
There is right speech as well as right livelihood;
that is to say,
the four types of sublime conduct of speech arising from non-greed.
There are those that are neither right speech nor right livelihood; namely,
all other types of bodily wholesome conduct apart from the three types of bodily sublime conduct arising from non-attachment.
If one possesses right action, does one possess right livelihood?
Conversely, if one possesses right livelihood, does one possess right action? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is right action that is not right livelihood; namely:
Excluding the three types of bodily sublime conduct arising from non-greed, all other bodily sublime conducts are such that there is right livelihood which is not right action.
That is to say:
The four types of sublime verbal conduct arising from non-attachment include right action and also right livelihood;
that is to say:
The three types of excellent bodily conduct arising from non-greed may not be right action or right livelihood;
that is to say:
Excluding the four types of excellent verbal conduct arising from non-attachment, there are all other types of excellent verbal conduct.
There are three unwholesome courses of action, and three crookednesses, corruptions, and turbidities—namely:

bodily crookedness, bodily corruption, and bodily turbidity; verbal crookedness, verbal corruption, and verbal turbidity; and mental crookedness, mental corruption, and mental turbidity—making three [sets].
What is crookedness?
It refers to the bodily, vocal, and mental actions arising from guile.
What is defilement?
It refers to the bodily, vocal, and mental karmas arising from hatred.
What is turbidity?
It refers to the bodily, vocal, and mental karmas arising from greed.
Are the three types of misconduct subsumed by crookedness (*vaṅka*), corruption (*doṣa*),
and turbidity (*kaṣāya*), or are crookedness, corruption, and turbidity subsumed by misconduct? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There are cases of misconduct that are neither crooked, nor corrupt, nor turbid.
That is to say:
Excluding the bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct arising from the deceit, anger, and greed of the desire realm, there are other remaining instances of bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct.
Furthermore, there are instances of crookedness, corruption, and turbidity that do not constitute misconduct.
That is to say:
the bodily, vocal, and mental karma arising from guile and greed in the first dhyāna, as well as the mental karma arising from greed in the remaining realms of form and formlessness.
There are unwholesome actions that are also crooked, defiled, and turbid; namely,
those unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind arising from deceit, hatred, and greed within the desire realm.
There are those that are neither unwholesome conduct nor crooked, defiled, or turbid;
namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Regarding the three types of wholesome conduct and the three purities—
namely, purity of body, speech, and mind—
is it that the purities are subsumed within the wholesome conduct?
Is it for the sake of purifying and encompassing sublime conduct? Answer:
It depends on the specific case.
They are mutually inclusive:
the three types of wholesome conduct and the three kinds of silence. Namely:
Regarding the tranquility of body, speech, and mind:
is tranquility subsumed by sublime conduct,
or is sublime conduct subsumed by tranquility?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions.
There is wholesome conduct that is not silence.
That is to say:
with the exception of the untrained (aśaikṣa) sublime conduct of body and speech, all other sublime conduct of body and speech,
as well as all sublime conduct of mind.
There is that which is silent but not sublime conduct;
namely, the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
There is that which is both sublime conduct and silence; namely,
the sublime conduct of body and speech of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
There is that which is neither sublime conduct nor silence;
namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Regarding the three purities and the three silences: do the purities subsume the silences, or do the silences subsume the purities? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is that which is pure but not silent; namely:
Excluding the purity of body and speech of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all other purities of body and speech, as well as all purities of mind, exist;
yet there is silence that is not purity. Namely:
The mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣacitta) is both pure and tranquil;
that is to say:
The body and speech of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are pure.
There is that which is neither pure nor silent; namely:
Excluding the aforementioned cases,
are all bodily misconducts instances of bodily action induced by what is unreasonable? Conversely,
are all instances of bodily action induced by what is unreasonable instances of bodily misconduct?
Answer: All bodily misconduct is entirely bodily action induced by what is unreasonable.
However, there is bodily action induced by what is unreasonable that is not bodily misconduct.
That is to say:
obscured-unspecified bodily action, and unobscured-unspecified bodily action induced by improper reasoning.
Are all verbal misconducts exclusively verbal actions induced by improper reasoning?
If it is vocal action induced by what is unreasonable, is it all vocal misconduct?
Answer: All vocal misconduct is vocal action induced by what is unreasonable.
There are vocal actions induced by improper reasoning that are not vocal misconduct; namely,
vocal actions that are obscured-neutral, as well as vocal actions that are unobscured-neutral and induced by improper reasoning.
Are all unwholesome mental actions necessarily mental karma that is induced by what is unreasonable?
Conversely, is all mental karma that is induced by what is unreasonable necessarily an unwholesome mental action?
Answer: This should be analyzed in four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There may be mental misconduct that is not induced by irrationality (ayoniśomanasikāra).
That is to say:
covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
There is mental action induced by improper reasoning that does not constitute an unwholesome mental course of action.
That is to say:
obscured-unspecified mental karma, as well as unobscured-unspecified mental karma induced by improper reasoning.
There is also mental misconduct that is mental karma induced by improper reasoning.
That is to say:
unwholesome mental action;
there is also that which is neither mental misconduct nor mental action induced by improper reasoning.
That is to say:
excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
are all those excellent bodily conducts entirely bodily actions induced by correct reasoning?
If it is bodily action induced by correct reasoning, is it all virtuous bodily conduct? Answer:
All virtuous bodily conduct is indeed bodily action induced by correct reasoning.
There is bodily action induced by correct reasoning that is not a sublime bodily conduct;
namely, unobscured-neutral bodily action induced by correct reasoning.
Are all instances of verbal good conduct necessarily verbal actions induced by correct reasoning?
Conversely, are all instances of verbal actions induced by correct reasoning necessarily verbal good conduct?
Answer: All excellent verbal conduct (*vāksucarita*) is entirely verbal action (*vākkarman*) induced by correct reasoning (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
However, there is verbal action induced by correct reasoning that is not excellent verbal conduct.
That is to say:
unobscured-neutral vocal karma that is induced by correct reasoning.
Are all mental sublime conducts likewise mental karma induced by correct reasoning?
If it is an mental action (manas-karman) induced by correct reasoning, is it necessarily a sublime mental conduct (manas-sucarita)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
Volitional good conduct refers to mental karma that is not induced by reasoning;
it consists of non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view.
There is mental karma that is induced by correct reasoning but is not a sublime mental action;
namely, unobscured-neutral mental karma induced by correct reasoning.
There is volitional wholesome conduct, which is also mental action induced by correct reasoning;
that is to say:
wholesome mental action.
There is mental misconduct that is also not mental action induced by correct reasoning;
namely, that which excludes the aforementioned characteristics.
If various phenomena are acquired through karma, should those phenomena be described as wholesome,
unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Answer: Based on the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), those phenomena which are acquired through karma are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This is stated with certainty.
"Is it the case that, by way of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), those dharmas which are acquired through karma are themselves indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Answer: "It is so."
What is it that you desire?
The Tathāgata speaks with a virtuous mind; his speech is a wondrous sound, a beautiful sound, a harmonious and elegant sound, and a pleasing sound—is this speech not virtuous?
Answer: It is so. If one were to say this:
If it were the case that "by way of the ripened fruit, all phenomena are acquired through karma, and those phenomena are indeterminate," then one should not say:
"The speech spoken by the Tathāgata with a virtuous mind— possessing a sublime voice, a beautiful voice, a harmonious and elegant voice, and a pleasing voice— is virtuous."
To speak in this manner is not reasonable. If one were to say:

"The words spoken by the Tathāgata with a virtuous mind—those with wondrous tones, beautiful tones, harmonious and elegant tones, and pleasing tones—these words are virtuous," [then it would be reasonable].
Then one should not say:
"Based on the fruit of maturation, various phenomena are acquired through karma, and those phenomena are indeterminate.
To make such a statement is unreasonable.
One should speak thus:
"In other previous lives, the Bodhisattva performed and accumulated karma that brings about the ripening fruit of great magnitude;
by reason of these causes and conditions, there has been produced, through a continuous succession, the subtle and sublime primary elements within the Tathāgata’s throat."
From this, wondrous speech and sounds can arise;
yet the sound itself is not a maturation (*vipāka*).
When actions (*karman*) have passed away, has their fruit (*phala*) also passed away?
Answer: Its fruit may be past, future, or present.
If various karmas are future, is their fruit also future?
Answer: It is so.
If various karmas are present, are their fruits also present?
Answer: Its fruit is either present or future.
Is it possible that while bodily karma produces a ripening result, vocal and mental karma do not?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one does not guard the body but guards speech;
At that time, he possesses either a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
Furthermore,
it is like guarding the body while not guarding speech.
At that time, he possesses either an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
Is it possible for verbal karma to produce a ripened result while bodily and mental karma do not?
