Answer: There is.
For example, there may be protection of the body while there is no protection of speech.
At that time, he possesses either a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
The same applies to the converse statement.
Is it possible for mental karma to produce a ripened result (*vipāka*) while bodily and vocal karma do not?
Answer: There is.
For example, as there is protection of the body, so too is there protection of speech.
At that time, he possesses an unwholesome mind,
such as when he does not guard his body and does not guard his speech;
at that time, he also possesses a wholesome mind.
Is it possible that bodily and verbal karma produce ripening results (*vipāka-phala*) while mental karma does not?
Answer: It is possible.
Just as when there is no guarding of the body, there is no guarding of speech;
at that time, one possesses either a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
Likewise, when there is guarding of the body, there is guarding of speech.
At that time, he possesses either an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
Is it possible that while his bodily and mental actions induce a ripened result (*vipāka-phala*), his vocal action does not?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one does not guard the body but guards speech, at that time one possesses an unwholesome mind.
Just as there may be protection of the body while there is no protection of speech, yet at that time one possesses a wholesome mind,
is it possible for vocal karma and mental karma to induce a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) while bodily karma does not?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one guards the body but does not guard speech, at that time one possesses an unwholesome mind.
If one is not restrained in bodily action but is restrained in verbal action, at that time one possesses a wholesome mind.
Is it possible for both bodily and verbal karma to produce a ripened result (*vipāka-phala*) in such a way that the same applies to mental karma?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one does not guard the body and does not guard speech, at that time one possesses an unwholesome mind.
Just as there is protection of body and protection of speech, at that time one possesses a virtuous mind.
Is it possible for there to be maturation produced by neither bodily, vocal, nor mental karma, yet still resulting in maturation?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Do the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) induce maturation (*vipāka*) in matter, mind and mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind?
Is there any karma—such as that to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and so forth—that undergoes its maturation result neither before nor after [the other two types]?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Karma to be experienced in the present life—matter (rūpa).
Karma to be experienced in the next life—the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma).
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives—conditioned factors dissociated from the mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
Furthermore:
karma to be experienced in the present life consists of formations dissociated from mind;
karma to be experienced in the next life consists of form.
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives consists of the mind and mental factors.
Furthermore,
karma to be experienced in the present life consists of the mind and mental factors.
Karma to be experienced in the next life consists of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives consists of form (*rūpa*).
Is there any karma to be experienced as pleasant feeling and so forth—the three types of karma—that does not experience its ripened fruit either before or after [the primary experience]?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Karma conducive to pleasant feeling—form;
karma conducive to painful feeling—mind and mental factors;
karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—factors dissociated from mind.
Furthermore:
karma conducive to pleasant feeling—dissociated mental formations;
karma conducive to painful feeling—form.
Karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling consists of the mind and mental factors.
Furthermore,
karma conducive to pleasant feeling consists of the mind and mental factors.
Karma conducive to painful feeling—dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—form (*rūpa*).
Is there karma belonging to the three realms that ripens its fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) neither before nor after [the other]?
Answer: There are. Namely:
Karma bound to the desire realm—form;
karma bound to the form realm—mind and mental factors;
karma bound to the formless realm—factors dissociated from mind.
Furthermore,
karma bound to the desire realm consists of formations dissociated from mind;
karma bound to the form realm consists of form.
Karma bound to the formless realm—the mind and mental factors.
Furthermore!
Karma bound to the desire realm—the mind and mental factors.
Karma of the form realm—dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Karma bound to the formless realm—form (*rūpa*).
Is there any wholesome or unwholesome karma whose maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is experienced neither before nor after [the other]?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Wholesome karma—form.
Unwholesome karma—the mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from the mind.
Furthermore!
Wholesome karma consists of mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Unwholesome karma consists of form (*rūpa*).
Is there any karma to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that undergoes its maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) neither before nor after [the other]?
Answer: There are. Namely:
Karma abandoned through seeing consists of form;
karma abandoned through cultivation consists of mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind.
Furthermore:
Karma to be abandoned by seeing consists of mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
Karma to be abandoned by cultivation consists of form (rūpa).
There are four types of taking life: two are karmic maturation (vipāka), and two are protective (ārakṣa).
The accomplishment of the body and its actions, Defilement, the ripening of fruits,
the unwholesome, and perversions; Bondage and non-bondage, the accomplishment [of these],
death, and the place of rebirth— In this chapter, may all these be fully explained.
Is it possible that one has already taken life, yet the impulse to kill has not yet been extinguished?
Answer: Yes.

If one has already taken another's life, but the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) has not yet ceased, is it possible that the living being has not yet been killed while the act of killing has already ceased?
Answer: Yes.
Yes. For example, when one has not yet taken another's life, but that preparatory effort has already ceased.
Is it possible that one has already killed a living being, yet the act of killing has already ceased?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one has already taken another's life, and that preparatory effort has ceased.
Is there anyone who has not yet harmed living beings, yet for whom the impulse to kill has not been extinguished? Answer: There is.
Suppose one has not yet taken another's life, and the preparatory effort for that act has not yet ceased.
Is it possible that, while no living being has been killed and the act of killing has not been extinguished, the maturation of this karma will nonetheless certainly result in birth in hell?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one dies while engaged in the preliminary application (*prayoga*) for an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).

Is there any unwholesome karma that accords with painful feeling, whose maturation has not yet ripened, such that one does not fail to experience its first karmic fruit, yet gives rise to a defiled mind?
Answer: There is.
For example, once one has performed and accumulated an uninterrupted karma (*ānantarya-karma*), the first retribution of that karma arises as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of that hell.
Is there a case where, after intentionally taking the life of a living being, one does not undertake the abstention [from killing], yet nonetheless achieves protection regarding all sentient beings?
Answer: There is.
Suppose one initiates the preparatory action for killing such that the victim certainly dies, yet in the interim realizes the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
If one has attained protection regarding all sentient beings,
has that person undertaken the abstention from harming all sentient beings?
Answer: This should be treated as a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the case where one attains restraint toward all sentient beings, yet does not undertake the formal abstention (virati).
For example:
there are those who realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) without having received the precepts (*śikṣāpada*);
and there are those who maintain distance from all sentient beings, yet do not attain formal restraint (*saṃvara*).
For example:
there are those who, having received the training rules, violate the abstentions;
and there are those who obtain protection regarding all sentient beings and also receive the abstentions.
For example:
there are those who receive the training rules and do not transgress them,
yet they have neither attained protection regarding all sentient beings nor undertaken the practice of renunciation.
That is to say:
excluding the aforementioned cases.
If one possesses the body, does one also possess bodily action?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the case where one possesses the body but does not possess bodily karma.
That is to say:

being within an eggshell; or being an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) dwelling in the womb; or being born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and abiding in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline (naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara), lacking bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), or having it but having lost it.
There are those who accomplish bodily karma but not the body, namely:
noble ones born in the formless realm.
There are those who possess both the body and bodily action.
This refers to:

noble ones dwelling within the womb; or those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint, non-restraint, or that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint, and who currently manifest bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), or who possess it from before without having lost it.
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
there are cases where one neither possesses the body nor possesses bodily action (kāyakarma).
That is to say:
When an ordinary person is born in the formless realm,
if they possess the body, do they also possess vocal karma? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There are those who possess the body but not vocal karma; namely:

Whether dwelling within an eggshell, or as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) residing in the womb, or being born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) while abiding in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline (*naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara*), there is entirely no vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*);
even if it were present, it would have been lost.
There are those who accomplish verbal karma but not bodily karma; namely,
the noble ones born in the formless realm.
There are those who accomplish both bodily and vocal karma; namely,
those noble ones dwelling within the womb, or those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint, or abide in non-restraint, or abide in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There is either a present vocal intimation, or one that existed previously and has not been lost.
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu),
there are those who neither possess bodily action nor vocal action.
That is to say:
when ordinary beings are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
if they possess the body, do they also possess mental karma (manaskarma)?
Answer: All those who possess the body necessarily possess mental action (manas-karma).
However, there are those who possess mental action but do not possess the body; namely:
Regarding those born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu):
if they possess the body, do they also possess bodily action (kāyakarman) and vocal action (vākkarman)? Answer:
There are those who possess the body but not bodily or vocal karma;
namely, those dwelling within the shell of an egg.

If an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) dwells in the womb, or is born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline (naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara), they lack bodily and vocal intimation (vijñapti); even if such intimation exists, it has been lost.
There are those who possess both the body and bodily action, but not vocal action.

This refers to one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, and who currently possesses bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), or who previously possessed it and has not lost it.
There is no manifest verbal action; even if it existed, it would have been lost.
There is the accomplishment of bodily and verbal karma, but not of bodily karma.
That is to say:
Born in the desire realm, abiding in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, one currently possesses vocal intimation, or possesses it as previously acquired and not yet lost.
One lacks bodily intimation; even if it were present, it has been lost.
There are those who possess both the body and bodily action as well as vocal action;
namely, noble ones dwelling in the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint;
or if one abides in non-restraint, or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint, and currently possesses bodily or vocal intimation, or has previously possessed it without losing it;
or if one is born in the form realm.
If one accomplishes bodily action and vocal action, does that person accomplish the body? Answer: Either they do, or they do not.
How is it accomplished?
It is as previously explained.
What is non-attainment?
It refers to noble ones born in the formless realm.
If one is endowed with the body, is that person also endowed with bodily action (kāyakarman) and mental action (manaskarman)?
Answer: There are cases where one is endowed with the body and mental action, but not with bodily action.
That is to say:
being within an eggshell;
or if an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is dwelling in the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm,
abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
and possesses no bodily intimation.
There is the case where, although something exists, it is lost;
that is, one possesses the body as well as bodily and mental karma. Namely:
The Noble One abides in the womb;

or, if born in the desire realm, he abides in either restraint or non-restraint, or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint, and currently possesses bodily intimation, or previously possessed it and has not lost it;
or, he is born in the form realm.
If one accomplishes bodily action and mental action, does that person accomplish the body?
Answer: Either they accomplish it, or they do not accomplish it.
How is it accomplished?
It is as previously explained.
What is non-attainment?
It refers to noble ones born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes the body, does that person accomplish verbal action and mental action?
Answer: There are those who accomplish the body and mental action, but not verbal action.
There is the accomplishment of bodily action, vocal action, and mental action.
These are all as previously explained regarding the body in relation to bodily action and mental action.
The difference is as follows:
This explains the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
Suppose one accomplishes vocal and mental karma; does that person also accomplish bodily [karma]? Answer:
It may be accomplished, or it may not be accomplished;
it is as stated there.
If one accomplishes the body, does one also accomplish bodily action, verbal action, and mental action?
Answer: There are those who possess the body and mental karma, but not bodily or vocal karma.
There are those who possess the body, bodily karma, and mental karma, but not vocal karma.
There are those who accomplish bodily and vocal actions, but not mental action;
there are those who accomplish bodily, vocal, and mental actions.
All of these cases are as previously explained regarding the relationship between the body and bodily or vocal actions.
If one accomplishes bodily action, vocal action, and mental action, does that person accomplish the body?
Answer: Either they accomplish it, or they do not.
It is also as stated there:
"If one accomplishes bodily action, does one also accomplish verbal action? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is the case of one who accomplishes bodily action, but not vocal action.
That is to say:
Born in the desire realm,
abiding in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
and currently possessing bodily intimation.
Either it was previously possessed and not lost;
or there was no verbal intimation (vāgvijñapti); or, even if it existed, it has been lost.
There are those who accomplish verbal karma but not bodily karma;
that is to say:
those born in the desire realm.
Abiding in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
one currently possesses vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*),
or possesses it as previously existing and not yet lost.
There is no bodily intimation;
even if it existed, it would have been lost.
There is, however, the accomplishment of bodily action and vocal action.
That is to say:
an noble one dwelling in the womb,
or one born in the desire realm.
Abiding in restraint, non-restraint, or neither restraint nor non-restraint,
one currently possesses bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*).
Alternatively, it may have existed previously and not been lost;
this applies if one is born in the form realm,
or if an noble one (ārya) is born in the formless realm.
There are those who do not accomplish bodily and vocal karma;
namely, those dwelling within the shell of an egg.
If an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) dwells in the womb,
or is born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
and abides in a state that is neither discipline (saṃvara) nor non-discipline (asaṃvara).
There are no bodily or vocal intimation;
even if they were present, they have been lost.
This is the case for those born as ordinary beings in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes bodily action, does one also accomplish mental action? Answer:
If one accomplishes bodily action, one necessarily accomplishes mental action.
There is the accomplishment of mental action, but not of bodily action;
namely, those dwelling within the eggshell.
If an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) dwells in the womb,
or is born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
and abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline (naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara).
There is no bodily intimation; even if it existed, it would have been lost.
If a non-Buddhist is born in the formless realm, and if he accomplishes bodily action, does he also accomplish vocal and mental actions?
Answer: There are those who possess bodily action (kāyakarman) and mental action (manaskarman), but not vocal action (vākkarman).
That is to say:
Born in the desire realm,
abiding in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
and currently possessing bodily intimation.
Either there was previously [a non-informative action] that has not been lost, or even if it existed, it has been lost; in either case, there is no manifest intimation (vijñapti).
There are those who accomplish bodily action, verbal action, and mental action; namely,
noble ones dwelling in the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in either restraint, non-restraint, or that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently possesses bodily and vocal informative intimation (vijñapti).
Or it may have existed previously and not been lost;
this applies if one is born in the form realm,
or if an noble one (ārya) is born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes verbal action and mental action, does one also accomplish bodily action?
Answer: One may accomplish it, or one may not accomplish it.
How is it accomplished?
It is as previously explained.
What is non-attainment?
It refers to being born in the desire realm.
Abiding in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
one currently possesses vocal intimation,
or possesses it as previously acquired and not yet lost.
There is no bodily intimation;
even if it existed, it would have been lost.
If one accomplishes vocal karma, does one also accomplish mental karma?
Answer: Those who accomplish verbal karma also accomplish mental karma.
However, there are those who accomplish mental karma but not verbal karma.
This is as previously explained regarding bodily karma in contrast to mental karma;
the difference here is that this refers to vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
If karma has not been freed from defilement, is its maturation also not freed from defilement?
Answer: All karma that has not been freed from defilement has its maturation also not freed from defilement.
There may be cases where the maturation has not yet been freed from defilement, while that karma has already been freed from defilement.
That is to say:
for a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), karma to be abandoned through seeing has already been freed from defilement, but its maturation has not yet been freed from defilement.
If an action has already been free from defilement, is its maturation also free from defilement?
Answer: Whatever maturations are free from defilement, those actions have already been free from defilement.
There may be karma that is already free from defilement, yet its maturation (*vipāka*) is not yet free from defilement.
That is to say:
for a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), karma to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) is already free from defilement, but its maturation is not yet free from defilement.
If an action has a fruit, does that action necessarily have a ripening (vipāka)?
Answer: Of all actions that have a ripening, those actions necessarily have a fruit.
There may be karma that has a fruit, yet that karma lacks maturation (vipāka).
That is to say:
indeterminate (avyākṛta) karma and untainted (anāsrava) karma.
If an action has no fruit, does that action lack all ripening?
Answer: There is no action that lacks a fruit.
There may be karma that has no maturation; namely,
neutral karma and untainted karma.
If an action is unwholesome, is that action necessarily inverted?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is unwholesome karma that is not based on inversion;
namely, as when someone gives rise to this view and establishes this doctrine:
"There is karma, and there is the ripening of the fruit of karma," yet one engages in misconduct of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore,
it is as with someone who:
Having seen, one has the perception that one did not see;
having heard, sensed, or known, one has the perception that one did not hear, sense, or know. Concealing this perception, this approval, and this desire, one says: "I saw; I heard, sensed, and knew."

Or, when not seeing, one has the perception of seeing; when not hearing, cognizing, or knowing, one has the perception of hearing, cognizing, or knowing. Concealing this perception, this approval, and this desire, one says:
"I did not see, hear, cognize, or know."
There is karma that is inverted, yet that karma is not unwholesome.
That is to say:
for example, there is one who gives rise to this view and establishes this doctrine:
"There is no karma, and no ripening of the fruit of karma," yet one performs sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore!

Suppose there is a person who has the perception of not seeing regarding what was seen, and the perception of not hearing, not sensing, or not cognizing regarding what was heard, sensed, or cognized; yet he does not conceal this perception, this approval, or this inclination, but says:
"I did not see; I did not hear, sense, or cognize."

Or, having not seen, one has the perception of seeing; having not heard, sensed, or known, one has the perception of hearing, sensing, or knowing. Without concealing this perception, this approval, or this desire, one says:
"I have seen; I have heard, sensed, and known."
There is karma that is both unwholesome and inverted; namely,
as when someone gives rise to this view and establishes this doctrine:
"Thinking, 'There is no action, there is no ripening of the fruit of action,' they further engage in misconduct of body, speech, and mind.
Moreover,
it is as if there were someone who:"

When there is seeing, one has the perception of seeing; when there is hearing, sensing, or knowing, one has the perception of hearing, sensing, or knowing. Yet, concealing this perception, this acceptance, and this inclination, one says:
"I have neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, nor known."

Or, having not seen something, one has the perception of not having seen it; having not heard, sensed, or known something, one has the perception of not having heard, sensed, or known it. Yet, concealing this perception, this acquiescence, and this inclination, one says:
"I have seen; I have heard, sensed, and known."
There is karma that is neither unwholesome nor perverted;
namely, as when someone gives rise to this view and establishes this doctrine:
"Thinking, 'There is karma; there is the ripening of the fruit of karma,' one further practices sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Moreover, it is as if there were someone who:"

When there is seeing, one has the perception of seeing; when there is hearing, sensing, or cognizing, one has the perception of hearing, sensing, or cognizing. Without concealing these perceptions, these acceptances, or these inclinations, one says:
"I have seen; I have heard, sensed, or cognized."

Or, when not seeing, one has the perception of not seeing; when not hearing, cognizing, or knowing, one has the perception of not hearing, cognizing, or knowing. Without concealing this perception, this acceptance, or this inclination, one says:
"I did not see; I did not hear, cognize, or know."
"If an action is wholesome, is that action non-perverted?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
The former second line becomes this first line;
the former first line becomes this second line;
and the former fourth line becomes this third line.
The former third clause is made the fourth clause here—
explained in detail as previously stated.
If one accomplishes unwholesome karma, does that person also accomplish karma bound to the realm of form and the formless realm?
Answer:
Those who possess unwholesome karma necessarily possess karma bound to the form and formless realms.
However, there are those who possess karma bound to the form and formless realms without possessing unwholesome karma.
That is to say:
one who is born in the desire realm and has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm;
or one who is born in the form realm.
If one accomplishes wholesome karma bound to the desire realm, does that person accomplish karma bound to the form and formless realms?
Answer:
All those who accomplish wholesome karma bound to the desire realm necessarily accomplish karma bound to the form and formless realms.
There are those who possess karma bound to the form and formless realms, but not karma bound to the desire realm that is wholesome.
That is to say:
a person (pudgala) who has severed their roots of goodness, if they are born in the form realm.
If one accomplishes wholesome karma bound to the desire realm, does that person accomplish wholesome karma bound to the form and formless realms?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are those who possess wholesome karma bound to the desire realm, but not wholesome karma bound to the form or formless realms;
that is to say:
one born in the desire realm who has not severed the roots of goodness, yet has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm.
There is the accomplishment of wholesome karma pertaining to the form and formless realms, but not of wholesome karma pertaining to the desire realm;
that is to say,
one born in the form realm who attains a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
There is one who accomplishes both wholesome karma bound to the desire realm and wholesome karma bound to the form and formless realms;
that is to say,
one born in the desire realm who attains a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
There are those who do not possess wholesome karma bound to the desire realm, nor wholesome karma bound to the form or formless realms;
namely, individuals who have severed their roots of virtue.
If one accomplishes karma bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish karma bound to the form realm? Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes karma bound to the form realm, does one also accomplish karma bound to the desire realm? Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes karma bound to the desire realm, does that person accomplish karma bound to the formless realm?
Answer:
All those who accomplish karma bound to the desire realm necessarily accomplish karma bound to the formless realm.
There are those who accomplish karma bound to the formless realm, but not karma bound to the desire realm;
namely, individuals born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes karma bound to the desire realm, does one also accomplish unbound karma?
Answer: One should formulate this as four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are those who accomplish karma bound to the desire realm, but not karma that is unbound.
That is to say:
ordinary beings born in the desire realm or the form realm.
There is the accomplishment of non-bound karma, which is not karma bound to the desire realm;
namely, when noble ones are born in the formless realm.
There are those who accomplish both karma bound to the desire realm and unbound karma; namely,
noble ones born in the desire or form realms.
There are those who neither accomplish karma bound to the desire realm nor accomplish karma that is unbound;
namely, ordinary beings born in the formless realm.

If one accomplishes karma bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-karma), does that person necessarily accomplish karma bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-karma)? Answer:
All those who accomplish karma bound to the realm of form necessarily accomplish karma bound to the formless realm.
There are those who accomplish karma associated with the formless realm, but not karma associated with the form realm;
that is to say,
sentient beings born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes karma bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-karma), does that person accomplish karma that is unbound (apratisaṃyukta-karma)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are those who accomplish karma bound to the realm of form, but not karma that is unbound.
That is to say:
ordinary beings born in the desire realm or the realm of form.
There is the accomplishment of non-bound karma, which is not karma bound to the form realm;
that is to say:
when noble ones are born in the formless realm.
There are those who possess karma bound to the realm of form as well as karma that is unbound; namely,
noble ones born in the desire realm or the realm of form.
There are those who neither accomplish karma bound to the form realm nor karma that is unbound.
That is to say:
ordinary beings born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes karma bound to the formless realm, does that person accomplish karma that is unbound?
Answer:
All those who accomplish unbound karma necessarily accomplish karma bound to the formless realm.
There are those who accomplish karma bound to the formless realm, but not karma that is unbound;
namely, all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
If one accomplishes karma bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, or that which is unbound, where will they be reborn at the end of life?
Answer:
Either in the desire realm, or the form realm, or the formless realm, or in a state of non-rebirth.
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Fascicle Eleven.
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Fascicle Twelve.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Manifest and unmanifest [karma], general and specific; The four natures, the three time periods, the formation of karmic fruits, The realms, the correct and the incorrect, The contaminated and so forth, the trainee and so forth.

Physical restraint and mental wisdom—whether these categories of restraint are cultivated collectively or individually, and whether they are cultivated or not—result in their formation across the three periods of time. I pray that this chapter will explain them in full detail.
If one accomplishes the physical manifest action (*vijñapti*), does one also accomplish its corresponding non-manifest action (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is one who accomplishes bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) but not this non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:

being born in the desire realm, abiding in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, one currently possesses bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) but does not obtain this non-intimation (avijñapti);
or, having previously possessed this intimation without losing it, one does not obtain this non-intimation.
There are those who possess the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of the body but not its informative matter (*vijñapti*).
This refers to:

noble ones dwelling in the womb; or those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint (*saṃvara*), yet have not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint, and thus lack bodily informative matter, or possessed it but have lost it.
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu), there is no bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti); even if it existed, it would have been lost.
If an noble one (ārya) is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is the possession of both bodily intimation and its corresponding non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:

being born in the desire realm and abiding in restraint, one does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint, yet presently possesses bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and also obtains this non-intimation (*avijñapti*);
or, having previously possessed this intimation without losing it, one also obtains this non-intimation.

Whether one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint, abides in non-restraint, or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint, if there is currently a bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), one also acquires this non-intimation (avijñapti);
or, if one previously possessed this intimation and has not lost it, one also acquires this non-intimation.
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and currently possesses bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), or previously possessed it and has not lost it,
there are cases where one neither possesses bodily intimation nor its non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:
dwelling within an eggshell;
or, if an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), dwelling in the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm, abiding in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, and lacks bodily intimation— or even if it exists, has been lost—
and if one is an ordinary being born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes a wholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), does one also accomplish its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: One should formulate this in four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There are those who accomplish wholesome bodily intimation but not its corresponding non-intimation;
that is to say:

one born in the desire realm who dwells in non-restraint, or in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, currently possesses wholesome bodily intimation but does not acquire its corresponding non-intimation.
Or, there may be cases where this manifest action (vijñapti) previously existed and has not been lost, yet one does not possess this non-manifest action (avijñapti).
There are those who possess the wholesome non-manifest action of the body but do not possess its manifest action. Namely:

When a Noble One dwells in the womb, or if he is born in the desire realm, he abides in restraint but does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint; he lacks virtuous bodily intimation, or if it exists, it has been lost.
If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*); even if it existed, it would have been lost.
If an noble one (*ārya*) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they possess both virtuous bodily intimation and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
That is to say:

being born in the desire realm and abiding in restraint, one does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint, yet currently possesses a virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and also obtains its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*);
or, having previously possessed this intimation without losing it, one also obtains this non-intimation.

Whether one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint, or abides in non-restraint, or abides in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint, if there is currently a virtuous bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), one also acquires this non-intimation (avijñapti);
or, if one previously possessed this intimation and has not lost it, one also acquires this non-intimation.
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and currently possesses a wholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), or previously possessed it and has not lost it;
yet there are cases where one neither possesses a wholesome bodily intimation nor its corresponding non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:
being within an eggshell,
or as an ordinary person dwelling in the womb.

If one is born in the desire realm and dwells in non-restraint, or in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, and lacks virtuous bodily intimation— or even if such exists, it has been lost—
and if one is an ordinary being born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does one also accomplish its non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: Those who accomplish unwholesome bodily non-intimation also accomplish this intimation.
There are cases where one accomplishes an unwholesome bodily intimation but not its corresponding non-intimation.
That is to say:
one born in the desire realm who abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint, and who currently possesses an unwholesome bodily intimation, yet does not obtain its corresponding non-intimation.
Or, perhaps one previously possessed this informative [action] without losing it, yet did not obtain this non-informative [action].
If one accomplishes an obscured-unspecified bodily informative action, does one also accomplish its corresponding non-informative action?
Answer: There is no one who possesses the unmanifest (avijñapti) body of obscured-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta) karma, yet there is one who possesses its manifest (vijñapti).
That is to say:
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and currently possesses a concealed-neutral bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),
and if they possess an unconcealed-neutral bodily intimation, do they also possess its non-intimation (avijñapti)?
Answer: There is no one who possesses the non-obscured neutral bodily non-informative action (kāyavijñapti), yet there are those who possess this informative action (vijñapti).
That is to say:
In those born in the desire realm or the form realm who currently possess unobscured-unspecified bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
if they have accomplished past bodily intimation, do they also accomplish this non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is one who accomplishes past bodily informative action (kāyavijñapti), but not its corresponding non-informative action (avijñapti).
That is to say:

one born in the desire realm who abides in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, having previously possessed a bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) which has not been lost, yet does not possess this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
Such a person possesses past bodily non-intimation, but not this [present] intimation.
That is to say:
when a noble one dwells in the womb;
or when born in the desire realm, they abide in restraint but have not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint, having previously lacked bodily intimation, or having possessed it, they have lost it.
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), one previously lacked bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), or if it existed, it has been lost.
If a learner (śaikṣa) is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
they possess past bodily intimation as well as its corresponding non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:

one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint, though not having obtained the prātimokṣa restraint, possesses an existing bodily intimation that has not been lost, and also obtains this non-intimation (avijñapti).

Whether one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint, in non-restraint, or in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint, if there was previously a bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) that has not been lost, one also acquires this non-intimation (avijñapti).
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and has not lost the previously existing bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),
there are cases where one does not possess past bodily intimation, nor does one possess its non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:
Whether dwelling within an eggshell,
or as an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) remaining in the womb,

or born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) while abiding in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, one previously lacked bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), or if it existed, it has been lost.
If an Arhat or an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
and they possess past virtuous bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), do they also possess this non-intimation (avijñapti)?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions.
There is one who has accomplished past virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), but not its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
That is to say:

one born in the desire realm who dwells in non-restraint, or in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, previously possessed an unlost wholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) but has not acquired its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
There are those who possess past unmanifest karma of wholesome bodily action, but not its manifest expression.
This refers,
for example, to noble ones dwelling in the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint, yet has not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint, there was previously no wholesome bodily intimation; even if it existed, it has been lost.
If one is born in the form realm, there was previously no wholesome bodily intimation; even if it existed, it has been lost.
If a learner (śaikṣa) is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
they possess the past wholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) and its corresponding non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:

Born in the desire realm and abiding in the discipline of restraint (*vinaya*), one who has not obtained the discipline of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*) retains previously existing wholesome bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) without losing it, and also acquires this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).

Whether one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint, or abides in non-restraint, or in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint, if there was previously a virtuous bodily intimation that has not been lost, one also acquires this non-intimation.
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and has not lost a previously existing wholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),
there are cases where one does not possess past wholesome bodily intimation, nor its corresponding non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:
Whether dwelling within an eggshell,
or as an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) abiding in the womb,

or born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) while abiding in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), or in neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint (*naivasaṃvaranāsaṃvara*), one previously lacked virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), or even if it existed, it has been lost.
If an Arhat or an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
and they possess past unwholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), do they also possess this non-intimation (avijñapti)?
Answer: Those who possess past unwholesome bodily non-informative action (avijñapti) also possess this [past] informative action (vijñapti).
However, there are those who possess past unwholesome bodily informative action but do not possess this non-informative action.
That is to say:

one born in the desire realm, abiding in either restraint, or neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint, who previously possessed an unwholesome bodily intimation that has not been lost, yet has not acquired this [corresponding] non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
If one accomplishes past obscured-unspecified bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), does one also accomplish its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There is no one who accomplishes both past obscured-unspecified bodily intimation and its corresponding non-intimation.
If one accomplishes past non-obscured neutral bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), does that person also accomplish this non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There is no accomplishment of both past non-obscured neutral bodily intimation and its corresponding non-intimation.
If one accomplishes future bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), does one also accomplish this non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: There is no accomplishment of future bodily intimation, but there is accomplishment of this non-intimation.
That is to say:
when a noble one dwells in the womb;
or, having been born into the desire realm, they attain a wholesome mind of the form realm.
If one is born in the form realm,
or if an noble one (ārya) is born in the formless realm,
and they possess future wholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), do they also possess this non-intimation (avijñapti)?
Answer: There is no one who possesses future virtuous bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), but there is one who possesses its non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
That is to say:
The Noble One dwells in the womb;
or, having been born in the desire realm, he attains a wholesome mind of the form realm;
or, he is born in the form realm.
If an noble one is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
and if they possess future unwholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), do they also possess this non-intimation (avijñapti)? Answer:
There is no one who achieves future unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
If one achieves future obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) bodily intimation, does that person also achieve its corresponding non-intimation?
Answer: There is no one who achieves future obscured-unspecified bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) or its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
If one achieves future unobscured-unspecified bodily intimation, does that person achieve its corresponding non-intimation?
Answer: There is no one who possesses future non-obscured-neutral bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
If one possesses present bodily intimation, does that person also possess its corresponding non-intimation?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the case where one accomplishes present bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) but not its corresponding non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:

one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint, yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint; who currently possesses bodily intimation but does not obtain this non-intimation; or who, even if previously possessing bodily intimation without having lost it, does not obtain this non-intimation.

If one abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, and currently possesses a bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), one does not obtain this non-intimation (*avijñapti*); even if a prior bodily intimation exists and has not been lost, one still does not obtain this non-intimation.
If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and currently possesses bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
there are those who possess the present bodily non-intimation (*kāyāvijñapti*) but not this [bodily] intimation.
That is to say:
Born in the desire realm, abiding in discipline, one who has not obtained the prātimokṣa discipline and is currently in meditative concentration;

or, even if not in concentration, if there is currently no bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) but one does not lose a previously existing bodily intimation—one obtains this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
If one abides in either the prātimokṣa restraint or non-restraint, there is currently no bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).

If one abides in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint, and there is currently no bodily intimation, yet one has not lost a prior bodily intimation, one acquires this non-intimation (avijñapti).
If one is born in the form realm and is currently in meditative absorption,
there is the accomplishment of both present bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
That is to say:

Born in the desire realm and abiding in restraint, one does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint; yet, while currently possessing bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), one obtains this non-intimation (avijñapti), or one possesses bodily intimation that was previously acquired and has not been lost, and thereby obtains this non-intimation.
If one abides in either the prātimokṣa restraint or non-restraint, there is currently a bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).

If one abides in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint, and there is currently a bodily intimation, one acquires this non-intimation (*avijñapti*); or, having previously possessed a bodily intimation without losing it, one acquires this non-intimation.
There are those who neither possess present bodily intimation nor its corresponding non-intimation;
namely, those dwelling within an eggshell or residing inside the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm, abides in restraint, but does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint, and is not in meditative concentration, there is currently no bodily intimation;
even if a prior bodily intimation existed and was not lost, one does not obtain this non-intimation.

If one abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, and currently lacks bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), or even if one previously possessed bodily intimation and has not lost it, yet does not obtain this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
If one is born in the form realm and is not in meditative concentration, there is currently no bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
If one is born in the formless realm,
or if one possesses a present wholesome bodily intimation, does that person also possess its non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions.
There is the case where one possesses the present virtuous bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) but not its non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:

one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint, yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint, currently possesses a virtuous bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) but does not obtain its corresponding non-intimation (avijñapti);
or, even if a previously existing virtuous bodily intimation has not been lost, one still does not obtain this non-intimation.

If one abides in non-restraint, or in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint, and currently possesses a virtuous bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), one does not obtain this non-intimation (*avijñapti*);
even if one previously possessed a virtuous bodily intimation that has not been lost, one still does not obtain this non-intimation.
If one is born in the form realm and currently possesses a virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
there are those who possess the present virtuous non-intimation (*avijñapti*) of the body but not this [bodily] intimation.
That is to say:
Born in the desire realm, abiding in restraint, one who has not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint and is currently in meditative absorption;

or, even if not in absorption, one who currently lacks a wholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) but does not lose a previously existing wholesome bodily intimation, thereby obtaining this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
If one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint and currently lacks a virtuous bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),

or if one abides in non-restraint or in neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint and currently lacks a virtuous bodily intimation, yet has not lost a previously existing virtuous bodily intimation, one thereby acquires this non-intimation (avijñapti).
If one is born in the form realm and is currently in meditative absorption,
there is one who possesses both the present virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
That is to say:

Born in the desire realm and abiding in restraint, though one has not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint, if there is currently a wholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), one also obtains this non-intimation (*avijñapti*); furthermore, having previously possessed a wholesome bodily intimation that has not been lost, one obtains this non-intimation.
If one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint, there is currently a virtuous bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).

If one abides in non-restraint or in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint, and there is currently a virtuous bodily intimation, one also acquires this non-intimation (avijñapti); furthermore, having previously possessed a virtuous bodily intimation that has not been lost, one acquires this non-intimation.
There are those who neither possess the present virtuous bodily intimation nor its non-intimation;
namely, those dwelling within the eggshell or residing in the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm, abides in restraint, yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint, and is not in meditative concentration, there is currently no virtuous bodily intimation;
even if a previously existing virtuous bodily intimation has not been lost, one does not obtain this non-intimation (avijñapti).
If one abides in non-restraint, or in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint, there is currently no virtuous bodily intimation;
even if a previously existing virtuous bodily intimation has not been lost, one does not acquire this [corresponding] non-intimation.
If one is born in the form realm and is not in meditative concentration, there is currently no wholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
If one is born in the formless realm,
or if one accomplishes an unwholesome bodily intimation in the present, does that person also accomplish its non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: This should be analyzed in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one accomplishes the present unwholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) but not its corresponding non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say:

being born in the desire realm, abiding in either restraint (*saṃvara*) or neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint (*naivasaṃvaranāsaṃvara*), one currently possesses an unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) but does not acquire its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*);
or, even if one previously possessed an unwholesome bodily intimation that has not been lost, one still does not acquire this non-intimation.
There is one who accomplishes the present unwholesome bodily non-informative [matter] but not its informative [matter].
That is to say:
one born in the desire realm who dwells in non-restraint and currently lacks unwholesome bodily informative matter.

If one abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint, and currently lacks unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), yet does not lose previously existing unwholesome bodily intimation, one acquires this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
There are those who accomplish both present unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
That is to say:
one born in the desire realm who dwells in neither restraint nor non-restraint, and who currently possesses unwholesome bodily intimation as well as has acquired this non-intimation.
If one has not lost a prior unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and acquires this non-intimation (*avijñapti*),
or if one abides in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and currently possesses an unwholesome bodily intimation,
[one is endowed with both]. However, there are cases where one neither accomplishes a present unwholesome bodily intimation nor this non-intimation.
That is to say:
dwelling within an eggshell,
or abiding within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint, there is currently no unwholesome bodily intimation;
even if a previously existing unwholesome bodily intimation has not been lost, one does not acquire this [unmanifest] intimation.
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) or the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
and if they possess present obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), do they also possess this non-intimation (avijñapti)? Answer:
There is no one who possesses the present non-informative (avijñapti) body that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta),
yet there are those who possess its informative (vijñapti). Namely:
One born in the form realm currently possesses obscured-unspecified bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
If one accomplishes present unobscured-unspecified bodily intimation, does that person also accomplish this non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer:
There is no one who possesses the present unobscured-neutral bodily non-informative [action], yet there is one who possesses its informative [action].
That is to say:
For those born in the desire realm or the form realm, there currently exists unobscured-neutral bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*).
As has been explained in detail regarding bodily intimation and non-intimation (*avijñapti*),
so it is with vocal intimation and non-intimation.
The detailed exposition is likewise.
If an action is bound to the desire realm, is its fruit also bound to the desire realm? Answer:
If various karmas are bound to the desire realm, their fruits are likewise so.
However, there are cases where the fruit of a karma is bound to the desire realm, yet that karma itself is not.
That is to say:
By means of a path belonging to the form realm,
one creates emanations of the desire realm and utters speech of the desire realm.
If an action is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), is its fruit also bound to the form realm?
Answer: All fruits of actions that are bound to the form realm, those actions are likewise so.
There is karma bound to the realm of form that does not have its fruit in that realm;
namely, that which is produced by the path of the realm of form.
One manifests transformations of the desire realm and utters speech of the desire realm; furthermore,
by means of the path of the form realm, one realizes the severance of all fetters.
If an action is bound to the formless realm, is its fruit also bound to the formless realm?
Answer: All fruits of actions that are bound to the formless realm, their corresponding actions are likewise so.
There is karma that is bound to the formless realm but whose fruit is not that karma.
That is to say:
by means of the path of the formless realm, one realizes the abandonment of all fetters.
If an action is not bound, is its fruit also not bound? Answer:
All actions that are not bound, their fruits are likewise so.
There are karmic fruits that are not bound [to a realm] but are not the result of that karma; namely,
the realization of the severance of all fetters through the paths of the form and formless realms.
If an action is not bound to the desire realm, is its fruit also not bound to the desire realm?
Answer: Whatever fruits of actions are not bound to the desire realm, those actions are likewise so.
There is karma that is not bound to the desire realm, yet its fruit is not [experienced] there;
namely, when,
by means of a path belonging to the form realm, one creates a transformation-body in the desire realm and utters speech belonging to the desire realm.
If an action is not bound to the form realm, is its fruit also not bound to the form realm?
Answer: All actions that are not bound to the form realm have fruits that are likewise not bound to the form realm.
There is karma whose fruit is not bound to the form realm, yet it is not that karma itself;
namely, when,
by means of a path belonging to the form realm, one produces emanations of the desire realm or utters speech of the desire realm.
And by means of the path of the form realm, one realizes the abandonment of all fetters.
If an action is not bound to the formless realm, is its fruit also not bound to the formless realm? Answer:
There are no karmas that are not bound to the formless realm, and the same applies to their fruits.
However, there are fruits of karma that are not bound to the formless realm, yet are not the fruits of such karmas. Namely:
Through the path of the formless realm, one realizes the abandonment of all fetters.
If an action is not "unbound," is its fruit also not "unbound"? Answer:
There are various karmic fruits that are not non-bound, and those karmas are likewise so.
There are karmas that are not non-bound, yet they do not have those [fruits].
That is to say:
Through the paths of the form and formless realms, one realizes the abandonment of all fetters.
Is there any karma that is both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and possesses an outflowing fruit? Answer: Yes.
There are; namely,
the outflowing fruit (niṣyanda-phala) and the ripening fruit (vipāka-phala).
Is there any karma that is with outflows (sāsrava) yet has an outflow-free (anāsrava) fruit? Answer: There is.
That is to say:
the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
Is there any karma that is outflowing (*sāsrava*) yet possesses both outflowing and non-outflowing fruits?
—Answer: There are. Namely:
The outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*), and the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
Is there any karma that is untainted (*anāsrava*) yet has an untainted fruit? Answer:
There are: namely,
the fruit of outflow and the fruit of dissociation.
Is there any karma that is untainted (anāsrava) yet has a tainted (sāsrava) fruit? Answer: No.
Is there any karma that is untainted (anāsrava) which has both tainted (sāsrava) and untainted fruits? Answer: No.
Is there any karma that is both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*), yet possesses both fruits of being with outflows and without outflows? Answer: No.
Is there any karma that is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), yet possesses a fruit that is with-outflows? Answer: No.
Is there any karma that is both with outflows and without outflows, yet has a result that is without outflows? Answer: No.
Is there karma that is training (śaikṣa) and whose fruit is training? Answer: Yes.
That is to say:
the outflowing fruit (niṣyanda-phala).
Can there be karma that is both "in training" (śaikṣa) and has a fruit that is "beyond training" (aśaikṣa)?
—Answer: There are. Namely:
Regarding the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*):
Can there be karma that is "in training" (*śaikṣa*) yet has a fruit that is neither "in training" nor "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*)? Answer: Yes.
There is; namely, the fruit of dissociation (visamyoga-phala).
Is there any karma that is both beyond training (aśaikṣa) and has a fruit that is beyond training? Answer: Yes.
That is to say:
the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Is there any karma that is of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) which has the fruit of the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*)?
—Answer: No. Is there any karma that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner which has as its fruit that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
—Answer: No. Is there any karma that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner which has a result that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
[The fruits are] the outflow fruit, the ripening fruit, and the fruit of dissociation.
Is there any karma that is neither trainee nor beyond-training, yet has a trainee fruit? Answer:
None. Is there any karma that is neither of the learner (aśaikṣa) nor of the non-learner (naivāśaikṣa), yet has a fruit that is of the non-learner? Answer: No.
No. As the Blessed One said:
"One does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate virtue, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom."
"What is meant by not cultivating the body? Answer:
It is when one has not yet become free from greed, desire, attachment, delight, and thirst regarding the body."
Furthermore, the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) can exhaust craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*); yet, he has neither cultivated nor stabilized that path.
How, then, could he not be cultivating ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
Answer: If one has not yet abandoned craving for the precepts, it is explained at length as in the case of the body.
How then could one not cultivate the mind?
Answer:
If one has not yet become free from greed, desire, moisture, delight, and craving toward the mind.
Furthermore!
The path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is capable of exhausting craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*); yet, one has not yet cultivated or stabilized that path.
Why has wisdom (*prajñā*) not been cultivated? Answer:
If one has not yet become free from craving for wisdom, it is explained at length as in the case of the mind.
If one does not cultivate the body, does that person not cultivate ethical discipline? Answer:
Thus it is.
Suppose one does not cultivate morality; does that person not cultivate the body? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one does not cultivate the body, does one also not cultivate the mind? Answer:
Those who do not cultivate the body do not cultivate the mind.
However, there are those who do not cultivate the mind but are not without cultivating the body.
That is to say:
One who is already free from the defilement of form but not yet free from the defilement of the formless:
if they do not cultivate the body, do they also not cultivate wisdom? Answer:
Those who do not cultivate the body do not cultivate wisdom.
There are those who do not cultivate wisdom but do not fail to cultivate the body, as previously stated.
If one does not cultivate ethical discipline, does that person not cultivate the mind?
Answer: Those who do not cultivate ethical discipline do not cultivate the mind.
However, there are those who do not cultivate the mind but do cultivate ethical discipline, as previously explained.
If one does not cultivate ethical discipline, does that person not cultivate wisdom?
Answer: Those who do not cultivate ethical discipline do not cultivate wisdom.
There are those who do not cultivate wisdom but are not non-cultivators of ethical discipline, as previously explained.
If one does not cultivate the mind, does that person not cultivate wisdom? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one does not cultivate wisdom, does one also not cultivate the mind? Answer:
It is so. As the Blessed One has said:
"Cultivate the body, cultivate ethical discipline, cultivate the mind, and cultivate wisdom."
“What is the cultivation of the body? Answer:
It is when one has become free from greed, desire, moisture, delight, and thirst regarding the body.”
Furthermore, the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is able to exhaust craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*); he has already cultivated and stabilized that path.
How does he cultivate ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
Answer: If one has already become free from craving regarding ethical discipline, it is explained at length as in the case of the body.
How, then, does one cultivate the mind?
Answer:
If one has already become free from greed, desire, moisture, delight, and thirst regarding the mind.
Furthermore!
The path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is able to exhaust craving for the formless realm; he has already cultivated and stabilized that path.
How does he cultivate wisdom? Answer:
If one has already become free from craving for wisdom, the detailed explanation is as with the mind.
If one cultivates the body, does that person cultivate ethical discipline? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one cultivates morality, does one cultivate the body? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one cultivates the body, does one also cultivate the mind? Answer:
Those who cultivate the mind also cultivate the body.
However, there are those who cultivate the body but do not cultivate the mind;
that is to say:
One who is already free from the defilement of form, but not yet free from the defilement of the formless:
if they cultivate the body, do they also cultivate wisdom? Answer:
All those who cultivate wisdom also cultivate the body.
However, there are those who cultivate the body but do not cultivate wisdom, as previously explained.
If one cultivates ethical discipline, does one also cultivate the mind?
Answer: Those who cultivate the mind also cultivate ethical discipline.
However, there are those who cultivate ethical discipline but do not cultivate the mind, as previously explained.
If one cultivates ethical discipline, does one cultivate wisdom?
Answer: All who cultivate wisdom also cultivate ethical discipline.
There is the cultivation of ethical discipline (śīla) without the cultivation of wisdom (prajñā), as previously explained.
If one cultivates the mind (citta), does one cultivate wisdom? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one cultivates wisdom, does one cultivate the mind? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one is endowed with past morality, is one also endowed with future and present morality of this same category?
Answer:
There are those who have accomplished past morality, but not future or present morality of this kind.
That is to say:
the manifest morality has already ceased but is not lost, while this kind of morality does not manifest before them.
There is that which exists in the future but not in the present; namely,
when the dhyāna-precepts and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts have already ceased but have not been lost, yet these types of precepts do not manifest before one.
There is that which exists in the present but not in the future; namely,
when the manifest precept has already ceased but is not lost, and this category of precept is presently manifest.
There is [possession] of both the future and the present.
That is to say:
when the dhyāna-precepts and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts have already ceased but are not lost, this category of precepts manifests before one.
If one accomplishes future precepts, does that person accomplish past and present precepts of this same category?
Answer: There are cases where one accomplishes future precepts, but not past and present precepts of this same category.
That is to say:
an Arhat born in the formless realm possesses [the outflows] of the past, but not those of the present.
That is to say:
the dhyāna-precepts and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts have already ceased but have not been lost; these types of precepts do not manifest.
They exist and are present, but are not past.
That is to say:
when untainted (anāsrava) morality first manifests,
it includes both the present and the past.
That is to say:
when the dhyāna-precepts and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts have already ceased but are not lost, these types of precepts manifest before one.
If one possesses present precepts, does one also possess past and future precepts of this same type?
Answer:
There is one who possesses present morality, but not past or future morality of this kind.
That is to say:
The initial manifestation of the manifest precepts (vijñapti-śīla) exists in the present and the past, but not in the future.
That is to say:
The precepts previously undertaken have been extinguished but not lost;
this type of precept is present, as well as future, but not past.
That is to say:
The untainted (anāsrava) precept first manifests;
it exists in the present as well as in the past and future.
That is to say:
The dhyāna and untainted (anāsrava) precepts, having already ceased, are not lost; this type of precept manifests before one.

The meaning of "one's own karma" is established in the world. Regarding the ripening [of karma], it is established through falling, knowledge, plotting harm, retaining, abandoning, mental distraction, the outbursts (paryavasthāna), and the Buddha’s teaching.
Writing, arithmetic, calculation, and seals; the training in the worldly arts and crafts;
and the precepts—may this chapter explain these in detail.
What is one’s own karma?
Answer: If karma has already obtained its maturation in the present existence (*vartamānabhava*), and the maturation of that karma has already arisen and is being experienced—
what is the meaning of "one's own karma" (*svakarma*)?
Answer: It has the meaning of attaining its own fruit, its own outflow, and its own maturation.
Furthermore:
The maturation (*vipāka*) summoned by this karma ripens within one's own continuum and not elsewhere;
it nourishes, follows in nourishing, nurtures, follows in nurturing, protects, follows in protecting, evolves, follows in evolving, and benefits, follows in benefiting one's own continuum.
Therefore, it is called "one's own karma" (*svakarma*).
If karma is one's own karma, should this karma be said to be past,
future, or present?
Answer: This karma should be said to be past.
If this karma is one's own karma, is this karma accomplished?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is karma that is one's own karma, yet this karma is not accomplished.
That is to say:

there is karma whose maturation (*vipāka*) in the present existence has already been obtained, and the maturation of that karma has already arisen and is currently being experienced, yet this karma itself has already ceased.
There is also karma that is accomplished, yet this karma is not one's own karma.
That is to say:
there is karma whose maturation has not yet been obtained in the present existence, and there is the maturation of karma that has not yet arisen or been fully experienced; such karma is not lost.
Furthermore, there is karma that is one's own karma, and this karma is also accomplished.
That is to say:
when karma has already obtained the maturation (*vipāka*) of the present existence, and the maturation of that karma has already arisen and is being experienced, this karma is not lost.
There is karma that is not one's own karma; such karma is not accomplished.
That is to say:
there is karma whose fruition has not yet been obtained in the present existence, and the fruition of that karma has not yet arisen and is not currently being experienced;
this karma has already been lost.
There are also four propositions regarding what is not [one's own karma], which should be explained in detail as being the opposite of the preceding.
If an action is one's own karma, must this karma necessarily undergo its maturation?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions.
There is karma that is one's own karma, yet this karma will certainly not result in the experience of its maturation (vipāka).
That is to say:

there is karma whose maturation (vipāka) in this present existence has already been obtained, and the maturation of that karma has already arisen and is being experienced, having reached its final stage.
There is also karma that is certain to undergo maturation, yet this karma is not one's own karma.
That is to say:

there is karma whose maturation has not yet been obtained in the present existence; and there is the maturation of karma that has not yet arisen or been fully experienced, such that this maturation of karma is still unripened.
There is also karma that is one's own karma, which is certain to be experienced as its maturation.
That is to say:

there is karma that has already obtained the maturation (*vipāka*) of the present existence, and there is the maturation of karma that has already arisen and is currently being experienced, yet has not reached its final stage.
There is also karma that is not one's own karma, which will certainly not undergo maturation.
That is to say:

there is karma whose maturation has not yet been obtained in the present existence, and there is the maturation of karma that has not yet arisen as a direct experience; this refers to the maturation of such karma having already ripened.
There are also four permutations regarding this, which are the opposite of the previous case, and should be explained in detail.
If karma is accomplished, will this karma necessarily undergo its maturation?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is karma that is accomplished such that this karma will certainly not undergo its maturation (vipāka).
That is to say:
when past unwholesome or wholesome-with-outflows karma has already matured its maturation, this karma is not lost.
If there is karma that is future, unwholesome, or wholesome with outflows (*sāsrava*) which has already been acquired but is certain not to arise;
or if there is karma that is neutral (*avyākṛta*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*) which is possessed (*samanvāgata*);
or if there is karma that is certain to undergo maturation (*vipāka*) but is not currently possessed—[these are cases where possession is absent despite the existence of the action].
That is to say:
there are past unwholesome or wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava*) karmas whose maturation has not yet ripened; these karmas have already been lost.
Or, there are future unwholesome or wholesome-with-outflows karmas that have not yet been acquired, yet are certain to arise.
There is karma that is accomplished, such that this karma will certainly undergo its maturation (*vipāka*).
That is to say:
when past unwholesome or wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava*) karma has not yet matured, this karma is not lost.
If karma that is future— whether unwholesome or wholesome with outflows— is already acquired and is also destined to arise;
or if karma that is present— whether unwholesome or wholesome with outflows—
is not yet accomplished, this karma is certain not to undergo its maturation.
That is to say:
past unwholesome or wholesome *sāsrava* (outflowing) karma has already ripened its maturation (*vipāka*),
and this karma has already ceased.
If an action is unwholesome or wholesome with outflows (*sāsrava*) in the future and is not acquired, it will likewise certainly not arise.
If an action is neutral (*avyākṛta*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is not accomplished.
