If one does not possess the eye faculty, one certainly does not possess one of the three time periods, seven of the past and future, and certainly possesses two of the past and future, one of the present, while the remainder are indeterminate.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, female, and male faculties.

If one does not possess the body faculty, one certainly does not possess ten [faculties] across the three periods of time: one from the past and future, five certainly from the past and future, two from the three periods, and one from the present; the remainder are indeterminate.
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), and the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*) are necessarily possessed by all.

If one does not possess the pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*), one certainly does not possess nine faculties across the three time periods: six from the past and future, seven from the past and future [of those nine], one from the present, while the remainder are indeterminate.

If one does not possess the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), one certainly does not possess five faculties of the three time periods; one certainly possesses six of the past and future; one certainly possesses seven of the past and future, one of the present, and the remainder are indeterminate.

If one does not possess the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one certainly does not possess eight faculties across the three time periods: six in the past and future, and certainly possesses seven in the past and future, one in the present; the remainder are indeterminate.

If one does not possess the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), one certainly does not possess one [faculty] of the three times, eight of the past and future, and certainly possesses seven of the past and future, one of the present, while the remainder are indeterminate.

If one does not achieve the faculty of faith, one certainly does not achieve eight [faculties] across the three times—namely, the eight of the past and future; one certainly achieves four of the past and future, two of the three times, and two of the present; the remainder are indeterminate.
The same applies to the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

If one does not possess the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), one certainly does not possess one from the three times—namely, the past, the future, and the present; one certainly possesses two from the past and the future, and one from the present; as for the remainder, it is indeterminate.
The same applies to the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) and the faculty of "fully knowing" (*ājñendriya*).
Regarding those faculties that are wholesome (*kuśala*), are those faculties caused by wholesome roots?
Conversely, if a faculty is caused by wholesome roots, is that faculty wholesome?
Answer: Those faculties that are wholesome have wholesome roots as their cause.
There are, however, faculties that have wholesome roots as their cause, yet those faculties themselves are not wholesome.
That is to say:
the faculties that constitute the maturation produced by wholesome roots.
If those faculties are unwholesome, are those faculties caused by unwholesome roots?
If a faculty has an unwholesome root as its cause, is that faculty unwholesome? Answer:
All faculties that are unwholesome have unwholesome roots as their causes.
There are faculties that have unwholesome roots as their cause, yet those faculties themselves are not unwholesome.
That is to say:

the faculties produced by the maturation (vipāka) induced by unwholesome roots, as well as the faculties associated with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extreme attachment (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) within the desire realm.
If the faculties are indeterminate, are those faculties caused by indeterminate roots?
Conversely, if the faculties are caused by indeterminate roots, are those faculties indeterminate? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There are faculties that are indeterminate, yet those faculties are not causes of indeterminate roots.
That is to say:
There are no indeterminate roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*). There are roots that have indeterminate roots as their cause, yet those roots themselves are not indeterminate.
That is to say:
Regarding the unwholesome roots:
there are roots that are indeterminate, and those roots are also caused by indeterminate roots. Namely:
The indeterminate has the faculty of having an object.
There are faculties that are not indeterminate, and those faculties are also not caused by indeterminate roots.
That is to say:
Regarding the wholesome roots:
Is there any root that is not caused by a wholesome root, not caused by an unwholesome root, and not caused by an indeterminate root, yet that root is not without a cause?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
The faculty that lacks an object-condition (anālambana) has matter (rūpa) and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) as its causes.
This chapter on the analysis of the faculties by way of cause and object-condition is hereby fully explained.
If the various faculties have the past as their cause, do those faculties take the past as their object? Answer:

Those faculties that have the past as their cause may take the past as their object, or they may take the future as their object, or they may take the present as their object, or they may take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object, or they may have no object at all.
Regarding those faculties that have the past as their cause and the past as their condition:
this refers to faculties that are past and have the past as their condition.
Furthermore, regarding faculties that are future or present, which have the past as their cause and the past as their condition;
and those which have the past as their cause and the future as their condition:
this refers to—
The faculties that are past have the future as their object.
Furthermore, those faculties that are future or present have the past as their cause and the future as their object.
Those that have the past as their cause and the present as their object [are as follows].
That is to say:
faculties that are past have present objects;
as well as faculties that are future or present, which have past causes and present objects.
That which has the past as its cause and the unconditioned as its condition refers to:
when the faculties are past, they have the unconditioned as their condition.
Furthermore, when the faculties are future or present, they have the past as their cause and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object.
Regarding those that have the past as their cause but no object:
it refers to—

If there is a faculty that does not have the past as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it has the past as its cause (*hetu*). Now, if a faculty has the past as its object-condition, does that faculty have the past as its cause? Answer:
Regarding those faculties that have the past as their object, those faculties are either conditioned by the past, or conditioned by the future, or conditioned by the present.
As for those faculties that have the past as their object and are conditioned by the past:
That is to say:
when the faculties are past, they have past objects;
and when the faculties are future or present, they have past causes and past objects.
That which has the past as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the future as its cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya) refers to:
when the faculties (indriya) are future, they have the past as their object-condition.
That which has the past as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) but the present as its cause (hetu) refers to:
when the faculties (indriya) are present, they have the past as their object-condition.
Furthermore, when the faculties are future and have the present as their cause, they have the past as their condition.
If all faculties have the future as their cause, do those faculties have the future as their condition? Answer:
Those faculties that have the future as their cause may have the future as their object,
or the past as their object,
or the present as their object.
Some take the unconditioned as their object;
some have no object at all.
As for those faculties that have the future as their cause and the future as their object:
That is to say:
when the faculties are future and take the future as their object;
and when they have the future as their cause and take the past as their object.
That is to say:
when the faculties (indriya) are future and take the past as their object;
and when the causes (hetu) are future and take the present as their object.
That is to say:
when the faculties are future and take the present as their object;
and when the causes are future and take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object.
That is to say:
faculties that are future, taking the unconditioned as their object;
and causes that are future, which have no object.
That is to say:
there are faculties that do not take the future as their object, yet have the future as their cause. Now, if a faculty takes the future as its object, does that faculty have the future as its cause?
Answer: Regarding those faculties that have the future as their object, those faculties are either conditioned by the future or conditioned by the past.
Or, taking the present as the cause,
the faculties take the future as their object; as for those that take the future as the cause,
it means:
Roots that are future have the future as their object.
Those that have the future as their object and have the past as their cause are as follows:
The faculties that are past have the future as their object;
and those faculties that are future or present have the past as their cause and the future as their object.
Those that have the future as their object and the present as their cause are as follows.
That is to say:
faculties that are present have the future as their object;
and faculties that are future, having the present as their cause, have the future as their object.
If the various faculties have the present as their cause, do those faculties take the present as their object? Answer:
If the various faculties have the present as their cause, those faculties may take the present as their object.
Some take the past as their object;
some take the future as their object;
some take the unconditioned as their object.
Or there are those that have no object of perception.
Those faculties that have the present as their cause and take the present as their object are as follows:
Roots that are present have present objects;
and roots that are future have present causes and present objects.
Those that have present causes and past objects:
That is to say:
a faculty that is present has the past as its object;
and a faculty that is future, having the present as its cause, has the past as its object.
Regarding that which has the present as its cause and the future as its condition:
this refers to when the faculties (indriya) are present and take the future as their condition.
And when the faculties are future, they have the present as their cause and the future as their condition.
As for those that have the present as their cause and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their condition,
it refers to:
The faculties that are present take the unconditioned as their object.
Furthermore, those faculties that are future have the present as their cause and the unconditioned as their object.
There are also cases where they have the present as their cause but no object.
That is to say:
if a faculty has no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it has the present as its cause.
Suppose a faculty has the present as its object-condition; does that faculty have the present as its cause?
Answer:
Regarding those faculties that have the present as their object, those faculties are either conditioned by the present, or conditioned by the past, or conditioned by the future.
As for those faculties that have the present as their object and are conditioned by the present:
That is to say:
faculties that are present have present objects;
and faculties that are future, having present causes, have present objects.
That which has the present as its object-condition and the past as its cause refers to:
when the faculties are past, they have the present as their object-condition.
Furthermore, regarding faculties that are future or present, having the past as their cause and the present as their condition;
or those that have the present as their condition and the future as their cause—
this refers to:
The faculties are future, with the present as their object.
If those faculties have the wholesome as their cause, do those faculties have the wholesome as their object? Answer:
Regarding those faculties that have wholesome roots as their cause, those faculties may take wholesome objects, or unwholesome objects, or indeterminate objects, or they may be without an object.
As for those faculties that have wholesome roots as their cause and take wholesome objects:
That is to say:
roots that are wholesome with wholesome objects;
and roots that are indeterminate, but which have wholesome causes and wholesome objects.
That which is wholesome by cause but unwholesome by condition refers to:
roots that are wholesome, yet have unwholesome objects.
Furthermore, regarding roots that are indeterminate (avyākṛta), there are those that have wholesome (kuśala) causes and unwholesome (akuśala) conditions;
and those that have wholesome causes and indeterminate conditions.
That is to say:
Roots that are wholesome with indeterminate objects;
and roots that are indeterminate, which have wholesome causes and indeterminate objects;
and those that have wholesome causes but no objects.
That is to say:

if there is a faculty that does not take the wholesome as its object, is that faculty caused by the wholesome? Furthermore, if a faculty takes the wholesome as its object, is that faculty caused by the wholesome?
Answer: Regarding those faculties that have wholesome objects, those faculties are either conditioned by the wholesome, or conditioned by the unwholesome, or conditioned by the indeterminate.
As for those faculties that have wholesome objects and are conditioned by the wholesome:
That is to say:
faculties that are wholesome with wholesome objects;
and faculties that are indeterminate, but which have wholesome roots as their cause and wholesome objects.
That which has a wholesome object-condition but an unwholesome cause refers to:
when the faculties are unwholesome, they have a wholesome object-condition.
Furthermore, regarding faculties that are indeterminate (avyākṛta), which have unwholesome (akuśala) causes and wholesome (kuśala) conditions;
and those that have wholesome conditions and indeterminate causes: these are as follows:

The faculties that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) take what is wholesome (*kuśala*) as their object. Furthermore, the faculties that are unwholesome (*akuśala*) have what is indeterminate as their cause and take what is wholesome as their object.
Are those faculties which have the unwholesome as their cause also those faculties that take the unwholesome as their object?
Answer: Those faculties that have unwholesome causes may either have unwholesome objects or have wholesome objects.
Some have neutral objects; some have no object.
As for those faculties that have unwholesome roots and take unwholesome things as their objects:
That is to say:
faculties that are unwholesome, conditioned by the unwholesome;
and faculties that are indeterminate, caused by the unwholesome and conditioned by the unwholesome.
That which has an unwholesome cause but a wholesome object refers to:
roots that are unwholesome, yet have wholesome objects.
And when the faculties are indeterminate, they have unwholesome roots as their cause and wholesome states as their object;
or they have unwholesome roots as their cause and indeterminate states as their object.
That is to say:
Roots that are unwholesome have neutral objects;
and roots that are neutral have unwholesome causes and neutral objects.
There are also unwholesome causes that have no objects.
That is to say:

Is there a faculty that does not take the unwholesome as its object, yet has the unwholesome as its cause? Furthermore, if a faculty takes the unwholesome as its object, does that faculty have the unwholesome as its cause?
Answer: Regarding those faculties that have unwholesome objects, those faculties are either conditioned by the unwholesome,
or conditioned by the wholesome, or conditioned by the indeterminate.
Those faculties that have unwholesome objects and have unwholesome causes refer to:
faculties that are unwholesome and have unwholesome objects.
Furthermore, regarding roots that are indeterminate (avyākṛta), which have the unwholesome (akuśala) as their cause and the unwholesome as their object;
and those which have the unwholesome as their object, yet have the wholesome (kuśala) as their cause: these are as follows:
Roots that are wholesome with unwholesome objects;
and roots that are indeterminate, which are wholesome by cause and have unwholesome objects;
and those that have unwholesome objects and are indeterminate by cause.
That is to say:
faculties that are indeterminate (avyākṛta) taking the unwholesome (akuśala) as their object;
and faculties that are unwholesome having the indeterminate as their cause (hetu) and the unwholesome as their object.
If the various faculties have indeterminate causes, do those faculties have indeterminate objects? Answer:
If the various faculties have indeterminate causes, those faculties may have indeterminate objects.
It may have a wholesome object, an unwholesome object,
or no object at all.
Those faculties that have an indeterminate cause and take an indeterminate object refer to:
faculties that are themselves indeterminate and take an indeterminate object.
Furthermore, when the faculties are unwholesome, they have indeterminate causes and indeterminate objects.
As for those that have indeterminate causes and wholesome objects,
it is said:
Roots that are indeterminate (avyākṛta) take wholesome (kuśala) objects;
as do roots that are unwholesome (akuśala) when they have indeterminate causes and take wholesome objects.
Regarding those with indeterminate causes that take unwholesome objects:
That is to say:
faculties that are indeterminate (avyākṛta) taking the unwholesome (akuśala) as their object;
and faculties that are unwholesome having the indeterminate as their cause and the unwholesome as their object.
Regarding "having indeterminate causes and no object of cognition":
this refers to the faculty of non-cognition, which has indeterminate causes.
If a faculty has an indeterminate object, does that faculty have an indeterminate cause?
Answer: Those faculties that have indeterminate objects may have indeterminate causes.
Either conditioned by the wholesome or conditioned by the unwholesome.
Those faculties that have the indeterminate as their object and are themselves conditioned by the indeterminate are as follows:
Roots that are indeterminate have indeterminate objects;
and roots that are unwholesome have indeterminate causes and indeterminate objects.
Those that have indeterminate objects and wholesome causes are as follows.
That is to say:
roots that are wholesome, having indeterminate objects;
and roots that are indeterminate, conditioned by the wholesome, having indeterminate objects.
That which is conditioned by the indeterminate and has the unwholesome as its cause refers to:
roots that are unwholesome and conditioned by the indeterminate.
Furthermore, regarding roots that are indeterminate (avyākṛta) yet have unwholesome (akuśala) causes and are conditioned by the indeterminate:
if various roots have the desire realm (kāmadhātu) as their cause, do those roots take the desire realm as their object (ālambana)? Answer:
Those faculties that have the desire realm as their cause may take the desire realm as their object,
or they may take the form realm as their object,
or they may take the formless realm as their object.
Some have as their object that which is unbound; some have no object at all.
As for those faculties that have the desire realm as their cause and have the desire realm as their object:
That is to say:
those faculties that belong to the desire realm and have the desire realm as their object;
and those that have the desire realm as their cause and the form realm as their object.
That is to say:
those whose faculties belong to the desire realm and take the form realm as their object;
and those whose causes belong to the desire realm and take the formless realm as their object.
That is to say:
when the faculties belong to the desire realm and take the formless realm as their object;
or when they have the desire realm as their cause and take that which is unconditioned (unbound) as their object.
That is to say:
faculties belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) that take what is unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta) as their object; and those belonging to the desire realm that have no object at all.
That is to say:

there are faculties that do not take the desire realm as their object, yet have the desire realm as their cause. If a faculty takes the desire realm as its object, does that faculty have the desire realm as its cause?
Answer: Those faculties that have the desire realm as their object may, as their cause,
be either the desire realm or the form realm.
Or, due to being unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*),
there are faculties that have the desire realm as their object and are conditioned by the desire realm.
That is to say:
The faculties belong to the desire realm and take the desire realm as their object.
Those that take the desire realm as their object but have the form realm as their cause are as follows:
The faculties belong to the form realm, while their objects belong to the desire realm.
Regarding those whose objects belong to the desire realm but whose causes are unconditioned (unbound):
that is to say:
If the faculties are not bound [to any realm] and take the desire realm as their object,
and those faculties have the form realm as their cause, do those faculties take the form realm as their object? Answer:
Regarding those faculties that have the form realm as their cause, those faculties may take the form realm as their object,
or they may take the desire realm as their object,
or they may take the formless realm as their object.
Some have as their object that which is unconditioned; some have no object at all.
As for those faculties that have the form realm as their cause and have the form realm as their object:
That is to say:
those whose faculties belong to the form realm (rūpadhātu) and take the form realm as their object;
and those whose causes belong to the form realm but take the desire realm (kāmadhātu) as their object.
That is to say:
those whose faculties belong to the form realm (rūpadhātu) take the desire realm (kāmadhātu) as their object;
and those whose causes belong to the form realm take the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) as their object.
That is to say:

when the faculties belong to the form realm (rūpadhātu) and take the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) as their object; and when they have the form realm as their cause and take that which is unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta) as their object.
That is to say:
the faculties belonging to the form realm have as their object that which is unconditioned;
those belonging to the form realm that lack an object have no object.
That is to say:

there are faculties that do not take the form realm as their object, yet have the form realm as their cause. Now, if a faculty takes the form realm as its object, does that faculty have the form realm as its cause?
Answer: Regarding those faculties that have the form realm as their object, those faculties are either conditioned by the form realm or conditioned by the desire realm.

That is to say:
the faculties belong to the form realm and take the form realm as their object;
those that take the form realm as their object but have the desire realm as their cause.
That is to say:
the faculties belong to the desire realm while having the form realm as their object;
those that have the form realm as their object while having the formless realm as their cause.
That is to say:
the faculties belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) take the form realm (rūpadhātu) as their object;
those that take the form realm as their object have non-tied factors (apratisaṃyukta) as their cause.
That is to say:
there are faculties not bound [to any realm] that take the form realm as their object.
Are those faculties which have the formless realm as their cause also those that take the formless realm as their object?
Answer: Those faculties that have the formless realm as their cause may either take the formless realm as their object,
or they may take the form realm as their object.
Some have as their object that which is unconditioned; some have no object at all.
As for those faculties that have the formless realm as their cause and take the formless realm as their object:
That is to say:
faculties belonging to the formless realm that take the formless realm as their object;
and those belonging to the formless realm that take the form realm as their object.
That is to say:
faculties belonging to the formless realm that take the form realm as their object;
and those belonging to the formless realm that take what is unconditioned (unbound) as their object.
That is to say:
faculties belonging to the formless realm that take what is non-bound as their object;
and those belonging to the formless realm that have no object.
That is to say:

there are faculties that do not have the form realm as their object, yet have the formless realm as their cause. If a faculty has the formless realm as its object, does that faculty have the formless realm as its cause?
Answer: Regarding those faculties that have the formless realm as their object, those faculties are either conditioned by the formless realm or conditioned by the desire realm.
Or [faculties] conditioned by the form realm,
or conditioned by that which is unconditioned (unbound).
Regarding those faculties that have the formless realm as their object and are conditioned by the formless realm:
That is to say:
the faculties belonging to the formless realm take the formless realm as their object;
those that take the formless realm as their object but have the desire realm as their cause.
That is to say:
the faculties belong to the desire realm while having the formless realm as their object;
and those that have the formless realm as their object while having the form realm as their cause.
That is to say:
the faculties belonging to the form realm take the formless realm as their object;
those taking the formless realm as their object have non-tied [factors] as their cause.
That is to say:
when the faculties are not bound [to any realm] and take the formless realm as their object—
do those faculties that have the state of training (*śaikṣa*) as their cause also take the state of training as their object?
Answer: Those faculties that have the state of training (śaikṣa) as their cause may have either the state of training or the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) as their object-condition (ālambana).
Or [there are those] conditioned by that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Those faculties that have learner-status as their cause and are conditioned by learner-status are as follows:

Roots that are training (śaikṣa) have as their object (ālambana) what is training. Furthermore, roots that are beyond training (aśaikṣa) have as their cause (hetu) what is training and have as their object what is training. [There are also roots] that have as their cause what is training and have as their object what is beyond training.
That is to say:

faculties that are *śaikṣa* (in training) and have as their object (*ālambana*) the *aśaikṣa* (beyond training); and faculties that are *aśaikṣa* and, having as their cause (*hetu*) the *śaikṣa*, have as their object the *aśaikṣa*.
With the state of training as the cause, the state that is neither training nor beyond training is the condition.
That is to say:
the faculties of one in training have as their condition the state that is neither training nor beyond training.

Furthermore, when the faculties are of the state beyond training (aśaikṣa), they have as their cause those of the state of training (śaikṣa) and as their object those that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
If a faculty has as its object that which is of the state of training, does that faculty have as its cause that which is of the state of training? Answer:
Regarding those faculties that have the state of training (*śaikṣa*) as their object, those faculties are either conditioned by the state of training,
or conditioned by the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or conditioned by that which is neither the state of training nor the state beyond training.
Those faculties that have the trainee as their object and have the trainee as their cause refer to:
faculties that are of the trainee and have the trainee as their object.

Furthermore, regarding the faculties that are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they have as their cause those that are in training (*śaikṣa*) and take as their object those that are in training. Those that take as their object those that are in training and have as their cause those that are beyond training are as follows:

The faculty that is beyond training (aśaikṣa) has as its object that which is in training (śaikṣa). That which has as its object that which is in training has as its cause that which is neither in training nor beyond training.
That is to say:
If the faculties are neither-learner-nor-non-learner and take the learner as their object:
Are those faculties which have the non-learner as their cause also taking the non-learner as their object? Answer:
Regarding those faculties that have the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as their cause, those faculties may take as their object the state beyond training,
or they may take as their object the state of training (*śaikṣa*), or they may take as their object that which is neither training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Those faculties that have the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) as their cause and have the state beyond training as their object:
namely, faculties that are beyond training and have the state beyond training as their object.
That which has the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as its cause and the state in training (*śaikṣa*) as its object refers to:
faculties that are beyond training.

Conditioned by the state of training (śaikṣa), that which has as its cause the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) and as its condition that which is neither training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa) is as follows:

If a faculty is without-learning (aśaikṣa) and takes as its object that which is neither-learning-nor-without-learning (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), does that faculty have as its cause that which is without-learning? Answer:
Regarding those faculties that have the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as their object, those faculties are either conditioned by the state beyond training,
or conditioned by the state of training (*śaikṣa*), or conditioned by that which is neither training nor beyond training.
Those faculties that have the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) as their object and are caused by the state beyond training are:
namely, faculties that are themselves beyond training and have the state beyond training as their object.

That which has the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but has the state in training (*śaikṣa*) as its cause (*hetu*). That is to say: the faculties (*indriya*) of one in training have the state beyond training as their object-condition.
Furthermore, when the faculties are of the aśaikṣa (beyond training) type, they have the śaikṣa (in training) as their cause and the aśaikṣa as their object.
When they have the aśaikṣa as their object, they have that which is neither-śaikṣa-nor-aśaikṣa as their cause.
That is to say:
If the faculties are neither-learner-nor-non-learner and have non-learner objects,
do those faculties, which have as their cause faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, have as their object faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer:
Those faculties that have as their cause neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee states may take as their object either neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee states or trainee states.
Either they take the state beyond training as their object, or they have no object at all.
These faculties have as their cause that which is neither-training-nor-beyond-training, and take as their object that which is neither-training-nor-beyond-training.
That is to say:
faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner take as their object that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner take as their cause that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, and take as their object that which is a learner.
That is to say:
when the faculties are neither-learner-nor-non-learner and take what is learner as their object;
and when they have what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner as their cause and take what is non-learner as their object.
That is to say:
faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, which take the non-learner as their object;
and those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, which have no object.
That is to say:

there are faculties that do not take as their object (ālambana) what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, yet have as their cause (hetu) what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner. Now, if a faculty takes as its object what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, does that faculty have as its cause what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

Answer: Regarding those faculties that have as their object that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, those faculties are either conditioned by that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, or they are conditioned by that which is learner.

Or, [there are cases] where, due to the faculties of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they have as their object that which is neither-learner-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), and have as their cause that which is neither-learner-nor-beyond-training.
That is to say:
The faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner take as their object that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
while having as their cause that which is learner.
That is to say:

When the faculties are "in training" (*śaikṣa*), they have as their object that which is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). Furthermore, when the faculties are "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) and have as their cause those that are "in training," they have as their object that which is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training.
This refers to those that have as their object that which is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training and have as their cause those that are beyond training.
That is to say:
the faculties that are beyond training (aśaikṣa) take as their object that which is neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Regarding those faculties that have as their cause that which is to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya), do those faculties take as their object that which is to be abandoned by insight?

Answer: Those faculties that have as their cause what is abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya) may have as their object either what is abandoned by seeing or what is abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Some have non-abandonment as their object;
some have no object at all.
As for those faculties that have abandonment through seeing as their cause and abandonment through seeing as their object:
That is to say:

those faculties that are abandoned by insight (darśana-heya), having as their object that which is abandoned by insight; and those that are abandoned by insight, having as their object that which is abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
That is to say:
faculties that are abandoned by seeing have objects that are abandoned by cultivation;
and faculties that are abandoned by cultivation have causes that are abandoned by seeing and objects that are abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding that which is abandoned through seeing as its cause, but not abandoned through seeing as its object:
this refers to those faculties that are abandoned through seeing as their cause, but are not abandoned through seeing as their object.
Regarding "those abandoned by insight that have no object":
this refers to the faculties that lack an object, which are abandoned by insight.
If a faculty has as its object that which is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), is that faculty caused by what is abandoned by seeing?
Answer: Those faculties that have as their object what is abandoned by seeing, those faculties are either caused by what is abandoned by seeing or [caused by other factors].
Or [the faculties] may have cultivation as their cause of abandonment, or non-abandonment as their cause.
Regarding those faculties that have vision as their object-condition and have vision as their cause of abandonment:
That is to say:

those faculties that are abandoned by seeing, which take as their object what is abandoned by seeing, and which, while taking as their object what is abandoned by seeing, have as their cause what is abandoned by cultivation.
That is to say:

when a faculty is abandoned through cultivation, it takes as its object that which is abandoned through seeing; and when it takes as its object that which is abandoned through seeing, it has as its cause that which is not abandoned.
That is to say:
there are faculties whose roots are not abandoned through seeing, yet which have objects abandoned through seeing.
Are those faculties whose roots are caused by what is abandoned through cultivation also such that their objects are abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: Those faculties whose causes are to be abandoned by cultivation may have objects that are to be abandoned by cultivation,
or they may have objects that are to be abandoned by vision.
Some have non-abandonment as their object;
some have no object at all.
As for those faculties that have cultivation-abandonment as their cause and cultivation-abandonment as their object:
That is to say:

those whose faculties are to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) and take as their object that which is to be abandoned through cultivation; and those whose causes are to be abandoned through cultivation and take as their object that which is to be abandoned through vision (darśana-heya).
That is to say:
those roots abandoned through cultivation that take as their object what is abandoned through seeing; and those [roots] abandoned through cultivation that take as their object what is not abandoned.
That is to say:

those factors whose faculties (*indriya*) are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), but which take as their object that which is not to be abandoned (*aheya*); and those factors whose causes (*hetu*) are to be abandoned through cultivation, yet have no object (*anālambana*).
That is to say:

there are faculties that have no object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya). If a faculty has an object-condition that is to be abandoned by cultivation, does that faculty have a cause that is to be abandoned by cultivation?
Answer: Regarding those faculties that have objects of cultivation for their abandonment, those faculties are either abandoned through cultivation or abandoned through vision.
Or, due to non-abandonment:
those factors whose sense-faculties have cultivation as their object and which have cultivation as their cause are as follows:
[namely:]...

Those whose roots are to be abandoned by cultivation take as their object that which is to be abandoned by cultivation. Those whose objects are to be abandoned by cultivation but whose causes are to be abandoned by insight are as follows:
Roots abandoned by seeing have objects abandoned by cultivation;
and roots abandoned by cultivation have causes abandoned by seeing and objects abandoned by cultivation.
There are also those with objects abandoned by cultivation that have causes not to be abandoned.
That is to say:
there are faculties whose causes are not abandoned, but whose objects are abandoned through cultivation.
Are those faculties whose causes are not abandoned also such that their objects are not abandoned?
Answer: Those faculties whose causes are not abandoned may have objects that are either not abandoned or abandoned through vision.

Or those that take as their object what is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), while having faculties that are not to be abandoned (*aheya*) as their cause and taking what is not to be abandoned as their object.
That is to say:
The roots are not severed, and the conditions are not severed.
As for that which is not severed by cause but is severed by the vision of conditions,
it refers to:

Those whose roots are not to be abandoned by insight, but whose objects are to be abandoned by insight; and those whose causes are not to be abandoned by insight, but whose objects are to be abandoned by cultivation.
That is to say:

If a faculty is not abandoned by means of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), it is abandoned by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Now, if a faculty has as its object that which is not abandoned by means of the path of seeing, is that faculty caused by that which is not abandoned by means of the path of seeing? Answer:

Regarding those faculties whose objects are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*), those faculties are either caused by what is not to be abandoned, or caused by what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), or caused by what is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
As for those faculties whose objects are not to be abandoned and which are caused by what is not to be abandoned:
That is to say:
when the faculties are not severed, the conditions are not severed;
and when the conditions are not severed, they are severed by means of vision.
That is to say:
a faculty that is abandoned through seeing has as its object that which is not abandoned;
and that which has as its object that which is not abandoned is abandoned through cultivation.
That is to say:

there are faculties that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and take as their object that which is not abandoned (*aheya*). If various faculties have as their cause that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), do those faculties take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering?

Answer: Those faculties whose cause is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) may have as their object that which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, or they may have as their object that which is to be abandoned through the vision of origination (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya).

Some take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation; some take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of the path; and some take as their object that which is abandoned through cultivation.
Some have non-abandonment as their object; some have no object.
As for those faculties that have as their cause what is abandoned through the vision of suffering, and have as their object what is abandoned through the vision of suffering:
That is to say:

faculties that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) and have as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering; and faculties that are abandoned through the vision of origination (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), are caused by that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering, and have as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering.

That which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) while having as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) refers to:
faculties (*indriya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering that take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of origination.

Furthermore, those [factors] whose roots are abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), which have as their cause those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and which have as their object those abandoned through the vision of origination; and those which have as their cause those abandoned through the vision of suffering, and which have as their object those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
That is to say:

Roots abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) that take as their object (*ālambana*) what is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*); and roots abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) or the vision of cessation that have as their cause (*hetu*) what is abandoned through the vision of suffering and take as their object what is abandoned through the vision of cessation;
and those that have as their cause what is abandoned through the vision of suffering and take as their object what is abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
That is to say:

faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) that take as their object what is abandoned through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya); and faculties abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) or the vision of the path, which have as their cause what is abandoned through the vision of suffering and take as their object what is abandoned through the vision of the path.
Those abandoned through the vision of suffering as their cause, but having the path of cultivation as their object:
this refers to faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering that take as their object that which is abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, regarding those faculties that are abandoned through the vision of the origin and through cultivation, which have as their cause those things abandoned through the vision of suffering, and take as their object those things abandoned through cultivation;
and those that have as their cause those things abandoned through the vision of suffering, and take as their object those things not to be abandoned: these are as follows:
The faculties are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path.

They have as their cause that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering, while they do not have as their object that which is not abandoned. There are also those whose causes are abandoned through the vision of suffering, yet which have no objects.
That is to say:

there are faculties that do not take [the truths] as objects, yet have their origination caused by what is abandoned through the vision of suffering. If a faculty takes what is abandoned through the vision of suffering as its object, does that faculty have its origination caused by what is abandoned through the vision of suffering?

Answer: Regarding those faculties that have as their object what is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), those faculties are either abandoned through the vision of suffering or abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Whether through being abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) or not abandoned,
those faculties that have as their object what is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) and are themselves abandoned by the vision of suffering: [these are the case].
That is to say:
faculties abandoned by seeing suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) which take as their object those abandoned by seeing suffering;
and faculties abandoned by seeing origination (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) which have as their cause those abandoned by seeing suffering and take as their object those abandoned by seeing suffering.

That which has its object of perception (*ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), yet has its cause (*hetu*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), refers to: faculties (*indriya*) that are abandoned through the vision of the origin, which have as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering.

Furthermore, regarding those faculties that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), have as their cause [factors] abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), and have as their object [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering; and those that have as their object [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering, yet have as their cause [factors] abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*):
these refer to—
Those factors abandoned through cultivation that take as their object those factors abandoned through seeing suffering,
yet have as their cause those factors not to be abandoned:
this refers to—
The faculty is not abandoned by means of the path; it is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
As it is with abandonment through the vision of suffering, so too is it with abandonment through the vision of the origin.

If the various faculties have as their cause that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), do those faculties have as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation? Answer:
Those faculties that have as their cause that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation, those faculties may have as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Some take what is to be abandoned by cultivation as their object; some take what is not to be abandoned as their object;
and some have no object at all.

Those faculties that have as their cause what is abandoned through the vision of cessation, and for which what is abandoned through the vision of cessation is the object-condition: this refers to those faculties that are themselves abandoned through the vision of cessation, and for which what is abandoned through the vision of cessation serves as the object-condition.
Regarding those whose causes are abandoned through the vision of cessation and whose conditions are abandoned through cultivation:

this refers to faculties that are abandoned through cultivation, which have as their cause factors abandoned through the vision of cessation and as their condition factors abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding "those abandoned through the vision of cessation, but whose objects are not abandoned":
this refers to faculties that are abandoned through the vision of cessation, yet have objects that are not abandoned.
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] that have no object:
this refers to the faculties that lack an object, which are abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering].
If a faculty has cessation through seeing (*darśana-heya*) as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), is that faculty caused by cessation through seeing? Answer:
Those faculties that have cessation through seeing as their object-condition may, in some cases, be caused by cessation through seeing.
Either abandoned through the vision of suffering,
or abandoned through the vision of the origin,
or abandoned through cultivation.

Or, [there are those] that are not abandoned by means of non-abandonment. Regarding those whose faculties have as their object what is abandoned through the vision of cessation and are themselves abandoned through the vision of cessation:
this refers to—

Those whose roots are abandoned through the vision of cessation and which take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation; and those which take as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation and have as their cause that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
That is to say:

Roots abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) have as their object (*ālambana*) that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*). Furthermore, roots abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) or the vision of cessation have as their cause (*hetu*) that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering and as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation.
[And there are those] that have as their object that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation and as their cause that which is abandoned through the vision of origin.
That is to say:

faculties abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) that take as their object what is abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya); and faculties abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) or abandoned by the vision of cessation, which have as their cause what is abandoned by the vision of the origin and take as their object what is abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Regarding those things that have cessation through seeing as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but have cultivation as their cause (*hetu*):
this refers to faculties that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which take cessation through seeing as their object-condition.
That which is conditioned by what is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, yet has as its cause that which is not to be abandoned,
refers to:
faculties that are not to be abandoned, which are conditioned by what is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
As it is with those abandoned by the vision of cessation, so it is with those abandoned by the vision of the path.

If the various faculties have as their cause that which is abandoned by the vision of suffering, do those faculties have as their object that which is abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering?

Answer: Those faculties whose cause is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) have as their object either the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya),
or the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-prahātavya).
Either it has as its object that which is abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of origination, or it has as its object that which is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origination,
or it has as its object that which is abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of cessation.
Either it takes the cessation of the subsequent knowledge of cessation as its object,
or it takes the path of the dharma-knowledge of the path as its object,
or it takes the path of the subsequent knowledge of the path as its object.
Either they take what is abandoned by cultivation as their object, or they take what is not abandoned as their object,
or they have no object at all.

Regarding those faculties whose cause is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and which are abandoned through the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*):
this refers to faculties that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and which have as their object that which is abandoned through the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering.

Furthermore, regarding those [factors] whose roots are abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), which have as their cause that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and which are abandoned through the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*);

and those which have as their cause that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering, and which are abandoned through the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*): these are as follows:

Roots abandoned through seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), which have as their object the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-prahātavya*); and roots abandoned through seeing origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), which have as their cause those abandoned through seeing suffering and as their object the subsequent knowledge of suffering;
and those which have as their cause those abandoned through seeing suffering and as their object the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*).
That is to say:

faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), which have as their object the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (samudaya-dharmajñāna-prahātavya); and faculties abandoned through the vision of origination, which have as their cause those abandoned through the vision of suffering and have as their object the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination.
Those abandoned through the vision of suffering as their cause, but abandoned through the subsequent knowledge of origination as their object,
refers to:
faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering as their cause, which have the subsequent knowledge of origination as their object and are thus abandoned.

Furthermore, regarding those [factors] whose roots are abandoned by the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), which have as their cause that which is abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and which are abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*); and those which have as their cause that which is abandoned by the vision of suffering, and which are abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*): namely, [The following factors: The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) associated with the mind; the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of mental satisfaction (*saumanasyendriya*) associated with the third dhyāna; the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) associated with the desire realm; the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) when they are associated with the aforementioned minds; the faculty of life (*jīvitendriya*) associated with the aforementioned minds; and the aggregates, elements, and bases associated with the aforementioned minds. These are the factors whose roots are abandoned by the vision of origination, which have as their cause that which is abandoned by the vision of suffering, and which are abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origination; and those which have as their cause that which is abandoned by the vision of suffering, and which are abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of cessation. They are as follows: [the list continues].
Roots abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), which have as their object the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna-prahātavya*);

and roots abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*) and the vision of cessation, which have as their cause the abandonment through the vision of suffering and as their object the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation.
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering as their cause, but abandoned through the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) as their object:
this refers to faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering that take as their object that which is abandoned through the subsequent knowledge of cessation.

Furthermore, regarding those [defilements] abandoned by the vision of origin and abandoned by the vision of cessation, which have as their cause those abandoned by the vision of suffering, and have as their object those abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation;
and those which have as their cause those abandoned by the vision of suffering, and have as their object those abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of the path.
That is to say:
faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) that take as their object the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (mārga-dharmajñāna-prahātavya);

and faculties abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) or the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya), which have as their cause those abandoned through the vision of suffering and take as their object the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path.
Those abandoned through the vision of suffering, which have the subsequent knowledge of the path as their object:
this refers to faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering that take the subsequent knowledge of the path as their object.

Furthermore, those [factors] abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) and abandoned through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya), which have as their cause those abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), and which are conditioned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna-prahātavya); and those which have as their cause those abandoned through the vision of suffering, and are conditioned by those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
That is to say:

faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) that take as their object those things abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya); and faculties abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) or abandoned through cultivation, which have as their cause those things abandoned through the vision of suffering and take as their object those things abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding those [factors] that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) as their cause,

while not being abandoned through the vision [of the truths] as their object (*ālambana*): this refers to faculties (*indriya*) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*), which have as their cause factors abandoned through the vision of suffering, while not having as their object factors abandoned through the vision [of the truths].
Those abandoned through the vision of suffering that have no object refer to the root-factors (mūla) without objects,
which are abandoned through the vision of suffering.

If a faculty has suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*) as its object, does that faculty have seeing-suffering-abandonment (*darśana-duḥkha-prahātavya*) as its cause? Answer:
Those faculties that have suffering-dharma-knowledge-abandonment as their object, those faculties may have seeing-suffering-abandonment as their cause.
Some are abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering], some are abandoned through cultivation,
and some are not abandoned.

Regarding those faculties that have the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) as their object-condition and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*):
this refers to faculties that are themselves abandoned through the vision of suffering and have the dharma-knowledge of suffering as their object-condition.

Furthermore, regarding those [factors] that are abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), have as their cause those abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and have as their object the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna-prahātavya*): those that have as their object the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering and have as their cause those abandoned by the vision of the origin are as follows: [The factors] which have as their object the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering and have as their cause those abandoned by the vision of the origin are: namely—

Roots abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) which have as their object the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna-prahātavya); and roots abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) which have as their cause those abandoned by the vision of the origin and have as their object the dharma-knowledge of suffering;
and those which have as their object the dharma-knowledge of suffering and have as their cause those abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
That is to say:

when the faculties are to be abandoned by cultivation, they take as their object that which is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering; yet, while taking as their object that which is to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering, they have as their cause that which is not to be abandoned.
That is to say:

there are faculties that are not abandoned [by the path], yet have as their object the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*). Are those faculties which have as their cause what is abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) also such that they have as their object what is abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-prahātavya*)?

Answer: Those faculties whose cause is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering may have as their object that which is to be abandoned through the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*), or they may have as their object that which is to be abandoned through the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*).
Either it is abandoned by means of the dharma-knowledge of origin,
or it is abandoned by means of the subsequent knowledge of origin,
or it is abandoned by means of the dharma-knowledge of cessation.
Either it takes as its object the abandonment through the subsequent knowledge of cessation, or it takes as its object the abandonment through the dharma-knowledge of the path,
or it takes as its object the abandonment through the subsequent knowledge of the path.
Some take what is abandoned through cultivation as their object; some take what is not abandoned as their object;
and some have no object at all.

Those faculties that have as their cause the abandonment through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), yet have as their object the abandonment through the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-prahātavya*),
are: namely,
faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering which take as their object the abandonment through the subsequent knowledge of suffering.

Furthermore, regarding those [factors] that are abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), have as their cause those abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and have as their object the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-prahātavya*); and those that have as their cause those abandoned by the vision of suffering, and have as their object the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-prahātavya*): namely, [The following factors: The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and so forth, which are associated with the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and are abandoned by the vision of the origin; the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) and so forth, which are associated with the view of self-existence and are abandoned by the vision of the origin; the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) and so forth, which are associated with the view of self-existence and are abandoned by the vision of the origin;
