It serves as the equal-immediate, object, and dominant condition for the pure [states] of the two higher formless realms.
It serves as the object and dominant condition for all untainted states of every stage, as well as the pure states of the six lower stages.
With respect to others, it serves as a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

As for the pure state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*śuddha-naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), with respect to the pure state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and so forth, how many conditions does it serve?
Answer: It acts as the cause, the equal-and-immediate condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition for the pure [states] of its own level.

It acts as the equal-and-immediate condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition for the pure and untainted [states] of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and the Sphere of Nothingness, as well as for those associated with the "taste" (āsvādana) of its own level.
It serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) states of the five lower stages.
For all others, it serves as only the dominant condition.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle Seventeen.
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Fascicle Eighteen.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
Inclusion, obtainability, association, accomplishment, non-obtainability, relinquishment, retrogression,
sudden and gradual cessation, and dependence on meditative concentration— may this chapter fully explain these ten perceptions.
That is to say:
the perception of impermanence, and the perception of suffering in what is impermanent.
The perception of suffering, the perception of non-self,
the perception of death,
and the perception of impurity.
The perception of repulsiveness in food;
the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in; and the perception of cessation.
The perception of detachment,
the perception of cessation,
and the four dhyānas.
The four immeasurables,
the four formless attainments,
and the eight liberations.
The eight bases of mastery,
the ten totalities,
and the eight knowledges.
Regarding the three samādhis:
how many dhyānas and so forth are subsumed within the perception of impermanence and the others? Answer:
The perception of impermanence encompasses the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the four liberations.
As it is with the perception of impermanence,

so it is with the perception of impermanence as suffering, the perception of suffering as non-self, the perception of death, the perception of abandonment, the perception of detachment, and the perception of cessation.
The perception of impurity (aśubha-saṃjñā) subsumes the third and fourth dhyānas and the first two liberations (vimokṣa).
As it is with the perception of impurity,
so it is with the perception of revulsion toward food (āhāre pratikūla-saṃjñā).
The perception of the lack of delight in all worlds subsumes the third and fourth dhyānas.
As for the first dhyāna and so forth, how many dhyānas and so forth do they subsume?
Answer:
The first dhyāna comprises the first dhyāna, the four immeasurables, the first two liberations, the first four bases of mastery, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.
The second dhyāna comprises the second dhyāna, the four immeasurables, the first two liberations, the first four bases of mastery, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.
The third dhyāna comprises the third dhyāna, the three immeasurables, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.

The fourth dhyāna comprises the fourth dhyāna, the three immeasurables, the pure liberation, the latter four bases of mastery, the first eight totalities, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.
How many immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are subsumed within the immeasurable of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and so forth? Answer:
Loving-kindness subsumes the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) of loving-kindness, and so on, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*), which subsumes the conventional knowledge of equanimity.
How many formless states (*ārūpya*) and so forth are subsumed by the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the others? Answer:

The Sphere of Infinite Space subsumes the Sphere of Infinite Space itself, as well as its corresponding liberation (*vimokṣa*), its corresponding totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), six types of knowledge (*jñāna*), and three meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
The sphere of infinite consciousness includes the sphere of infinite consciousness, its corresponding liberation, its corresponding totality, six types of knowledge, and three meditative absorptions.
The sphere of nothingness includes the sphere of nothingness, its corresponding liberation, six types of knowledge, and three meditative absorptions.

The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception includes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself, its corresponding liberation, the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling, and conventional knowledge.
Regarding the first liberations and so forth, how many liberations and so forth do they encompass? Answer:
The first, second, and third liberations encompass the first, second, and third liberations, as well as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The liberation of the sphere of infinite space includes the liberation of the sphere of infinite space, its corresponding totality (kṛtsnāyatana), six knowledges, and three samādhis.
The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness includes the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, its corresponding totality, six knowledges, and three samādhis.
The liberation of the sphere of nothingness includes the liberation of the sphere of nothingness, six knowledges, and three samādhis.
The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception includes the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and conventional knowledge.
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling includes the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling.
Regarding the first base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth, how many bases of mastery and so forth do they include? Answer:

The first *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery) subsumes the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the first *abhibhvāyatana*, and so on, up to the eighth *abhibhvāyatana*, which subsumes the conventional knowledge of the eighth *abhibhvāyatana*.
As for the first *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality sphere) and so forth, how many *kṛtsnāyatana*s and so forth do they subsume?
Answer:

The first universal base (kṛtsnāyatana) includes the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) of the first universal base, and so on, up to the tenth universal base, which includes the conventional knowledge of the tenth universal base.
How many knowledges (*jñāna*), etc., are subsumed within the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), etc.? Answer:
The knowledge of phenomena subsumes the knowledge of phenomena and a portion of five other knowledges.
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) comprises subsequent knowledge and a portion of five knowledges.
Knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) comprises knowledge of others' minds and a portion of four knowledges.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) comprises conventional knowledge and a portion of one knowledge.
The knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) subsumes the knowledge of suffering and a portion of two other knowledges.
The knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) subsumes the knowledge of origin and a portion of two other knowledges.
The knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) subsumes the knowledge of cessation and a portion of three knowledges.
Path-knowledge (mārgajñāna) subsumes path-knowledge and a portion of three other knowledges.
Regarding the concentration on emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi) and so forth, how many concentrations do they subsume? Answer:
Emptiness subsumes emptiness; wishlessness subsumes wishlessness; signlessness subsumes signlessness.
As it is with their subsumption, so it is with their obtainability.
With how many dhyānas and so forth are the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*) and the others associated? Answer:
The perception of impermanence is associated with the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the four liberations (*vimokṣa*), the four knowledges (*jñāna*), and one samādhi.
Just as it is with the perception of impermanence,

so it is with the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of death, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of detachment, and the perception of cessation.
The perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) is associated with the latter two dhyānas, the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Just as with the perception of impurity,
so it is with the perception of revulsion toward food (*āhāre pratikūla-saṃjñā*).
The perception that all worlds are unattractive is associated with the two subsequent dhyānas and with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
With how many dhyānas and so forth is the first dhyāna and the others associated?
Answer:
The first dhyāna is associated with the first dhyāna, the four immeasurables, the first two liberations, the first four bases of mastery, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.
The second dhyāna is associated with the second dhyāna, the four immeasurables, the first two liberations, the first four bases of mastery, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.
The third dhyāna is associated with the third dhyāna, the three immeasurables, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.

The fourth dhyāna is associated with the fourth dhyāna, the three immeasurables, the pure liberation, the latter four bases of mastery, the first eight spheres of totality, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.
With how many immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are the immeasurables such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) associated? Answer:
Loving-kindness is associated with loving-kindness and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and so on, up to equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is associated with equanimity and conventional knowledge.
With how many formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and so forth is the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) associated? Answer:

The sphere of infinite space is associated with the sphere of infinite space itself, its corresponding liberation (*vimokṣa*), its corresponding totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), six knowledges (*jñāna*), and three meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
The sphere of infinite consciousness, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, its corresponding base (kṛtsnāyatana), the six knowledges, and the three samādhis are associated with it.
The sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the liberation of the sphere of nothingness, and those six knowledges are associated with the three samādhis.

The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are associated [with the three samādhis].
With how many liberations, etc., are the first liberation and the others associated? Answer:
The first, second, and third liberations are associated with the first, second, and third liberations, as well as with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

The liberation of the sphere of infinite space, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space itself, and its corresponding universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) are associated with six types of knowledge and three samādhis.

The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, along with the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness and its corresponding totalities, is associated with six knowledges and three samādhis.
The liberation of the sphere of nothingness is associated with the liberation of the sphere of nothingness, six types of knowledge, and three samādhis.

The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is associated with the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling is not associated [with mental factors].
With how many masteries (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth are the first mastery and the others associated? Answer:

The first sphere of mastery is associated with the conventional knowledge of the first sphere of mastery, and so on, up to the eighth sphere of mastery, which is associated with the conventional knowledge of the eighth sphere of mastery.
With how many universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), etc., are the first universal base, etc., associated? Answer:

The first universal base is associated with the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the first universal base; likewise, up to the tenth universal base, it is associated with the conventional knowledge of the tenth universal base.
With how many samādhis are the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and the others associated? Answer:
Dharma-knowledge is associated with three samādhis to a small degree.
As it is with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), so it is with subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
Knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is associated with a small portion of one samādhi.
As it is with the knowledge of others' minds,
so it is with the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path.
The knowledge of suffering is partially associated with two or three samādhis.
If one accomplishes the first dhyāna and so forth, how many of the four dhyānas and so forth does that person accomplish,
and how many do they not accomplish? Answer:
If one achieves the first dhyāna, one may possess one, two, three, or all four of the dhyānas.
"One" refers to:
The craving for the Brahma world has not been exhausted.
The second refers to:
the craving for the Brahma world has been exhausted, but the craving for what is above it has not been exhausted.
The third refers to one who has exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara Heaven but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The fourth refers to:
With the exhaustion of craving for the Sphere of Utmost Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*),
there are either none, three, or all four of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
"Non-existent" refers to those born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
"The three" refers to:
They are reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna and Bṛhatphala [heavens].
The fourth refers to those reborn in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, and the Ābhāsvara [heaven].
Regarding the four formless attainments:
there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to:
Attachment to the realm of form is not yet exhausted.
The first refers to:
attachment to the realm of form is exhausted, but attachment to the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
The second refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space, but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The third refers to:
The craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness is exhausted, but the craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted.
The fourth refers to the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of nothingness.
Regarding the eight liberations:
there may be none, or one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or all eight.
"None" refers to:
One who is born in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven] and whose craving for the Śubhakṛtsna has not yet been exhausted.
This refers to one person:
One is born in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven].
There, craving for the Śubhakṛtsna has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
Or, one is born in the Bṛhatphala [heaven], where craving for that very place has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space, craving for that very place has not yet been exhausted.
The second case refers to those born in the Desire Realm, the Brahma World, or the Ābhāsvara Heaven, whose craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala [heavens], craving for the Bṛhatphala has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Ākāśānantyāyatana, craving for that very realm has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, craving for that very sphere is not yet exhausted.

The third case refers to those born in the Desire Realm, the Brahma-world, or the Ābhāsvara Heaven, who have exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven but have not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala [heavens], craving for the Sphere of Infinite Space is exhausted, but craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.

If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space or the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, craving for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness is exhausted, but craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), craving for that very realm has not yet been exhausted.

The fourth case refers to those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*), or the Ābhāsvara heaven, who have exhausted craving for the Bṛhatphala heaven but have not yet exhausted craving for the realms above it.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala [heavens], craving for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness is exhausted, while craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Ākāśānantya, Vijñānānantya, or Ākiṃcanyāyatana [realms], craving for the Ākiṃcanyāyatana is exhausted.
If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), one does not attain the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
The five cases are:

being born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the Brahma-world (brahmaloka), or the Ābhāsvara heaven; having exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), yet not having exhausted craving for the higher realms.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala heavens and has exhausted craving for the Ākiñcanyāyatana, yet has not attained the nirodhasamāpatti;
or if one is born in the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana and has attained the nirodhasamāpatti.

The sixth refers to one who is born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, or the Ābhāsvara heaven; who has exhausted craving for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness but not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms;
or who is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala heavens and has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

The seventh refers to one who is born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, or the Ābhāsvara heaven, has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness, but has not attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
The eighth refers to:
Born in the desire realm, the Brahma world, or the Ābhāsvara heaven, one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Regarding the eight bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), one may possess none, four, or all eight.
"Non-existence" refers to being born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven with craving for that realm not yet exhausted,
or being born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The fourth refers to those born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, the Ābhāsvara heaven, or the Śubhakṛtsna heaven whose craving has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, then that very craving is exhausted.
If one is born in the Bṛhatphala [heaven],
there are eight [factors], namely:
being born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, the Ābhāsvara [heaven], and having exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven].
Regarding the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*):
there may be none, or one, two, eight, nine, or all ten.
"None" refers to:
One who is born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, or the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and whose craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven has not yet been exhausted;
or one who is born in the Ākiñcanyāyatana or the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana.
The first refers to being born in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), where craving for that very state has not yet been exhausted;
or being born in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
The second refers to:
being born in the sphere of infinite space, wherein craving for that very state has been exhausted.
The eighth refers to:

One who is born in the Desire Realm, the Brahma-world, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, or the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, has exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms.
Or, one who is born in the Bṛhatphala Heaven has not yet exhausted craving for that very realm.
The ninth refers to those born in the desire or form realms who have exhausted their craving for the desire and form realms, but whose craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
The tenth refers to:
For one born in the desire realm or the form realm who has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space,
there are two, four, five, six, seven, or eight of the eight knowledges.
The second refers to the stage of the ordinary person’s patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*pṛthagjana-duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
The fourth refers to:
The dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) occurs at the stage of the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*).
The fifth refers to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), occurring at the stage of the dharma-patience regarding origination (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*).
The sixth refers to the stage from the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the dharma-patience regarding cessation.
The seventh refers to:
from the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (nirodha-dharma-jñāna) up to the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of the path (mārga-dharma-kṣānti).
The eighth refers to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna) and the stages above it.
Regarding the three samādhis:
there may be none, or two, or all three. "None" means:
First, all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, those who are noble (*ārya*) but in whom the patience regarding the cessation of phenomena (*nirodhadharmakṣānti*) has not yet arisen.
The third refers to the arising of the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*),
as when one has attained the first dhyāna.
This continues up to the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna; it is likewise according to what is appropriate for each.
There are seven types of individuals (pudgala), namely:
Those who follow by faith,
those who follow by dharma,
and those with liberation through faith.
The one who has attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), the one who has realized through the body (kāyasākṣin), and the one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta).

Regarding those liberated through both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), as well as those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and so forth: among the four dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana*) and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), how many do they possess (*samanvāgata*) and how many do they not possess?
Answer: For one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin),
regarding the four dhyānas associated with relish (āsvādana-samprayukta), there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"Non-existence" refers to the exhaustion of craving for form.
"The one" refers to:
The craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm is exhausted, but the craving for the realms above is not yet exhausted.
"Up to the fourth" refers to the fact that the craving for the Brahma-world has not yet been exhausted.
Regarding the four pure dhyānas:
there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"None" means:
When sensual craving has not yet been exhausted:
the first case refers to when sensual craving is exhausted, but craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
Up to the fourth [level], which refers to the exhaustion of craving for the Sphere of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*).
Regarding the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas:
There may be none, or one, two, three, or four.
"None" refers to entering the state of rightness and separation from birth based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The first refers to:
entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the first dhyāna or the intermediate dhyāna.
Up to the fourth refers to:
Relying on the fourth dhyāna, one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with relish (āsvādana),
there may be one, two, three, or all four.
The first refers to:
the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of nothingness, while craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted.
This continues up to the fourth, which refers to:
If craving for the sphere of infinite space has not been exhausted,
then regarding the four pure formless attainments,
there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"Non-existent" refers to one whose craving for form has not yet been exhausted.
"One" refers to:
The craving for form is exhausted, but the craving for what is above is not yet exhausted.
... Up to the fourth, which refers to the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Regarding the three untainted formless attainments, one does not possess them at all;
as it is with the faith-follower,
so it is also with the Dharma-follower.
For those with faith-based liberation (*śraddhādhimukta*), regarding the four dhyānas associated with relishing (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*): there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"Non-existence" refers to the exhaustion of craving for form.
"The one" refers to:
The craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm is exhausted, but the craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
"Up to the fourth" refers to the fact that the craving for the Brahma-world has not yet been exhausted.
Regarding the four pure dhyānas:
there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to:
If sensual desire has not been exhausted and one is born in the formless realm, there is one [type]: namely, [the fetter of attachment to existence].
Born in the desire realm, one has exhausted craving for the desires but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms.
Or, born in the Brahma-world, one has not yet exhausted craving for that very realm.
Or, born in the Ābhāsvara heaven, one has not yet exhausted craving for that very realm.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven], that craving has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Bṛhatphala [heaven]—these are the two. That is to say:
Born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world, one has exhausted craving for the Brahma-world but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
Or, born in the Ābhāsvara heaven, one has exhausted craving for that very place but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, craving for that very place is exhausted.
The third case refers to:
being born in the desire realm or the Brahma world, where craving for the Ābhāsvara heaven is exhausted, but craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven is exhausted.
The fourth refers to those born in the Desire Realm or the Brahma-world, for whom craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven is exhausted.
Regarding the four untainted dhyānas:
there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to:
Desire and lust have not yet been exhausted.
The first refers to:
desire and lust being exhausted, while higher attachment has not yet been exhausted.
Up to the fourth, which refers to the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of universal purity (*śubhakṛtsna*).
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*):
Or there may be one, two, three, or four.
"One" refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
Up to the fourth [level], namely:
the craving for the sphere of infinite space has not been exhausted.
Regarding the four pure formless attainments:
It may be absent, or it may be one, two, three, or four.
"Absent" refers to those born in the desire realm or the form realm whose craving for form has not yet been exhausted.
The first refers to:
one born in the desire realm or the form realm who has exhausted craving for form but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above;
or one born in the sphere of infinite space whose craving for that very state is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, craving for that very state is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Nothingness, craving for that very state is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception...

The second refers to those born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the sphere of infinite space, who have exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space but have not yet exhausted craving for what is above it;
or those born in the sphere of infinite consciousness, who have exhausted craving for that very sphere but have not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
If one is born in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), craving for that very place is exhausted. The third case refers to those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),

the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), for whom craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) is exhausted, while craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, craving for the Sphere of Nothingness is exhausted.
The four cases are:
being born in the Desire Realm, the Form Realm, or the Sphere of Infinite Space, while craving for the Sphere of Nothingness is exhausted.
Regarding the three untainted formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there may be none, or one, two,
or three. "None" refers to:
Attachment to the realm of form is not yet exhausted.
The first refers to:
attachment to the realm of form is exhausted, but attachment to the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
Up to the third [stage], namely:
the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness;
as with those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta).
The same applies to the "attained-by-seeing" (dṛṣṭiprāpta). As for the "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin):
with respect to the four dhyānas associated with relishing (āsvādana), he does not possess them at all.
Regarding the four pure dhyānas:
there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to:
Those born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are of one kind: namely,
those born in the Fruit of Vastness (Bṛhatphala).
"Up to four" refers to those born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world;
they fully accomplish all four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas.
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with flavor (*sāsrava*):
one is accomplished and three are not.
Regarding the four pure (*anāsrava*) formless attainments:
Either one or four. "One" refers to those born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The fourth refers to those born in the desire realm and the form realm;
they fully possess all three untainted formless attainments.
One liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) does not possess any of the four dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana*).
Regarding the four pure (*śuddha*) dhyānas:
There may be none, or one, two, three, or four.
"None" refers to those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The first refers to being born in the Bṛhatphala heaven;
up to the fourth, which refers to:
Born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
one possesses all four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas.
One does not possess any of the four formless attainments associated with attachment (*āsvādana*).
Regarding the four pure formless attainments:
there may be one, two, three, or all four.
"One" refers to:
Birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
up to the fourth, refers to birth in the desire realm, the form realm, and the sphere of infinite space.
Regarding the three untainted formless attainments, one possesses them all. As for the one liberated through both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*),
one does not possess any of the four meditative absorptions associated with relishing (*āsvādana*).
Regarding the four pure dhyānas:
there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"None" means:
Those born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are of one type: namely,
those born in the Fruit of Vastness (Bṛhatphala).
As for "up to four," this refers to those born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world;
they fully accomplish all four untainted dhyānas.
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with flavor (*sāsrava*), one possesses none of them.
Regarding the four pure (*anāsrava*) formless attainments:
one may possess either one or all four.
The first refers to being born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The fourth refers to:
Those born in the desire realm and the form realm all possess the three untainted (anāsrava) formless attainments.
Is it possible to possess the four dhyānas associated with tasting (āsvādana), yet neither pure (śuddha) nor untainted?
Answer: There is. Namely:
If sensual desire has not been exhausted, is there one who possesses the pure four dhyānas, yet neither those associated with relish nor those that are untainted?
Answer: Yes.
There is. That is to say:
an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world has exhausted their craving for the form realm.
Is there anyone who has accomplished the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas that are neither associated with relish (*āsvādana*) nor pure (*śuddha*)?
Answer: There is.
That is to say:
an noble one born in the formless realm.
Is there anyone who possesses the pure and untainted four dhyānas, yet does not possess those associated with relishing?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
When a noble one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma world, they have exhausted attachment to the form realm.
Is it possible for them to possess any two or three of the remaining [attainments]? Answer:
No. Is there anyone who does not achieve the four dhyānas associated with relishing (*āsvādanā*), yet neither achieves those that are pure (*śuddha*) nor those that are untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: No.
There is. That is to say:
when a noble one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma world, their craving for the form realm is exhausted.
Is there anyone who has not attained the pure four dhyānas, yet neither those associated with attachment (sāsrava) nor those that are untainted (anāsrava)? Answer: No.
Is there anyone who does not achieve the untainted (anāsrava) four dhyānas, yet neither possesses those associated with relish (āsvādanasamprayukta) nor those that are pure (śuddha)? Answer: No.
Is there anyone who has not attained the four dhyānas associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) or the pure (*śuddha*), yet has not failed to attain the untainted (*anāsrava*) ones?
Answer: There is.
That is to say:
when a noble one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Is there anyone who does not possess the four dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), yet does not lack the pure (*śuddha*) ones?
Answer: There is. Namely:
Ordinary beings are born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world and have exhausted their craving for the form realm.
Is there anyone who does not possess the pure and untainted four dhyānas, yet is not dissociated from those associated with relishing?
Answer: There is. Namely:
If sensual desire has not been exhausted,
is it possible for one to be non-possessed of the four dhyānas associated with relishing (*āsvādana*), the pure (*śuddha*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*)? Answer:
There is. That is to say:
ordinary beings born in the formless realm.
Is there anyone who has attained the four formless attainments associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*), yet neither pure (*śuddha*) nor outflow-free (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: There is.
That is to say:
one whose craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is not yet exhausted.
Is it possible to possess the pure (*śuddhaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) without them being associated with relish (*āsvādana*)?
Answer: There is. Namely:
Regarding those born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the sphere of infinite space who are Arhats:
could there be any who possess other [attainments]?
Answer: Yes.

No. Is there anyone who does not accomplish the four formless attainments associated with relishing (*āsvādana*), yet neither accomplishes those that are pure (*śuddha*) nor those that are outflow-free (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: No.
There are. Namely:
Arhats born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the sphere of infinite space.
Is there anyone who has not attained the pure and untainted (anāsrava) four formless attainments, yet is not associated with attachment to the flavor (āsvādana) of them?
Answer: There is.
That is to say:
craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) has not yet been exhausted.
Is it possible that one does not accomplish the remainder?
Answer: No.
Is there any attainment of the four dhyānas associated with relishing (*āsvādanā-samprayukta*) that is neither pure (*śuddha*) nor untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
When one who has exhausted craving for the form realm falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm;
or when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm.
Is there any case where one attains the four dhyānas that are pure (*śuddha*), yet neither associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) nor untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: No.
Is there any attainment of the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas that is neither associated with relish (āsvādanasamprayukta) nor pure (śuddha)?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Entering into the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on the fourth dhyāna,
when one attains the fruit of arhatship,
is there anything else that is attained?
Answer: No.
Is there any case where one relinquishes the four dhyānas associated with relish, yet they are neither pure nor untainted?
Answer: No.
Is there any case where one abandons the pure four dhyānas, yet they are neither associated with relishing nor are they untainted?
Answer: There is. Namely:
When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), having exhausted craving for the *śubhakṛtsna* [heaven], falls away due to the arising of fetters (*paryavasthāna*) belonging to the desire realm;
or when one dies from the desire realm or the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*) and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Is there any case where one abandons the pure (*anāsrava*) and the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) without them being associated with relish (*āsvādana*)?
Answer: There is. Namely:
When a noble one who has exhausted craving for the realm of universal purity (śubhakṛtsna) falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
is there any other [defilement] that is abandoned? Answer:
No. Is there any attainment of the four formless states associated with relish that is neither pure nor outflow-free?
Answer: No.
There is. That is to say,
when an Arhat falls away due to the arising of the fetters (paryavasthāna) of the desire realm or the form realm.
Is there anyone who attains the three formless attainments that are untainted (*anāsrava*), yet neither associated with relish (*āsvādana*) nor pure (*śuddha*)?

That is to say:
at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship,

Answer: No.

Answer: No.

Answer: There is. That is to say:

When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), having exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), falls away due to the arising of fetters (paryavasthāna) belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu).

is it possible that they abandon the pure (*śuddhaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) formless attainments, yet not those associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*)?

Answer: No.
There is. That is to say:
when an ordinary person who has exhausted craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm.
Is there a case where one falls away from the pure (*śuddha*) or untainted (*anāsrava*) four dhyānas, but not from those associated with relish (*āsvādanā-samprayukta*)? Answer: There is.

when a noble one who has exhausted craving for the Realm of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the Desire Realm,

Is there any falling away from the four formless attainments associated with relishing (*āsvādana*), which is neither pure (*śuddha*) nor untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: No.
Is there any case of falling away from the pure (śuddha) four formless attainments that is neither associated with relishing (āsvādanasamprayukta) nor untainted (anāsrava)?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
When an ordinary person who has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness regresses due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire or form realms,
is there a regression from the pure or untainted [attainments] of the four formless spheres that is not associated with relishing?
Answer: There is. Namely:

When a noble one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm or the form realm, is there any other [falling away] besides this?
Answer: Yes.

when one who has exhausted craving for the Realm of Universal Purity falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the Desire Realm.

There are. By which meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) and non-intimation (*avijñapti*) ceased? Answer:
Bodily and vocal intimation depend on the first dhyāna or the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage).
Bodily and vocal non-intimation depend on the four dhyānas or the *anāgamya*.
Upon which meditative absorption do the three types of unwholesome conduct, the three types of wholesome conduct, the three unwholesome roots, and the three wholesome roots cease?
Answer: Based on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration.

Upon which meditative absorption (*samādhi*) do the four non-noble utterances, the four noble utterances, the four modes of birth, the four types of entry into the womb, and the four stations of consciousness cease?
Answer:
The four non-noble utterances, the four noble utterances, the four modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and spontaneous—and the four ways of entering the womb;
these depend on the stage of *anāgamya*.
Beings of apparitional birth (upapāduka) abide in the last three stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti),
based either on the seven [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya). As for the station of consciousness of form (rūpavijñānasthiti):
— Based on the four [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage],

what meditative absorption (*samādhi*) brings to cessation the five aggregates (*skandha*), the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*), the five destinies (*gati*), the five objects of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), and the five precepts (*śikṣāpada*)?
Answer: The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of grasping at form (*rūpopādānaskandha*):—
these depend on the four [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage].
The four aggregates, the four clinging-aggregates, and the heavenly realm:
these depend on the seven [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The remaining four realms, the five objects of sensual pleasure, and the five precepts: [these depend on the same].

Based on the *anāgamya* [concentration], there are the six internal bases, the six external bases, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, the six groups of volition, and the six groups of craving. By means of which meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are these extinguished?
Answer: The five internal bases, as well as the external bases of visible form, sound, and tangibles—
these depend on either the four dhyānas or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The internal sense base of mind, the external sense base of phenomena, the mental consciousness aggregate, and their associated aggregates of contact, feeling, perception, volition, and craving:
these depend on either the seven [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The external bases of odor and flavor; the groups of nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness;
and their associated aggregates of contact, feeling, perception, volition, and craving:
these depend upon the *anāgamya* (threshold) stage.
The groups of visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses,
along with their associated contact, feeling, perception, volition, and craving:
these depend on either the first dhyāna or the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage.

Regarding the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the eight worldly dharmas (*lokadharma*), the nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*), and the ten paths of action (*karmapatha*), by which meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are they extinguished?
Answer: The first station of consciousness, the eight worldly dharmas, the first abode of sentient beings, and the ten paths of action [are extinguished by the first dhyāna].
The second station of consciousness and abode of sentient beings is based on the *anāgamya* (threshold) concentration— or,
alternatively, on the first dhyāna or the *anāgamya*.
The third station of consciousness, the abode of sentient beings:
[it is] based on two dhyānas or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The fourth station of consciousness, the abode of sentient beings:
—Based on the third dhyāna or the preparatory stage (anāgamya).
The fifth abode of sentient beings:
—Based on the fourth dhyāna or the preparatory stage.
The fifth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the sixth abode of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*):
these depend on the five [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage].
The sixth station of consciousness and the seventh abode of sentient beings:

The sixth or the *anāgamya* [dhyāna] serves as the basis for the seventh station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*); the eighth and ninth abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*) are based on the seventh or the *anāgamya*.

Regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the ten totalities—by which concentration are they extinguished?
Answer: The first dhyāna:
— Based on the first dhyāna or the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage),
there are the second dhyāna, the immeasurable joy (*muditā*), the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
— Based on the second dhyāna or the *anāgamya*.
The third dhyāna:— based on the three [lower dhyānas] or the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage).
The fourth dhyāna, the three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the pure liberations (*śuddhavimokṣa*), the latter four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the first eight totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Based on four [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya* stage,
there are the Sphere of Infinite Space and its corresponding liberation and totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Based on five [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya* stage, there are the remaining ones.
The sphere of infinite consciousness, along with its corresponding liberation and totalities,
relies upon the sixth [dhyāna] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The latter two formless attainments and the latter three liberations rely upon the same.
— — Based on which [dhyāna] or the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage) do the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) cease? Answer:
Knowledge of others' minds:
based on the four dhyānas or the *anāgamya* stage. Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*): [based on all nine stages].
Based on the seven [stages] or the *anāgamya*,
the non-returners (*anāgāmin*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) abide in the forward and reverse orders;

the two supreme [knowledges] of the Bodhisattvas, the prophetic knowledge (*vyākaraṇa*), the vow-knowledge (*praṇidhijñāna*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*), and the four pairs of distinctions.
The one who dwells in the abandonment of phenomena, is disciplined, follows the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma,
and turns the wheel of the Dharma— such a person is a true follower of the True Dharma in this world. In this chapter,
I shall fully explain the five types of Non-returners.
That is to say:

those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion, those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion, and those who ascend to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Do the five [aggregates] encompass all [phenomena],
or do all [phenomena] encompass the five? Answer:
All [factors] are subsumed within the five [aggregates], but the five do not subsume all [factors].
What is not subsumed? Namely:
Between one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin) and one who goes to the formless realm as a non-returner (ārūpya-gāmy anāgāmin),
and between one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) and one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin), which is superior? Answer:
If one abides in the equal severance [of fetters], then parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) is superior;
if one attains parinirvāṇa upon birth (upapadyaparinirvāyin) with a greater severance of fetters, then that is superior.
Among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state up to those who go upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, which is superior?
Answer: If one attains abandonment while dwelling in equanimity, then parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) is superior;
if, up to the point of being a "stream-winner to the Peak of Existence" (ūrdhvasrotas), one has abandoned many fetters while proceeding to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, then that [latter] is superior.

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, up to those who go upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven and attain parinirvāṇa through exertion, and up to those who go upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven and attain parinirvāṇa without exertion—among those who go upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, which is superior?
Answer: If one abides in equal abandonment [of defilements], then those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) and so forth are superior;
if one has more abandonment of fetters through effortful practice (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) and so forth, then they are superior.
Are all those who train training for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained?
And if they are training for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, are they all [considered] those who train? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is the learner (*śaikṣa*) who does not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained;
that is to say:
One who trains abides in their original nature.
To train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained within the conditioned is not true training.
That is to say:
Arhats and ordinary beings advance in their quest for higher dharmas;
those in training also train in order to attain what they have not yet attained.
That is to say:
One who trains seeks the higher Dharma.
There is also that which is neither training, nor is it training for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained; namely:
Do Arhats and ordinary persons abide in their original nature?
Are all those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) such that they do not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained?
Conversely, if they do not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, are they all beyond training?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions.
There are those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa), yet it is not the case that they do not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained.
That is to say:
an Arhat who progresses to seek the higher Dharma does not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained; he is not one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
That is to say:
those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abide in their own nature.
There are also those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), yet they do not [strive] to attain what has not yet been attained among the qualities of one beyond training.
That is to say:
an Arhat abides in his original nature.
He is not one who has not yet attained the state of a non-learner (aśaikṣa), nor is he one who learns for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained.
That is to say:
those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) who strive for higher dharmas.
What is the meaning of "flowing with the stream" (anuloma)?
Answer:

To serve as a limb, a gateway, a basis, a path, and a track toward all births, destinies, existences, classes of beings, and cycles of birth and death—this is the meaning of "flowing with the current."
What is the meaning of "逆流" (逆流, *pratikūla*)? Answer:

It means to serve as a factor (*aṅga*), a gateway (*mukha*), a basis (*vastu*), a path (*mārga*), and a track leading toward the cessation of birth and death, the cessation of rebirth, the cessation of existence, the cessation of the categories of existence, and the cessation of saṃsāra; this is the meaning of "逆流."
What is the meaning of "abiding for oneself"? Answer:
It does not mean being a constituent factor (*aṅga*) for any birth, nor even for the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), nor even being a track or a path toward it.
Nor is it that arising and ceasing, up to the cessation of birth and death, constitute the factors or the path leading toward [liberation];
this is the meaning of "abiding in oneself. Are all those who are Arhats likewise abiding in themselves?
If one abides in oneself, is one necessarily an arhat? Answer: All arhats abide in themselves.
There are those who abide in their own state but are not arhats;
namely, non-returners (anāgāmin).
As the Blessed One said:
"Having forever severed the five afflictions, With training complete and no further rebirths remaining,
Attaining mastery over concentration and the faculties— Such a person is called 'one who abides in themselves.'"
Is it the case that all who have attained the ultimate restraint (uttama-saṃvara) have also attained the ultimate track (uttama-pada)?
Conversely, is it the case that all who have attained the ultimate track have also attained the ultimate restraint? Answer:
All those who have attained the ultimate restraint have all attained the ultimate track.
However, there are those who have attained the ultimate track but have not attained the ultimate restraint. Namely:
He does not return.
As the Blessed One said:
"How does a bhikṣu attain the ultimate goal?"
That is to say:
"It is the thorough knowledge of the permanent abandonment of the five lower fetters.
To what extent is one called a bodhisattva?
Answer: Up to the point where one is able to perform and increase karma that results in maturation with distinct characteristics,
by what name is such a person called a bodhisattva?
Answer: It is the karma that results in the maturation of the acquisition of marks (*lakṣaṇavipākakarma*).
As it is said:
“Maitreya! In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Tathāgata Maitreya, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
What kind of knowledge is this?
Answer: It is due to the knowledge of causes (hetu-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna). In what respect do these operate?
Answer: There is that which operates with respect to the maturation of karma regarding characteristics; by this it is called "knowledge of causes" (*hetujñāna*).

There is that which operates with respect to the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; by this it is called "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*).
As it is said:
"O Bhikṣu! You shall realize the noble goal even in this very life."
"What kind of knowledge is this?
Answer: "It is the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)."
In what does this operate? Answer:

It operates with respect to the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), whereby the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) is attained; it is for this reason that it is called "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*).
What is the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*)? Answer:

It is when an Arhat, having accomplished the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and attained mastery over the mind, forms a correct aspiration to know a particular object according to his desire, and then enters the ultimate fourth dhyāna.
Having arisen from meditative concentration, one knows all things according to one's wish.
Should this "knowledge through aspiration" (praṇidhijñāna) be described as wholesome?
Is it indeterminate?
Answer: It may be wholesome.
Or it is indeterminate.
What is the practice of non-contention? Answer:

When all Arhats have thoroughly mastered the internal [time], they do not do so regarding the external; if they also thoroughly master the external, it is called "conduct free from contention" (*araṇā-vihāra*).
What dharma is designated as "freedom from contention"?
Answer: It causes the mental continuum of others to proceed without defilement.
As it is said:
"I have declared that among my disciples, Kolita (Maudgalyāyana) is foremost in wisdom, while Bhāradvāja and others are foremost in quickness of wit.
What is the difference between these two? Answer:

Because of the Venerable Māṇava, the Venerable Bhārgiva and others have an upright mind, a mind free from crookedness, and a preeminent mind of pure sincerity; they have a gentle mind, a pliant mind, and a preeminent mind of harmony and compliance.
As it is said:
"Among my disciples, Cūḍapanthaka excels in the transformation of the mind, while Mahāpanthaka excels in the transformation of perception.
What is the difference between these two?
Answer: Venerable Cūḷapanthaka dwells frequently in the practice of mindfulness by observing the mind as mind;
Venerable Mahāpanthaka dwells frequently in the practice of mindfulness by observing phenomena as phenomena.
As it is said:
"Among my disciples, Śāriputra possesses great wisdom and eloquence; he upholds the Great Treasury and has attained unimpeded understanding.
What is the distinction between these two?
Answer: Venerable Śāriputra dwells frequently in the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid).
Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila dwells frequently in the four analytical knowledges (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ).
As it is said:
"Among my disciples, Mahākāśyapa has few desires and is content, possessing the practice of the dhūtas;
Bakkula has little illness and is frugal, possessing the practice of pure precepts."
"What is the distinction between these two? Answer:
"As for the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, whether the food and drink he receives be coarse or exquisite, he eats them according to their order without making any discrimination."
Venerable Bakkula—whatever food he obtained, whether coarse or refined—he would set aside the refined and eat the coarse.
Furthermore!
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa was widely known and possessed great merit; it was easy for him to obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites.
Although he had not previously undertaken the ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*), he was nonetheless able to practice them.
Venerable Bakkula does not possess extensive renown or great merit; it is difficult for him to obtain clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites.
Nevertheless, he has previously undertaken the virtues of the dhūtas and is able to practice them faithfully.
For a monk with little learning who practices the virtues of *dhūta* and follows them accordingly, this is not difficult.
As it is said:
"O Mahānāman, train yourself to dwell frequently in the gradual abandonment of the five hindrances."
In this context, what is meant by "training"? Answer:
A stream-enterer, or a once-returner.
How does one who trains dwell frequently in the gradual abandonment of the five hindrances? Answer:
By gradual abandonment, gradual separation, gradual suppression, and gradual turning away.
As it is said:
"O Bhikṣus! Because the Dharma is relinquished, the Vinaya is relinquished."
"Because of the relinquishing of the Vinaya, there is the relinquishing of the Dharma. What is the Dharma? Answer:
The Noble Eightfold Path.
What is the Vinaya? Answer:
Greed, hatred, and delusion are extinguished.
How is it that through the relinquishing of phenomena there is the relinquishing of the Vinaya,
and through the relinquishing of the Vinaya there is the relinquishing of phenomena?
Answer:
If one does not cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path, one cannot realize the cessation of greed, hatred, and delusion.
If one does not realize the cessation of greed, hatred, and delusion, one cannot cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.
For this reason, it is said: "Practice in accordance with the Dharma.
As it is taught:
"The practice that accords with the Dharma."
"What is the Dharma? Answer:
"It is the quiescent nirvāṇa."
What is conformity to the Dharma? Answer:
The Noble Eightfold Path.
What is the practice in accordance with the Dharma? Answer:
It is when one practices according to the meaning within this [Dharma].
Furthermore,
the Prātimokṣa is called the Dharma, and the Prātimokṣa restraint is called the "conformity to the Dharma" (anudharma).
If one practices in accordance with the meaning within this context, it is called "practice in conformity with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
Furthermore, bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood are called the Dharma; to receive these and follow them is called "following the Dharma.
If one acts in accordance with the meaning within this context, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
What is the Wheel of Dharma? Answer:
The Noble Eightfold Path.
In what sense should one say that the wheel of Dharma was turned? Answer:
It was when the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya saw the Dharma.
What is the True Dharma? Answer:
The untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and factors of the path.
Question: At what time should it be said that the True Dharma abides? Answer:
It is when those who practice the Dharma abide.
When can it be said that the True Dharma is extinguished? Answer:
When those who practice the Dharma have perished.
If one first enters the untainted (anāsrava) first dhyāna, by virtue of attaining this, one attains all other untainted mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma).
To which time period do they belong? Answer: The future.
If one first enters, up to the untainted sphere of nothingness, by virtue of attaining this, one attains all other untainted mental states and mental factors; to which time period do these belong?
Answer: They belong to the future.
To which period do all births belong?
Answer: They belong to the future.
To which time period do all cessations belong?
Answer: The present.

According to the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, fascicle eighteen, the second refers to one who has exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara Heaven but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The third refers to one who has exhausted craving for the Brahma-world but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The fourth refers to one who has not yet exhausted craving for the Brahma-world regarding the four pure dhyānas.
There may be none, or one, two, three, or four.
"None" refers to one for whom desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmarāga*) has not yet been exhausted.
"One" refers to one for whom desire for the realm of sensuality has been exhausted, but higher desire (*ūrdhvārāga*) has not yet been exhausted.
The second refers to one for whom craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
The third refers to one for whom craving for the Ābhāsvara realm has been exhausted, but craving for what is above the Śubhakṛtsna realm has not yet been exhausted.
The fourth refers to one for whom craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm has been exhausted.
Regarding the four untainted dhyānas,
there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to entering the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on the preparatory stage (anāgamya).
The first refers to entering rightness and departure from birth based on the first dhyāna or the intermediate dhyāna.
The second refers to entering rightness and departure from birth based on the second dhyāna.
The third refers to entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the third dhyāna.
The fourth refers to entering the state of rightness and departure from birth based on the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with relish (*āsvādana-samprayukta*):
Or [there are] one, two, three, or four.
The first refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The second refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The third refers to one for whom craving for the sphere of infinite space has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
The fourth refers to one for whom craving for the sphere of infinite space has not yet been exhausted,
[and who is bound] to the four pure formless spheres.
There may be none, or one, two, three, or four.
"None" refers to those who have not yet exhausted their craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*).
"One" refers to those who have exhausted their craving for the realm of form but have not yet exhausted their craving for the higher realms.
The second refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The third refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The fourth refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness.
They do not possess any of the three untainted formless attainments.
This is likewise true for those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
As for those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta), they [do not possess] the four meditative absorptions associated with relishing (āsvādana).
There may be none, or one, two, three, or four.
"None" refers to the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*).
"One" refers to the exhaustion of craving for the Subhakṛtsna heaven, while craving for the higher realms has not yet been exhausted.
The second refers to those who have exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara heaven but have not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The third refers to those who have exhausted craving for the Brahma-world but have not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The fourth refers to those who have not yet exhausted craving for the Brahma-world.
Regarding the four pure dhyānas,
there may be none, one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to those whose craving for the desire realm has not yet been exhausted, or those born in the formless realm.
The first refers to one who is born in the desire realm and has exhausted craving for the desire realm but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms;
or one who is born in the Brahma-world and has not yet exhausted craving for that very world;
or one who is born in the Ābhāsvara heaven and has not yet exhausted craving for that very world.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven], craving for that very state is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Bṛhatphala [heaven],
these two cases refer to being born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
When craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted,
if one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, then craving for that [level] is exhausted but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted;
if one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, then craving for that [level] is exhausted.
The third refers to one born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who has exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara Heaven but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms;
or one born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven who has exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
The fourth refers to one born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who has exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Regarding the four untainted dhyānas, there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to those who have not yet exhausted desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*).
"One" refers to those who have exhausted desire for the realm of sensuality but have not yet exhausted desire for the higher realms.
The second refers to one for whom craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
The third refers to one for whom craving for the Ābhāsvara realm has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
The fourth refers to one for whom craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm has been exhausted.
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with craving for taste, there may be one, two, three, or four [fetters].
The first refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The second refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The third refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The fourth refers to one who has not yet exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space regarding the four pure formless spheres.
There may be none, or one, two, three, or four.
"None" refers to those born in the desire realm or the form realm whose craving for form has not yet been exhausted.
"One" refers to those born in the desire realm or the form realm whose craving for form has been exhausted, but whose craving for the higher [realms] has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the sphere of infinite space and craving for it is not yet exhausted;
or if one is born in the sphere of infinite consciousness and craving for it is not yet exhausted;
or if one is born in the sphere of nothingness and craving for it is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
there are two types: those born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the sphere of infinite space,
who have exhausted their craving for the sphere of infinite space but have not yet exhausted their craving for the higher realms.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), craving for that level is exhausted, but craving for the higher levels is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), craving for that level is exhausted.

The third case refers to those born in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), or in the Spheres of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) or Infinite Consciousness, where craving for those levels is exhausted, but craving for the higher levels is not yet exhausted.
First, it is when one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and has exhausted craving for the Sphere of Nothingness.
Fourth, it is when one is born in the Desire Realm, the Form Realm, or the Sphere of Infinite Space, and has exhausted craving for the Sphere of Nothingness.
Regarding the three untainted formless attainments, there may be none, one, two, or all three present.
"None" refers to one whose craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) has not yet been exhausted.
"One" refers to one whose craving for the realm of form has been exhausted, but whose craving for the higher realms has not yet been exhausted.
The second refers to one for whom craving for the sphere of infinite space is exhausted, but craving for higher spheres is not yet exhausted.
The third refers to one for whom craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness is exhausted.
This is likewise true for those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
One who has realized through the body (kāyasākṣin) does not possess any of the four dhyānas associated with relishing (āsvādana).
Regarding the four pure (śuddha) dhyānas,
they may have none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"Non-existence" refers to being born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"The first" refers to being born in the Fruit of Vastness (Bṛhatphala).
"The second" refers to being born in the All-Pure (Śubhakṛtsna) realm.
The third refers to being born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
the fourth refers to being born in the Brahma-world of the desire realm.
In both cases, one fully accomplishes all four untainted dhyānas.
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with flavor (*sāsrava*), one is accomplished and three are not.
Regarding the pure (*śuddha*) four formless attainments,
either one or all four are accomplished.
The first refers to birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The fourth refers to birth in the desire or form realms, wherein one achieves all three untainted formless attainments.
One liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) does not possess any of the four meditative absorptions associated with relish (āsvādana-samprayukta).
Regarding the four pure (śuddha) meditative absorptions,
they may possess none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"Those who do not [possess it]" refers to those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
"The first" refers to those born in the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhatphala*).
"The second" refers to those born in the Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*).
The third refers to being born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
the fourth refers to being born in the Brahma-world of the desire realm.
In both cases, one fully accomplishes all four untainted dhyānas.
One does not possess any of the four formless attainments associated with relishing (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*).
Regarding the pure (*śuddha*) four formless attainments,
one may possess one, two, three, or all four.
The first refers to being born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
the second refers to being born in the sphere of nothingness;
the third refers to being born in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The fourth refers to those born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the sphere of infinite space.
They possess all three untainted (anāsrava) formless attainments,
yet they do not possess any of the four dhyānas associated with relishing (āsvādana).
Regarding the four pure dhyānas,
there may be none, one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to those born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The first refers to those born in the Bṛhatphala heaven;
the second refers to those born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven;
the third refers to those born in the Ābhāsvara heaven.
The Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Fascicle Nineteen.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
Seven or six factors are cultivated in a single session; there are two types of abandonment, two types of right nature, two knowledges, and two types of pleasure.

There are differences in their arising; the factors of enlightenment are categorized as being with signs, signless, in concentration, out of concentration, through hearing, determinate, or indeterminate. There are also the knowledges of abandonment, the divine eye, and the divine ear.
Having attained the fruit of the five supernormal powers, this chapter shall fully explain the three samādhis, namely:
emptiness (śūnyatā), wishlessness (apraṇihita), and signlessness (animitta).
If one accomplishes emptiness, does one also accomplish wishlessness? Answer: It is so.
If one achieves the wishless (*apraṇihita*), does one [also] achieve the empty (*śūnya*)? Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes emptiness, does one also [accomplish] signlessness?
Answer: If one has attained it.
If one achieves the signless, does one achieve the empty? Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes wishlessness, does one [also] possess signlessness?
Answer: If one has attained it.
If one achieves the signless (animitta), does one also achieve the wishless (appaṇihita)? Answer: It is so.
If one has accomplished the past emptiness, has one accomplished the future as well? Answer: It is so.
If one has attained the future emptiness, has one also attained the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it. If one possesses past emptiness, does one also possess it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifested in the present.
If one has attained present emptiness, has one also attained it in the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes future emptiness, does one also accomplish it in the present? Answer:
If it is present before one,
and if one accomplishes present emptiness, does one also accomplish it in the future? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one is endowed with past emptiness, is one also endowed with future and present [emptiness]? Answer:
If one achieves [the emptiness] in the future, and it is present before one in the present:
if one achieves the emptiness of the future and the present, does one also achieve it in the past? Answer:
If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one possesses it;
if it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses the future emptiness, does one also possess the past and present?
Answer: There is one who possesses the future emptiness, but not the past or present;
there is also one who possesses it together with the past, but not the present.
