There is [the case where one] possesses it in the present, but not in the past;
there is [the case where one] possesses it in both the past and the present;
and there is [the case where one] achieves the future emptiness, but not in the past or the present.
That is to say:
emptiness has already been attained, but not yet extinguished;
or, even if it has been extinguished, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
Regarding those that are past but not present:
this refers to that which has already ceased through emptiness yet is not lost, and does not manifest before one.
As for that which is present but not past:
it refers to when emptiness is manifest before one, yet has not yet ceased.
If it has already ceased and been lost,
as well as that which is past and present,
this means:
The emptiness that has already ceased is not lost; it manifests in the present.
If one is endowed with past and present emptiness, is one also endowed with future [emptiness]? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one is endowed with present emptiness, is one also endowed with past and future [emptiness]? Answer:
Regarding future [dharmas], one achieves them.
Regarding past [dharmas], if they have already ceased but have not been lost, then one achieves them;
if they have not yet ceased, or even if they have ceased but have been lost, then one does not achieve them.
If one has attained the emptiness of the past and the future, has one also attained that of the present?
Answer: If it is manifest before one.
As with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), six permutations (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) should be applied;
it should be understood that the same applies to wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) and signlessness (*animitta*).
If one has attained past emptiness, has one also attained past wishlessness?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished the past wishlessness (apraṇihita), has one also accomplished the past emptiness (śūnyatā)?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one has accomplished it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses past emptiness, does one also possess future wishlessness?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the future *apraṇihita* (wishless), does one also possess the past *śūnyatā* (emptiness)?
Answer: If it has already been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished past emptiness, does one also have present wishlessness?
Answer: If it is presently manifest.
If one has attained present wishlessness, has one also attained past emptiness?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses past emptiness, does one also possess past and present wishlessness?
Answer: There is one who possesses the past emptiness (*śūnyatā*), but not the past or present wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
There is also one who possesses [the past emptiness] together with the past, but not the present.
There is [the case of] possessing both the present and the past, but not the future;
there is [the case of] possessing both the past and the present.
There is one who accomplishes the emptiness of the past, but does not possess the wishlessness of the past or the present.
That is to say:
emptiness has already ceased but has not been lost;
wishlessness has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
Regarding those that are past but not present:
this refers to when emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) have already ceased but are not lost, while wishlessness is not currently manifest.
And that which is present, but not past,
refers to:
emptiness that has already ceased but has not been lost.
The wishless (*apraṇihita*) has not yet manifested, or although it has already ceased, it has been lost;
as well as those that are past and present.
That is to say:
When emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has already ceased but is not lost, and wishlessness (*apranihita*) is present before one,
if one accomplishes both past and present wishlessness, does one also possess past emptiness?
Answer: If [the defilement] has already been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished past emptiness, has one also accomplished future and present wishlessness?
Answer: One has accomplished it in the future; as for the present, it is so if it is currently manifest.
If one accomplishes the future and present wishlessness (apraṇihita), does one also accomplish the past emptiness (śūnyatā)?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one accomplishes it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses past emptiness, does one also possess the past and future wishlessness?
Answer: One accomplishes it in the future.
Regarding the past, if it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one accomplishes it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes the past and future *apraṇihita*, is that past *śūnyatā* as well?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes past emptiness (*śūnyatā*), does that person also accomplish past, future, and present wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)? Answer:
There are those who accomplish past emptiness and future wishlessness, but not the past or present.
There is [existence] that includes the future and the present, but not the past.
There is [existence] that includes the past and the future, but not the present.
There is [existence] that includes the past, the future, and the present.
It is the accomplishment of past emptiness and future wishlessness, but not of the past or present.
That is to say:
emptiness has already ceased but has not been lost.
The wishless [concentration] has not yet been extinguished; or, having already been extinguished, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
This includes that which is future or present, but not past.
That is to say:
When emptiness has already ceased but is not lost, wishlessness manifests before one; it is not something that has already ceased, nor is it something that, having already ceased, is lost.
This applies to the past and future, but not to the present.
That is to say:
emptiness and wishlessness have already ceased but are not lost, while wishlessness does not manifest before one;
as well as those [factors] belonging to the past, future, and present.
That is to say:
emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has already ceased but is not lost, and wishlessness (*apranihita*) is present before one.
If one accomplishes past, future, and present wishlessness, does one also possess past emptiness?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one has accomplished past emptiness, has one also accomplished past signlessness?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one has accomplished it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has already ceased but has been lost, then it is not accomplished.
If one accomplishes the past signless, is that the past empty?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes past emptiness, does one also possess future signlessness?
Answer: If one has attained it.
If one has attained the future signless (*animitta*), has one also attained the past emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses past emptiness, does one also possess present signlessness?
Answer: If it is present before one,
and one has attained the signless (animitta) of the present, does one also possess the empty (śūnya) of the past?
Answer: If [the defilement] has already been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes past emptiness, does that person also accomplish past and present signlessness?
Answer: There are those who accomplish past emptiness, but do not accomplish past and present signlessness.
There are those who possess [the fruit] in the past but not in the present;
there are those who possess it in the present but not in the past;
and there are those who possess it in both the past and the present.
To accomplish past emptiness while not being [characterized by] past or present signlessness means:
emptiness has already ceased but is not lost.
The signless has not yet been extinguished; or, having already been extinguished, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
Furthermore, regarding that which is past and not present, it is said:
Emptiness and the signless have already ceased but are not lost, yet the signless does not manifest before one.
As for that which is present but not past, it is as follows:
When emptiness has already ceased, it is not lost.
When the signless manifests before one, it has not yet ceased; even if it has ceased, it is lost.
This applies to both the past and the present.
That is to say:
emptiness has already ceased but is not lost, and signlessness is present before one.
If one accomplishes past and present signlessness, does one also possess past emptiness?
Answer: If [the defilement] has already been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
If one accomplishes past emptiness, does one also accomplish future and present signlessness?
Answer: There are those who accomplish past emptiness, but do not accomplish future and present signlessness.
One possesses [the attainment] in the past and the future, but not in the present.
One possesses [the attainment] in the past, the future, and the present.
Regarding one who has accomplished the emptiness of the past, but does not possess the signlessness of the future or the present:
That is to say:
emptiness has already ceased, yet the signless has not yet been attained;
and that which belongs to the future, rather than the present.
That is to say:
emptiness has already ceased but its efficacy is not lost;
signlessness has already been attained, yet it does not manifest before one.
Regarding the future and the present:
it means that what was previously empty has ceased but its efficacy is not lost, and the signless (animitta) manifests before one.
If one has attained the signless (animitta) of the future and the present, has one also attained the empty (śūnya) of the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
If one possesses past emptiness, does one also possess past and future signlessness?
Answer: There is one who accomplishes past emptiness, but not past or future signlessness;
there is one who accomplishes [past emptiness] and future [signlessness], but not the past.
There are those who possess both the past and the future.
One who has accomplished the emptiness of the past, yet does not possess the signlessness of the past or the future,
refers to:
Having already ceased through emptiness, one has not yet attained the signless.
As for that which is future and not past,
it is said:
Emptiness has already ceased but is not lost.
Signlessness has already been attained but has not yet ceased; even if it has ceased, it is lost.
This also applies to those that are past and future.
That is to say:
emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the signless (*animitta*) have already ceased but are not lost.
If one has attained the past and future signless, does one also possess the past emptiness?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
If one achieves past emptiness, does that person also achieve the signless of the past, future, and present?
Answer: There are those who achieve past emptiness, but do not achieve the signless of the past, future, and present.
There is [the case] where there is [possession] of the future, but not of the past or the present;
where there is [possession] of the future and the present, but not of the past;
and where there is [possession] of the past and the future, but not of the present.
There are those who possess the past, future, and present.
One may achieve the emptiness of the past, yet not possess the signlessness of the past, future, or present.
That is to say:
emptiness has already ceased, yet the signless has not yet been attained;
and that which belongs to the future, rather than the past or the present.
That is to say:
emptiness has already ceased but has not been lost;
signlessness has already been attained but has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
And those belonging to the future and present, but not the past,
refer to that which has already perished through emptiness yet has not been lost.
The signless has not yet manifested, or although it has manifested, it has already ceased;
as well as that which is past or future, but not present.
That is to say:
When emptiness and signlessness have already ceased and are not lost, yet signlessness does not manifest before one—
this refers to those [states] belonging to the past, future, and present. Namely:
When emptiness and the signless have already ceased but are not lost, the signless manifests before one.
If one has attained the signless of the past, future, and present, does that entail the emptiness of the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
Just as emptiness corresponds to signlessness;
one should know that wishlessness corresponds to signlessness in the same way.
This is like the "small seven."
It should be understood that the "great sevens" are likewise;
the difference is that two are paired with one.
As with emptiness regarding the past;
there are seven [contemplations] when the past is without aspiration (apraṇihita) in relation to the past being signless (animitta).
If one cultivates emptiness, does one also cultivate without aspiration?
If one practices wishlessness (apraṇihita), is that emptiness (śūnyatā)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of emptiness, but not of wishlessness;
that is to say,
when one who has already attained emptiness brings it into manifestation.
There is the cultivation of wishlessness, but not of emptiness;
that is to say,
when one who has already attained wishlessness brings it into manifestation.
If one has not yet attained the manifestation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), one does not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
There are cases where both are cultivated simultaneously, namely:
If one has not yet attained emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and it is not present before one, one cultivates emptiness; if one has not yet attained wishlessness (*apranihita*),
or if one has not yet attained signlessness (*animitta*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is not present before one, one cultivates both emptiness and wishlessness.
There is that which is neither cultivated; namely,
when one who has already attained the signless brings it into manifestation.
If one has not yet attained the manifestation of the signless (*animitta*), one does not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
If one has already attained the manifestation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), [one cultivates them].
If one has not yet attained the manifestation of conventional knowledge, one does not cultivate emptiness or wishlessness.
Regarding all ordinary beings with defiled minds, neutral minds, those in the attainment of non-conception, the attainment of cessation, or those born in the heaven of non-conception:
if they cultivate emptiness, do they also cultivate the signless?
If one cultivates signlessness, is that emptiness?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of emptiness, but not of signlessness;
that is to say,
when emptiness, having already been attained, manifests before one.
If emptiness has not yet been attained and does not manifest before one, one does not cultivate signlessness.
If wishlessness has not yet been attained and does not manifest before one, one cultivates emptiness but not signlessness.
There are cases where one cultivates signlessness but not emptiness.
That is to say:
when the signless (animitta) has already been attained and is present before one;
or, if the signless has not yet been attained and is present before one, one does not cultivate emptiness (śūnyatā).
There is simultaneous cultivation;
that is to say,
when emptiness has not yet been attained, one brings the signless into presence and cultivates it.
If one has not yet attained the manifestation of the signless (*animitta*), one cultivates emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
If one has not yet attained the wishless (*apraṇihita*), nor the manifestation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), one cultivates both emptiness and the signless.
There is the case where neither is cultivated: namely,
when the already attained wishlessness is present before one, or when the not-yet-attained wishlessness is present before one, and one does not cultivate emptiness or signlessness.
Whether one has already attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that is currently manifest,
or whether one has not yet attained mundane knowledge that is currently manifest, one does not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or signlessness (*animitta*).

This includes all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) with afflicted minds (*kliṣṭacitta*) or neutral minds (*avyākṛtacitta*), those in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and those born in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
If one cultivates wishlessness, does that involve signlessness?
And if one cultivates signlessness, does that involve wishlessness? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is the cultivation of the wishless (apraṇihita), which is not the signless (animitta).
That is to say:
If one has already attained the wishless (apraṇihita) and it is present before one,
or if one has not yet attained the wishless and has not yet attained the empty (śūnyatā),
one does not cultivate the signless (animitta).
There is the cultivation of signlessness (animitta) that is not wishlessness (apraṇihita); namely,
when one who has already attained signlessness brings it into manifestation.
If one has not yet attained the manifestation of the signless (animitta),
one does not cultivate the wishless (apraṇihita); however, there are cases where both are cultivated together.
That is to say:
when one has not yet attained the manifestation of wishlessness (apraṇihita), one cultivates the signless (animitta);
or if one has not yet attained the manifestation of the signless, one cultivates wishlessness.
If one has not yet attained emptiness (*śūnyatā*), nor has the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) currently manifest, one cultivates the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and the signless (*animitta*).
There are cases where neither is cultivated, namely:
Having already attained emptiness and having already attained conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) such that it is present before one;
or, if conventional knowledge has not yet been attained and is not present before one, one does not cultivate wishlessness (apraṇihita) or signlessness (animitta).
All the defiled minds and neutral minds of ordinary beings;
those in the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation;
and those born in the Heaven of Non-conception.
Are there any fetters that are abandoned by emptiness, but not by the wishless or the signless? Answer: No.
Are there any fetters that are abandoned by the wishless (apraṇihita), but not by the empty (śūnya) or the signless (animitta)?
Answer: There are.
That is to say:
the fetters abandoned through the vision of origin and the vision of the path are abandoned by means of the wishless (*apranihita*).
Are there any fetters that are abandoned by means of the signless (*animitta*), yet not by means of the empty (*śūnya*) or the wishless?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
The fetters abandoned through the vision of cessation are abandoned by means of the signless (*animitta*).
Is there any fetter that is abandoned by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or the wishless (*apraṇihita*), but not by means of the signless? Answer:
There are. Namely:
the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of suffering are abandoned by means of emptiness and the wishless.
Are there any fetters that are abandoned by emptiness and signlessness, but not by wishlessness? Answer: No.
Are there any fetters that are abandoned by the wishless and the signless, but not by the empty? Answer: No.
Are there any fetters that are abandoned by means of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness?
Answer: There are.
That is to say:

the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation by one who has attained the vision of the tracks (the *śaikṣa*) are abandoned by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*). Are there any fetters that are not abandoned by means of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, yet are nonetheless abandoned?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Regarding the fetters to be abandoned by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*),
how does one enter the state of rightness and departure from corruption (*samyaktva-niyāma*) through mental attention? Answer:
Whether one contemplates impermanence, suffering, emptiness, or non-self,
by what type of fettered practice does one enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)? Answer:
Regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) bound to the desire realm,
should it be said that one dwells contemplating the body as the body?
...up to: "Should it be said that one dwells contemplating phenomena in accordance with phenomena? Answer:
Regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna),
it should be said that one dwells contemplating the body as body, or contemplates feelings, or the mind, or phenomena as phenomena.
As it is with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), so it is with the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is the difference between the bliss of the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna and the bliss of the factor of enlightenment that is pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: There is no difference.
What is the distinction between the pleasure of the various untainted second dhyāna and the pleasure of the various factors of enlightenment such as pliancy?
Answer: There is no difference.
If one emerges from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), is it that [concentration] which is its object (*ālambana*)?
If one emerges from the object of focus, is that concentration [still present]?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one emerges from meditative concentration (samādhi) without its object.
That is to say:
for instance, there is someone who, having contemplated this sign, enters the first dhyāna, and then, contemplating that same sign again, enters the second dhyāna.
There is that which emerges from the object of focus but not from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
That is to say:
for example, there is one who, having contemplated this sign, enters the first dhyāna; without emerging from the first dhyāna, he then contemplates another sign.
There are cases where one emerges from meditative concentration and yet remains focused on the same object.
That is to say:
for example, when someone contemplates this particular sign and enters the first dhyāna, they then contemplate another sign and enter the second dhyāna.
There are cases where one neither emerges from meditative concentration nor [shifts] the object of focus.
That is to say:
for example, there is someone who, contemplating this sign, enters the first dhyāna and remains therein for a long time.
As it is said:

"O Bhikṣus! Even those who have attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and reached the holy intent, the disciples of the Blessed One are born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
"By relying on which meditative concentration does he attain the fruit of arhatship?
Answer: "The untainted sphere of nothingness."
As it is said:
"The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke: 'O Āyuṣmat!'"
"I recall that while dwelling in the meditative concentration of the sphere of nothingness, I heard the sounds of many dragon-elephants roaring and so forth by the side of the Mandākinī Lake.
Did that venerable one hear these sounds while remaining in meditative concentration?
Is it for the purpose of emerging from meditative concentration? Answer:
It is heard while emerging from concentration, not while remaining in concentration.
Are all those who are indeterminate likewise unwise and destined for ignorance?
Answer: All those who are indeterminate are indeed unwise and destined for ignorance.
There are those who lack wisdom and proceed toward ignorance, yet are not indeterminate;
that is to say, those who are fixed in error (mithyātva-niyata).
"Are all those who are wise and of clear understanding also established in meditative concentration? Answer:

All those who are wise and of clear understanding are indeed established in meditative concentration; however, there are those established in meditative concentration who are not wise and are of unclear understanding."
That is to say:
those with wrong concentration and those who are indeterminate— do they all fail to accomplish the factors of enlightenment?
Answer: All those that are indeterminate do not possess the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga).
However, there are cases where one does not possess the factors of enlightenment without being indeterminate.
That is to say:
regarding wrong concentration and all concentrations, are they all accomplished as factors of enlightenment?
Answer: All those who possess the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) necessarily possess concentration (samādhi).
However, there are those who possess concentration but do not possess the factors of enlightenment.
That is to say:
those who are of wrong determination and have accomplished the factors of enlightenment— have they accomplished untainted phenomena?
Answer: Those who accomplish the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) also accomplish untainted phenomena (anāsravadharma).
However, there are those who accomplish untainted phenomena who do not accomplish the factors of enlightenment.
That is to say: regarding all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
those who do not possess the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), do they also not possess the untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)?
Answer: There is no one who does not accomplish untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*).
However, there are those who do not accomplish the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
That is to say:
regarding all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
do those who have attained the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) necessarily attain untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)?
Answer: Those who attain the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) attain those untainted dharmas (anāsravadharma).
However, there are those who attain untainted dharmas that are not factors of enlightenment.
That is to say:
regarding all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana),
when they abandon the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga), do they abandon the untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma)?
Answer: There is no total relinquishing of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), nor is there any total relinquishing of untainted phenomena (anāsravadharma).
If one falls away from the factors of enlightenment, does one also fall away from the untainted phenomena?
Answer: There is no complete retrogression from the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), nor is there any complete retrogression from untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).
Are all those that have not been abandoned also those that have not been fully known (*aparijñāta*)?
Answer: All those that have not been fully understood have not been abandoned;
however, there are those that have not been abandoned which have not been fully understood.
That is to say:
if something has been fully known because it was thoroughly understood by wisdom, but has not been abandoned because it was not abandoned through the thorough knowledge of abandonment—
then is that which has been abandoned necessarily that which has been thoroughly understood?
Answer: All that has been abandoned has been fully understood.
However, there is that which has been fully understood but not yet abandoned.
That is to say: if,

by means of thorough knowledge through wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*), something has already been thoroughly known, but has not yet been abandoned through thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*),
then for those who possess this birth and do not see forms with their physical eyes, by relying on what dharma do they bring forth the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)?
Answer:
For example, there is one who has attained birth by way of their own nature and recalls that in a previous life they saw forms with their eye; based upon this, they bring forth the divine eye.
Regarding those beings who are born here and do not hear sounds with their ears, by means of what dharma do they produce the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*)? Answer:
It is as when someone attains birth through their own nature (*svabhāvajāti*), and recollects that in other previous births their ears once heard sounds; based upon this, they produce the divine ear.
For what reason do the fetters to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation increase when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) falls away,
whereas only the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation increase when a disciple of the Blessed One (śrāvaka) falls away?
Answer:
An ordinary person (pṛthagjana) uses this very path to abandon the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through seeing, and uses that same path to abandon the fetters abandoned through cultivation.
Therefore, when they fall away, both types of fetters increase simultaneously.
When a disciple of the Blessed One uses this path to abandon the fetters abandoned through vision, they are certain not to fall back from that path.
When they use another path to abandon the fetters abandoned through cultivation, they may or may not fall back from that other path.

If a disciple of the Blessed One were to say, "By means of this very path one abandons the fetters abandoned through vision, and by means of this very same path one abandons the fetters abandoned through cultivation," such a person would likewise not fall away.
Why is it that there is falling away from the three higher fruits, but not from the fruit of stream-entry?
Answer: The fetters to be abandoned through cultivation arise based on existing entities (*vastu*).
That is to say:
there are signs of purity and signs of impurity. When one contemplates the sign of purity through improper attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), one then regresses from the perception of impurity.

The fetters to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) arise based on non-existent objects; since there is not a single dharma that is "self" or "belonging to self" which could be made an object of contemplation for them, they regress from the view of selflessness (*anātma-dṛṣṭi*).

When one falls away from the three higher fruits, regarding all the untainted faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and factors of the path (mārgāṅga) that have been attained: should it be said that they are attained as something previously attained, or as something never before attained?
Answer: One should say they are "previously acquired acquisitions.

When one passes away from the formless realm and is born into the desire realm, regarding all the aggregates, elements, bases, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate factors, faculties, fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and envelopments that are acquired at that time—should these be called "previously acquired acquisitions"?
"Is it that what was never previously obtained is now obtained? Answer:

"It should be said that wholesome and defiled dharmas are obtained by means of what was previously obtained, whereas resultant (vipāka) dharmas are obtained by means of what was never previously obtained."

When one passes away from the formless realm and is born into the form realm, there are the aggregates, elements, bases, wholesome factors, indeterminate factors, faculties, fetters, bonds, latent dispositions, secondary afflictions, and envelopments that are acquired.
Should it be said that what was previously attained is attained,
or that what was never before attained is attained? Answer:
It should be said that wholesome and defiled dharmas have been previously acquired through acquisition (*prāpti*), whereas resultant dharmas have not been previously acquired through acquisition.

When one dies in the form realm and is born in the desire realm, the aggregates, elements, and bases thus acquired are as explained in the case of dying in the formless realm and being born in the desire realm.
When one induces the supernormal power of travel by means of the first dhyāna, how far does it extend?
Answer: It reaches as far as the Brahma-world.
When one induces the supernormal power of the divine ear based on the first dhyāna, what kind of sounds does one hear from such a great distance?
Answer: Up to the Brahma-world.
When one induces the supernormal power of knowing others' minds based on the first dhyāna, what level of bound (saṃyojana) mental states and mental factors does that knowledge reach?
Answer: Up to the Brahma-world.
When one induces the supernormal power of recollecting past lives by relying on the first dhyāna, what range of past existences does one recollect?
Answer: Up to the Brahma-world.
When one induces the channel of the divine eye based on the first dhyāna, what kind of forms does one see at the furthest distance?
Answer: Up to the Brahma-world.
Just as it is based on the first dhyāna, so it is for each of the others up to the fourth dhyāna; the detailed explanation for each respective stage is likewise.
If one contemplates suffering as suffering and attains the fruit of arhatship, what kind of bound suffering does that person contemplate?
Answer: It is suffering associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If, while contemplating origination as origination, one attains the fruit of arhatship, what kind of origination associated with which realm does that person contemplate?
Answer: It is the cessation associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If one contemplates cessation regarding cessation and attains the fruit of Arhatship, what kind of cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) does that contemplation pertain to?
Answer: It is the cessation of those formations (saṃskāra) that are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form and formless realms.
If one contemplates the path with respect to the path, [it is the cessation of those formations].
Having attained the fruit of arhatship, what kind of path does he contemplate that is capable of severing the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to which realms? Answer:
It is either the path capable of severing the conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm, or those bound to the form or formless realms.
The foundations of mindfulness have six doors; there are eight ways of knowing things as they truly are.
Greed, hatred, and delusion increase or decrease. The disciple dies and receives parinirvāṇa before the Buddha;
the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa while emerging from meditative absorption.
The four [realms] and the three realms of existence have their respective practices. In this chapter, I wish to explain in detail the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), namely:
the foundation of mindfulness of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
If one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the body, does one [also] cultivate that of sensation?
And if one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of sensation, does one [also] cultivate that of the body? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is the establishment of mindfulness of the body, but not of sensation;
that is to say:
When the mindfulness of the body has already been attained and is present before one,
there may be cultivation of the mindfulness of feelings, but not of the body.
That is to say:

If one has already attained the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), it is present before one; if one has not yet attained the application of mindfulness to feelings, it is present before one, but one does not cultivate the body.
If one has not yet attained the applications of mindfulness to the mind (*citta*) or phenomena (*dharma*), one cultivates feelings, but not the body.
There is simultaneous cultivation;
that is to say,
when the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained but is now present before one.
If one has not yet attained the mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) manifesting before one, one cultivates the body (*kāya*).
If one has not yet attained the mindfulness of mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*) or the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) manifesting before one, one cultivates the body and feelings.
There is that which is neither cultivated: namely,
when the mind and dharma foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have already been attained and are currently manifest.
If the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna has not yet been attained and is present before one, one does not cultivate the body or feelings.
This applies to all defiled minds and neutral minds.
In the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation,
and birth in the heaven of non-perception;
as with the foundation of mindfulness of the body and the foundation of mindfulness of feeling.
One should know that the same applies to the foundation of mindfulness of the body and the foundation of mindfulness of the mind.
If one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the body, does one cultivate the [foundation of] dharmas?
And if one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas, does one cultivate the body?
Answer: One should formulate four propositions.
There is the cultivation of the application of mindfulness to the body that is not in accordance with the Dharma.
That is to say:
one who has already attained the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) and brings it to presence,
may practice the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), but not that of the body.
That is to say:
when the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna already attained has become manifest;
or, when the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna not yet attained has become manifest, one does not cultivate the body.
If one has not yet attained [the attainment of] mindfulness of feelings or mindfulness of mind, and brings them to presence, one cultivates the dharma-foundation but not the body-foundation.
There is simultaneous cultivation when one brings the unattained mindfulness of the body to presence.
If one has not yet attained the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) and brings it into presence, one cultivates the body.

If one has not yet attained the mindfulness of sensation (vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna) or the mindfulness of mind (cittasmṛtyupasthāna) and brings them into presence, one cultivates both the body and phenomena.
There is the case where neither is cultivated: namely,
when the mindfulness of sensation and the mindfulness of mind that have already been attained are present before one.
All defiled minds, indeterminate minds,
and those existing in the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation.
One is born in the Heaven of Non-conception.
If one cultivates the mindfulness of feeling, is that the mind?
If one cultivates the mindfulness of mind, is that the feeling?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the mindfulness-establishment of feeling, but not of the mind.
That is to say:

when the mindfulness-establishment of sensation (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna) has already been attained and is present before one, there is cultivation of the mindfulness-establishment of mind (citta-smṛtyupasthāna), but not of sensation.
That is to say:
when the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) has already been attained and is present before one, there is simultaneous cultivation (*ubhayabhāvanā*).
That is to say:
when the mindfulness of body, feeling, or mind has not yet been attained, it is brought into presence;
or, if the mindfulness of phenomena has not yet been attained, it is brought into presence while one cultivates mindfulness of feeling and mind.
There is that which is neither cultivated; namely,
when the mindfulness establishments of body and dharmas have already been attained and are present before one.
If the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna that has not yet been attained is present before one, one does not cultivate [the smṛtyupasthānas of] sensation or mind,
nor any defiled or neutral minds.
In the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of cessation,
or being born in the heaven of non-perception—
if one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, are those [feelings] that same phenomena?
If one practices the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna), does one [also] practice that of sensation (vedanā)?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the mindfulness of feeling that is not the Dharma;
that is to say,
when the mindfulness of feeling already attained is present before one.
There is the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena, but not of sensation;
that is to say,
when the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena already attained is present before one.
If the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna that has not yet been attained is present before one, one does not cultivate the feeling-smṛtyupasthāna.
There are cases where both are cultivated simultaneously, namely:
If one has not yet attained the presence of the applications of mindfulness on the body, feelings, or mind,
and if one has not yet attained the presence of the application of mindfulness on phenomena, one cultivates feelings;
there are also cases where neither is cultivated.
That is to say:
when the mindfulness of body and mind has already been attained and is present before one;
and all defiled states of mind.
The indeterminate mind exists in the attainment of non-conception, the attainment of cessation,
and upon being born in the heaven of non-conception.
Just as with the mindfulness-establishment of feelings and the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena,
one should know that the mindfulness-establishment of mind and the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena are likewise.
Regarding the mindfulness-establishment of contemplating the body within the body:

Should it be said that these are the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)?
Should they be said to be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without both vitarka and vicāra?
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity?
Should it be said that it is accompanied by the samādhis of emptiness or wishlessness?
Should it be said that it takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm or the form realm?
And as for those that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*): when one dwells in the contemplation of feelings within feelings during cultivation,

should these be said to be the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), or the knowledges of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), origin (*samudayajñāna*), and the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
Should it be said that it possesses vitarka and vicāra, and so forth among the three?
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity?
Should it be said that it is conjoined with the samādhis of emptiness or wishlessness?
One should say that it takes as its object those things bound to the three realms or those that are unbound;
as it is with feeling, so it is with the mind.
Regarding the cultivation of this mental application toward phenomena (*dharma*),

should it be described as the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), or the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path?
Or should it be described as being with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), and so forth, according to the threefold classification?
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity?
Should it be said that it is conjoined with the three samādhis of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness?
Should it be said that it takes as its object that which is bound to the three realms or that which is unbound?
As it is said:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.
These are the four knowledges, namely:
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge.
When experiencing a painful feeling, one knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a painful feeling.
This is one type of knowledge, namely:
In the mundane world, when experiencing a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, one knows as it truly is: "I am experiencing a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.
These are the four knowledges, namely:
The Dharma-knowledge, the subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of the path.
When experiencing a pleasant bodily feeling, a painful bodily feeling, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily feeling, or a painful mental feeling, one knows them as they truly are.
This is one wisdom, namely: conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
When experiencing a mental feeling of pleasure or a mental feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, one knows it as it truly is.

—These are the four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

When experiencing pleasant sensation with attachment, painful sensation with attachment, neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation with attachment, as well as painful sensation without attachment, one knows them as they truly are.
This is one wisdom, namely:
conventional wisdom.
When experiencing a flavorless feeling of pleasure or a flavorless feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one knows it as it truly is.

These are the four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

When experiencing the feeling of pleasure based on attachment, the feeling of pain based on attachment, the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure based on attachment, and the feeling of renunciation from suffering, one knows them as they truly are.
This is one wisdom, namely: conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
When experiencing the feeling of renunciation based on pleasure, or the feeling of renunciation based on neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one knows it as it truly is.
These are the four knowledges, namely:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge.
As it is said: "When there is a mind possessed of greed, one knows the mind possessed of greed as it truly is."
This is one kind of knowledge, namely:
conventional knowledge.
One knows, as it truly is, a mind free from greed as a mind free from greed.
These four knowledges are: the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
They are like [the knowledge of] a mind with greed and a mind free from greed;
One should know that there is a mind associated with delusion and a mind free from delusion;
a defiled mind and an undefiled mind.
The concentrated mind and the distracted mind;
the depressed mind and the uplifted mind;
the narrow mind and the expansive mind.
A restless mind and an unrestless mind;
an unpacified mind and a pacified mind;
an unconcentrated mind and a concentrated mind.
It is the same for the uncultivated mind and the cultivated mind,
as well as for the unliberated mind and the liberated mind. When there is a mind with anger,
one knows "there is a mind with anger" in accordance with reality.
This is one wisdom, namely:
conventional wisdom.
It knows the mind free from hatred as it truly is—a mind free from hatred.
These three knowledges are: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga*).
As it is said: "When there is the hindrance of internal sensual desire, one knows as it really is that there is the hindrance of internal sensual desire."
This is one kind of knowledge, namely:
conventional knowledge.
When there is no hindrance of internal sensual desire, he knows as it really is: "There is no hindrance of internal sensual desire."
—These are the three knowledges, namely: knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
For example, when the internal hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) has not yet arisen, one knows it as it truly is.
"This is one kind of knowledge, namely:
conventional knowledge.
Having arisen, it is immediately abandoned; having been abandoned, it does not arise again—this is knowing it as it truly is."
These three knowledges are: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga*).
They are like the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*);
It should be understood that the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor, the hindrance of restlessness-and-regret, and the hindrance of doubt are likewise.
Just as it is said that there is an internal fetter of the eye, one knows truly that there is an internal fetter of the eye.
This is one kind of knowledge, namely:
conventional knowledge.
When there are no internal fetters of the eye, one knows as it truly is: "There are no internal fetters of the eye."
—These four knowledges are: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge.
One knows as it truly is when internal fetters of the eye have not yet arisen but are about to arise.
—This is one wisdom, namely: conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Having arisen, it is immediately abandoned; having been abandoned, it does not arise again; this he knows as it truly is.
These four knowledges are: the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
They are like the fetter of the eye;
It should be understood that the fetters of the ear, body, and mind are likewise.
The fetters of the nose and tongue are as explained for the [ear] cover.
As it is said, there is the internal factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness; one knows, as it truly is, that there is the internal factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness.
These four knowledges are: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge.
When there is no factor of enlightenment of mindfulness internally, one knows as it truly is that there is no factor of enlightenment of mindfulness internally.
This is one kind of knowledge, namely: conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

Just as the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, when not yet arisen, comes into being; and having arisen, remains and is not forgotten, becoming perfected, increased, and extensively realized through wisdom—these are the four knowledges:
namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
Just as it is with the mindfulness factor of enlightenment,
one should know that the same applies to the factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, diligence, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
As it is said:
"One observes with equanimity that one's own greed, hatred, and delusion increase.
How do greed, hatred, and delusion increase?
Answer: Because there are the lower fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, it is middling;
because there are the middling ones, it is superior.
This is called "increase.
As it is said:
"One contemplates with equanimity the diminishing of one's own greed, hatred, and delusion.
What is meant by the diminishing of greed, hatred, and delusion? Answer:
Because of being bound by the supreme fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion, it is "middling.
Because there is no middling, it is "inferior.
This is what is meant:
[The category] "diminution. What is the experience at the limit of death? Answer:
Due to the severance of these vital points (*marmans*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) ceases.
To what extent should one say that this constitutes the experience at the limit of death? Answer:
When these vital points (*marmāṇi*) are severed, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) ceases.
Wherein is this included? Answer:
Regarding the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana): with how many consciousnesses is it associated? Answer:
Regarding body-consciousness and mind-consciousness:
the sensation experienced when the initial vital point (*marmaccheda*) is severed is associated with body-consciousness;
the final sensation is associated with mind-consciousness.
Regarding the mind of an Arhat at the moment of parinirvāṇa, should it be described as wholesome or as indeterminate? Answer:
It should be said that this is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Why is it that the two noble disciples enter parinirvāṇa first, and only then the Buddha? Answer:
Those two venerable ones, having previously during the long night performed and accumulated karma that brings about uninterrupted results, so that it may not be in vain or without its maturation.
Furthermore:
By the nature of things (*dharmatā*), as it is said:
"The Blessed One has entered parinirvāṇa while abiding in the immovable and tranquil meditative absorption; the Eye of the World has been extinguished."
"Is this one remaining in meditative absorption,
or has one emerged from it? Answer:
Emerging from meditative absorption.
As it is said: there are four modes of existence (*bhava*).
That is to say:
existence at birth (pūrvakālabhava), existence at death (maraṇabhava), intermediate existence (antarābhava), and existence at rebirth (upapattibhava). What is existence at birth?
Answer: With the exception of the aggregates at the stage of birth and the stage of death, there are the intermediate states of existence.
What is the existence at death?
Answer: It consists of the aggregates at the moment of death.
What is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Answer: With the exception of the aggregates at the stage of death and the stage of birth, there are the intermediate states of existence.
What is the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*)?
Answer: Regarding the aggregates that constitute birth:
are all those belonging to the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) comprised within the five modes of existence (pañcagati)?
If one posits the five aggregates, are they all part of the realm of desire?
Answer: One should formulate this in four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are those who possess desire but do not possess the five aggregates.

This refers to sentient beings of the desire realm who abide in a state of non-congruent mind, as well as those abiding in the meditative attainment of non-conception or the meditative attainment of cessation.
There are five types of existence that do not belong to the realm of desire. They are:
the gods with perception in the form realm who abide in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāga-citta*).
If one in the Heaven of Non-conception does not attain non-conception,
they possess desire-existence and likewise the five aggregates.
That is to say:
Sentient beings of the desire realm abide in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāga-citta*).
There are those who do not belong to the existence of desire, nor do they belong to the five destinies (*gati*).
That is to say:

In the realm of form, there are those in the heavens of perception who abide in a mind of a different category, as well as those abiding in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation.
Or, they may be those in the heaven of non-perception who have attained non-perception,
or those born in the formless realm.
Regarding those beings in the realm of form who possess perception: are they all of five aggregates?
Or, if they are of five aggregates, are they all beings in the realm of form who possess perception? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There are beings with form and with perception who do not belong to the five aggregates.
That is to say:
In the form realm, there are the gods of the realm of perception who abide in a mind of a different category;
as well as those abiding in the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation.
There are five types of beings who are neither in the formless realm nor among the gods of the realm of perception.
That is to say:
sentient beings of the desire realm abide in a mind of homogeneous character;
or, those in the Heaven of No-Thought who have not yet attained the state of no-thought.
There are beings who possess form and possess perception; these also consist of five types.
That is to say:
the gods of the realm of form who possess perception and abide in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāga-citta*).
There are beings who possess neither form nor perception, yet are not of the five aggregates.
These are: sentient beings of the desire realm who abide in a dissimilar state of mind, as well as those abiding in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation.
If one attains non-perception in the Heaven of Non-perception,
or is born in the Formless Realm—
regarding all those beings with form who exist in the Heaven of Non-perception, are they all characterized by both modes of activity?
If one posits two categories, are all those who possess form necessarily non-percipient gods?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations.
There are beings with form who dwell in the Heaven of Non-perception, yet they do not possess the two modes of activity;
that is to say,
those in the Heaven of Non-perception have not attained non-perception.
There are two types of beings who do not possess form yet reside in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva): namely,

sentient beings of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), and those of the heaven of perception in the form realm (rūpadhātu) who abide in a dissimilar state of mind (visabhāga-citta), as well as those abiding in the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
There are beings with form who belong to the Heaven of Non-perception; they also possess two types of formations, namely:
the attainment of non-perception within the Heaven of Non-perception.
There are those who are neither of the form realm nor of the non-percipient heavens, and yet do not possess the two types of formations; namely,
sentient beings of the desire realm and those of the percipient heavens in the form realm who abide in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāgata*).
If one is born in the formless realm,
are all those formless existences characterized by the four modes of activity? Conversely,
if they are characterized by the four modes of activity, are they all formless existences?
Answer: All four modes of conduct (cārī) are included within the formless existence (ārūpyabhava).
However, there is formless existence that is not comprised of the four modes of conduct.
That is to say:
when sentient beings of the formless realm abide in a mind of a different category (asabhāga-citta),
can there be five courses of action (karmapatha)?
Answer: There is. Namely:
Sentient beings of the desire realm and the gods of the form realm who possess ideation abide in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāga-citta*).
As for the gods of the non-ideation realm, they do not attain non-ideation.
Is there, then, a case of four modes of activity?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Sentient beings in the formless realm abide in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāgacitta*).
Is it possible for them to possess the three types of formations (*saṃskāra*)?
Answer: Yes.
No. Is there perhaps that which has two modes of activity? Answer:

There are. Namely: sentient beings of the desire realm and those in the heavens of the form realm who possess perception, when they abide in a state of mind that is dissimilar [to their current state].
If one abides in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation,
or if one attains non-perception in the Heaven of Non-perception,
could there be a single mode of conduct?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Regarding sentient beings in the formless realm who abide in a dissimilar state of mind (*asabhāga-citta*),
is there any presence or absence of mental formations (*saṃskāra*)? Answer:
There are none.
There are three types of latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with perception; six types of vitarka;
and the presence or absence of clarity and ignorance regarding causes and so forth. This chapter shall explain these in full.

Is it the case that for all those who relinquish existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhava*) and continue in existence in the desire realm, all phenomena of the desire realm cease and phenomena of the desire realm manifest?
Answer:
For all those who relinquish existence in the desire realm and continue in existence in the desire realm, all phenomena of the desire realm cease and phenomena of the desire realm manifest.
There are cases where dharmas of the desire realm cease and dharmas of the desire realm manifest, yet one does not abandon existence in the desire realm, and existence in the desire realm continues.
That is to say:
without passing away, dharmas of the desire realm cease and dharmas of the desire realm manifest.

Is it the case that for all those who relinquish existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and take up a continuity of existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), all phenomena of the desire realm cease and phenomena of the form realm manifest?
Answer:
For all those who relinquish existence in the desire realm and take up a continuity of existence in the form realm, all phenomena of the desire realm cease and phenomena of the form realm manifest.
There are cases where dharmas of the desire realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest, yet one does not abandon existence in the desire realm while existence in the form realm continues.
That is to say:
without passing away, dharmas of the desire realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest.

Is it the case that for all those who abandon existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and continue in existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all phenomena of the desire realm cease and phenomena of the formless realm manifest? Answer: It is so.

If the dharmas of the desire realm cease and the dharmas of the formless realm manifest before one, does that person abandon all existence in the desire realm and continue with existence in the formless realm? Answer: It is so.

Is it the case that for all those who relinquish existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and continue in existence in the realm of form, all phenomena of the realm of form cease and phenomena of the realm of form manifest?
Answer:
For all those who relinquish existence in the realm of form and continue in existence in the realm of form, all phenomena of the realm of form cease and phenomena of the realm of form manifest.
There are cases where dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest, yet one does not relinquish existence in the form realm, and existence in the form realm continues.
That is to say:
without passing away, dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest.

Is it the case that for all those who relinquish existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and continue in existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the desire realm manifest?
Answer:
For all those who relinquish existence in the form realm and continue in existence in the desire realm, all dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the desire realm manifest.
There are cases where dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the desire realm manifest, yet one does not abandon existence in the form realm while existence in the desire realm continues.
That is to say:
without passing away, dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the desire realm manifest.

Regarding all those who abandon existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and continue their existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): do all those for whom the phenomena of the realm of form cease have the phenomena of the formless realm manifest before them? Answer:

For all those who abandon existence in the realm of form and continue their existence in the formless realm, all phenomena of the realm of form cease, and the phenomena of the formless realm manifest before them.

There are cases where dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest, yet one does not relinquish existence in the form realm and existence in the formless realm continues.
That is to say:
without passing away, dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest.

Is it the case that for all those who abandon existence in the formless realm and continue their existence in the formless realm, all dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest?
Answer:

All those who relinquish existence in the formless realm and continue their existence in the formless realm—therein all phenomena of the formless realm cease, and phenomena of the formless realm manifest in the present.

There are cases where dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest, yet one does not relinquish existence in the formless realm, and existence in the formless realm continues.
That is to say:
without passing away, dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest.

Is it the case that for all those who abandon existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and take up a rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the desire realm manifest? Answer: It is so.

If the dharmas of the formless realm cease and the dharmas of the desire realm manifest before one, does that person relinquish all existence in the formless realm and continue in the existence of the desire realm? Answer: It is so.

Is it the case that for all those who relinquish existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and take up a continuity of existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), all dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the realm of form manifest?
Answer:

For all those who relinquish existence in the formless realm and take up a continuity of existence in the realm of form, all dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the realm of form manifest.

There is the cessation of dharmas of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and the manifestation of dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), yet there is no relinquishing of existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*), and existence in the form realm (*rūpabhava*) continues.
That is to say:
without passing away, there is the cessation of dharmas of the formless realm and the manifestation of dharmas of the form realm.
Why do the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm not increase with respect to the phenomena (*dharma*) of the form and formless realms?
Answer: Because the realms would become confused, and it would be impossible to establish [their distinctions].
Because they are free from the defilement of desire.
Why do the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) not increase with respect to the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? Answer:
The realms would then become confused; furthermore,
because those [unconditioned phenomena] are not objects of perception for this [form realm],
why do the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm not increase with respect to the phenomena of the formless realm?
Answer: The realms would become confused and disordered;
furthermore, they could not be known.
Because they are free from attachment to form (*rūparāga*).
Why do the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) not increase with respect to the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)? Answer:
The realms would then become confused,
and because those [dharmas] are not the objects of this [desire].
Why is it that the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm do not increase in accordance with all dharmas of the desire realm?
Answer: This would entail that it is a universal [defilement],
and because those [other objects] are not its object-condition (*ālambana*).
For what reason do the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm not increase in relation to all phenomena of the form realm?
Answer: As previously stated.
The same applies to the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are ten perceptions (*saṃjñā*), namely:
the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*) … up to … the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā*).
If one cultivates the perception of impermanence, does that person contemplate the perception of impermanence?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the perception of impermanence without the mental application of the perception of impermanence;
that is, cultivating the perception of impermanence by taking other phenomena as its object.
There is one who contemplates the perception of impermanence but does not cultivate the perception of impermanence;
that is to say,
taking the perception of impermanence as an object, they cultivate other perceptions.
There is one who cultivates the perception of impermanence and also contemplates the perception of impermanence;
that is to say,
taking the perception of impermanence as an object, they cultivate the perception of impermanence.
There are those who neither cultivate the perception of impermanence nor contemplate the perception of impermanence;
that is to say,
excluding the aforementioned cases.
Just as it is with the perception of impermanence,
so it is with the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, and the perception of non-self in what is suffering.
Other perceptions should also be understood accordingly.
If one gives rise to a thought of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*), does that person contemplate the thought of sensual desire?
Answer: One should formulate this in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is the arising of sensual thought, yet one does not dwell upon that sensual thought;
that is to say,
one gives rise to a sensual thought by taking other phenomena as its object.
There is one who, while contemplating the thought of sensual desire, does not give rise to that thought of sensual desire;
that is to say,
taking the thought of sensual desire as an object, they give rise to another thought.
There is the arising of sensual thought, and one also contemplates sensual thought;
that is to say,
taking sensual thought as an object, one gives rise to sensual thought.
There are those who do not give rise to thoughts of desire, nor do they contemplate thoughts of desire;
that is to say,
excluding the aforementioned cases.

As it is with the thought of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*), so it is with the thought of ill will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*), the thought of harm (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*), the thought of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-vitarka*), the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-harm.
Regarding all phenomena that have ignorance as their cause, do those phenomena have ignorance as their condition?
Answer: If a phenomenon has ignorance as its cause, that phenomenon takes ignorance as its condition.
There are phenomena that take ignorance as their condition but do not have ignorance as their cause.
That is to say:
with the exception of the maturation of ignorance, all other non-obscured neutral formations (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-saṃskāra*) and wholesome formations (*kuśala-saṃskāra*).
If all phenomena have clarity as their cause, do those phenomena have clarity as their condition?
Answer: If a phenomenon has clarity as its cause, that phenomenon has clarity as its condition.
There are phenomena that take light as their object, yet do not depend on light;
namely, the initial light itself.
And as for all contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*):
if various phenomena have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their cause, do those phenomena have clear knowledge (*vidyā*) as their condition? Answer:
If a phenomenon has ignorance as its cause, that phenomenon takes clarity as its condition.
There are phenomena that take clarity as their condition but do not have ignorance as their cause; namely:
Excluding the maturation of ignorance (*avidyā-vipāka*), all other non-obscured neutral formations (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-saṃskāra*) and wholesome formations (*kuśala-saṃskāra*).
If those phenomena have ignorance as their cause, do those phenomena have ignorance as their condition?
Answer: If a phenomenon has ignorance as its cause, that phenomenon takes ignorance as its object.
There are phenomena that take ignorance as their object but do not have ignorance as their cause.
That is to say:
ignorance itself, as well as all contaminated formations.
If various phenomena have ignorance as their cause, are those phenomena unwholesome?
Answer: If a phenomenon is unwholesome, that phenomenon has ignorance as its cause.
However, there are phenomena that have ignorance as their cause but are not unwholesome.
That is to say:
the maturation of ignorance and obscured-unspecified formations.
Are those phenomena which have clarity as their cause necessarily wholesome?
Answer: If a phenomenon is caused by clear knowledge (*vidyā*), that phenomenon is wholesome (*kuśala*).
There are phenomena that are wholesome but are not caused by clear knowledge.
That is to say:
initial illumination and wholesome contaminated formations.
Is there any such dharma?
Is it not the case that those phenomena do not arise because of clarity (*vidyā*), nor because of ignorance (*avidyā*), and thus have no cause?
Answer: Yes, there are.
That is to say:
with the exception of the maturation of ignorance,
all other non-obscured neutral formations.
And at the beginning of the exposition, there are wholesome contaminated formations (*sāsrava-kuśala-saṃskāra*).

The four—perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), knowledge (*vidyā*), and so forth—are included in the categories of those without objects (*anālambana*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), causes (*hetu*), paths (*mārga*), and so on. This chapter shall explain them in detail.
If phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence, are those phenomena associated with the perception of impermanence?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena that arise from the perception of impermanence but are not associated with the perception of impermanence;
namely, those instances where the perception of impermanence is present and necessarily ceasing.
When other perceptions manifest, they necessarily give rise to the mental factors associated with them.
There are phenomena that are associated with the perception of impermanence, yet are not produced by the perception of impermanence; namely:
When other perceptions manifest, they must necessarily cease;
when the perception of impermanence manifests, the factors associated with it must necessarily arise.
There are factors for which the perception of impermanence arises and which are also associated with the perception of impermanence.
That is to say:
when the perception of impermanence manifests, that which is subject to cessation necessarily ceases;
and when the perception of impermanence manifests, those factors associated with it necessarily arise.
There are phenomena that neither arise from the perception of impermanence nor are associated with the perception of impermanence;
namely, other perceptions that are present and must necessarily cease.
When any other perception manifests before one, it will necessarily give rise to the mental states associated with it.
This is true for the perception of impermanence,
and likewise for all others up to the perception of cessation.
If various phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence, do those phenomena share the same object as that perception of impermanence?
Answer: This should be treated according to four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena that arise from the perception of impermanence, yet do not share the same object as the perception of impermanence;
namely, those phenomena which must necessarily cease once the perception of impermanence has become manifest.
When other perceptions manifest and are necessarily produced, they have other conditions.
There are phenomena that share the same object as the perception of impermanence, yet do not give rise to the perception of impermanence. Namely:
