When other perceptions appear before one, they must necessarily cease;
when the perception of impermanence appears before one, it must necessarily arise. For such a person, there exists this condition:
there is a phenomenon wherein the perception of impermanence arises, having the perception of impermanence as its single object-condition.
That is to say:
when the perception of impermanence manifests, that which is certain to perish must cease;
when impermanence manifests, that which is certain to arise must be produced. He possesses these conditions.
There are phenomena that do not arise from the perception of impermanence, nor share the same object as the perception of impermanence;
namely, other perceptions that are present and must necessarily cease.
When other perceptions manifest, they will necessarily arise, provided there are other conditions present.
This is as with the perception of impermanence;
it is the same up to the perception of cessation.
All phenomena arise from the mind; they do not arise apart from the mind.
When the mind arises, do those phenomena arise at that same time? Answer:
The mind arises first, and subsequently that phenomenon.
At the time the mind ceases, does that phenomenon [cease] at that same time? Answer:
The mind ceases first, and subsequently that phenomenon.
At the time the mind is attained, is that phenomenon also attained at that same time? Answer:
The mind is acquired first, and those phenomena afterwards.
At the time when the mind is relinquished, are those phenomena also relinquished at that same time? Answer:
Those dharmas are first abandoned, and only afterwards is the mind [abandoned].
At the time when the mind receives maturation (*vipāka*), at that time do those dharmas [also receive it]? Answer:
Whether at that time or at another time,
is there perhaps any phenomenon (*dharma*) that is thoroughly penetrated and fully known, yet is not to be abandoned, not to be cultivated, and not to be realized?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Regarding space and non-analytical cessation:
is there any phenomenon that is thoroughly penetrated and fully known, yet is neither to be abandoned nor to be cultivated, but is rather to be realized?
Answer: There is. Namely:

Regarding analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): Is there any phenomenon that is something to be thoroughly penetrated (*abhisamita*) and something to be fully known (*parijñeya*), yet is not something to be abandoned (*prahātavya*), but is something to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) and something to be realized (*sākṣātkartavya*)?
Answer: Yes.
There are. That is to say:
untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Is there any phenomenon that is to be thoroughly penetrated, to be fully known, to be abandoned, to be cultivated, or to be realized?
Answer: There is.
That is to say:
wholesome contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*).
Is there any dharma that is thoroughly penetrated (*abhisamita*), fully known (*parijñeya*), abandoned (*prahātavya*), yet is neither cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) nor realized (*sākṣātkartavya*)?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
Regarding the divine eye and ear produced by meditative concentration:
is there any phenomenon that is thoroughly penetrated and fully known, which is to be abandoned, yet is neither to be cultivated nor to be realized?
Answer: There are. Namely:
Excluding the divine eye and ear produced by meditative concentration, there are other indeterminate formations and unwholesome dharmas.

Is there any dharma that has no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), yet is an object-condition for a dharma without an object, arises simultaneously with a dharma without an object, exists, possesses the nature of existence, is not non-existent, does not lack the nature of existence, and is distinct from form, distinct from feeling, perception, and consciousness, and distinct from associated formations?
Answer: There is. That is to say:
The five groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors, as well as the objects of form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind;

and all the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of the group of mental consciousness and its associated factors—these phenomena have no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), they do not take an objectless phenomenon as an object-condition, and they do not arise simultaneously with an objectless phenomenon.
This exists and has existence; it is not non-existent, nor does it lack the nature of existence.
It is distinct from form, distinct from feeling, perception, and consciousness, and distinct from the formations associated with them.
Regarding these phenomena in relation to those phenomena, should one say they are causes?
Should it be said that it is a condition?
Answer: It should be said that it is a cause, and it should be said that it is a condition.
Should this dharma be called wholesome, unwholesome,
or indeterminate?
Answer: Regarding what is wholesome, one should say it is wholesome;
regarding what is unwholesome, one should say it is unwholesome.
Regarding that which is indeterminate, it should be said to be indeterminate.
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in association with this dharma?
How many fetters (saṃyojana) bind it?
Answer: In the three realms, the latent tendencies (anuśaya) increase in accordance with the objects that are tainted (sāsrava). There is bondage by the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
Regarding feeling associated with views (dṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta-vedanā), how many latent tendencies increase?
Answer:

Regarding the objects of the outflows (āsrava) within the three realms and the views (dṛṣṭi) that take the outflow-free as their object, the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of ignorance (avidyā) associated with them increase therein.
As for feeling (vedanā) not associated with those views, how many latent tendencies increase therein?
Answer: With the exception of the outflow-free (anāsrava) objects of vision and the ignorance associated with them, the remaining latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with it.
Regarding the feeling associated with doubt, how many latent dispositions increase in association with it?
Answer:
For the outflow-tainted objects of the three realms that are abandoned by vision, as well as for doubt with untainted objects, the latent tendencies of ignorance associated with them increase.
Regarding the feeling dissociated from doubt, how many latent tendencies increase?
Answer: With the exception of doubt directed toward the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with it, the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.
Regarding the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as causes and paths, how many elements (*dhātu*) do they comprise?
In how many bases (āyatana) and how many aggregates (skandha) is it included? Answer:
The eighteen elements (dhātus),
the twelve bases (āyatanas),
and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Excluding the phenomena associated with perception, feeling, and mind arising from eye-contact, as well as the phenomena dissociated from perception, feeling, and mind arising from ear-contact;
how many elements (*dhātu*) do the remaining phenomena comprise?
How many bases (āyatana)?
How many aggregates (skandha) do they comprise? Answer:
The eighteen elements (dhātus),
the twelve bases (āyatanas),
and the five aggregates (skandhas).

Excluding, furthermore, the factors associated with perception, feeling, and mind that arise from body-contact, as well as the factors dissociated from perception, feeling, and mind that arise from mental-contact;
how many elements (*dhātu*) are these remaining factors?
In how many bases (āyatana) and how many aggregates (skandha) is it included? Answer:
The eighteen elements (dhātus),
the twelve bases (āyatanas),
and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Fascicle Nineteen.
Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty.
Composed by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree:
Wisdom, abandonment, disenchantment, and cultivation; Conditions, contact, pride, karma, and entities;
Inclusion of the remainder and inclusion of all— This chapter shall explain them in full.
If one can penetrate a given matter, does one thereby fully know that matter?
Answer: This should be analyzed in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are matters that can be thoroughly understood but cannot be fully known;
namely, the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, which does not sever the afflictions.
There are instances where one can fully know something but not yet penetrate it;
namely, when the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path sever the afflictions.
There are matters that can be thoroughly penetrated and fully understood;
namely, the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, which sever the afflictions.
There are matters that one cannot fully penetrate nor fully comprehend:
namely, the patiences regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, which do not sever the afflictions.
If a phenomenon can be brought about through weariness with it, can that phenomenon also be abandoned?
Answer: This should be treated in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are instances where one is able to feel revulsion but not yet able to achieve detachment;
that is to say,
the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin do not sever the afflictions.
There are instances where one is able to become detached but not yet able to feel revulsion;
that is to say,
through the patiences and knowledges regarding cessation and the path, one abandons the afflictions.
There are matters that can both cause weariness with and lead to detachment from:
namely, the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin, which sever the afflictions.
There are objects that are neither capable of being weary of nor capable of being detached from;
namely, the receptivities and knowledges regarding cessation and the path, which do not sever the afflictions.
If a thing can induce weariness, is that thing also cultivated as weariness? Answer:
If a thing can induce weariness, that thing is also cultivated as weariness.
There are instances where one cultivates revulsion toward an object but does not possess the capacity for revulsion; that is,
the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, which sever the afflictions.
If a phenomenon can be detached from, is that phenomenon cultivated with revulsion?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are instances where one is able to abandon [defilements] without practicing revulsion;
that is, through the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding cessation and the path, one abandons the afflictions.
There are instances where one cultivates revulsion but is not yet able to become detached;
that is to say,
when through the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin, one does not abandon the afflictions.
There are matters that can be abandoned through cultivation of revulsion; namely:
the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin, as well as the knowledge of cessation and the path, which sever the afflictions.
There are instances where there is neither detachment nor the cultivation of revulsion;
namely, the patience and knowledge regarding cessation and the path, which do not sever the afflictions.
If a phenomenon acts as a cause for another phenomenon, is there ever a time when this phenomenon is not a cause for that one?
Answer: There is no time when it is not a cause.
If a phenomenon acts as the equal-and-immediate condition for another phenomenon, is there ever a time when this phenomenon is not the equal-and-immediate condition for that one?
Answer: Yes;
when this phenomenon has already arisen but has not yet reached [the state of being] that [condition].
If a phenomenon serves as an object-condition for another phenomenon, is there ever a time when this phenomenon is not its object-condition?
Answer: There is never a time when it is not its object-condition.
If a phenomenon acts as a dominant condition for another phenomenon, is there ever a time when this phenomenon is not a dominant condition for that one?
Answer: There is never a time when it is not a dominant condition.
Are all instances of mental contact (manas-saṃsparśa) necessarily contacts arising from the conjunction of the three?
Answer: All instances of mental contact are necessarily contacts arising from the conjunction of the three.
There is contact through the conjunction of the three that is not mental contact;
namely, contact associated with the five groups of consciousness.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Bhikṣus! You should know that there is the element of mind, the element of phenomena, and the element of ignorance.”
Because they are touched by the feeling born of contact with ignorance, the unlearned and foolish person clings to existence, clings to non-existence, or clings to both existence and non-existence.
Regarding all forms of conceit, are they all instances of self-clinging?
Answer: All forms of conceit (*māna*) are instances of self-clinging (*svābhiniveśa*).
However, there is self-clinging that is not conceit, namely:
Because of these various views,
the Blessed One said:
"O Bhikṣus!..."
One should know this:
"I" is grasped as self, and "mine" is grasped as belonging to the self.
Are all forms of conceit entirely non-quiescent?
Answer: All forms of conceit are entirely non-quiescent.
However, there are states that are non-quiescent but are not conceit; namely:
Because other afflictions manifest,
the Blessed One said:
"O Bhikṣus!..."
"You should know:
those who move are bound by Māra; those who do not move are liberated from evil. Are all karmas non-restraint?
Answer: This should be treated as four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are karmas that are not non-restraint (asaṃvara).
That is to say:
there is restraint of body and speech that is non-restraint but not karma. Namely:
There are faculties that are non-restraint,
and there is also karma that is non-restraint; namely:
There are cases of non-restraint of body and speech that are neither karma nor non-restraint; namely:
Regarding the restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*): Are all karmas that [restraint]? Answer:
One should formulate four propositions.
There is karma that is not discipline (avijñapti).
That is to say:
There are instances of non-restraint of body and speech that are not karma.
That is to say:
Restraint of the sense faculties.
There is also action that is restraint, namely:
There are physical and vocal restraints.
There are also those that are neither karma nor restraint, namely:
Regarding the non-restraint of the faculties:
if a particular object has not yet been acquired, is that [non-restraint] not accomplished?
Answer: Yes.
If a thing has not been acquired, it is not accomplished.
However, there are cases where a thing is not accomplished even though it has been acquired.
That is to say:
Attained, yet lost. If a thing has already been attained, is it accomplished? Answer:
If a matter is accomplished, it has already been attained.
There are matters that have already been attained but are not yet accomplished; namely:
Acquired and then lost.
Excluding the Noble Truth of Suffering and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), one sphere, and one aggregate (*skandha*).
The same applies to the teaching regarding the noble truth of the origin and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Excluding the noble truth of cessation and the sphere of phenomena,
the remaining factors are subsumed under seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
The same applies to the explanation regarding the Noble Truth of the Path and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Excluding material phenomena and the sphere of mental objects,
the remaining phenomena are subsumed under seven elements (*dhātu*), one sphere, and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Excluding formless phenomena (*ārūpya-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Excluding visible phenomena (*sanidarśana-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects.
Other dharmas are subsumed under sixteen elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha).
Excluding the invisible dharmas and the dharma-base (dharmāyatana),
the remaining dharmas are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate.
Excluding the resistant dharmas and the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
the remaining dharmas are subsumed under seven elements (dhātus), one sphere, and one aggregate (skandha).
Excluding the non-resistant dharmas and the sphere of mental objects.
Other phenomena are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Excluding contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and the base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed under two elements, one base, and one aggregate.
Excluding the untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects.
Excluding all dharmas, to inquire about other dharmas is a groundless and empty discourse.
Excluding unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining dharmas are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding past phenomena and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
The same explanation applies when excluding future and present phenomena, as well as the sphere of mental objects.
Excluding wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
The same explanation applies when excluding unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*) and the sphere of phenomena.
Excluding indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The remaining phenomena are subsumed under nine elements (*dhātu*), three spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects.
Other phenomena are subsumed under thirteen elements, nine bases, and two aggregates.
Excluding phenomena bound to the form realm and the base of mental objects,
other phenomena are subsumed under seventeen elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates.

Excluding the factors bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), the factors of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), the factors beyond training (*aśaikṣa-dharma*), and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), the explanation is likewise.
Excluding the factors that are neither of training nor beyond training (*naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa-dharma*) and the sphere of phenomena.
Other phenomena are subsumed under two elements, one base, and one aggregate.
Excluding phenomena abandoned by vision and the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
other phenomena are subsumed under seventeen elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates.
Excluding the factors abandoned through cultivation and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining factors are subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), one sphere, and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Excluding the factors that are not to be abandoned and the sphere of mental objects...
Other phenomena are subsumed under seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha).
Excluding phenomena that have already arisen and those that are destined never to arise,
other phenomena are subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
Except for dharmas already arisen and those determined not to arise—this excludes all dharmas while one asks about other dharmas; this is a groundless and empty discourse.
[This applies] except for material dharmas (*rūpadharma*) and those determined not to arise.
Other phenomena are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates.
Excluding formless phenomena and those phenomena that are determined not to arise,
the remaining phenomena are subsumed under eleven elements, eleven bases, and one aggregate.
Excluding visible phenomena (*sanidarśana-dharma*) and those phenomena that are necessarily non-arising,
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding invisible phenomena (*anidarśana-dharma*) and those phenomena that are necessarily non-arising...
Other dharmas are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate.
Excluding obstructive dharmas and those dharmas that are determined not to arise,
the remaining dharmas are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and five aggregates.
Excluding non-obstructive phenomena (*apratigha-dharma*) and phenomena that are necessarily non-arising,
the remaining phenomena are subsumed under ten elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Excluding contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and phenomena that are necessarily non-arising...
The remaining dharmas are subsumed within the three realms, the two bases, and the five aggregates.
Excluding the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and those dharmas that are determined never to arise,
the remaining dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates.
Excluding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and those phenomena that are definitely not to arise—this excludes all phenomena;
yet to ask about "remaining phenomena" [under such conditions] is a groundless and empty argument.
Excluding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) and those phenomena that are definitely not to arise.
The remaining dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
The same explanation applies when excluding past dharmas, present dharmas, and those dharmas that are determined never to arise.
Excluding future dharmas and those dharmas that are determined not to arise—this excludes all dharmas and yet you inquire about "remaining dharmas"; this is a groundless and empty argument.
Excluding wholesome dharmas and those dharmas that are determined not to arise.
The remaining dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
The same applies to the explanation regarding unwholesome dharmas and those dharmas that are determined never to arise.
Excluding indeterminate dharmas and those dharmas that are determined never to arise,
the remaining dharmas are subsumed within ten elements, four bases, and five aggregates.
Excluding dharmas bound to the desire realm and those dharmas that are determined never to arise...
Other dharmas are subsumed within fourteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding those dharmas bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and those dharmas that are definitely not to arise,
the remaining dharmas are subsumed within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.

The same applies to the teaching regarding the exclusion of factors bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*), factors of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), factors beyond training (*aśaikṣa-dharma*), and factors that are definitely not to arise (*aniyatānutpatti-dharma*).
This also applies to the exclusion of factors that are neither of training nor beyond training (*naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa-dharma*) and factors that are definitely not to arise.
Other dharmas are subsumed under the three realms, the two bases, and the five aggregates.
Excluding those dharmas abandoned by insight and those dharmas that are determined never to arise,
the remaining dharmas are subsumed under the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
Excluding those dharmas abandoned through cultivation and those dharmas that are definitively non-arising,
the remaining dharmas are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates.
Excluding those dharmas that are not to be abandoned and those dharmas that are definitively non-arising.
The remaining phenomena consist of the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Is there perhaps one element, one base, or one aggregate that encompasses all phenomena?
Answer: There is. One realm refers to:
The dharma-element.
One base refers to the mind-base (manāyatana).
The one aggregate refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
[Therein lie] the views of wrong abandonment and wrong permanence, as well as the views of wrong morality and wrong observances, and wrong permanence.
The six views, the five [types of] nirvāṇa, the nine types of pride,
and the deluded attachment to the permanence [of self] and the agency of self and others; upon awakening, both are non-existent,
yet one possesses pride, attainment, and so forth— this chapter I pray you explain in full.
Those who hold such views as:

"There is no giving, no offering of affection, no sacrifice; there is no wholesome conduct and no unwholesome conduct"—this is a false view that denies causality, which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin [of suffering].
"There is no fruit of wholesome or unwholesome conduct"—
this is the false view that denies the fruit, which is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
"There is no this world, there is no other world, and there are no beings born by transformation."
— This is either abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
"There is no father, there is no mother"—
this is the false view that denies causes (*hetu-apavāda-mithyādṛṣṭi*), which is abandoned through the vision of origination.
Those who hold the view that "there are no arhats in the world"—
this is a false view that slanders the Path, and it is abandoned through the vision of the Path.
There is no right attainment.
This is the false view that slanders cessation; it is abandoned through the vision of cessation.

There is no right practice regarding this world and the next, such that one knows for oneself in this very life, attains realization, and dwells in its fulfillment, knowing as it truly is: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
This is a false view that slanders the Path, abandoned through the vision of the Path.
It is the view held by those who think:
"As long as a living being exists, once it has died, it is annihilated and ceases to be."

When this person composed of the four great elements dies, the earth-body returns to earth, the water-body returns to water, the fire-body returns to fire, and the wind-body returns to wind; the sense-faculties follow along with space, and the bier serves as the fifth, carrying that corpse away to be discarded in the cemetery. Before it is burned, it can still be recognized; once burned, it becomes ashes, leaving behind only bones the color of pigeons.
The fool praises giving, while the wise person praises receiving.

All those who maintain the theory of existence speak nothing but empty falsehoods; they claim that both fools and the wise exist as long as they live, but once dead, they are annihilated and cease to be.
This view of extremes is subsumed under the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
It refers to those who hold this view:
that there is no cause and no condition for the defilement of sentient beings.
"There is defilement of sentient beings without cause and without condition"—
this is the false view of denying causes, which is abandoned by the vision of the origin [of suffering].
"There is purification of sentient beings without cause and without condition";
Sentient beings are purified without cause and without condition—this is the false view of slandering the Path, which is abandoned by the vision of the Path.
That there is no cause and no condition that renders sentient beings ignorant and without vision; [this is the false view of slandering the Path].
It is not that there are no causes and no conditions, yet sentient beings lack wisdom and vision.
This is the wrong view of denying causes; it is abandoned by the vision of the origin [of suffering].
It is not that there are no causes and no conditions that bring about wisdom and vision in sentient beings.
"There is no cause and no condition, yet sentient beings possess wisdom and vision"—
this is a false view that slanders the Path, abandoned by the vision of the Path.
For those who hold this view:

They are without power, without diligence, without the power of diligence; they are without a person, without majesty, without the majesty of a person; they are without self-creation, without other-creation, and without creation by both self and other. All sentient beings, all births, and all species are without power, without sovereignty, without diligence, and without majesty; being fixedly subject to the transformation of their inherent nature, they experience various forms of suffering and pleasure within the six superior realms of birth.
This wrong view:
if it slanders the power of the out-flowing (sāsrava) forces, diligence, and so forth,
then it is a wrong view that slanders the cause, which is abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya).
If one slanders the untainted powers, diligence, and so forth,
this constitutes the false view of slandering the Path, which is abandoned through the vision of the Path.
All those who hold such a view:

They commit acts themselves or incite others to do so; they cook or incite others to cook; they harm or incite others to harm; they kill various sentient beings, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods knowingly, and intentionally drink intoxicants;
they break through walls and untie knots to seize all that belongs to others;
they guard passes and block roads, destroying villages, destroying cities, and destroying the lives of nations.

With swords and wheels, one might seize and ravage the great earth, cutting, severing, and dismembering all sentient beings therein, piling them up and heaping them together into a single mass of flesh;
yet it should be known that by this, no evil is produced, nor any cause for evil.
If one were to cut, sever, and beat beings on the south bank of the Ganges,
while simultaneously practicing generosity and cultivating merit on the north bank of the Ganges, you should know that because of this,
there would be neither sin nor merit, nor any conditions for sin or merit.
The four means of attraction—generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—do not bring about any merit when used to gather sentient beings.
This is a slanderous view based on false views, abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
There are those who hold this view:
"These seven classes of beings—uncreated and not made by a creator, unevolved and not evolved by a transformer, indestructible, eternally abiding—stand as firm as an *īṣikā* reed;
they remain unmoving, undergo no transformation, and do not interact with one another."
What are the seven? They are:
earth, water, fire, wind, as well as suffering, pleasure, and life.
These seven constituent elements of the person are uncreated, and so forth, remaining as immovable as a mountain peak (*īṣāka*).
Whether it be demerit, merit, or both; whether it be suffering, pleasure, or both—none can transform them, nor can they cause them to obstruct one another.

Suppose a person were to cut off another person’s head; this would still not be called harming a living being of the world. Whether walking or standing, within the interval of the seven bodies, although the blade may turn, it does not harm life.
In this, there is no one who can harm and no object to be harmed; there is no one who can strike and no object to be struck; there is no manifestation and no locus of manifestation.
This view of extremes is subsumed under eternalism and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Regarding those who hold this view:
there are fourteen billion, sixty thousand, six hundred gateways to rebirth, as well as five types of karma, three types of karma, and two types of karma.
One karma and half a karma; sixty-two modes of conduct; sixty-two intermediate kalpas; one hundred and thirty-six hells;
one hundred and twenty faculties; thirty-six realms of dust; forty-nine thousand families of nāgas;
forty-nine thousand families of garuḍas; forty-nine thousand families of heterodox practitioners.
There are forty-nine thousand families of livelihoods: seven treasuries of perception, seven treasuries of non-perception, and seven treasuries of detachment;
seven asuras, seven piśācas, seven devas, and seven humans;
seven dreams and seven hundred dreams; seven awakenings and seven hundred awakenings; seven ponds and seven hundred ponds.
The seven perils and seven hundred perils; the seven decreases and seven hundred decreases; the seven increases and seven hundred increases;

the six classes of superior rebirths; and the eight stages of the great beings—within these states, for eighty-four thousand great kalpas, whether foolish or wise, one wanders and transmigrates back and forth until one is finally able to bring an end to suffering.
The limit is like throwing a ball of thread: when the thread is exhausted, it comes to rest.
Within this, there is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can say otherwise.

"By means of ethical discipline, or by means of diligence, or by means of the holy life, I cause all karma that has not yet ripened to ripen; once it has ripened, upon contact, it is immediately vomited out."
By thus weighing the limits of birth and death, and of suffering and pleasure, they cannot be established as having increase or decrease, nor can it be said whether they are so or not.

This is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is the misapprehension of what is not a cause as a cause; it is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
It consists of those who hold this view: "Whatever is experienced by all persons (*pudgala*) and individuals (*sattva*) has no cause other than past actions (*pūrvakṛta*)."
This is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which takes what is not a cause to be a cause; it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).

It consists of those who hold this view: "Whatever is experienced by all persons (*puruṣa*) and individuals (*pudgala*), there is nothing that does not have the transformations of Īśvara as its cause."

This is not taking what is non-causal to be a cause; it is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
It refers to those who hold this view: "Whatever is experienced by all persons (*puruṣa*) and individuals (*pudgala*) is entirely without cause and without condition."
This slander arises from false view and is abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
There are those who hold such views:
that pleasure and pain are created by oneself, that pleasure and pain are created by another, or that pleasure and pain are created by both oneself and another.
This is not the view of grasping at precepts and observances that takes what is not a cause to be a cause; it is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
It refers to those who hold this view:
"The suffering and pleasure one experiences are neither self-made nor made by another; they arise without cause."
—This slander arises from wrong view and is abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
Those who hold this view:
"The self and the world are eternal, permanent, stable, unchanging by nature, and remain exactly as they are."
This extreme view is subsumed under the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Those who hold this view think:
"Because it is real and because it persists, there is a self; there is what belongs to a self."
—This is the view of extremes, subsumed under the view of permanence, and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Those who hold this view:
"The self exists as a reality and as something enduring; there is no non-self."
—This is an extreme view (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) subsumed under the view of nihilism (ucchedadṛṣṭi), which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya).
Those who hold this view say:
"I perceive the self; the eye and form are the self."
—This is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Those who hold this view:
"I perceive the non-self as the self; the eye is the self, and visible forms are its requisites."
This view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Those who hold this view—
viewing what is non-self as a self— assert that "form is the self" and that "the eye is the instrument [of the self]."
This view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Those who hold this view think:

"This is my self; this is a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-principle (*jīva*), a living being (*jantu*), a nourisher (*poṣa*), a person (*pudgala*), a mind-born (*manuja*), a human (*mānava*), an agent (*kartṛ*), an instigator (*vedaka*), a producer (*janaka*), a procreator (*saṃjanaka*), a speaker (*vaktṛ*), a knower (*boddhṛ*), and an experiencer (*pratisaṃvedaka*); it has not been non-existent in the past, nor will it be non-existent in the future; having performed wholesome or unwholesome karma in various places, it experiences the ripening of the fruit (*vipāka*) in various places."
To abandon these aggregates and continue into other aggregates—

this is the eternalist view (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) subsumed under the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*). Those who hold this view:
To experience the five sublime sensual pleasures is called attaining the foremost *nirvāṇa* in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*).
This is the view of grasping at inferior dharmas as superior (*hīnagrahābhiniveśadṛṣṭi*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Those who hold this view:

"Having abandoned sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one enters and dwells in the first dhyāna; this is called attaining the first nibbāna in the present life."

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind, being without applied or sustained thought, and possessing the joy and happiness born of concentration, one enters and dwells in the second dhyāna; this is called attaining the first nirvāṇa in the present life.

Detached from joy, one dwells in equanimity, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension; experiencing bliss with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare, "One who is equanimous and mindful dwells in bliss," one enters and abides in the third dhyāna, fully endowed with it; this is called attaining the first nirvāṇa in the present life.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, one enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness; this is called attaining the first nirvāṇa in the present life.
This grasping of inferior phenomena as superior is the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
There are nine types of pride (*māna*):

namely, "I am superior," "I am equal," "I am inferior"; "there is one superior to me," "there is one equal to me," "there is one inferior to me"; "there is no one superior to me," "there is no one equal to me," and "there is no one inferior to me."
"I am superior" refers to the pride of overestimation arising from views.
"I am equal" refers to the pride arising from views.
"I am inferior" refers to the pride of self-deprecation arising from views.
To think "there is one superior to me" is conceit arising from the view of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
To think "there is one equal to me" is conceit arising from the view of equality (*māna*).
To think "there is one inferior to me" is overweening conceit arising from the view of superiority (*adhimāna*).
"I have no superior"—this is conceit arising from [false] views.
"I am equal to those who are equal to me"—this is overweening conceit arising from [false] views.
"I am not inferior to those who are superior to me"—this is inferiority conceit arising from [false] views.
Those who hold this view:

that the wind does not blow, rivers do not flow, fire does not burn, milk does not curdle, the womb does not conceive, and the sun and moon neither rise nor set; that defilement and purity abide in their own nature without increasing or decreasing.
This extreme view is subsumed under the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) and is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Sentient beings cling to the notion that 'I' am the agent; likewise, they cling to the notion that 'another' is the agent."
What is the meaning of the statement that "each [of these] cannot be observed and known as they truly are"? Answer:
“Sentient beings” refers to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
They hold this view: “I am the agent; I am the progenitor; I am the transformer.”
Therefore it is said:
"Sentient beings grasp at the self as the agent.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who grasp that "another can act, another can produce, and another can transform."
Therefore it is said:
"The same applies to the grasping of another's action. "Each" means:
Each one is not all. "Arrow" refers to evil views,
because they can pierce and wound.
Regarding these views, they are unable to perceive them as they truly are—that they are arrows.
One should observe that this is an arrow; when sentient beings are firmly attached in this way, there is neither "I who act" nor "another who acts."
"Regarding 'one should contemplate this as an arrow':
it means that one should contemplate and understand this view as it truly is—an actual poisoned arrow, for it serves as the precursor to old age, sickness, and death."
Regarding the phrase "sentient beings are firmly attached":
"sentient beings" refers to those of external paths; within their respective views and inclinations, they are firmly attached and unable to achieve liberation.

If one can thus observe and know things as they truly are, then there will no longer be the grasping that "I am the creator," "I am the progenitor," or "I am the transformer," nor will there be the grasping that "another is the creator," "another is the progenitor," or "another is the transformer."
Sentient beings possessed of pride, Attached to pride and bound by pride,
Opposed in their views and unable to transcend birth and death. "Those possessed of pride" indicates that they have accomplished the seven types of pride.
"Sentient beings" refers to those of external paths (tīrthikas).
Because they are attached to, excessively attached to, and universally attached to the seven types of pride, they are said to be "attached to pride."
Because it binds, binds extensively, and binds universally, it is called the "bond of pride" (*māna-bandhana*).
Regarding the phrase "contrary to views":
this refers to the categories of the views of annihilationism and eternalism, which are mutually opposed.
"Those who do not transcend birth and death" refers to those who,
within the beginningless cycle of birth and death, are unable to cross over and attain nirvāṇa.
Both those who have attained [the goal] and those who are yet to attain it are defiled by the inferior training of mere ritual precepts and ascetic observances.
The first side is the suffering of the Brahma-world; the second is the purity of those who indulge in sensual desires.
Seeing that they are not free from extreme sinking or wandering, the one with clear vision perceives their difference.
Being without the conceit of being dust-free, he cuts off the path and reaches the end of suffering.
"Attained" (*prāpta*) means:
it indicates that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) have already been attained.
"To be attained" (*prāptavya*) means:
This demonstrates that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases have not yet been attained.
Regarding "dusty together":
these two are both dusted, thoroughly dusted, and intensely dusted by greed, hatred, and delusion.
"Inferior" has two meanings:
first, it refers to the sick; second, it refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Here, non-Buddhists are described as inferior because they study according to this [teaching]; hence, they are called "inferior learners."
He speaks as follows:

"All individuals who train in riding elephants, horses, boats, chariots, and palanquins; who handle bows, staves, hooks, wheels, lassos, writing, seals, and arithmetic—making them all skillful therein—thereby attain purification, liberation, and transcendence, reaching the end of suffering and pleasure."

"This is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that regards what is not a cause as a cause; it is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*). Regarding "rules":
there are certain non-Buddhists who give rise to this view and establish this doctrine:

"Various individuals uphold the vows of oxen, deer, dogs, naked ascetics, and so forth, and by means of these, they attain purification, liberation, and transcendence, reaching the end of suffering and pleasure."
"This is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that takes what is not a cause to be a cause; it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding "observances" (*vratas*):
there are certain non-Buddhists who give rise to this view and establish this doctrine:

"Various individuals observe the crows' vow, the owls' vow, the silence vow, and so forth; by means of these, they attain purification, liberation, and transcendence, reaching the end of suffering and pleasure."

"This is the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) that falsely regards what is not a cause as a cause; it is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). As for 'bathing':
there are certain non-Buddhists who give rise to this view and establish this doctrine:"

"Various individuals bathe in the three pools of Manaḥśa, Vimanāśa, and Gaṅgādvāra; by means of this, they attain purification, liberation, and transcendence, reaching the end of suffering and pleasure."

"This is the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) that regards what is not a cause as a cause; it is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
'Brahman' refers to the holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
There are certain non-Buddhists who give rise to this view and establish this doctrine:

"When individuals practice the holy life and remain far removed from sexual desire, they thereby attain purification, liberation, and transcendence, reaching the ultimate limit of suffering and pleasure."
"This is the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) which regards what is not a cause as a cause; it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha).
'Suffering' here refers to ascetic practices."
There are certain non-Buddhists who give rise to this view and establish this doctrine:
"When individuals undergo various ascetic practices, by means of these they attain purification, liberation, and transcendence, reaching the ultimate limit of suffering and pleasure."
"This is the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) that regards what is not a cause as a cause; it is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
'Service' (vastu) means attending upon."
There are certain non-Buddhists who give rise to this view and establish this doctrine:

"By taming elephants, horses, and oxen, and by serving the sun, moon, stars, fire, jewels, medicinal herbs, and so forth, individuals thereby attain purification, liberation, and transcendence, reaching the end of suffering and pleasure."
"This is the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) which regards what is not a cause as a cause; it is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
'One extreme' refers to that which was mentioned above: namely, the extreme of asceticism (duṣkaracaryā)."
Regarding "purity through the enjoyment of sensual desires":
there are certain non-Buddhists who give rise to this view and establish this doctrine:
"All sensual desires are pure and wonderful; their joyful enjoyment is without fault."
“This grasping at inferior dharmas as superior is the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
As for “the second”: this refers to what has been described as the extreme of indulgence in pleasure (*sukhallikānta*).
"Non-seeing" refers to the various non-Buddhists who do not see the two extremes as they truly are.
"Utterly sinking and running" means:
This refers to those non-Buddhists who, due to their lack of vision:
one class gives rise to craving and is thus called "extremely sunken";
another class gives rise to views and is thus called "extremely running."
Furthermore, one class is characterized by indolence and is therefore called "extreme sinking";
another class is characterized by restlessness and is therefore called "extreme wandering."
Furthermore,
one class gives rise to pride, and is thus called "extremely sunken";
another class gives rise to overweening pride.
Therefore, it is called "running to the utmost.
Regarding "seen by those with clear eyes":
"clear eyes" refers to the Buddha and his disciples.
"Vision" refers to knowing and seeing,
as they truly are, the two extremes mentioned above.
"Able to differ" means:

Because of knowing and seeing things as they truly are, one does not fall into those extremes of excessive sinking or excessive wandering, for one is able to avoid giving rise to craving, views, and so forth.
"Therein there is no dust" means that regarding the aggregates,
elements, and sense-fields— both those already attained and those not yet attained— one does not give rise to the dust of greed, hatred, and delusion.
"Being without pride therein" means that although one has distanced oneself from both extremes, the mind does not rely upon [that achievement].
"Cutting off the path" means:
If one can act in this way, one severs the three paths, namely: afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*).
Regarding the phrase "reaching the end of suffering":
"suffering" refers to the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
"Limit" (*anta*) refers to *nirvāṇa*.
If one cuts off the three paths, one will reach the limit of this mass of suffering.
Seeing the Brahma-father, the Victorious Net, the chariot is originally set in motion by faith.
The Mother, the King, Wisdom, Liberation, and the Faculties— may this chapter be fully explained so that those who have seen may see;
that those who have seen and those who have not yet seen may see, and that those who have not seen and those who have already seen may likewise see.
"Those who have already seen" refers to those who have already seen suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
"Able to see what has been seen and what has not yet been seen" means:
This means that they are able to see others who have already seen, as well as those who have not yet seen, the suffering, its origin,
its cessation, and the path. "Those who have not seen" refers to those who have not yet seen suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

"Neither seeing what has not been seen, nor what has already been seen" means that he does not see other instances of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path that have not yet been seen, nor those that have already been seen.
"One should not harm a brahmin, nor should one abandon him;
whether one harms him or abandons him, both are censured by those who possess worldly wisdom.
Regarding "one should not harm a brahmin": [this refers to...]
"Brahmin" refers to an Arhat; that is to say, one should not harm an Arhat with one's hands, clods of earth, knives, or staves.
"Nor should one abandon them" means:
That is to say, one should respectfully provide an arhat with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessary requisites, and should not neglect or abandon them.
Regarding the phrase, "If one harms them or abandons them, both are censured by those of worldly wisdom":

this means that if one harms an Arhat with one's hand, a clod of earth, or the like, or if one abandons them and fails to honor or support them, both acts are condemned and reviled by all wise people in the world.
"Having perversely harmed one's parents, a king, and two who are learned;
having destroyed a kingdom and its followers—such a person is an unimpeded [transgressor], surpassing even a brahmin.
Regarding "having perversely harmed one's parents, a king, and two who are learned": [this refers to...]
"Mother" is a metaphor for "craving," because it gives birth [to existence].
As the Blessed One said:
"Born from craving, O man, you run about driven by the mind."
"Sentient beings dwell in birth and death, / Suffering is their great terror.
Here, "father" is a metaphor for "outflow-tainted karma" (*sāsrava-karma*), because it is that which draws [beings] [into existence].
As the Blessed One said:

“Monks! It is because sentient beings create wholesome, out-flowing karma produced through cultivation that they are born there and experience its ripened fruit; therefore, I say that they proceed according to their karma.”
"King" is a metaphor for "consciousness with grasping" (*sopādāna-vijñāna*).
As the Blessed One said:
"The sixth is the sovereign king; when it is defiled, it takes defilement as its own."
"Though unstained, they appear stained. Regarding "stained," it refers to the foolish commoner.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "O Bhikṣus!"
"You should know:
when I speak of the city lord, this refers to the consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*).
'The two types of much-hearing' are metaphors for the 'clinging to views' (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the 'clinging to precepts and observances' (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)."

Just as two learned men—one a ritualist and one a silent ascetic—might engage in play together amidst filth and impurity, so too do these two types of grasping regard tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as supreme and preeminent, or else as pure, liberated, and transcendent.
Because one abandons and forever severs craving, karma, consciousness, and grasping, it is called "counter-attack.
"Country" is a metaphor for "afflictions" (*kleśa*).
"Concomitants" are a metaphor for "the associated discursive thoughts and investigations" (*vitarka-vicāra*) that correspond to them.
"Execution" (zhū) means to execute and slay.
Because one abandons and eternally severs afflictions (*kleśa*) and discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is called "execution."
Regarding "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*):
there are three kinds of "impediments," namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because one has already abandoned and fully understood these three, it is called "unimpeded."
"Transcending" means emerging.
Because it is unimpeded, it emerges and transcends the three realms.
Because they have forever eliminated unwholesome dharmas, they are called "Brahmins.
As the World-Honored One said:
"The Buddha dwells constantly in right mindfulness, wandering and transforming throughout the world."
"One who has extinguished evil dharmas and exhausted all fetters is therefore called a brahmin.
One who has slain their father and mother, the king, the two learned ones,
and the fifth enemy, the tiger— such a person is said to be pure."
Regarding the meaning of the first half of this verse, it is as previously explained.
"Tiger" is a metaphor for the "entanglement of hatred.
Just as the nature of a tiger is violent, cruel, and fierce, devouring flesh and blood; so too is this entanglement.
The obsession with anger (*pratigha-paryavasthāna*) is likewise violent, cruel, and treacherous, destroying all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

"The fifth enemy" is a metaphor for the fifth of the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*), or it is a metaphor for the fifth of the five fetters conducive to the lower realms (*pañcāvarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
Because they have abandoned and forever severed [defilements], it is called "removal.
Because such a person has forever severed greed, hatred, and delusion, it is called "purity."

This refers to those afflictions that have already been abandoned and fully understood.
Among them, some are further surpassed, while others are not further surpassed. Which ones are further surpassed?
That is to say:
one who has already severed the afflictions but later regresses.
Who would not surpass such a person?
That is to say:
one who has already severed the afflictions and does not regress.
The phrase "no further superiority" distinguishes this from those who might attain further superiority.
"Having triumphed, there is nothing to follow" means that if afflictions have not been abandoned and fully understood, one will continue to circulate and transmigrate through the three realms;
since all afflictions have already been abandoned and fully understood, there is nothing to follow.
Regarding the phrase "The Buddha’s conduct is boundless":

it means that the World-Honored Buddha has attained the realization of the wisdom and vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the clear awakening of *bodhi*, and the manifest penetration of wisdom; because he has brought these to fulfillment and accomplishment, he is called "Buddha."
The four foundations of mindfulness are called "the practice of the Buddha.
Since these four foundations of mindfulness have both modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects of focus (*ālambana*) that are without limit, they are called "boundless" (*ananta*).
Regarding the phrase "Without traces, by what means does one go?":
"Traces" refers to footprints, which here serve as a metaphor for "afflictions" (*kleśa*).
If these afflictions have not been severed or fully understood, one proceeds through them toward the evil destinies within the three realms.
Since all afflictions have already been abandoned and fully understood, there is no means by which he could go.
No nets can be spread; what can craving lead? The Buddha’s range of action is boundless;
since he leaves no tracks, by what way could he go?
Regarding the phrase "no nets may be spread":
"net" is a metaphor for "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
As the Blessed One said:
"I say that the net of craving covers the groves and ponds.
If craving has not been abandoned and fully understood, it can spread its snares throughout the three realms;
since it has already been abandoned and fully understood, it cannot be spread."
Regarding the phrase "Craving has nowhere to lead":
if craving has not been abandoned and fully understood, it can lead one toward the three realms;
since it has already been abandoned and fully understood, there is nowhere for it to lead.
The meaning of the latter half of the verse is as explained previously:
"One whose carriage is destroyed and whose ropes are severed, who has crossed the stream, followed along,
and traversed the trench— only such a one in the world is called a *brahmin*."
Regarding the phrase "the chariot has been destroyed, the ropes severed, and the flow along with its attendants [ceased]":
"chariot" is a metaphor for "ego-conceit" (asmimāna);
"ropes" is a metaphor for "craving" (tṛṣṇā).
Just as the load carried by a cart is elevated because of the cart,
and is transported to a distant destination because it is bound and held by ropes,
so too it is with sentient beings: they are elevated because of pride, and because they are bound and held by craving, they wander through birth and death.
"Flowing forth" (*anusrotas*) is a metaphor for "all afflictions" (*sarvakleśa*).
"Following along" (*anugata*) is a metaphor for "the vitarka and vicāra associated with them.
Having severed and fully understood the vitarka and vicāra associated with the afflictions of pride (*māna*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is called "severed and destroyed."
Regarding "crossing the moat":
"moat" is a metaphor for "ignorance" (*avidyā*); because it has been severed and fully understood, it is called "crossed.
As the Blessed One said:
"What is it called 'having already crossed the moat'? It means having completely abandoned and fully understood ignorance.
Regarding the phrase "In the world, only the Buddha is called a *brahmin*":
the meanings of "Buddha" and "*brahmin*" are as explained previously.
In all the worlds, only the Buddha may be called a true brahmin;
for it is only the Unsurpassed Awakened One who can eternally extinguish all unwholesome dharmas.
One root, two eddies, three stains, and five currents of transmigration.
The Great Ocean and its twelve perils— The Muni has already crossed them all.
"Single root": this is a metaphor for "ignorance" (*avidyā*), for it is the fundamental cause of birth and death.
As the Blessed One said:
"All evil destinies, both in this world and in future births,
have ignorance as their root, with sensual desire and so forth acting as their support."
"The two eddies" is a metaphor for "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*),
because it is difficult for sentient beings to emerge from within them.
The "three impurities" refer to the impurities of greed, hatred,
and delusion. The "five flows" refer to:
This is a metaphor for the "five destinies" (*pañca-gati*),
because sentient beings constantly transmigrate within them.
As for the "great ocean":
This is an analogy for the "six internal bases.
As for "twelve," it refers to the twelve aspects.
This metaphor refers to the six internal and six external bases (*āyatana*).
"Precipice" refers to a steep pit,
which is a metaphor for "all afflictions" (*kleśa*).
Regarding the phrase "The Munis have all crossed over":
there are two kinds of "Munis"— first, those in training (śaikṣa),
and second, those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Those in training (śaikṣa) are on the path toward perfect deliverance; those beyond training (aśaikṣa) have already attained deliverance.
Lacking faith and ignorant of gratitude, they sever intimacy and find no room for it;
constantly longing for change and revulsion—such is the supreme man.
"Those without faith" refers to arhats.
Regarding the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths, they have all personally realized and known them; they do not rely on the words of others.
Regarding "not knowing gratitude":
"gratitude" refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it possesses functional activity.
Nirvāṇa is called "non-gratitude"; since the Arhats possess superior wisdom and vision and know it to be non-gratitude, they are said to be "not knowing gratitude."
Regarding "severing the secret":
"secret" refers to continuity.
This is of two kinds:
First, the continuity of the desire and form realms;
second, the continuity of the form and formless realms. Because an Arhat has departed from these continuities, he is called "one who has severed the secret" (prahīṇaguhyaka).
“Lack of a place of residence” means that because an Arhat has severed the continuity [of the aggregates], there is no place within the three realms where they can be born.
“Constantly hoping for transformation and vomiting” means:
There are two kinds of "hope":
first, hope for wealth and status; second, hope for longevity.
Since that Arhat has already abandoned and fully understood these two types of hope, he is called "one who has vomited out [desire]."
This means the sense of abandoning constant longing.
Regarding the phrase "the supreme person" (*puruṣottama*):
it refers to the Arhat who has attained the aforementioned supreme, most excellent, and foremost qualities; therefore, among all persons, he is called the foremost, most excellent, and supreme.
The thirty-six swift currents: those who are led by the mind and are dominated by intense wrong views ride upon them; they are the basis for conceptual attachment.
Regarding "the thirty-six swift currents":
This is illustrated by the "thirty-six modes of craving.
Regarding "that which is led by the mind":
this means that the mind is the accumulation, it is produced from the mind, and it belongs to the category of the mind.
"Excessive" means: superior, intense, and complete.
"Those with wrong views" refers to:
This refers to the various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
They "ride upon" this [view] to travel toward the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; therefore, it is called "riding upon.
As for the term "those who discriminate":
There are three kinds of discursive thought:
first, discursive thought of desire; second, discursive thought of ill-will; and third, discursive thought of harm.
Regarding "clinging to a basis":
"Attachment" refers to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because these arise based upon that [body], it is called the "basis.
One abandons misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
Furthermore, regarding the abandonment of other faults and bodily misconduct:
this refers to abandoning the three types of bodily misconduct; and regarding verbal misconduct: this refers to abandoning the four types of verbal misconduct.
"Abandoning unwholesome mental conduct" means:
severing the three types of unwholesome mental conduct as well as other faults;
that is, abandoning the ten aforementioned types of unwholesome conduct and all other remaining faults.
Regarding what you see and hear, there is only seeing and hearing;
regarding what you perceive and know, there is only perceiving and knowing.
Because these exist only for you, there is no "this" or "that," no near or far.
Nor is there anything between these two; thus one reaches the limit of suffering.
These two verses further elucidate what was said in the Sūtra:
"The Buddha told the Elder Mother:..."

In what you see, there is only that which is seen; in what you hear, there is only that which is heard; in what you perceive, there is only that which is perceived; in what you know, there is only that which is known.
Because you have only what is seen, heard, and so forth, you do not possess this;
because you do not possess this, you do not possess that;
because you do not possess that, you have neither near nor far, nor anything in between the two.
"By means of these causes and conditions, one reaches the end of suffering. In this context:
that which is experienced and cognized by visual consciousness is called "the seen."
There are those for whom what is seen is merely what is seen; there are those for whom what is seen is not merely what is seen.
Who are those for whom what is seen is merely what is seen?—namely:
One does not give rise to afflictions regarding what is experienced and discerned by eye-consciousness.
Who is it that, regarding what is seen, does not consist of merely the seen?
It is said:
One gives rise to various afflictions regarding what is experienced and cognized by visual consciousness.
What is experienced and discerned by auditory consciousness is called "the heard.
Regarding the heard, there is that which is merely the heard, and there is that which is heard but is not merely the heard.
Who is it that, regarding what is heard, experiences only what is heard? That is to say:
one who, with respect to what is received and discerned by the auditory consciousness, does not give rise to afflictions.
Who is it that, regarding what is heard, does not merely have what is heard?
It refers to one who gives rise to various afflictions toward that which has been apprehended and discerned by the ear-consciousness.
That which is experienced and discerned by the three consciousnesses of the nose, tongue, and body is called "the sensed.
Regarding the sensed, there is that which is merely the sensed, and there is that which is not merely the sensed.
Who is it that, while having only objects of cognition, possesses nothing but those objects of cognition? That is to say:
one who does not give rise to afflictions regarding what has been experienced and discerned by the three consciousnesses.
Who is it that, regarding what is perceived, does not merely perceive it?
It refers to one who gives rise to various afflictions toward that which has been experienced and cognized by the three consciousnesses.
That which is experienced and cognized by the mental consciousness is called the "knowable.
Regarding the knowable, there is that which is merely the knowable, and there is that which regarding the knowable is not merely the knowable.
Who possesses only the knowable among all that is knowable?
It refers to one who does not give rise to afflictions regarding what is experienced and cognized by the mental consciousness.
Who is it that, regarding the objects of knowledge, does not merely possess those objects of knowledge?
It refers to one who gives rise to various afflictions toward what is experienced and discerned by the mental consciousness.
"Because, regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, and known, he has only what is seen, heard, sensed, and known, and does not give rise to afflictions, therefore this does not exist."
That is to say:
not giving rise to conceit, arrogance, or haughtiness, nor having a mind that is uplifted or a mind that is resolute and bold.
"Because these do not exist, those do not exist," which means:
"One does not give rise to greed, hatred, or delusion.
Because these are absent, there is neither near nor far, nor anything intermediate between the two.
This means that within the desire realm, as well as the form and formless realms, there is no place of birth.
"By means of such reasoning, one reaches the very limit of suffering":

"Suffering" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). This "limit of suffering" is the relinquishing of all bases of existence, the exhaustion of craving, detachment from passion, and the eternal cessation that is *nirvāṇa*.
"Medini and Medini, Tappuṭa and Kaṇṭhapuṭa, Mucilinda and Saṃkhapāla;
having completely abandoned [suffering], one reaches the end of suffering.
Thus, this single verse further elucidates what was taught in the Sūtra:
"The Buddha spoke the Four Noble Truths and so forth to the two kings who protect the world using the Mleccha language,
and they immediately understood. "Medini" (醫泥) signifies the Noble Truth of Suffering.
“Mi-ni” means the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. “Da-pu” means:
The Noble Truth of Cessation is revealed. "Dakṣapu" reveals the Noble Truth of the Path.
"Should not aspire" means:
one exhorts them not to aspire for the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
"Should rejoice" means:
One should encourage them so that, upon hearing: "The Buddha has realized awakening; the Dharma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha practices the sublime path;
form is impermanent, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent;
the truth of suffering is well-established, as are the truths of origin, cessation, and the path," they should give rise to joy.
"Should be tranquilized" means:
one should exhort them that when greed, hatred, or delusion arise, they should be tranquilized, thoroughly tranquilized, and completely pacified.
"Should be universally detached from" means:
One should encourage that mind to become detached from the desire realm, as well as the form and formless realms.
Regarding "reaching the end of suffering":
it means that if one can act in this way, one will then reach the limit of suffering.
The phrase "the end of suffering" has the same meaning as previously explained.
Knowing the body to be like a mass of foam, and likewise perceiving it to be identical to a mirage,
one cuts off the small flowers of Māra and does not see the messengers of the King of Death.
"Knowing the body to be like a mass of foam" means knowing the body as it truly is: like a mass of foam, it is powerless, frail, and cannot be grasped or rubbed.
"Also perceiving it to be identical to a mirage" means:
This means awakening to the body as it truly is: like a mirage, born of the affliction of heat, shifting and unstable.
Regarding the phrase "severing the flower and small flower of Māra":
there are four kinds of "Māra," namely:
The māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), and the māra of the sovereign devas (*devaputra-māra*).
It should be understood that among these, the māra of afflictions is being discussed here.
Those [afflictions] to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) are called "the flowers of Māra" (*māra-puṣpa*).
That which is to be abandoned through cultivation is called "small flowers";
the permanent abandonment of those is called "cutting off.
Regarding the phrase "not seeing the messengers of the King of Death":
That which can extinguish through impermanence is called the "King of Death";
old age and sickness press and pursue it, and are termed the "Messengers of the King of Death.
Contemplating the proximity or distance of dwelling in awakening, one should rejoice that all karmic actions are non-existent.
Knowing that the world has its rise and fall, one whose virtuous mind is universally liberated [attains this].
Regarding "contemplating abiding":
it means one should observe that there are three kinds of abiding.
First, emptiness; second, wishlessness; third, signlessness.
Regarding the phrase "awakening to the near and the far":
"awakening" refers to awakening-wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*).
With intelligence and full application, one should correctly give rise [to joy] regarding internal and external objects.
"One should rejoice" means:
if one hears it said, "The Buddha has realized awakening; the Dharma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha practices the sublime conduct."
Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Thus is the truth of suffering well-established, and the truths of origin, cessation, and the path are well-established.
"One should give rise to joy.
Regarding "the non-existence of all karmas":
this refers to the failure to accomplish those bodily, verbal, and mental karmas that would induce a future birth.
Regarding "knowing that the world has its rise and fall":
"knowing" means thorough comprehension; "the world" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*); "rise and fall" refers to arising and ceasing.
This means observing that the five contaminated aggregates (pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ) possess the nature of arising and ceasing.
"Wholesome mind" refers to a mind of discernment, a skillful mind, and a pliant mind.
"Universal liberation" means:
having been liberated, thoroughly liberated, and completely liberated from all realms of existence, all states of being, and all modes of birth.

Regarding the phrase "although they have escaped the desire realm,

"‘The gluttonous one returns again’" means that although he has slightly severed the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), because the remainder is still great, greed will inevitably arise later, and he will return to be born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding "attaining peace":
"peace" refers to the realm of nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
Because the arhats have already realized it, it is called "attained."
Regarding "still delighting in delight":
"delight" refers to the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*); because one constantly aspires to it, it is called "delight.
Regarding "riding on delight to reach the place of delight":
That is to say, one who delights in the path and reaches the bliss of nirvāṇa;
who has no roots in the realm of earth, nor leaves, nor branches—
that heroic one, liberated from bonds— who could possibly revile him?
"Roots" is a metaphor for "consciousness with grasping.

"The five seeds represent consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*)."
"The earth element" reveals the four stations of consciousness.

"Ignorance has already been abandoned and fully understood.
As for the "branch," it is a metaphor for "craving."
As the Blessed One said:
“If a branch of craving grows within the palace of the five exquisite forms,
the Muni sees its arising and swiftly cuts it off with wisdom.”
Among the four stations of consciousness, the various Arhats possess no consciousness that grasps for existence and draws forth future becoming; they are free from conceit and free from craving.
Therefore, it is said: "They have no roots in the earth element, nor leaves, nor branches."
"Vīra" (the Heroic) means that those Arhats have accomplished it;
because they have achieved the dharmas of heroism, they are also called "Vīras."
Regarding "liberation from bonds":
there are three kinds of bonds, namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
He has already become liberated from these bonds, completely liberated, and utterly liberated.
Regarding the phrase "Who else should criticize or disparage him?":

it refers to such a person (pudgala) who should only be praised and not disparaged; if one were to disparage him, the offense incurred would be boundless, for he is a true field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) for the world. Thus, he must be damaged and destroyed [by such an act].
As the Blessed One said:
"If one praises those who should be censured, and censures those who should be praised, that mouth accumulates calamity and misfortune;
such a person shall certainly not enjoy peace and happiness."
